R ussia has only recently opened up its sector of the Caspian Sea to offshore production of oil and natural gas. LUKoil, Russia's second largest oil company, began exploring the northern portion of the Russian sector in 1995; by 2004, the company had identified six viable fields for production. The first offshore platform, over the Yuri Korchagin field, started producing oil for the commercial market in 2010; the sector's largest field is anticipated to begin producing oil for market in 2015. Although Russia's total reserves are small in comparison to three other Caspian Sea states (Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, and Turkmenistan), these recent events signal the further diversification in sites of extraction for the Russian oil and gas industry (Joyner and Walters 2006). 1 The Russian state is increasingly engaging in oil and gas production in resource peripheries (Bradshaw 2003; Hayter, Barnes, and Bradshaw 2003).

Further to the south along Russia's Caspian Sea littoral, in Dagestan, increased offshore oil and gas production has previously been proposed and was recently reiterated by the republic's president (Ekho 2014). Preemptive to any such development, two of this article's coauthors conducted a survey ( N = 956) in sixteen settlements proximate to Dagestan's coast in the summer of 2010. The survey queried respondents on a variety of questions related to this planned expansion. In this article, we draw on the results of the survey to evaluate public opinion on support for offshore oil and gas production among Dagestan's residents, its environmental consequences, and potential alternative development strategies as evaluated by those queried.

First, the article reviews the role of oil and gas production in Russia's sector of the Caspian Sea. The expansion of this production reflects the further consolidation of hydrocarbons as the basis for Russia's economy. We then detail the process of expanding capacity as spearheaded by LUKoil; although the future of oil and gas production in the region is linked to offshore fields, the three regions (the republics of Dagestan and Kalmykia and Astrakhan oblast') that make up Russia's Caspian Sea littoral have previously established oil and gas infrastructure. The article then presents the survey results, reporting public opinion on the economic and environmental consequences of expanding offshore capacity in Russia's Caspian. We conclude by situating the case of Dagestan within the wider literature on economic geography, the environment, and resource peripheries and subsequently offer a recommendation about how the Russian state and oil companies should move forward in consonance with the local population in the republic.
sections.Oil and Gas Production in the Russian Se:
The transition away from communism-an economic system associated with top-down planning, an overweighting toward the military and armaments in industrial production, and single-industry settlements-consolidated Russia's dependency on oil and natural gas exports (Kotkin 2001). The decline in world oil prices from their peaks during the 1970s weakened the USSR's economic position during the mid- and late 1980s and is commonly viewed as one of the contributing factors to the country's breakup. In post-Soviet Russia, the devaluation of the ruble in 1998spurred domestic production and consumption in the broader economy, although much of this growth was subsidized through rents from natural resource extraction. Gustafson (2012) argues that the state is now even more dependent on rents to fund its budget; Russia's current situation can be characterized as a dual economy, with its reliance on natural resources, while failing to diversify into other growth sectors (Bradshaw 2008). Some parts of the Russian Federation, including resource-rich areas in the country's north and east, have benefited disproportionately from the extraction and export of resources such as oil, gas, and timber.

At the national scale, Russia's long-term prospects for an economy based on hydrocarbons are tenuous; Gustafson (2012) cautions that the future of world oil prices is uncertain in terms of both supply and demand. Other concerns revolve around the failure of the oil industry to diversify its technology platform, the approach of peak oil, and the lack of an effective working relationship with Western partners (Hill and Fee 2002; Gustafson 2012).

In Russia, there is little concern for the consequences of continued oil and gas production that have been articulated in the conceptual literature on resource extraction: anthropogenic climate change, economic overdependence on resource production, and the finite nature of such resources, among other topics. A report from the Pew Research Center's (2009) Global Attitudes Project found that 44 percent of respondents in Russia-an equal percentage to the United States-consider global warming to be a very serious problem. For now, resources remain useful and valuable to the Russian economy; the country is pursuing opportunities to extend hydrocarbon production capacities into areas, such as the Caspian Sea, that have previously received little attention as sites of production.

As illustrated in Figure 1, the Caspian Sea can be divided into four main areas of oil and gas production: (1) the Northwest, in Russia and centered offshore proximate to the cities of Astrakhan and Makhachkala; (2) the Apsheron peninsula in Azerbaijan, near the country's capital of Baku; (3) the Atyrau-Mangistau complex in Kazakhstan; and (4) the West Balkan province of Turkmenistan. The region's potential oil and gas reserves play an important role in prospective development plans for the five states-Russia, Azerbaijan, Iran, Turkmenistan, and Kazakhstan-that border the Caspian Sea; the various states have offered contrasting proposals on the division of the seabed to maximize their access to offshore oil and gas (O'Lear 2004).

Someoftheseareashaveonlyrecentlybeenexplored for oil reserves; for example, Kazakhstan's Tengiz field was discovered in 1974, with production ramping up in 1993 only after Kazakhstan became independent (Kaiser and Pulsipher 2007). Other areas have long been centers of oil production; Baku's first oil boom, in the late nineteenth century, made the fortune of the Nobel Brothers (LeVine 2007). Today, nearly 70 percent of the region's oil comes from Kazakhstan. The Kashagan field, located in the northern Caspian Sea near Atyrau, has estimated recoverable reserves of 7 to 9 billion barrels. It is the largest find since the discovery of oil in the North Sea during the 1960s (Rutland 2008). In 2009, total oil production from existing fields in the region amounted to approximately 130 million tons. Estimates of potential reserves vary quite widely, from 7 to 20 billion tons; in the Russian sector, the estimates of unproven reserves are 2 billion tons (Eldarov and Ismailov 2009).

The Russian sector of the Caspian Sea has received less attention from scholars and policymakers due to the zone's small proven reserves. Other considerations-including U.S. policy toward the greater Caspian region and the discourse of the 'new great game,' the search for alternative energy corridors for exporting oil and gas by Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan, and Russia's relative economic weakness in the first decade after the breakup of the Soviet Union-all served to shift focus away from Russian production in the region (Shaffer 2010). Moreover, although Russia is one of the world's leading oil producers, ranking second to Saudi Arabia in total production in 2012 (BP 2013), little of the country's production comes from the Caspian. In part, this is because the Russian sector remains underdeveloped relative to other parts of the country.

There are approximately twenty commercial fields currently operational in Dagestan, the southernmost of the three regions that make up Russia's Caspian Sea littoral. There is a small refinery, operated by Dagestan Oil, located in Makhachkala (U.S. Energy Information Administration 2013). The city is also a transit point for offshore production, with oil delivered there before entering the pipeline to Novorossiysk for export.

In the republic of Kalmykia, to Dagestan's north, the deposits are generally smaller, with probable oil reserves estimated at 65 million tons; there are two main fields, the Caspian and the Promyslovie, in the republic's coastal sector. There is a large gas condensate field in Astrakhan oblast', the third region of Russia's Caspian Sea littoral; the field is located approximately 30 km to the north of the region's main city of Astrakhan (Eldarov and Ismailov 2009). Overall, Dagestan and Kalmykia experienced declines in oil production between 1991 and 2006, although this was offset by substantial growth in the third region, Astrakhan oblast' (Sagers 2006).

As such, the expansion of oil and gas production in the Russian sector of the Caspian Sea is a longer term project; Sagers (2006, 517) wrote, 'The area is likely to provide a sizable contribution to national output in the future, but not in the near term.' LUKoil has spearheaded exploration efforts of offshore reserves in the Caspian Sea. Between 1995 and 2004 the company identified six fields for development, the largest being the Vladimir Filanovskiy field. 2 Of these six fields, only one, the Yuri Korchagin field, is currently producing oil. The Korchagin field has been profitable thanks to a reduction in export duties collected on oil produced from the field (U.S. Energy Information Administration 2013). The Filanovskiy field is much larger in terms of probable reserves, and LUKoil estimates that this field will produce 120,000 barrels per day at its maximum output (U.S. Energy Information Administration 2013). The company reported completing the first stage of site development in December 2013; drilling is slated to begin during 2014, with production for market starting by the end of 2015 ( Oil &Gas Journal 2013).

The Korchagin and Filanovskiy fields are located in the north central portion of Russia's Caspian Sea sector, close to the agreed-on maritime boundary between Russia and Kazakhstan. A second, and smaller, grouping of oil and gas fields is located in Dagestan, to the southeast of the republic's capital, Makhachkala. These fields range along Dagestan's Caspian Sea coast between Makhachkala and the southern Dagestani city of Izberbash (where oil was first produced in the republic in 1936). This area contains estimated oil reserves of 340 million tons and 540 billion cubic meters of natural gas. The development of these reserves is still in the proposal stages; in January 2014, Dagestan's acting president, Ramazan Abdulatipov, expressed a desire to increase exploration work along the republic's coast in collaboration with leading Russian oil companies, including Rosneft and LUKoil (Ekho 2014). Any such development will have a direct impact on rural residents of Dagestan's southern coast, and those living to the north of the capital would be affected by any oil spills resulting from offshore production and the transit of oil in the northern part of Russia's Caspian Sea sector.
sections.Opinions on Resource Development in Dage:
To evaluate the potential impact of hydrocarbon development on the rural residents of Dagestan, in the summer of 2010 two of the article's coauthors conducted a survey ( N = 956) among residents living near Dagestan's Caspian Sea coast. The survey consisted of a structured questionnaire with twenty-three questions that queried respondents on the following subjects: demographic information such as age, gender, and educational level; baseline economic statistics such as employment status, socioeconomic condition, and migration preferences; opinions on the economic situation in Dagestan; and prospects for expanded oil and gas production (Eldarov et al. 2011). Broadly stated, the survey had two aims to (1) evaluate economic and environmental conditions in rural Dagestan; and (2) gauge residents' positions on nascent oil and gas development in Dagestan's coastal region.

The survey used convenience sampling at fourteen rural locations. Local contacts at each site distributed the survey among their social and employment networks. 3 Acknowledging the nonrepresentative nature of the sample, we do not perform more advanced statistical analysis on the data. Given the large sample size and the targeted nature of the survey, however, and its questions at locations that will be affected by increased oil and gas production (both offshore in the north Caspian and near Dagestan's southern coast), these data provide valuable insight into receptiveness to the proposed longer term expansion of such production.

The fourteen villages and urban-type settlements ( poselki gorodskogo tipa ) that were surveyed are sited either near or along the republic's coast (see Figure 2). 4 In the south, this included the villages of Kayakent, Novokayakent, Berikey, Mamedkala, Belidzhi, and Samur; in the republic's central region, it included Dakhadaevka, Zelenomorsk, Manaskent, and the urban-type settlement of Glavniy Sulak. The southern section of the republic's coastline is a site for industrial facilities but also an area for recreation, with large urban settlements. Roughly one third of the sample was drawn from the north of the republic, an area of comparatively less economic development. The primary economic activities in this section are tied to the fisheries sector and include fishing and the processing of the catch. The hydrocarbon potential of much of this northern section has yet to be evaluated for recoverable reserves, although these villages would be impacted by any spills occurring further out in the Caspian Sea. The sample points in this area were the villages of Kochubey, Bryansk, and Kraynovka, as well as the settlement of Staroterechnoe.

A majority of respondents to the survey were men (64 percent). With respect to age, roughly three fifths of those surveyed reported that they are older than thirty years of age. Similarly, approximately 60 percent of the sample reported that they were born in Dagestan's lowlands; the remainder have resettled there from other parts of the republic, specifically the mountainous regions of the republic's south and west (on this process of resettlement, see Eldarov et al. 2007). The overall educational level was lower than expected given the convenient nature of the sampling and its reliance on employment and social networks, with only a quarter of respondents reporting some university-level work.
sections.The Economy in Rural Dagestan:
The subset of questions on the economy of rural Dagestan underscores the region's poverty relative to muchof the Russian Federation. Of particular note are the data on income for the sampled population. The overwhelming majority of respondents (73 percent) manage to carve out a living on a monthly income less than 20,000 RR (US $ 660) for their family as a whole. Given that the average family in Dagestan is composed of four to five persons, this amount corresponds to a subsistence-level existence for many of those surveyed. Only 105 respondents, or 11 percent of the total, reported family incomes above 40,000 RR per month per family, which is close to the average for Russia as a whole when assuming two wage earners (just below 38,000 RR).

The proportion of those employed in industry (approximately 29 percent) in comparison to those en- gaged in service work (approximately 71 percent) is in line with global trends; in developed countries the number of individuals engaged in service work generally ranges from 50 to 70 percent. In Dagestan's coastal areas, however, such a ratio is somewhat anachronistic and is linked to two negative socioeconomic trends. The first is the dominant role that is played in real economic production by subsistence farming, as well as illicit fishing in the nearby Caspian. Building on the latter point, despite the proximity of the villages and settlements sampled to the Caspian Sea, only 7 percent of respondents reported that they are employed in the fisheries sector. It could well be that survey participants did not want to respond positively to this question, given the prevalence of poaching and the processing and selling of fish that frequently occurs in the region, and report employment in the service sector to mask this activity. Second, high levels of employment in nonindustrial sectors reflect the primary, and frequently only, type of governmental investment in the rural areas of the republic: in infrastructure and increased employment in the state bureaucracy (including local and regional administration, law enforcement, health services, education, and information services). In sum, there is little industry in rural Dagestan in which employment can be secured. Given the employment and economic situation in the republic, and perhaps somewhat surprisingly, most of those surveyed indicated that they were uninterested in moving away from their place of residence; nearly two thirds of the sample (568 respondents, or 59 percent) responded in the negative to the question about resettlement: 'If you had the opportunity to move somewhere in the next two years, would you take advantage of this opportunity?'

When asked which type of economic activity is most promising for the region, a majority of respondents indicated support for the idea of developing large-scale tourist facilities, specifically beach resorts along the Caspian coast. Without question, the geographic location and unique natural amenities that exist along Dagestan's littoral make the republic's Caspian Sea coast a possible tourist destination. sections.The State of the Environment:
As a baseline measure of public opinion on the environment, a majority of respondents view the current situation in their locality as unsatisfactory (11 percent of respondents characterized the situation as 'poor,' and a further 45 percent viewed the situation as 'more poor than good'); only 1 percent of those surveyed responded that they consider the ecological situation in the region to be 'excellent.' These responses reflect the dire state of the Caspian Sea's environment. As with other regions of the former Soviet Union, the Caspian Sea's environment has been significantly altered through human action (Dumont 1995; Barannik, Borysova, and Stolberg 2004). The health of the Caspian Sea is further compromised by pollution, the continued extraction of nonrenewable resources including sturgeon, and a loss in biodiversity also linked to the incursion of invasive species (Henry and Douhovnikoff 2008). Two thirds of respondents identified the Caspian Sea and sandy beaches as most susceptible to the continued deterioration of the environmental situation along Dagestan's coast. For example, raw sewage from the republic's settlements is commonly discharged, untreated, into the Sea.

A set of questions in the survey dealt with the opinion of rural residents on the development of offshore oil and gas fields. A clear majority of respondents-79 percent-learned about the existing plans for offshore oil and gas development in the Caspian Sea through the questionnaire process; they had no prior knowledge that the proposed expansion of hydrocarbon extraction would take place offshore in the Caspian (this percentage is notably lower than the measure of environmental awareness reported for Azerbaijan, located just to Dagestan's south, by O'Lear and Gray 2006). Wereturn to the implications of this result in the article's concluding section. Processing this information, and in turn responding to the question, 'In your opinion, will the extraction of offshore oil improve life in your village?,' more than half of those queried (54 percent) answered in the negative. Twenty-seven percent of respondents indicated that they viewed this develop- ment as having little impact on their current situation, and only 4 percent responded that they viewed such developments as having a positive impact on the lives of local residents. As noted earlier, the level of official unemployment in the rural areas of the republic is currently very high; but, curiously, 593 respondents (62 percent of the total sample) replied in the negative to the question: 'Would you like to be employed in the oil and gas industry?' Taken as a whole, the survey found that residents of these rural settlements along Dagestan's Caspian Sea coast generally view oil and gas development negatively; in turn, the majority is opposed to being employed in this sector. On the one hand, economic interests defer to the desire to live in a clean environment but, on the other hand, few people now believe in the idea of the state as 'good uncle,' with the ability to provide villages with employment in the relatively high-paying oil sector. It is entirely possible that residents of Dagestan's coastal villages are aware of the fact that the oil industry in neighboring Kalmykia currently employs temporary workers, known in Russian as vakhtoviki (F¨ ullsack 2001), who come from outside of the republic. In other words, the respondents realize that they stand to benefit very little from the development of this offshore oil and gas industry.

These findings were further corroborated through responses to the following question: 'Are you for or against the initiation of oil production offshore in the Caspian Sea at a site near your residence?' Almost the entirety of the sample (98 percent) responded that they were against such development if it occurred in proximity to their home. To some extent, survey participants attempted to express their concern with respect to the future condition of the environment, particularly if this was to be affected by an oil spill or other environmental disaster as a result of such offshore development. This type of 'environmental ethic,' in theory, should contribute to our understanding of analogous environmental catastrophes occurring elsewhere in the world.

That the residents of coastal Dagestan are concerned about the potential environmental consequences associated with hydrocarbon development makes sense. Given the increasing use of offshore extraction techniques, an accident on the magnitude of the Deepwater Horizon oil spill in the Gulf of Mexico could occur in the Caspian Sea (the Russian press speculated on this possibility; see Zhil'tsov 2010); the consequences of such a spill for the environment would be substantially higher, given that the Caspian is shallow, landlocked, and already in a parlous environmental state. 7 Nevertheless, drilling operations with the aim of developing new sites for oil extraction in the waters of the Russian section of the Caspian shelf are likely to proceed. The dependence on oil and gas revenue for Russia's economy is well known, as is the need for the further diversification of supply and the increased development of the economies of Dagestan and the other regions along the Caspian Sea littoral.
sections.Discussion and Conclusion:
Skepticism of the economic benefits of hydrocarbon development among those surveyed could stem from a variety of factors. There is little trust in the resourceextracting monopolies that characterize the Russian market. Primarily due to the legacies of Soviet-era development, these companies disregard local socioeconomic needs, employing shift workers who have little job security or connection to the communities in which they work (F¨ ullsack 2001). This development also lends itself to the defacement of the landscape and environment, resulting in the clogging of the marine environment with oil platforms and similar objects linked to production. To address this negative opinion, greater accountability on the part of oil companies and the state must be achieved through public advocacy and increased awareness about future plans for development in the Russian sector of the Caspian Sea. In reality, however, this work has often been limited to drawing up a colorful booklet with detailed instructions and guarantees of security, despite the impending development of offshore oil fields. Moreover, these attempts at public relations are usually subject to no further scrutiny other than by the oil companies and aligned governmental institutions themselves.

We have little optimism that the findings reported here will lead to the modification by either the companies involved or the Russian state of their approach to offshore hydrocarbon production in the Caspian Sea. The results of our survey in Russia's Dagestan do have resonance with local-scale debates about energy production and associated development that are occurring elsewhere, however. Why should local-level opinion factor in to such discourses? First, the geographies of energy production reflect a shift toward more marginal locations; in Russia, this includes not only the country's Caspian Sea sector but also Sakhalin Island in the Russian Far East and the Arctic Ocean (Bradshaw 2003; Harsem, Eide, and Heen 2011; Graybill 2013). 8 To this end, Hayter, Barnes, and Bradshaw (2003, 16) have called for increased attention in economic geography to resource peripheries, where economic, environmental, cultural, and geopolitical conditions come together in unique ways to structure relations between the core and the margins; 'the reality is that the economic geography of resource production is far from straightforward and seldom just an economic matter.' The paths to development are influenced by decisions occurring at a range of scales and are being made by a variety of actors; as Zimmerer's (2011, 705) recent overview of new energy geographies states: 'The resource systems of energy production, distribution, and consumption are thoroughly entwined as social-environmental interactions occurring across multiple scales.' As with other resource peripheries, the case of Dagestan is unique in its specifics, including the ecological vulnerability of the Caspian Sea, the reliance of locals on subsistence farming and fishing, and the region's ongoing security concerns. More broadly, this particularity reflects the fact that resource systems are entwined with human systems, through which individuals interpret the value of such development, the associated environmental impact, and the need for viable alternatives if this impact is too great. In resource peripheries, which are often viewed solely as sites of production within larger energy economies, the dissenting voices of local residents often go unnoticed; this project articulates public concerns about the environmental impact of oil and gas development in one such periphery.

Second, and building on this interplay of the economic and the environmental, the case of Dagestan reflects the importance of including local-scale preferences in decision making about development paths. With the majority of the sample indicating a preference for tourism as an economic approach in the region, the regional and federal governments (in tandem with the major state oil companies brought on for the project) should address concerns regarding potential spills and their environmental and economic consequences.

Although tourism itself has measurable social impacts (see, e.g., Mansfeld 1992) and security concerns are relevant to any attempts to further develop tourist facilities along Dagestan's coast (Lally 2012), the option of tourism should remain open as a possibility for regional economic development; the extensive development of oil and gas production along the republic's coast would potentially foreclose this option. Tourism facilities would be threatened by any large-scale spill; in the case of the Deepwater Horizon accident in the Gulf of Mexico, preliminary estimates put losses to the travel industry at $ 23 billion over three years (Harzl and Pickl 2012). At the least, the regional and federal governments in Dagestan and Russia should further evaluate how resource development and tourism can coexist.

The particularities of production in resource peripheries-in this case, Russia's sector of the Caspian Sea-reflect specific, localized concerns regarding the economy and the environment. At the same time, our use of surveys identifies a lack of knowledge at the local scale regarding this project; in turn, our findings support the use of surveys as an intervention to generate a baseline of knowledge about and awareness of environmentally impactful development projects. Through such work we have identified potential alternatives in terms of economic development as supported by local populations in the republic of Dagestan. ■

Opinions on Resource Development in Dagestan

sections.Magomed-Kamil B. Kamilov:
Dagestan State University

This article considers public opinion in the republic of Dagestan on the expansion of hydrocarbon production in the Russian sector of the Caspian Sea. The article reports the findings of a survey ( N = 956) conducted in 2010 in fourteen rural locations in the republic. Overall, respondents uniformly oppose the proposed expansion of offshore oil and gas production in the Russian sector of the Caspian Sea, seeing little economic benefit from this development and expressing concern about the environmental consequences. These findings resonate with work in geography on resource peripheries and development alternatives available in these locations. Key Words: Caspian Sea, environment, oil and gas production, public opinion survey, Russia.
sections.Oil and Gas Production in the Russian Se: The transition away from communism-an economic system associated with top-down planning, an overweighting toward the military and armaments in industrial production, and single-industry settlements-consolidated Russia's dependency on oil and natural gas exports (Kotkin 2001). The decline in world oil prices from their peaks during the 1970s weakened the USSR's economic position during the mid- and late 1980s and is commonly viewed as one of the contributing factors to the country's breakup. In post-Soviet Russia, the devaluation of the ruble in 1998spurred domestic production and consumption in the broader economy, although much of this growth was subsidized through rents from natural resource extraction. Gustafson (2012) argues that the state is now even more dependent on rents to fund its budget; Russia's current situation can be characterized as a dual economy, with its reliance on natural resources, while failing to diversify into other growth sectors (Bradshaw 2008). Some parts of the Russian Federation, including resource-rich areas in the country's north and east, have benefited disproportionately from the extraction and export of resources such as oil, gas, and timber.
sections.Opinions on Resource Development in Dage: To evaluate the potential impact of hydrocarbon development on the rural residents of Dagestan, in the summer of 2010 two of the article's coauthors conducted a survey ( N = 956) among residents living near Dagestan's Caspian Sea coast. The survey consisted of a structured questionnaire with twenty-three questions that queried respondents on the following subjects: demographic information such as age, gender, and educational level; baseline economic statistics such as employment status, socioeconomic condition, and migration preferences; opinions on the economic situation in Dagestan; and prospects for expanded oil and gas production (Eldarov et al. 2011). Broadly stated, the survey had two aims to (1) evaluate economic and environmental conditions in rural Dagestan; and (2) gauge residents' positions on nascent oil and gas development in Dagestan's coastal region.

records.title: We Plant Only Cotton to Maximize Our Earnings: The Paradox of Food Sovereignty in Rural Telengana, India
records.abstract: This article critically examines the role of food sovereignty interventions in the mitigation of the impacts of neoliberal economic policies on poor farmers in the Telengana region of India. Findings based on eighteen months of ethnographic research in the Telengana region reveal that small and poor farmers face socioeconomic and cultural constraints to the adoption of food sovereignty practices and ideals. Food sovereignty prescriptions based on localized, sustainable, and subsistence agriculture paradoxically constrained farmers' chances of maintaining viable rural livelihoods in a harsh economic climate. Based on these findings, I argue that contrary to assertions by advocates that food sovereignty is a precondition to genuine food security, farmers must first have food and livelihood security to exercise truefood sovereignty that allows them more control over their livelihoods. ???????, ?????????????????????????????, ?????????????????????????????????????, ???????????, ??????????????, ????????????????????????????????????, ??????????????, ????????????????????????, ???????????????????????, ?????????????, ?????????????????????? Este articulo examina criticamente el papel de las intervenciones de la soberania alimentaria en la mitigacion de los impactos ejercidos por politicas economicas neoliberales sobre los agricultores pobres de la region Telengana, en la India. Los hallazgos logrados con base en dieciocho meses de investigacion etnografica en esa region revelan que los agricultores pequenos y pobres tienen que enfrentar restricciones socioeconomicas y culturales para la adopcion de las practicas e ideales de la soberania alimentaria. Las prescripciones de la soberania alimentaria basada en una agricultura localizada, sostenible y de subsistencia paradojicamente restringen las oportunidades de los agricultores de mantener un sistema de vida rural viable en medio de un clima economico dificil. Basandome en estos hallazgos, sostengo que al contrario de lo que proclaman sus mentores, en el sentido de ver la soberania alimentaria como condicion previa para una genuina seguridad alimentaria, los agricultores primero deben tener comida y seguridad de medios de vida para ejercer una verdadera soberania alimentaria que les permita mayor control sobre su subsistencia.

Based on these findings, I argue that contrary to assertions by advocates that food sovereignty is a precondition to genuine food security, farmers must first have food and livelihood security to exercise true food sovereignty that allows them more control over their livelihoods. Key Words: food sovereignty, food security, rural livelihoods.

I n this article I critically examine the role of food sovereignty interventions in the mitigation of the impacts of neoliberal economic policies on poor farmers in the Telengana region of India. The Telengana region has experienced high levels of agrarian distress, especially after India introduced neoliberal economic policies in the 1990s (Ghosh 2005; Nagaraj 2008). The commodification of agriculture has intensified processes of environmental degradation, land fragmentation, and water stress, which, combined with decreasing state supports and safety nets, have made rural livelihoods increasingly precarious.

Food sovereignty is put forth as a principal strategy to counteract the negative outcomes of the commodification of agriculture, which is blamed on the global corporate food regime, a system that favors particular Western nation-states and corporate interests in food and agriculture (McMichael 2005). Food sovereignty seeks to curb this trend through a strategic focus on upholding small farmers and agroecological practices (V´ ıa Campesina 1996; McMichael 2005; Desmarais

2007; Altieri 2009; Patel 2009; Martinez-Torres and Rosset 2010; Wittman, Desmarais, and Wiebe 2010). It distinguishes itself from the productivist food security paradigm that emerged after World War II as a state-sponsored strategy to increase food production to achieve food self-sufficiency, revive economies, and increase political legitimacy (McMichael 2005). Where food security is dominated by its focus on high production and efficiency, food sovereignty is animated by the principles of equity and ecological integrity. Food sovereignty's promotion of 'the peasant way' as the solution to the ills of the corporate food regime is also critiqued, however, as being a set of principles with little political analysis of how they would translate in practice (Akram-Lodhi 2013; Trauger 2013; Bernstein 2014; Edelman 2014).

This research supports emerging critiques of food sovereignty and seeks to contribute to debates on food security. Findings based on eighteen months of ethnographic research in the Telengana region reveal that small and poor farmers face socioeconomic and cultural constraints in the adoption of food sovereignty practices and ideals. These include compulsions to participate in the market economy, changing geographies of labor, and shifting values and knowledge relating to agriculture. Food sovereignty prescriptions based on localized, sustainable, and subsistence agriculture paradoxically constrained farmers' chances of maintaining viable rural livelihoods in a harsh economic climate. Based on these findings, I argue that contrary to assertions by advocates that food sovereignty is a precondition to genuine food security, farmers must first have food and livelihood security (hereinafter food security) to exercise true food sovereignty that allows them more control over their livelihoods.

To examine the disjuncture between food sovereignty and food security, I draw on historical and contemporary critiques of neopopulist ideas promoted by alternative agricultural movements as well as more recent empirical research examining food sovereignty in the Global South. This research supports recent assertions that food sovereignty is an idea that fails to consider the complex nature of peasant societies and as a result is unable to offer concrete alternatives to the existing market and state-led programs for food security.

In the following section, I chronicle debates surrounding food sovereignty and food security. I then describe the field site and provide a brief history of agrarian transitions in the region. This is followed by a discussion of my findings on the outcomes of food sovereignty interventions in the Telengana region. I conclude by discussing the contradictions between food sovereignty and food security and highlighting the myriad problems rural dwellers face in the Telengana.
sections.Drawing the Lines: Food Security and Foo:
The ideological basis of food sovereignty implies control and autonomy over the food system, something that is not addressed by food security paradigms. The term attained global significance after V´ ıa Campesina, a transnational peasant coalition, deployed food sovereignty to oppose the General Agreement on Trade and Tariffs (GATT) as compromising the rights of nations to produce their basic foods and being inimical to the interests of peasant farmers (Edelman 2014). Since then, food sovereignty has been widely adopted, and its definition expanded, reflecting its growing appeal as a discursive weapon to protect the interests not only of small food producers but increasingly of consumers and states (Wittman, Desmarais, and Wiebe 2010).

Food sovereignty is a call to address the failings of the food security paradigm that do not address who produces the food, how food is produced, and who benefits from its production and sale (Desmarais 2007). The diverse array of ideological positions and class interests of those advocating for food sovereignty make it challenging to define what it actually entails, but most call for supporting small and peasant farming systems and agroecological practices-a neopopulist ideal-as essential to resist the corporate food regime (V´ ıa Campesina 1996; McMichael 2005; Windfuhr and Jons´ en 2005; Desmarais 2007; Patel 2009; MartinezTorres and Rosset 2010). Advocates highlight how the commodification of agriculture has impinged on the sovereignty of states, communities, and individuals to determine their own food policies. Food sovereignty's most identifiable battles are those that oppose the research, marketing, and cultivation of genetically modified crops, landlessness, corporate 'land grabs' for biofuels, large-scale commercial agriculture, resource extraction such as mining, and other large-scale development that displaces poor farmers or impedes their ability to make a livelihood from farming.

As food sovereignty is a relatively new concept, only recently have scholars made attempts to theorize it. Although most scholars support its progressive agenda in that it questions the unsustainability of neoliberal agriculture, they highlight how food sovereignty ideals represent a resurgence of agrarian populism and hence do little to respond to the varied, complex, and contradictory problems faced by different classes of rural dwellers (Kay 2008; Bernstein 2014).

In its simplest form, populism is defined as 'a mode of thought opposed to orthodox large-scale concentrated production in favor of small-scale individual enterprise' (Watts 1983, 80). Contemporary agrarian populists have foisted ecological sustainability onto this ideal and envision peasant farmers as supporters of a decentralized socialism who base their practices on ecological values (Cochrane 2007). Populist economic doctrines date back to the work of Russian neopopulists such as Chayanov from the early 1900s (Watts 1983). E. F. Schumacher (1993), author of Small Is Beautiful, and influential writers and scholars such as Wendell Berry and Michael Lipton and others kept these ideas alive in the 1960s and 1970s (Watts 1983).

Critiques of neopopulism highlight that strategies that uphold a localized, smallholder farming model are ahistoric and static as they fail to adequately acknowledge how the economic logic of small farms are not distinct from those of other capitalist production systems (Watts 1983; Byres 2004; Brass 2005; Bernstein 2009). Rural society is dynamic. Peasants accumulate surpluses and diversify out of agriculture. This dynamic necessarily includes the accompanying structural change, the inequality of access to resources, the necessary relations between agriculture and industry, the role of the state in these processes, as well as the relationship of peasants to other classes (Watts 1983; Byres 2004; Kay 2008; Bernstein 2009; Borras 2010). Yet, it is common for food sovereignty advocates to make claims about small farming systems that capitalist market relations are external to indigenous and peasant communities, whereas noncapitalist relations, based on a moral economy of reciprocity and production for subsistence, exist on the inside (MartinezTorres and Rosset 2010, 154).

Recent empirical research in the Global South examining food sovereignty stresses that food sovereignty as it is currently defined is at odds with farmers' lived realities and does not enable them to achieve food security. Boyer's (2010) research in Honduras among peasant organizations belonging to V´ ıa Campesina found that there were historical, cultural, and structural constraints that prevent the acceptance of food sovereignty ideals among Honduran peasants. He concluded that Honduran peasant understandings of food security were at odds with V´ ıa Campesina's discourse of food sovereignty.

Bhattarai (2013) found that in the context of an increasingly monetized economy in rural Nepal, even a voluntary shift to agroecological farming practices by farmers who want to cut the cord of corporate dependence is not enough to provide food security that included access to education, health care, and housing. Furthermore, the younger generations' aspirations of progress moved them away from agriculture. Thus, Bhattarai calls for an expanded version of food sovereignty that does not base its solutions only in agriculture. Gartaula et al. (2013) similarly found that in rural Tamil Nadu, food sovereignty practices would not address the particular challenges farmers faced within a neoliberal agrarian economy nor meet their needs and aspirations. They found that food sovereignty was too narrow and ideological and needed to include sustainable development policies that went beyond agriculture.

Therefore, critiques of the neopopulist vision of food sovereignty are borne out by empirical research that in the context of developing countries, food security and food sovereignty ideals are contradictory. Empirical research highlights that food sovereignty strategies based solely on small farming ignore the changing realities of the contemporary countryside where the move to commercial farming and the diversification out of farm-based livelihoods is integral to achieving food security. That many 'peasants' no longer can (or want to) depend only on agriculture alone (Bernstein 2009) is also true of the Telengana region, which, as the following two sections demonstrate, pits the food security struggles of small farmers against food sovereignty ideals.
sections.The Telengana Context:
Research was conducted among fifteen villages of the Western Medak district of the Telengana region, with two villages being the focal point of the ethnographic research. Food sovereignty interventions have been actively promoted by a nongovernmental organization (NGO), Rural Development Initiatives (RDI), in seventy-five villages in the area since the early 1990s. This research used a political ecology approach that combined a place-based study of local actors contextualized with a historical analysis of the capitalist transition of agriculture and a multiscalar treatment of food sovereignty. Methods included focus group discussions, surveys, semistructured interviews, life histories, informal discussions, and participant observation.

Secondary data in the form of land records, crop histories, and local news articles were also used.

The Telengana region (see Figure 1) forms part of a contiguous semi-arid belt and is considered 'backward' in terms of its human development (Nagaraj 2008). The region is characterized by rain-fed agriculture, poor soils, drought, and cultural and economic marginalization. Since India adopted neoliberal economic policies, already vulnerable farming systems have given way to widespread agrarian distress in the form of farmer suicides (Nagaraj 2008).

The region still primarily cultivates food crops such as sorghum, lentils, and oilseeds in nonirrigated lands and commercial crops such as sugarcane, potato, and banana in irrigated lands. Genetically modified (GM) cotton, considered by local farmers to be a high-risk crop, has in the past been cultivated by mainly large farmers. Yet, within the last seven to eight years, GM cotton and hybrid corn sold by Monsanto's local affiliates have been adopted on a large scale, even by small and marginal farmers.

Distress is not new to small and marginal farmers 2 in the region. Historically, lower castes have dealt with extreme oppression, exploitation, and hunger. Under late-Mughal rule, land and power were highly concentrated among the high castes, while untouchables and lower castes provided wage and unfree labor (Pavier 1981). Examples of earlier hardships were recounted several times during life history interviews by Dalit and lower caste families at the field site. They talked about the indignity of being hungry into the 1970s and 1980s, of having to beg for food and the compulsory unpaid labor called vetti.

The era of state-led development after independence brought some positive changes with land reforms, abolition of feudal institutions, investments in agriculture, the provision of safety nets resulting in agricultural growth, and increased food security. Many interviewees benefited from land reforms and became owner-cultivators. They reported that the availability of subsidized rice and rural employment programs greatly contributed to their food security. For the lower castes, these developments brought self-respect as culturally sanctioned poverty and social exclusion lessened.

The adoption of neoliberal economic reforms in the 1990s led to massive cuts in farming subsidies, reduced safety nets, and privatization and disinvestment in several key institutions for agriculture including credit, seeds, research, and extension services (Ghosh 2005). Costs of cultivation rose substantially as a result, leading to high debt. The reforms had differentiated impacts for the poor at the field site. Increased market engagement created new opportunities but also increased vulnerability in the face of ecological and market perturbations. Although most small farmers continued to struggle to meet their basic needs and their lives were extremely vulnerable, a majority of Dalits felt that they were better off than the past. Maniamma, an elder Dalit farmer who recounted hardships during a life history interview in 2009, explained:

Things are better now. We are eating well because of subsidized rice, state-provided rural employment, and the ability to cultivate our land. Our own hard work brings in wages that are high. Before we could not work in our own fields and had to work the landlord's fields. If we did not work for them they would not give us the grain we needed to survive.

This comment suggests that a combination of higher wages that came with neoliberal reforms, state welfare measures, and the breaking down of traditional feudal institutions have allowed them to cultivate their own land and sell their labor freely. These have been key to their improved food security. Small farmers are still up against insurmountable obstacles in their quest to eke out a livelihood in the Telengana region, however.

It is within this context of historical vulnerability, hunger, and marginalization and rapid commercialization that food sovereignty interventions have been promoted by RDI among small and marginal mainly Dalit women farmers. Their strategies reflect food sovereignty's overarching model for resisting the neoliberal agro-food regime, promoting localized agroecological farming that intends to improve farmers' capacity to subsist, focusing on traditionally cultivated food crops such as sorghum, millets, oilseeds, and lentils.

The majority of small and poor farmers, however, were unable to adopt localized subsistence-focused agriculture even if it improved their ability to subsist. Farmers faced many constraints including (1) compulsions to participate in an increasingly monetized economy with all the opportunities and risks that markets bring, (2) changing geographies of labor, and (3) changing values and knowledge relating to agriculture.
sections.Constraints to Adopting Food Sovereignty:
Debt, Risk, and a Monetized Economy

Chinnapuram 1 Village was the locus of the 1995 anticotton protests led by the NGO with the participation of local farmers. The protests were an attempt to draw attention to the displacement of food crops by cotton and the increasing commercialization of the countryside. RDI was prescient regarding the potential of cotton to cause major upheavals in a primarily food-crop cultivating area. When they staged the protest, mainly rich farmers were cultivating cotton. Today, however, small farmers are rapidly adopting cotton cultivation, andsomelandless farmers are leasing land at exorbitant rates to cultivate cotton, a trend not seen in the field site before. Historical crop reports for one research village show that cotton was first planted in 1996. Until 2003, it averaged less than 10 percent of the cultivable area. By 2004 almost half of the cultivable area was planted in cotton, representing drastic shifts in cultivation.

Cotton and corn (corn is another new commercial crop grown for chicken feed; it is not considered a food crop in the field areas) are displacing food crops like sorghum, pigeonpea, and other lentils, as well as certain high-value food crops like chickpea. Farmers explained that cotton is the only crop that brings such high returns in nonirrigated areas (Figure 2). They are well aware of the risks but also want to profit from agriculture. Balappa, a small Dalit farmer who owns two acres of nonirrigated land, explained:

Traditional crops are not being cultivated as much because with a crop like cotton one can make twenty to thirty thousand rupees in profit as opposed to very low profits from traditional crops.

Localized agriculture focused on food crops imposes limits. For example, one of RDI's most celebrated Dalit women farmers noted in a focus group discussion:

Although we have control over our agriculture, and are secure in food, shelter, and agriculture, we do not have enoughcashtoeducate our children, for marriages, sickness, and so on.

Over the last fifteen to twenty years local economies are becoming increasingly monetized. Villages have moved beyond subsistence and needs for cash are more urgent than before. In most Dalit households at the field site, children are being educated for the first time and farmers reported that health and education costs had increased dramatically. Of the 150 households surveyed, 50 percent borrowed money for costs of cultivation (including leasing land and sinking borewells), about 40 percent for marriages and other ceremonies, 30 percent for housing construction, and 25 percent for education and health.

Muniamma, a small woman farmer, noted during an interview:

If we had more land then we could afford to plant food crops, but since we have only one acre we plant only cotton to maximize our earnings.

Small farmers like her have no choice but to maximize their cash-earning opportunities and are more constrained in their cultivation choices.

Those who planted cotton and corn, however, were not happy with the absolute dominance of private actors in the seed sector. Farmers complained that the state had abdicated its role in providing the research and extension support they felt was crucial to their success as agriculturists. They preferred to buy their seeds from state extension outlets but complained that the seeds were of poor quality, making it even riskier.
sections.Changing Geographies of Labor:
Since the RDI established itself in the region nearly thirty years ago, local geographies of labor have changed in ways that have had direct impacts on households' abilities to mobilize labor for labor-intensive farming practices. Food sovereignty practices tend to be more labor intensive in all aspects of the agricultural cycle, including selecting and storing seed, preparing the land, building soil fertility through the application of organic matter, controlling weeds and pests, harvesting, processing, and storing grain. Because agriculture is becoming increasingly feminized in the region, this work burdens women more.

Before subsidized rice became cheaply available in the early 1980s, most poor households ate traditional food such as millets. Preparing millets is time consuming and women especially appreciated the reduced labor needs of preparing a rice-based meal. Anaamma, a landless Dalit farmer who depends primarily on wage work and safety nets for food security, explained:

Subsidized rice has made things easy for us. We had to do a lot of work to prepare foxtail millet, finger millet, and other grains, pounding them with our hands to dehusk the grain.

Farmyard manure is a key input into agroecological farming and a household's ability to maintain livestock depends on labor availability. Children have traditionally taken care of livestock, but they are increasingly unable or unwilling to tend to animals. When asked why they were not growing traditional crops, Maisappa, a small Dalit farmer belonging to one of RDI's project villages, explained in a focus group discussion:

If we want traditional agriculture and food security we should not send our children to school. We can only have animals if we have people to graze them. This was done by our children. Animals give us farmyard manure that we can use on our fields. In school children are not learning anything, neither are they useful at home . . . . If I go to graze cattle then who will earn the money?

As Maisappa indicates, the formal education system not only takes children physically away from agri- cultural work, but it also leads youth to devalue an agriculture-based livelihood.

The prevalence of higher wages in the area presents high opportunity costs for small farmers who would rather earn wages than expend time and labor growing food crops that would limit them to a subsistence lifestyle (Figure 3). Lalamma, a small woman farmer in an RDI project village, for example, remarked:

From one acre I can get three bags [300 kg] of sorghum. . . . If I weed my field, I lose my daily wages from other work. To hire bullocks for ploughing costs Rs. 300 a day. The investment is so high for only three bags of sorghum. For this reason many small farmers prefer doing wage work to cultivating their own fields.
sections.Shifting Values Around Traditional Agric:
Within households, there is a shift in knowledge and values around traditional subsistence crops due to the introduction of the subsidized rice program, increased material wealth, changing food preferences, and shifting values on a subsistence-focused lifestyle.

Indicating that increased material wealth has changed their diets, Somamma, a small woman farmer, recalled changed food habits during a life history interview:

Nowweeatmorewhite sorghum, subsidized rice, green gram, pigeonpea, and chickpea and less uncultivated greens like punti koora, doggal koora, and payal koora [referring to uncultivated greens from the Amaranthus and Hibiscus families]. Those days we ate more greens and less dal [prepared lentils] and hardly any vegetables. Now we eat more vegetables and also eat mutton one or two times a month.

For many Dalits, traditional foods and systems of cultivation were associated with exploitative labor institutions, hunger, and social exclusion. Valiamma, an elderly small Dalit farmer, shared her perspective on traditional foods in one of RDI's project villages:

Ambali [finger millet porridge] is poor peoples' food. It is associated with the hungry days. In those days, there was no summer work and that was the hungriest season. Now that there is chai and government subsidized rice, there is no need to make ambali.

Older farmers like her associated traditional foods and farming with the marginality and poverty of the past. Within households, there is a clear generational shift in food tastes away from traditional subsistence crops, especially the coarser grains. The younger generation frequently sought to distance themselves from traditional foods, which were perceived as a signifier of progress. Farmers confirm that because their children are not interested in eating these coarser traditional millets there is less incentive to cultivate them; as a consequence, knowledge about traditional food crops is waning. In a focus group discussion of male small farmers, the older farmers said that their diets were 50 percent rice and 50 percent sorghum bread, whereas the younger farmers said that their they preferred rice to sorghum bread and it made up around 25 percent of their diets. Although some forms of sorghum are widely eaten in the region and form a staple along with rice, the more drought-resistant or nutritious varieties are not as preferred because they are considered to be coarser, do not taste as good, or do not make white flour or soft rotis. AsoneDalitwomansmallfarmersuccinctly stated, 'People do not even eat yellow sorghum because it is not white.'

The director of RDI, who has actively promoted food sovereignty initiatives for the last two decades, shared that one of their biggest challenges is motivat- ing the younger generation to value traditional agriculture, as their situations are vastly different from their parents' and grandparents' generations. He explained:

Most of the farmers we originally worked with were farm labor and were earning small wages, sometimes as grain. They have felt hunger and complete deprivation. Attaining food security [with RDI] is precious for them. But we are not sure what will happen twenty years from now when the children go to school. The two generations that we have worked with will continue to practice traditional and agroecological cultivation.
sections.Discussion: Disjuncture Between Food Sec:
The constraints previously discussed underscore that food sovereignty prescriptions were not rooted in the changing material conditions of peasant existence in the Telengana region and depend on an essentialized notion of peasant motivations. At the field site, all those who practiced farming, regardless of their socioeconomic standing, gender, and caste, wanted more control over their agriculture. This control, they explained, would come from access to credit, support prices, subsidies on seeds, fertilizer, power for irrigation, research and extension services, market supports, and safety nets-for which they put faith in and assigned responsibility to the state. For poor farmers and the landless, their already precarious livelihoods would be far more difficult without existing state supports, such as summer work (Figure 4), subsidized food, and other welfare measures.

In addition to state supports, the farmers' ability to negotiate their position within the market economy is crucial for achieving livelihood security. This is in contrast to food sovereignty's foundation that farmers are better served if they can limit their engagement with the market economy through a focus on agroecological farming and subsistence food crops. Unless farmers are completely isolated from the market and live subsistence livelihoods, they cannot but feel pressured to participate in an increasingly monetized economy, and move to commercial crops. Many were supportive of agroecological agriculture in principle but did not think it would allow them to gain food security. Food sovereignty thus had little to do with localization and self-sufficiency strategies promoted by RDI.

A political ecology analysis of food emphasizes the importance of power, place, context, and difference at the conjuncture of social, political, and environmental relations (Jarosz 2014). In the Telengana region, rural dwellers are confronted by several problems, including (1) chronic food insecurity and nutritional insecurity of the very poor; (2) highly ecologically unsustainable farming practices especially of high-input crops such as cotton; (3) high cost of farming and debt; (4) water stress and climate change; (5) the loss of control over biological resources and loss of biological diversity with the corporatization of agriculture; (6) social inequity; and (7) livelihood insecurity and the inability of farming to provide it and a consequent desire to leave farming. Therefore, achieving food security, supporting farming, increasing ecological sustainability of farming, and resisting the corporate global food regime might need different strategies especially in the context of landscapes where small farmers are food insecure and where agrarian landscapes are experiencing rapid commercialization.

Analyzing this disjuncture between food sovereignty andfoodsecurity highlights that both food security and food sovereignty narratives are hegemonic. A hegemonic food security narrative with its focus on productivist modes of agriculture has enabled corporate capital's control of the food system and is laying waste to our ecosystems, bodies, local knowledges, and communities (Goodman 2014). In the Telengana region, the impact of corporate capital's foray into agriculture has had profound impacts as seen in the high number of suicides among small farmers (Nagaraj 2008).

Is the food sovereignty narrative also not hegemonic in that it privileges the views of those who favor a neopopulist vision of agriculture over the needs and aspirations of small farmers? Food sovereignty narratives link environmental and social justice concerns with food security and serve as an important critique of the corporate food regime and the food security paradigm. When myriad and complex rural issues are conflated by food sovereignty advocates, however, they do not serve to improve the lives of small farmers.

This does not mean that the food sovereignty model is not viable, only that it is limited. When food crops are grown locally and sustainably, it does increase access to food for the most marginalized, especially women, and brings other benefits to the local economy. Thus the answer to the myriad and complex problems of rural Telangana might lie at the conjuncture of food security and food sovereignty and not within one or the other approach. Peasants to- day negotiate their lives within the constraints and opportunities posed by state, market, and civil society, and these should be the starting point of initiatives that aim to help them (Bebbington 2000). Unless food sovereignty movement proponents are able to recognize the constraints faced by small farmers, the limits of their radical horizon are weakened. Food sovereignty ideologues need to be willing to test their ideas against critical, empirically grounded research to consider how food sovereignty plays out in specific localities for impoverished farmers, particularly the pressures and challenges they face to shift toward commercial agriculture and high-capital-input crops (Louis 2013). ■

sections.Elizabeth Louis:
Texas A&M University

This article critically examines the role of food sovereignty interventions in the mitigation of the impacts of neoliberal economic policies on poor farmers in the Telengana region of India. Findings based on eighteen months of ethnographic research in the Telengana region reveal that small and poor farmers face socioeconomic and cultural constraints to the adoption of food sovereignty practices and ideals. Food sovereignty prescriptions based on localized, sustainable, and subsistence agriculture paradoxically constrained farmers' chances of maintaining viable rural livelihoods in a harsh economic climate. Based on these findings, I argue that contrary to assertions by advocates that food sovereignty is a precondition to genuine food security, farmers must first have food and livelihood security to exercise true food sovereignty that allows them more control over their livelihoods. Key Words: food sovereignty, food security, rural livelihoods.
sections.Drawing the Lines: Food Security and Foo: The ideological basis of food sovereignty implies control and autonomy over the food system, something that is not addressed by food security paradigms. The term attained global significance after V´ ıa Campesina, a transnational peasant coalition, deployed food sovereignty to oppose the General Agreement on Trade and Tariffs (GATT) as compromising the rights of nations to produce their basic foods and being inimical to the interests of peasant farmers (Edelman 2014). Since then, food sovereignty has been widely adopted, and its definition expanded, reflecting its growing appeal as a discursive weapon to protect the interests not only of small food producers but increasingly of consumers and states (Wittman, Desmarais, and Wiebe 2010).
sections.The Telengana Context:
Research was conducted among fifteen villages of the Western Medak district of the Telengana region, with two villages being the focal point of the ethnographic research. Food sovereignty interventions have been actively promoted by a nongovernmental organization (NGO), Rural Development Initiatives (RDI), in seventy-five villages in the area since the early 1990s. This research used a political ecology approach that combined a place-based study of local actors contextualized with a historical analysis of the capitalist transition of agriculture and a multiscalar treatment of food sovereignty. Methods included focus group discussions, surveys, semistructured interviews, life histories, informal discussions, and participant observation.

Secondary data in the form of land records, crop histories, and local news articles were also used.

records.title: Household Water Insecurity in the Global North: A Study of Rural and Periurban Settlements on the Texas-Mexico Border
records.abstract: This article examines household-level characteristics that predict water insecurity in low-income rural and periurban communities on the Texas-Mexico border. We employ two logistic regression models (binary and ordered) to identify household characteristics that are more likely to result in water insecurity. Our analyses yielded unexpected findings: Whereas socioeconomic factors are weak predictors, immigration status of household members is a significant variable that contributes to household water insecurity. Policymakers need to pay more attention to marginalized communities as universal water access still leaves populations without adequate, reliable, and affordable water in the Global North.

sections.Wendy Jepson and Emily Vandewalle:
Texas A&M University

This article examines household-level characteristics that predict water insecurity in low-income rural and periurban communities on the Texas -Mexico border. We employ two logistic regression models (binary and ordered) to identify household characteristics that are more likely to result in water insecurity. Our analyses yielded unexpected fi ndings: Whereas socioeconomic factors are weak predictors, immigration status of household members is a signi fi cant variable that contributes to household water insecurity. Policymakers need to pay more attention to marginalized communities as ' universal ' water access still leaves populations without adequate, reliable, and affordable water in the Global North. Key Words: colonias, household water security, logistic regression, Texas, water resources.

T he pervasive view that households in developed countries have universal, indoor plumbing and secure water belies everyday experiences in lowincome and marginalized communities, where access to and bene fi t from adequate, affordable, and safe drinking water are daily struggles. In the United States, more than 600,000 households, or approximately 1.5 million people, live without complete plumbing facilities (American Communities Survey 2012). Many are homeless or belong to migrant or economically distressed populations. In Europe, Roma settlements lack access to safe water and sanitation (Harper, Steger, and Fil  c  ak 2009; Laurent 2011). For economically distressed households with access to water infrastructure, water service might not be affordable and water reliability and quality might be inadequate (Cory and Rahman 2009). In Detroit, thousands face water shutoffs due to an inability to pay their monthly bills (Lukacs 2014), and in the United Kingdom, almost 24 percent of households are ' water poor, ' paying more than 3 percent of household monthly income for water and sanitation services (Bradshaw and Huby 2013). Water quality threatens human health and well-being for rural communities and the urban poor. Small rural water suppliers chronically violate federal statutes protecting safe drinking water (Balazs et al. 2011; Satija 2014), and Native American communities face increased risk of drinking water contamination in water systems (Mascarenhas 2007). Yet, as some have pointed out, the poor in developed countries ' do not count among the world ' s 1.1 billion who lack access to safe drinking water or 2.4 billion who lack access to improved sanitation ' (Wescoat et al. 2008, 802).

Technical challenges are regularly cited as the cause of domestic water service delivery problems in the Global North. Poor water-system design, lack of trained operators, and insuf fi cient economies of scale for rural community water systems are cited as the causes leading to chronic boil water advisories (Patrick 2011a, 2011b). Geographic isolation, paired with poverty, is also posited as a reason for poor drinking water access (Wescoat, Headington, and Theobald 2008). In other places, dishonest land developers, minimum enforcement of plumbing codes, inadequate lowincome housing stock, and water pricing schemes are cited as contributing factors to poor water service in low-income areas in the United States (Ward 1999; Olmstead 2003).

Although previous studies on drinking water access are meritorious, current explanations narrow the discussion to technical gaps or pricing problems that interrupt physical fl ows of water to consumers despite the growing scholarship in human -environment geography that examines water provision as more than infrastructure. Drinking water is part of a larger hydrosocial waterscape, de fi ned as a system bound together by dynamic circuits of knowledge, measurements, devices, organizations, institutional practices, and governance regimes (Linton and Budds 2014). Social and political processes constitute and mediate these circuits that allocate water fl ows and hydrological services through communities and across regions to water users and bene fi ciaries. Thus, our starting point is to frame the problem of drinking water provision in the Global North in terms of relational patterns of water access, everyday water practices, and the experiential or subjective dimensions of the hydrosocial cycle that dynamically reconstitute the waterscape (Sultana 2011; Jepson and Lee 2014). The challenge is how to operationalize the relational approach in a manner that is analytically robust, while offering opportunities to translate results into public policy that can materially improve drinking water quality for the marginalized in the Global North.

This article contributes to recent work on domestic water provision among marginalized communities in the Global North. First, we build on previous studies to advance the multidimensional concept of water security as a promising metric to assess the everyday experiences of water (Jepson 2014). Water security, de fi ned in terms of human development, is considered adequate, reliable, and affordable water for a healthy life (Lundqvist, Appasamy, and Nelliyat 2003; Wolf 2011; Cook and Bakker 2012). One can re fi ne water security for human development into three dimensions: water access, quality, and water affect (Wutich and Ragsdale 2008; Jepson 2014). This framework allows for the assessment of how gaps in water reliability, quality, and affordability erode the functioning for basic human activities. Water security includes, but is not limited to, water access; other characteristics such as affordability, quality, and the subjective experiences of domestic water provision are equally important. This is different than the concept of water poverty, which primarily addresses water access as a function of scarcity in terms of infrastructural and environmental issues at larger scales. Second, we examine the question of water security at the household level. By documenting water security variability among households in similar low-income populations, we might reveal contributing factors to water insecurity that have been previously overlooked at other scales.

Nowhere else does the relationship between domestic water provision and social exclusion come into such stark relief than in communities called colonias.

Colonias are impoverished and mostly unincorporated subdivisions populated by Mexican Americans located on urban fringes or in rural areas along the 2,000-mile U.S. -Mexico border. Although conditions have improved over the past decades (Durst and Ward 2013), colonias, home to more than 400,000 residents, are typically characterized by inadequate water and sanitation services, lack of electricity, and unpaved roads (Ward 1999; Donelson and Esparza 2010; McDonald and Grineski 2012; Of fi ce of the Attorney General 2012; Korc and Ford 2013). Recent work has examined the complex and dynamic social life of water prevalent in border colonias (Jepson and Lee 2014; Vandewalle and Jepson 2014). This article poses a further question: What household-level characteristics predict water insecurity within border colonias?

After placing the study in its regional context and describing the study ' s qualitative research and survey methods, we propose a novel measurement to assess household water insecurity and then employ two logistic regression models (binary and ordered) to identify household characteristics that are likely to result in household water insecurity. In the binary logistic regression model, the dependent variable is water insecurity. In the ordered logistic regression model, we use the natural order of dependent variables (water secure, marginally water secure, marginally water insecure, water insecure) where higher categories indicate increased household water insecurity. Our analysis, although preliminary, is signi fi cant because it is the fi rst regression model using a measurement of water security at the household scale.

Our results yield some unexpected fi ndings concerning the relevance of immigration status to household water insecurity. Notwithstanding some weaknesses in the study, it is clear that adequate, reliable, and affordable water for a healthy life is a ' material emblem of citizenship ' (Bakker 2010, 55); for colonias communities on the border, immigration status might in fl uence household water insecurity more than previously expected. Broadly, these results underscore the need to examine the social and political determinants of household water insecurity in marginalized communities rather than ascribing water insecurity to technical gaps in water delivery systems.
sections.Household Water Insecurity Along the U.S:
The waterscape on the Texas -Mexico border is de fi ned by complex hydrosocial interactions among institutions, organizations, and technologies that allocate the fl ow of water across the region and through infrastructure to different water users (Jepson 2012; Jepson and Brannstrom 2015). Rio Grande water eventually fi nds its way to poor households through circuits of irrigation-district canals, quasi-public community water networks, inadequate household connections, water vending machines, and garden hoses to be stored in fi fty-gallon barrels, buckets, or fi ve-gallon plastic bottles. A fragmented regime of water governance institutions, water markets, housing codes, and private corporations direct the water fl ow to households in border colonias. The focus of this study is two of the poorest regions in the United States: (1) Hidalgo County in the Lower Rio Grande Valley, with the largest concentration of colonias (over 240,000 people), and (2) El Paso County in West Texas (Figure 1).
