Residents in border colonias have few reliable, affordable, and adequate options for drinking water. They face a ' no-win ' waterscape. Existing domestic water provision is available but expensive, highly variable, and unreliable, and water quality is demonstratively precarious. Residents face service interruptions due to lack of payment, unreliable water service, and concerns over tap water quality. Some households avoid existing water utilities altogether and use garden hoses to connect to a neighbor ' s water meter (Figure 3).

Several households not connected to community water service might live in areas not served by a water supply corporation. For example, 4,500 residents living in sixty El Paso colonias are not connected to community water systems. In other cases, households cannot afford the water connection costs, or they cannot afford the household improvements necessary to comply with building codes, a prerequisite for waterline hookups. Instead, residents rely on water delivery trucks to fi ll large 1,500- to 2,500-gallon plastic storage tanks. Trucked water, despite claims to the contrary, is not considered potable, and many residents experience skin rashes due to contamination (Graham and VanDerslice 2007; McDonald and Grineski 2012; Figure 4). Finally, most households, whether connected to a community water system or not, depend on unreliable water vending machines because of generalized tap water quality concerns (Chaidez et al. 1999; Schillinger and Knorr 2004; Figure 5).
sections.Household Surveys: Qualitative research was conducted in Hidalgo County during nine visits between January 2009 and August 2011. The fi rst author led a research team, including a local community health worker ( promotora ), as they conducted forty-one semistructured interviews and two focus groups. The fi rst author used qualitative information to develop a household water security survey, which was then completed for seventy-one households in Hidalgo County (sixty-eight households used in study) in July 2012. The second author conducted sixty-six household surveys in El Paso County and Do ~ na Ana County (New Mexico) in July 2013. We used the State of Texas colonia classi fi cation system to stratify our sample of households (Parcher and Humberson 2009). We selected households in eleven different colonias in eastern Hidalgo County and fourteen different colonias in eastern El Paso, with households representing each colonia classi fi cation: red, yellow, green, and unclassi fi ed (Table 2). We also surveyed colonias not classi fi ed in the Texas database. We removed six household surveys from adjacent counties in New Mexico when we ran the logistic regression models to limit our analysis to Texas counties. The surveys were conducted in Spanish or English with the available head of household. The survey, which took between thirty and forty- fi ve minutes, was divided into four parts: (1) household demographics (age, occupation, health care access, country of origin, etc., for each household member), (2) water usages and practices, (3) series of yes -no questions related to the three water dimensions, and (4) income and wealth. Descriptive statistics of households are provided in Table 3.
sections.Data Analysis:
We analyzed household survey data using three techniques. First, we used an experiential scalogram technique (Guttman 1945) to draw inferences about a latent variable (water insecurity) in the observed data (Guttman 1945; Guest 2000). In this study we created three scalograms for each dimension of water security. Guttman scalograms provide a measurement of cumulative or progressive objective, subjective, and biocultural experiences; it has been particularly useful when related to domestic water access and food security (Wutich and Ragsdale 2008; Hadley and Wutich 2009; Stevenson et al. 2012). For Hidalgo County, we used household scales and classi fi cations from previously published data (Jepson 2014), and we followed the same procedure to create the water security scales and classi fi cation for households in El Paso.

Survey item responses were entered 0 or 1 into a respondent-by-item matrix for each dimension of water security, with each row representing a household respondent and each column representing an indicator for each dimension of water security (water access, water quality acceptability, water distress). Guttman scalograms order item responses such that the individual who responded more positively will rank higher than an individual who responded negatively, and the positions of the item responses and individuals are given numerical values. Three conventional measures of reliability for each scale were calculated: coef fi cient of reproducibility (CR), coef fi cient of

We did not explicitly ask immigration status of household members; however, a combination of responses from several survey questions -place of birth, sources of income (including public bene fi t), time of residency, insurance coverage -allowed us to deduce and estimate documented or undocumented status. We noted households receiving Temporary Assistance for Needy Families, Social Security (including SSI Disability), and Supplementary Nutrition Program (SNAP, or food stamps) because monthly bene fi ts require documented status. We also noted whether the distribution of these bene fi ts varied between and within each household. For example, we surveyed households in which all of the children under the age of eighteen would be eligible for Children ' s Health Insurance Program or Medicaid but not all of them receive the bene fi ts. Similarly, a household might receive SNAP bene fi ts for some children but not as a household or at the maximum eligible under current state provision. We recognize that SNAP eligibility for adults is variable, but since July 2002 children under eighteen who are legal residents are eligible for bene fi ts (Wight et al. 2014). This intrahousehold variability, paired with other data on birthplace, strongly suggests whether the household is a mixedstatus or all-undocumented household. If no proxy evidence for residency status was obtained, we classifi ed the household as all documented.

An odds ratio less than 1.0 indicates a negative effect or a lower likelihood that the outcome will occur. Second, we performed an ordered logistic regression (OLR) model, which is similar to the binary logistic regression model but for multiple outcome variables that are categorical (water secure, marginally water secure, marginally water insecure, and water insecure). OLR models the relation between the previous independent variables and the four household water security classifi cations while controlling for the covariates. Regression results are reported as adjusted odds ratios (ORs) and 95 percent con fi dence intervals (CIs) for moving to higher water insecurity categories versus remaining in the same category. That is, OLR models cumulative probability, or the factors that increase or decrease the likelihood of being in a higher category of household water insecurity. For the OLR, an odds ratio higher than 1.0 for the explanatory variable indicates a greater likelihood of being in higher water insecurity categories versus remaining in the same category. Conversely, an odds ratio less than 1.0 indicates a negative effect or a lower likelihood of being in higher water insecurity categories versus remaining in the same category.

sections.Results:
Comparing Scalograms and Household Water Security

Guttman scalograms for each of the three dimensions of water security offer a means to compare regional differences among colonias surveyed in El Paso and Hidalgo Counties (Table 6). The analysis clustered scale scores so that each household was classi fi ed in terms of household water security: (1) water secure, (2) marginally water secure, (3) marginally water insecure, or (4) water insecure (Table 6, Figure 7). In general, more households are water secure in Hidalgo County than in El Paso County. Although the analysis indicates that 10 percent of the colonia households in both regions are water secure, more than a third of the surveyed households in Hidalgo County are marginally water secure (35%), whereas only a quarter of the households in El Paso County are marginally water secure (25%). Similarly, the percentage of households classi fi ed as marginally water insecure is almost equal in each county (32 percent, El Paso; 31 percent, Hidalgo), but one third of the surveyed households in El Paso County are water insecure (33 percent), whereas a quarter of the households in Hidalgo County (24 percent) are classi fi ed as water insecure.

sections.Binary Logistic Regression:
Table 7 summarizes the outcome and explanatory variables used in the regression models. Table 8 presents the results from the logistic regression model for household water insecurity. Overall the model is reasonably strong as indicated by the likelihood ratio chi-square value, which is statistically signi fi cant ( p < 0.05).

Household immigration status is an important factor to consider in household water insecurity. The analysis indicates that ' mixed status ' households were 4.2 times more likely to be water insecure than households with members who were all documented (legal residents or U.S. citizens). Households in which all members are unauthorized residents increase the likelihood (1.2 times) of water insecurity, but the results were insigni fi cant. Birthplace, which is different than legal status, also signi fi cantly affected household water insecurity. Households with both U.S.- and foreignborn members are 20 percent less likely to be water insecure than households in which all members were born in the United States.

Other socioeconomic variables such as size of household increase the likelihood of household water insecurity, but the results are all insigni fi cant. Poverty level runs in the direction anticipated. Households between 50 percent and 99 percent of the FPL are almost twice as likely to be water insecure than those above the FPL, and the households below 49 percent of the FPL are 1.5 times more likely to be water insecure than those above the FPL. Households with members that include children, adults, and elderly are 6.3 times more likely to be water insecure than households with only adults or only elderly. Although the p value is slightly more than 0.01 ( p value D 0.127), it approaches signi fi cance and therefore is an important fi nding.

The model also considers residential factors on household water insecurity. Living in a manufactured home (recreational vehicle [RV] or mobile home) was not an important predictor of household water insecurity. The model con fi rms expectations, however, that households in ' red ' colonias were more likely (4.7 times) to be water insecure as compared to households in the ' green ' classi fi ed colonia. Although living in a colonia classi fi ed ' red ' signi fi cantly increased the likelihood of water insecurity, the other colonia classi fi cations are poor predictors of household water insecurity. sections.Ordered Logistic Regression:
The OLR model reports many similar relationships between the independent and dependent variable (household water insecurity) as the fi rst binary logistic regression but with some notable differences (Table 8). Households with residents of mixed documentation are 2.4 times more likely to be classi fi ed in a higher category of household water insecurity than households with all members documented. Although signi fi cant, this is less than predicted in the binary logistic regression model. The OLR model also indicates that households with all undocumented residents are three times more likely to be classi fi ed in higher levels of household water insecurity. Although this fi nding was not statistically signi fi cant, the p value was approaching signi fi cance and therefore we consider an important relationship between all undocumented households and water insecurity. Households with mixed U.S.- and foreign-born residents are 38 percent less likely to be classi fi ed in higher levels of water insecurity than households with all U.S.-born residents, which is a higher likelihood than in the binary logistic regression. Households with all foreign-born members are also less likely to be in a higher water insecurity category than all U.S.-born households. Although insigni fi cant, it is notable that this is a shift in direction from the binary logistic regression model.

Similar to the binary regression model, other socioeconomic variables, such as size of household, increases the likelihood of household water insecurity, but the results are insigni fi cant. In addition, relative poverty level runs in the direction anticipated, but results from our analysis are all insigni fi cant. Households between 50 and 99 percent of the FPL are about twice as likely to be in a higher household water insecurity category than those above the FPL, a very similar result from the binary regression. Households below 49 percent of the FPL are 2.6 times more likely to be in a higher water insecure category than those above the FPL, which is notably different than the result from the binary regression. Similarly, households that receive public bene fi t run in the negative direction to household water insecurity but, as with the binary logistic regression model, this is statistically insigni fi cant. As in the binary logistic regression model, households with members that include children, adults, and elderly are more likely to be water insecure (2.8 times) than households with only adults or only elderly. Although the p value is more than 0.01, it approaches signi fi cance with a p value of 0.163

and therefore is an important fi nding. The OLR model con fi rms that dwelling type and time in residence are poor predictors of household water insecurity.

The OLR model presents a clearer relationship between households living in ' red ' colonias and higher levels of household water insecurity than those in the binary regression. These households are 7.8 times more likely to be in a higher category of household water insecurity and with a stronger signi fi cance value. In the binary regression model, households in ' yellow ' colonias are less likely to be water insecure than households in ' green ' colonias, but the OLR model changes sthe direction of this relationship. There is an increased chance that a household in the ' yellow ' category will be observed in a higher category of household water insecurity but, again, the p value value indicates that this is not signi fi cant.
sections.Discussion:
Our research suggests that households living in border colonias -communities that are both connected to community water service and not connected to community water service -face signi fi cant levels of household water insecurity. Water insecurity varied, however, within similar subdivisions; thus, our work challenges the notion that colonias households form a homogenous group in terms of living conditions and access to resources. Our analysis attempted to determine what household-level characteristics would predict water insecurity in colonias households. The binary logistic regression modeled signi fi cant predictors for presence of household water insecurity; the OLR modeled the odds for a household moving to higher water insecurity categories versus remaining in the same category. Overall, household water insecurity is dif fi cult to predict with statistical signi fi cance, but there were some unexpected results in our fi ndings, particularly if we examine our preliminary fi ndings in comparison with recent scholarship on experience of insecurity of everyday life on the U.S. -Mexico border.

First, we would have expected relative poverty to increase the likelihood of water insecurity, but our results indicate that the degree to which a household lives in poverty might not strongly in fl uence water insecurity among this population. Although the reasons need to be investigated further, one can deduce that water is not affordable for most of the households because most are impoverished, and a majority of the surveyed households experience problems buying water or engage in practices to economize water use. Therefore, differences in terms of household water insecurity might re fl ect the experiences related to the other dimensions of water insecurity (quality and distress) and not to different levels of affordability or access.

Second, we would also expect that living in a mobile home would increase the likelihood of water insecurity because those units can be more easily located on land that does not necessarily follow water and sanitation codes. Moreover, colonia residents more frequently rely on the secondary market to buy aging mobile homes and RVs (Durst 2014); therefore, the internal infrastructure could be signi fi cantly depreciated, degrading water quality through the connection between the housing and the water supply. In addition, the literature would suggest that an increase in residence time might decrease the likelihood of water insecurity because of housing consolidation and dwelling improvements made over the life course (Durst and Ward 2013). Yet, our analysis indicates that factors related to the dwelling (e.g., dwelling types [mobile or RV vs. house] and time in residence [years]) do not increase the likelihood of household water insecurity to any signi fi cant degree.

Although we were not surprised that households in ' red ' colonias have a higher likelihood of being water insecure than households in ' green ' colonias, the result that other state-mandated colonias classi fi cations were poor predictors of household water insecurity was unexpected. In many cases, especially in the El Paso ' red ' colonias, lack of either water or sanitation services set the stage for household water insecurity, whereas in Hidalgo County, households in ' red ' colonias lacked mainly sanitation. Moreover, although classi fi cation was a predictor, we documented various household levels of water insecurity in ' red ' colonias. Therefore, we can only conclude that the colonia classi fi cation system, although perhaps helpful in identifying the worst-case scenarios, is an inadequate proxy to assess the larger and more diverse experiences of household-scale water insecurity.

Finally, our analysis revealed a major unexpected predictor of household water insecurity -immigration status of household members -with mixed-status households as the most signi fi cant predictor of household water insecurity. Our fi ndings, paired with existing research on mixed-status families, suggest that the quotidian behaviors and choices in response to precarious immigration status might ' spill over ' into other insecurities, including household water insecurity. Negotiating the immigration regime is de fi ned by avoiding exposure to authorities. This can be achieved in terms of location of residences, and many colonias provide this protection as they are within the sparsely patrolled rural and periurban areas. Connection to public services might also be a perceived vulnerability and exposure point. Another form of ' protection, ' con fi rmed anecdotally in fi eld research, is the reliance or dependency on private water delivery -either trucked or vending machines. This allows individuals to manage chronic problems of water access and quality without directly addressing problems with the water supply corporations or municipal services. The impact could include increased costs of water, dependency on unregulated water sources, and increased water distress. Exploring these speci fi c interactions is beyond the scope of this study, but we believe that future research should explore how immigration status might in fl uence interactions with local water governance regimes as a signi fi cant factor in water insecurity.

Several important limitations should be considered when reviewing the results of this study and could inform future research. Although the study included an adequate number of households, a larger sample size might improve the robustness. Second, housing tenure -either rental, ownership (title), or contractfor-deed ( fi nal or interim) -would be another important variable to include in future surveys. Our current survey did not delineate the speci fi c status of housing tenure, so we could not include this variable in our current model. As time in residence, the variable we used, might autocorrelate with housing tenure, future research would have to determine the best independent variable. Third, our analysis provided preliminary means to assess gaps in water reliability, quality, and affordability, but we recognize the need to re fi ne the scalogram and classi fi cation analysis. For example, household water security classi fi cations were generated based on experiential scales re fl ective of each place studied yet were aggregated in the regression analyses. That said, our study is in line with the experience-based scales, as these communities are similar in terms of culture and socioeconomic demographics.
sections.Conclusion: Ourstudy advanced current research on domestic water provision among marginalized communities in the Global North by applying methods to quantify household water insecurity. The empirical focus of this study was low-income, periurban and rural communities in two impoverished regions on the Texas -Mexico border: the Lower Rio Grande Valley and west Texas. The novel scale and classi fi cation system offered a systematic means to assess the three dimensions of household water security in a common measurement for households for two study areas. The results reveal notable regional differences. Households in both regions have an equal percentage classi fi ed as water secure, but there is a higher percentage of households surveyed in El Paso classi fi ed as marginally water insecure or water insecure. We also used household water security classifi cations developed from household survey data to run two statistical analyses: binary logistic regression and OLR. We determined that demographics, poverty, and housing infrastructure are relatively weak and statistically insigni fi cant predictors of household water insecurity, whereas immigration status signi fi cantly increased the likelihood of household water insecurity. Our study suggests that future research should investigate why immigration status might be a predictor of water insecurity, repeat the logistic regression analysis with a larger sample size, and broaden the geographical distribution of study areas to advance our knowledge of the unevenness of household water insecurity. These research directions will enable further tests of the household water security measurement as a robust, reliable indicator, similar to the food security measurements, in the Global North. &

sections.Wendy Jepson and Emily Vandewalle:
Texas A&M University

This article examines household-level characteristics that predict water insecurity in low-income rural and periurban communities on the Texas -Mexico border. We employ two logistic regression models (binary and ordered) to identify household characteristics that are more likely to result in water insecurity. Our analyses yielded unexpected fi ndings: Whereas socioeconomic factors are weak predictors, immigration status of household members is a signi fi cant variable that contributes to household water insecurity. Policymakers need to pay more attention to marginalized communities as ' universal ' water access still leaves populations without adequate, reliable, and affordable water in the Global North. Key Words: colonias, household water security, logistic regression, Texas, water resources.
sections.Household Water Insecurity Along the U.S:
The waterscape on the Texas -Mexico border is de fi ned by complex hydrosocial interactions among institutions, organizations, and technologies that allocate the fl ow of water across the region and through infrastructure to different water users (Jepson 2012; Jepson and Brannstrom 2015). Rio Grande water eventually fi nds its way to poor households through circuits of irrigation-district canals, quasi-public community water networks, inadequate household connections, water vending machines, and garden hoses to be stored in fi fty-gallon barrels, buckets, or fi ve-gallon plastic bottles. A fragmented regime of water governance institutions, water markets, housing codes, and private corporations direct the water fl ow to households in border colonias. The focus of this study is two of the poorest regions in the United States: (1) Hidalgo County in the Lower Rio Grande Valley, with the largest concentration of colonias (over 240,000 people), and (2) El Paso County in West Texas (Figure 1). The boxes indicated in Figures 1

Figure 1 Study sites: El Paso County and Hidalgo County. (Color figure available online.)
sections.Household Surveys: Qualitative research was conducted in Hidalgo County during nine visits between January 2009 and August 2011. The fi rst author led a research team, including a local community health worker ( promotora ), as they conducted forty-one semistructured interviews and two focus groups. The fi rst author used qualitative information to develop a household water security survey, which was then completed for seventy-one households in Hidalgo County (sixty-eight households used in study) in July 2012. The second author conducted sixty-six household surveys in El Paso County and Do ~ na Ana County (New Mexico) in July 2013. We used the State of Texas colonia classi fi cation system to stratify our sample of households (Parcher and Humberson 2009). We selected households in eleven different colonias in eastern Hidalgo County and fourteen different colonias in eastern El Paso, with households representing each colonia classi fi cation: red, yellow, green, and unclassi fi ed (Table 2). We also surveyed colonias not classi fi ed in the Texas database.

-Ambrosio Cerd  an de Landa, Lima Water Judge (1828, 3 -4)

H istorical perspectives have long been considered integral to political ecology (Zimmerer and Bassett 2003; Peet and Watts 2004; Robbins 2004), although how and to what end historical content and analysis could be incorporated into this research approach has not been fully resolved and remains an ambiguous pursuit (Offen 2004). In general, the historical political ecology approach calls for the application of historical perspectives within a broadly de fi ned political ecology point of view and has been de fi ned as ' a fi eld-informed interpretation of society -nature relations in the past ' (Offen 2004, 21). This includes using historical material to contextualize current environmental con fl icts, especially the continuing in fl uences of European expansion and colonialism, often with the explicit motivation of improving social justice or environmental conservation in the present (Brannstrom 2004; Offen 2004; D. K. Davis 2009). Historical political ecology might also include asking questions about environmental change or natural resource use in historical periods, either recent (e.g., Swyngedouw 1999; Biehler 2009; Carey 2010; Lane 2011; Carey, French, and O ' Brien 2012) or more distant (e.g., Watts 1983; Sluyter 1999; Zimmerer 2000; Carney 2001; M. Davis 2004; End fi eld and Fern  andez Tejedo 2006; D. K. Davis 2007; End fi eld 2008). Although this latter purpose -using a political ecological analysis to closely examine nature -society relations in the past and not just provide context for current-day issues -is lesser used, it represents a powerful framework for historical research.

In this article, I apply such a framework to municipal drinking water access and governance in colonial Lima, the capital city of the Viceroyalty of Peru. I draw on approaches and questions inspired by political ecology to examine patterns and politics of water use in a colonial context, focusing on the in fl uence of power dynamics on sociospatial patterns of resource access and control (following McCarthy 2002; Ribot and Peluso 2003; Turner 2009). Using material analysis of water infrastructure and technology recorded in sixteenth- and seventeenth-century archives, I explain how water access formed, reinforced, and re fl ected colonial social divisions, as well as in fl uenced the spatial development of the colonial city.

The city of Lima, originally called Ciudad de Los Reyes , was founded in 1535 as the seat of the Spanish Viceroyalty of Peru. It can be considered one of the most prominent of the Spanish colonial cities, second perhaps only to Mexico, the capital of New Spain. Lima is located on the central coast of Peru in a desert climate where true rainfall rarely occurs. All water used for drinking, irrigation, sanitation, and industry must be drawn from river watersheds and related aquifers. The urban design of Lima followed the wellknown Spanish colonial grid pattern, and the city was speci fi cally sited along the banks of the Rímac River and in relation to the numerous pre-Hispanic irrigation canals drawn from this river. 1 The Spaniards, however, established their own drinking water pipeline infrastructure. This underground pipe network, fi rst inaugurated in 1578, was controlled by the Cabildo (City Council) and was one of the earliest in the New World. The Cabildo, or municipal branch of colonial government, was of fi cially charged with managing Lima ' s water and, not surprisingly, the careful division of measured amounts of drinking and irrigation water occupied much of its energy. 2 Although the Cabildo ' s explicitly stated objective was to provide access to clean and copious drinking water for the entire urban population, this goal was only partially achieved. Therefore, this article seeks to examine how municipal governance strategies contributed to inequality in access to drinking water among colonial Lima ' s urban residents. The methodological approach to answering this question incorporates two major components: fi rst, asking questions inspired by political ecology and, in particular, the political ecology of water and, second, applying data collection and analysis techniques appropriate to the historical period being studied.

Three key themes drawn from the recent literature on the political ecology of water inform my interpretations of the Lima case. Most important, unequal water access (Swyngedouw 2004; Bakker 2011; Loftus 2011) and the related politics of surface water or aquifer management (Swyngedouw 1999; Norman and Bakker 2008; Brooks and Linton 2011; Jepson 2012) have proven integral themes in understanding current-day water systems and have been shown to have both important historical antecedents and long-term legacy effects. Second, analyses of urban development and urban -rural relations related to water demonstrate strong urban bias, with urban uses often privileged in cases of con fl icting multiple uses of water (multifunctionality). This bias, or unequal relationship between urban and rural areas, is evidenced by the urban hydraulic reach (or water footprint; Swyngedouw 1997, 2004; Bakker 2003; Kaika 2005; Scott and Pablos 2011). Third, combining spatial, social, political, and economic aspects of the previously mentioned themes, Bakker (2003) indicated that water supply in urban areas, especially urbanizing areas of the Global South, should be understood in terms of archipelagos instead of networks, given the discontinuous and partial coverage of public water supply and the frequency of multiple and overlapping methods of public and private water delivery mechanisms. Together, these themes provide a foundational perspective from which to examine urbanization, water supply, and inequality. They suggest the primacy of urban water use and indicate unequal infrastructural coverage and access to water within urban spaces.

Although these topics, questions, and themes from political ecological research can be easily transferred to historical contexts, the research methods typically used by political ecologists might not always be applicable, especially when more distant historical periods are studied. For such older cases, it is necessary to combine multiple methods and data sources, which might include fi eld-based ethnographic and landscape observations, archival analysis, archaeological investigation, biophysical data, mapping, and more. The multidisciplinary research area called hydraulic archaeology provides a framework for analysis of (pre) historical water systems (Kirchner and Navarro 1996; Glick and Kirchner 2000; Barcel  o 2004; Glick 2005). Here, practitioners seek to reconstruct the design, layout, construction, and modi fi cation of hydraulic systems, to identify the social groups participating in the use of these systems and thus to determine the relative political and demographic strengths of these groups as demonstrated by their ability to access water resources. The major unit of investigation in hydraulic archaeology is the concept of hydraulic space (Barcel  o 1996), which is basically equivalent to what Swyngedouw (1999) termed the ' waterscape ' and can be de fi ned as a landscape of water use, at once both natural and social. It is a space designed to take advantage of a natural fl uvial system, and incorporates (1) the aquifer or drainage area, (2) the local and regional topography in relation to desired water conduction, and (3) the irrigated parcels or other uses of water. It includes the biophysical context controlling the quantity of water available and the direction of its fl ow, as well as the human division of water among houses, fi elds, orchards, and other uses. The orientation and design of a hydraulic space is based on features of the fl uvial system, but the conduction and distribution of water in canals and pipes follows patterns that are neither natural nor casual. This water infrastructure is closely linked to the organization of productive activities and therefore to social, political, and economic relationships.

The focus on infrastructure (e.g., canals, pipelines), achieved through consideration of a range of data sources (e.g., archaeological survey and excavation, historical documents and maps, legal traditions, toponyms, and remotely sensed imagery), makes hydraulic archaeology a useful guide for pursuing historical political ecology work on water in colonial Lima. Given the nearly 500 years of Lima ' s urban development, few material or archaeological remains of colonial water infrastructure can still be found (or reasonably accessed), so in this case archival sources contain the best information. The major source for the analysis of Lima ' s hydraulic space is the Libros de Cabildos de Lima (the books of the City Council of Lima, hereafter LCL ). These books, which record the minutes from the weekly or biweekly meetings of Lima ' s Cabildo, span almost the entire colonial period, from the city ' s foundation in 1535 to after Peru ' s independence in 1821, 3 and provide an incredibly comprehensive and continuous record of the Cabildo ' s actions related to drinking water governance. 4 In this article I examine the period 1578 to 1700, which was the interval during which most of Lima ' s public and private drinking water infrastructure was installed, the vast majority of potable water connection licenses were issued, and the most signi fi cant water management and governance strategies were developed. Speci fi cally, I analyze all references to springs, reservoirs, pipes, tanks, fountains, petitions for water connections, and other related topics in the LCL of the period in question to determine both spatial and temporal aspects of water supply in the pipeline network. I consider such basic questions as these: Where were pipelines constructed and when? Which residents and populations did these pipelines serve? How reliable was water supply in the network overall? This included mapping the pipeline routes and the locations of public and private running water connections. 5 I used this analysis of written descriptions of material aspects of Lima ' s hydraulic space to interpret the biophysical, social, political, and economic signi fi cance of patterns of drinking water access and control in the early colonial period and to evaluate the Cabildo ' s role in contributing to or alleviating inequality in water access.
sections.Lima's Hydraulic Space and Its Governanc:
In 1671, Lima ' s solicitor general called water ' the element most necessary after air ' ( LCL 29.X.1671), 6 and indeed it was the natural resource most frequently discussed by Lima ' s Cabildo. The provision of drinking water was considered one of the principal responsibilities of the Cabildo: ' the fi rst thing given attention in the foundation of all of the cities of the world [is] that this element, inexcusable for human life, is provided with cleanliness and security ' ( LCL 17.XI.1649). To this end, the Spanish located their capital city along the banks of the Rímac River, to provide residents with water for irrigation, drinking, sanitation, and industry. The Rímac dominates Lima ' s hydraulic space (Figure 1). Like all of Peru ' s coastal rivers, it fl ows westward, cutting down from the glacial lakes of the high Andes to the Paci fi c, descending from a height of over 5,500 m above sea level to its mouth near Lima ' s port El Callao over a distance of about 130 km. Its fl ow varies seasonally, increasing during the highland rainy season (October -April), when it often threatens to overrun its banks, and all but drying up during the dry months (May -September). The Rímac was the source of the irrigation canals that supported all agriculture in the region around the city (Domínguez 1988). It was also the source of numerous springs used for drinking water during the colonial period. Seepage and fi ltration from the river and the Andean cordillera fi lls the large alluvial aquifer -of approximately 390 km 2 in area and 100 to 500 m in depth -located underneath the city and its surroundings, recharging this resource on a seasonal basis (Lerner et al. 1982; Quintana and Tovar 2002).

The Spanish designed and built their linked agricultural and hydraulic system ( fi elds, canals, reservoirs, and pipelines) around the natural topography as well as the pre-Hispanic canals already in existence. This multipurpose hydraulic space linked Lima ' s urban core with its rural surroundings and was of fi cially controlled by the Cabildo, which exercised jurisdiction over the urban zone (approximately 2.6 km 2 ), as well as the surroundings of the city (approximately a 113km radius around the city). A diverse population resided within this larger territory, primarily made up of Spaniards, Africans, and Indians. 7 Although the Cabildo claimed great authority over the city, it actually governed through a complicated relationship with other branches of colonial government, especially the Viceroy (the Spanish monarch ' s representative in Peru) and the Real Audiencia (Royal Audience, the highest court in Peru). With respect to water administration, responsibilities of the Cabildo included protection of the urban riverbank and construction of levees, distribution of rights to irrigation waters, canal maintenance, concession of milling licenses, and, of primary importance here, construction and maintenance of a municipal drinking water pipeline network and allocation of permits to install private connections to this network for homes and other institutions. To manage all aspects of municipal water governance, a water judge ( Juez de Aguas ) was elected annually from among the city councilmen ( Regidores ). The water judge post was established in 1556, with power to enforce the water ordinances for the city and surrounding countryside. It was a lucrative position, with a salary of 800 pesos a year, yet election as water judge rotated among the councilmen and did not seem to require much specialized knowledge (Bell forthcoming).

To provision the city with drinking water, Lima ' s Cabildo carried out three functions: (1) It secured the source of the water in springs on the outskirts of the city; (2) it installed and maintained a network of reservoirs, tanks, and pipelines; and (3) it awarded licenses for running water connections from the pipes to private houses, monasteries and convents, and other institutions. For this, beginning in 1611, each year the Cabildo named three or four pipeline commissioners ( Comisarios de Ca ~ nerías ). 8 These pipeline commissioners were councilmen or mayors, and in fi fty-eight of the seventy-nine years for which we have data in the seventeenth century, one of the commissioners was simultaneously the water judge (or

The pipeline commissioners ' work centered on evaluating petitions for private water connections through site visits and engineer ' s reports, determining how much water should be awarded and from which pipeline, and setting the price and conditions of each license or concession. Commissioners also attempted to ensure that no one took more water than their title allowed and coordinated the construction and maintenance of the pipe network in general. In this case some specialized knowledge was developed; for example, Councilman Ordo ~ no de Samudio was selected thirty times as pipeline commissioner between 1650 and 1683 and was considered an expert on the topic.

The engineer ( alarife ) in charge of the pipelines was another important person and one who gained in fl uence over the course of the seventeenth century. In 1609 the Cabildo determined that the municipal pipelines and public fountains should be maintained by a specialist ( LCL 14.XII.1609), and from 1625 the post was always held by one of the of fi cial city engineers (see also San Crist  obal 1993). 10 In reality, only three engineers managed the pipelines for the majority of the century: Clemente de Mansilla (1625 -1634), Juan de Mansilla (1635 -1661), and Pedro Fern  andez de Vald  es (1661 -1706). 11 The inheritance and concentration of knowledge about the urban drinking water system in these men was extraordinary, and their opinions were commonly heard (and heeded) during Cabildo meetings. Finally, it is necessary to mention that the engineers worked with African slaves, for whom little documentary evidence exists. In only one Cabildo meeting from the period in question was one of these men mentioned by name: Pedro Angola, who was Juan de Mansilla ' s slave ( LCL .18.IV.1654). 12 Apparently this was a position requiring skill, but also entailing damp and dif fi cult conditions.

(Bromley and Barbagelata 1945, 41; Raimondi [1824] 2009, 257 -58). The location of both springs, topographically above the city by approximately 100 m, provided the necessary inclination to canalize the water toward the main water tank located in the urban core, called the Caridad water tank ( Caja de Agua de la Caridad ) for its location next to the Caridad Hospital ( Hospital de la Caridad ). Water was distributed from this central storage point into the public and private pipelines. From the outset, this infrastructure contributed to inequality in water access. The pipeline network ' s center of gravity was the Caridad water tank in the northeast section of the city center. Those who lived above this key point in the network, including the farmers in the rural area around the springs, had to cede their rights to the zones lower in the fl ow of water. 13

The momentous inauguration of the fi rst public fountain in Lima ' s Plaza Mayor in 1578 was part of a larger municipal project to bring piped drinking water to city residents. 14 This project, in planning since 1552, culminated in the three main municipal pipelines that were constructed by 1613 (Bromley and Barbagelata 1945; see also LCL 26.XI.1610). The pipes were ceramic, made by city potters, and buried below city streets ( LCL 14.IX.1660; see also San Crist  obal 2005, 185 -86). The water for all three fl owed from the Caridad water tank (routes and construction dates summarized in Table 1 and illustrated in Figure 3). The Cabildo received petitions for private connections of running water from these three main municipal pipelines, to be installed in homes, monasteries and convents, and institutions (like hospitals). These connections were for speci fi c amounts of water withdrawn from the main pipelines, called pajas or reales , which were units of measurement based on the fl ow of water through pipes of controlled circumference (Table 2). The majority of petitions were submitted during the twenty-year period in which the three pipelines were being constructed (summarized in Table 3).

A total of sixty-three petitions for drinking water connections were recorded in the LCL from 1578 to 1700 for Municipal Pipelines 1 to 3, and a total of eighty connections could be identi fi ed for these three pipelines using additional data from Bromley and Barbagelata (1945). 15 Information about these petitions and the eventual concession of titles is listed in Tables 4 through 6, including biographical and institutional information about the petitioners and the locations of these concessions are mapped in Figures 3 and 4. Several signi fi cant patterns can be observed. Spatially, below the Caridad water tank the three original municipal pipelines were distributed fairly evenly over the central section of Lima ' s original thirteen-bynine city block grid, which would have been the main area populated when the original water system plans were initiated in the 1550s. As visible on the map of the pipeline system in 1613 (Figure 3), however, there is a clear concentration of concessions in the area just below (west and northwest of) the Caridad water tank, with distribution tapering off the farther outward one travels below this tank (especially to the southwest). The map of concessions along the municipal pipelines after 1613 demonstrates a similar geographic concentration, albeit with more connections, especially to the immediate southwest of the Caridad. The branching of Municipal Pipeline 3 speaks to the need to serve several key points, including religious institutions (e.g., the Jesuit Novitiate College and the Encarnacion Monastery, map references n and c, respectively), and residences of important people not included along prior municipal pipeline routes (e.g., Councilmen don Martin de Ampuero and don Diego de la Presa, map references i and j).

Straightforward social patterns are also apparent. Of the eighty concessions, seven were for public fountains, four were for government institutions (Cabildo and Viceregal), twenty were for religious or charitable institutions (including schools), and forty-nine were for private individuals. families. The vast majority of the remaining private individuals were of high status, including royal and viceregal of fi cials, church of fi cials, university rectors, and more. Women seem to be mentioned on water petitions only when they were high-status individuals themselves; for example, if they were daughters, mothers, or widows of conquistadores, Cabildo members, or high-ranking royal or viceregal of fi cials. Among the religious and charitable institutions, convents and monasteries received the most water: 82 percent of total water conceded (see Bell [forthcoming] for this calculation), with the Jesuits controlling the largest water concessions of all -nearly nine reales of water -among their various properties. 16

Taken together, the sociospatial patterns of the water concessions paint a picture of the distribution of power in the city. The Cabildo designed and implemented the original municipal water system and, not surprisingly, it served many of the homes of the mayors and councilmen. Indeed, many of these connections were awarded for free, in recognition of service to the pipeline projects and other public works. Public fountains, ostentatiously part of the original plans, experienced delays in construction and many interruptions in service. For example, in 1596 the San Sebastian fountain was completed but no water was fl owing ( LCL 19.IV.1596), in 1612 the drainage of the San Marcelo fountain failed, causing problems, and in 1621 the public fountains were found to be in a general state of disrepair ( LCL 5.VII.1621). When an important individual ' s house was located outside of the basic layout of the three pipelines, this layout was adjusted, as demonstrated by the repeated branching of Pipeline 3 described earlier. Overall we fi nd that powerful people were living in close proximity to one another and that the municipal pipelines passed by many of their houses. Additional water connections were easier to install near previous connections. For example, Captain Juan Fernandez de Heredia ' s connection on Municipal Pipeline 3 (map reference i) was facilitated by the prior existence of a water storage tank at the corner of the Carvajal Statue ( Marmol de Carvajal ) that served both a public fountain and don Diego de la Presa ' s connection (map references k and i). Religious institutions also in fl uenced pipeline routes: The powerful Dominican, Franciscan, and Jesuit orders, among others, were all served by the original municipal pipelines. These features all contributed to the concentration of water connections in certain sectors of the city; power, wealth, status, and water connections went hand in hand.

Nearly no concessions were given to merchants or professionals (who were not royal of fi cials) and none at all to artisans, laborers, or other lower ranking members of society. The Indian neighborhood -Santiago del Cercado -was not served at all by the three original municipal pipelines and was only provided with one public fountain. 17 This neighborhood, reported to be home to 800 Indians and eighty African slaves in 1629 (Bromley and Barbagelata 1945, 59), provides a key illustration of the sociospatial patterns of access described earlier: The Cercado was actually located right along the water main leading from the springs to the Caridad water tank, very near to the main area with springs. Because it was located ' above ' the Caridad, however, it had only limited access to the city ' s drinking water (Ram  on 2011). The African population is only referenced with regard to the pipelines in terms of slave labor toward their construction and maintenance and as water sellers. These lower status populations used the public fountains, purchased water from sellers who made deliveries via mule cargo, or collected water from the river, even though from 1552 river water was considered too polluted for most domestic uses (Cogorno 2011).

This list was compiled using Bromley and Barbagelata's (1945) reconstruction of Lima's water system in 1613 and from the petitions recorded in the Libros de Cabildos de Lima . The connections listed as pre-1613 by Bromley and Barbagelata are not included in Tables 1 or 3. Of the twenty-four connections, two were for public fountains, five for religious or charitable institutions, including a hospital, and the remaining seventeen were for private individuals. Of these individuals, thirteen were for mayors or city councilmen or families of Cabildo members. This includes two water judges and eight pipeline commissioners. The other private individuals were also high ranking, including two member judges of the Royal Court (one of whom was interim governor between Viceroys), a viceregal secretary, and a rector of San Marcos University (also Canon of the Cathedral). Again, the only woman mentioned seems to be in relation to her family members, especially her son, who was the sitting mayor. Of special note here is the branched form of the pipeline, which seems to be designed to include important individuals not served by the first two pipelines (e.g., Martin de Ampuero, j). Biographical information comes from the Libros de Cabildos de Lima , Bromley (2005), Bromley and Barbagelata (1945), and Lohmann Villena (1983a, 1983b, 1983c, 1993).

of private pipelines. Private pipelines were designed to serve only their fi nal points, and typically petitions could not be submitted to install additional connections to take water from along their courses (although there were several exceptions). The person or group who requested a private pipeline paid for its construction. These pipes generally served religious orders or neighborhoods where the municipal pipelines did not reach, which were called far neighborhoods ( LCL 28. XI.1651; San Crist  obal 2005). The Cabildo supervised the construction of at least twenty-one private pipelines between 1600 and 1700. Information about these pipelines is presented in Table 7 and they are mapped in Figure 4.

Examination of the petitions for private pipelines demonstrates that from the perspective of potable water provision, the city below the Caridad water tank was divided into two zones: that of ' above ' and that of ' below. ' The zone below suffered from continuous water shortages. This zone, identi fi ed as ' below the principal plaza ' and ' the bottom half of the city ' ( LCL 20.III.1629), included the far neighborhoods ( LCL 28. XI.1651) like La Merced, La Encarnaci  on, San Sebastian, San Marcelo, and Guadalupe (see also LCL 9. III.1620, 29.X.1671). These neighborhoods all had public fountains that experienced water shortages. The word below references actual topographic position but also location at the end of the pipelines; in other words, the lowest point in the water fl ow, to the northwest and southwest of the Plaza Mayor. These zones lacked water because those located above (along the pipeline) used the water, often taking water in excess of what their titles allowed and consequently letting little water fl ow to the end of the pipe ( LCL 9. III.1606, 11.VIII.1621, 20.III.1629). Other ' poor ' zones were left totally outside of the network; their residents had to buy water from water sellers or collect it themselves from distant public fountains or the river ( LCL 11.VII.1621, 20.III.1629). 18

The construction of private pipelines was an imperfect solution to the problem of supplying the general population with drinking water. For example, each monastery or convent that constructed a private pipeline was also required to install a public fountain for general use. In theory, this would contribute to a more egalitarian distribution of water. In practice, though, the convents did not comply with this obligation. In 1670, for instance, the Cabildo found that none of the public fountains were running as they should, and some were not even built ( LCL 3.IX.1670; see also 25. II.1671, 12.V.1671). These fountains are mapped in Figure 4, but this is an important case where installation of infrastructure did not necessarily equate to proper functioning of infrastructure. Therefore, in the second half of the century, the Cabildo decided that it was also necessary to expand the municipal pipeline network. It built two new municipal pipelines. The fi rst was built for a new fountain in the Plaza Mayor and was fi nished in 1650. The second was constructed to serve the San Marcelo neighborhood. Plans for this were initiated in 1668, although the pipeline was still not completed or functioning properly in 1692, mainly due to lack of funding ( LCL 20.IV.1668, 20.VII.1668, 30.VII.1668, 16.1.1669, 12.II.1669, 16.IX.1692). Details about these pipelines are also included in Table 7 and Figure 4.

In general, the Cabildo was not able to provide adequate drinking water to all of the residents of the city. Some problems were due to the slow construction of the municipal pipelines, like that of San Marcelo, which took nearly thirty years to complete. Others were due to the dif fi culty of controlling illegal water connections ( LCL 21.I.1605, 7.I.1611, 2.I.1636), which was compounded by the fact that the Cabildo lacked a registry -either a list or a map -that detailed the legal connections. The Cabildo had sought to create such a map of the pipelines and connections at several times throughout the seventeenth century without success (Bell 2012). In 1665 it ordered engineer Clemente de Mansilla to make a pipeline map, but he died before completing this work. In 1691 Pedro Fern  andez de Vald  es was similarly reprimanded for failing to submit his Cabildo-ordered map. As far as is known, the fi rst map of the pipeline network was made in 1787, of which only a copy from 1862 remains (Ram  on 2010). It is unclear why this project was so dif fi cult to complete, although it might relate to the way knowledge of the pipelines was stored: as practical working knowledge held by the engineers and their slaves. This was observed in Cabildo records from 1790, which described the ' depositing ' of knowledge of the water system in an elderly engineer and his still living slave (Ram  on 2011, 88).

From a broader perspective, it is easy to note social distinctions in the patterns of drinking water access that were both purposefully and inadvertently in fl uenced by the Cabildo ' s governance strategies. Even though the Cabildo (and some religious orders) employed a discourse supporting the necessity of providing water to all, and especially to poor neighborhoods, in reality it was the most powerful residents and the monasteries and convents that enjoyed running water. These areas were strategically located just below the Caridad water tank in the city center or, perhaps better said, the Caridad water tank had been strategically located near this neighborhood. No titles were awarded to either African or Indian individuals, and the Indian neighborhood (Santiago del Cercado) had only one public fountain, located ' above ' the Caridad water tank and thus in a relatively low-power location in the network. Moreover, the spatial distribution of the pipelines was one of the features that produced the differences between a rich neighborhood and a poor one. The division of water not only re fl ected social inequalities but also created and reinforced divisions between groups and zones. sections.Discussion and Conclusions:
Lima ' s hydraulic space was oriented by the east -west fl ow of the Rímac River and the location of the springs to the northeast and topographically above the city. The installation of its components, though, especially the drinking water pipeline, followed the desires, objectives, and values of Lima ' s human residents more than it did natural features. The LCL demonstrates that effective governance of Lima ' s hydraulic space was dif fi cult. The Cabildo repeatedly failed to achieve its primary objective of securing a clean and copious fl ow of drinking water in the municipal pipeline network. Problems with water supply were nearly always attributed to infrastructural and management problems, rather than ' natural ' issues like aquifer depletion or spring location. Although biophysical aspects of water availability and conduction were signi fi cant to drinking water supply, especially the seasonality of aquifer levels and the slope needed for gravity-based fl ow, drinking water access was most closely linked to the installation of infrastructure and to the spatial proximity down- fl ow from the Caridad water tank. The unequal distribution of drinking water infrastructure re fl ected colonial social divisions but also helped to create and widen gaps between groups based on access to water. Although the Cabildo made grand statements about the importance of providing water to all city residents, only the most powerful members of colonial society had running water in their homes.

This interpretation of Lima ' s municipal water system was only possible through interrogation of the Cabildo archives from a political ecology perspective. Most signi fi cantly, this perspective asks direct questions about the linked biophysical, material, social, political, and economic in fl uences on patterns of water access of individuals, groups, and regions. Political ecological analysis of contemporary urban drinking water systems shows strong inequality in access, and historical cases like that of Lima suggest that such patterns are not new (although the speci fi c relationships between past inequality and current conditions need to be clearly demonstrated and not assumed). Bakker ' s (2003) archipelago metaphor is also helpful for historical water analysis because it suggests that multiple, overlapping strategies are commonly used in urban drinking water delivery, including public and private supply systems, and that spatial coverage of water infrastructure is typically partial and uneven. This level of nuance is not always considered in historical situations, even though it was likely present. Finally, political ecological work has shown how uneven water access also leads to further social differentiation and thus shapes and in fl uences power relations, instead of merely re fl ecting or responding to them (Swyngedouw 1999; Gandy 2004; Loftus 2009). This can also be observed at a broader level, in terms of urban -rural relations, and usually results in signi fi cant urban bias. In colonial Lima, the governance strategies applied in the management of potable water resources not only led to the development of the urban space and the speci fi c sociospatial patterns of access to water within the city but also contributed to differentiation between urban and rural spaces. A signi fi cant urban bias was observed, with the city ' s hydraulic reach or water footprint extending beyond the urban zone into surrounding farmland. Although these questions and approaches might seem basic to political ecology, they have not frequently been applied to the study of early colonial natural resource access and never before to water in colonial Peru.

The relationship between the history of water systems and the history of cities also warrants further consideration (Swyngedouw, Kaika, and Castro 2002; Gandy 2003, 2004; Swyngedouw 2004). As Bakker (2003, 332) wrote, ' The water network is, in part, an artefact of urbanization. ' Given the great investment in construction and the dif fi culty of changing a pipeline network already built, water systems typically re fl ect water needs at one point in time and generally only cover a portion of a city, usually the most af fl uent part. Although such observations are generally made for contemporary urban situations, they are also true for colonial Lima and likely for other colonial Spanish cities in the Americas, which were established early in the colonial period and incorporated complicated and sophisticated water systems from the start. There are interesting remnants and traces of these colonial water systems in modern ones. For example, even though the city of Lima now draws drinking water from distant Andean lakes, the location of the Atarjea spring used from 1578 is still the location of Lima ' s central reservoir and water treatment plant (SEDAPAL 2013). This speaks to an enduring orientation of Lima ' s hydraulic space, even amidst modernization, development, and great change. With further historical analysis, it might be possible to reconstruct additional legacies of the colonial system with greater signi fi cance to modern patterns of water access.

There are clear advantages of applying a political ecology approach to historical water systems, but moving backward in time has methodological implications for the types of questions that can be asked and the types of data that might be available. Closer attention to material traces left on the landscape, including both biophysical and sociocultural features, is necessary, and a useful guide can be found in the hydraulic archaeology approach. In this article, I used written descriptions to explain the design and construction as well as the day-to-day management of infrastructure. In other cases, archaeological analysis of infrastructure might provide a useful complement, as historical documents have signi fi cant limitations for a political ecological analysis. With the LCL we have only the fi nalized or ' clean ' version of the Cabildo meeting agendas, and rarely hear dissent among Cabildo members, let alone direct contributions from lesser heard voices, like Indians or African slaves. The LCL and other similar sources do, however, provide key insights into ' how Europeans conceptualized ' their ' colonial landscapes and how those imaginations produced material consequences for colonized people, environments and wildlife ' (Offen 2004, 29). In the case of Lima ' s water, we have a clear representation of the administrative, legal, engineering, and measurement concepts developed and applied to water. Understanding these colonial practices and conceptualizations, as well as their consequences and legacies for postcolonial resource management and environmental science, is a principal goal of historical political ecology (Offen 2004; D. K. Davis 2009). Although here I have delved only brie fl y into one history of water access, I have endeavored to show the utility of the historical political ecology perspective for explaining sociospatial patterns of natural resource access in the past. &

The Cabildo claimed authority in Lima and its hinterland over issues such as urban planning and land grants; trade and business; food production, supply, and distribution; water rights and

- infrastructure; management of natural resources (e.g., fi rewood, pasture); and social support (e.g., assistance for the poor, education, annual fi estas). The Cabildo governed through nomination of commissioners and inspectors from among the mayors and city councilmen, as well as through appointment of outside specialists like engineers, architects, police of fi cials, surveyors, measurement inspectors, and secretaries.

sections.Introduction:
Historical political ecology provides a powerful framework for understanding nature -society relations in the past. This approach is applied to municipal drinking water governance in early colonial Lima, Peru, with a focus on how power dynamics in fl uenced sociospatial patterns of water access and control. Sixteenth- and seventeenth-century archival sources are analyzed for material aspects of Lima ' s drinking water pipeline network and for the management strategies employed by the municipal government. Access to water is demonstrated to have shaped, reinforced, and re fl ected colonial social divisions and to have been linked to the spatial development of the city, including urban -rural relations. Key Words: colonialism, historical political ecology, Peru, water governance, water infrastructure.

The public utility in the fair distribution of waters . . . has excited in all times continuing controversies.

H istorical perspectives have long been considered integral to political ecology (Zimmerer and Bassett 2003; Peet and Watts 2004; Robbins 2004), although how and to what end historical content and analysis could be incorporated into this research approach has not been fully resolved and remains an ambiguous pursuit (Offen 2004). In general, the historical political ecology approach calls for the application of historical perspectives within a broadly de fi ned political ecology point of view and has been de fi ned as ' a fi eld-informed interpretation of society -nature relations in the past ' (Offen 2004, 21). This includes using historical material to contextualize current environmental con fl icts, especially the continuing in fl uences of European expansion and colonialism, often with the explicit motivation of improving social justice or environmental conservation in the present (Brannstrom 2004; Offen 2004; D. K. Davis 2009). Historical political ecology might also include asking questions about environmental change or natural resource use in historical periods, either recent (e.g., Swyngedouw 1999; Biehler 2009; Carey 2010; Lane 2011; Carey, French, and O ' Brien 2012) or more distant (e.g., Watts 1983; Sluyter 1999; Zimmerer 2000; Carney 2001; M. Davis 2004; End fi eld and Fern  andez Tejedo 2006; D. K. Davis 2007; End fi eld 2008). Although this latter purpose -using a political ecological analysis to closely examine nature -society relations in the past and not just provide context for current-day issues -is lesser used, it represents a powerful framework for historical research.
sections.Lima's Hydraulic Space and Its Governanc: In 1671, Lima ' s solicitor general called water ' the element most necessary after air ' ( LCL 29.X.1671), 6 and indeed it was the natural resource most frequently discussed by Lima ' s Cabildo. The provision of drinking water was considered one of the principal responsibilities of the Cabildo: ' the fi rst thing given attention in the foundation of all of the cities of the world [is] that this element, inexcusable for human life, is provided with cleanliness and security ' ( LCL 17.XI.1649). To this end, the Spanish located their capital city along the banks of the Rímac River, to provide residents with water for irrigation, drinking, sanitation, and industry. The Rímac dominates Lima ' s hydraulic space (Figure 1). Like all of Peru ' s coastal rivers, it fl ows westward, cutting down from the glacial lakes of the high Andes to the Paci fi c, descending from a height of over 5,500 m above sea level to its mouth near Lima ' s port El Callao over a distance of about 130 km. Its fl ow varies seasonally, increasing during the highland rainy season (October -April), when it often threatens to overrun its banks, and all but drying up during the dry months (May -September).
sections.Lima's Drinking Water Pipelines and the: The pipeline network began at the springs located on the outskirts of the city (Figure 2). In the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, Lima drank mainly from two springs located approximately 6 km from the Plaza Mayor, called locally Atarjea and Sabana Figure 2 Connections of the two major springs Atarjea and Sabana with the municipal pipeline network and the important reservoirs and water tanks. The springs are located at an elevation of approximately 250 m above sea level and 100 m above the main plaza. Source: Bromley and Barbagelta (1945), 'Plan[o] Topogr  afico' (1787), GoogleMaps. (Color figure available online.)

records.title: Protecting a Broken Window: Vandalism and Security at Rural Rock Art Sites
records.abstract: The majority of the ancient rock art sites of the U.S. Southwest are located in rural locations that are difficult to monitor or police. These sites seem to exert a pull on humans, an attraction that not only provokes curiosity and wonder but also what can be classed as destructive responses or vandalism. Many crime control methods for reducing vandalism are based on traditional theories such as defensible space and broken window theory. In the case of rock art, however, these methods do not yield expected results and in some cases are even detrimental. Rural crime, including rural vandalism, as a whole is marginalized in criminology, which has been dominated by urban-focused approaches and theories. In the case of rock art, considering how security is approached and maintained ultimately leads to questions about human-object relationships with regards to crime and about object agency. By focusing on the policing challenges of one particular type of rural vandalism, we hope to contribute to the discussion of vandalism in rural spaces.

Archaeology Southwest, USA

The majority of the ancient rock art sites of the U.S. Southwest are located in rural locations that are difficult to monitor or police. These sites seem to exert a pull on humans, an attraction that not only provokes curiosity and wonder but also what can be classed as destructive responses or vandalism. Many crime control methods for reducing vandalism are based on traditional theories such as defensible space and broken window theory. In the case of rock art, however, these methods do not yield expected results and in some cases are even detrimental. Rural crime, including rural vandalism, as a whole is marginalized in criminology, which has been dominated by urban-focused approaches and theories. In the case of rock art, considering how security is approached and maintained ultimately leads to questions about human -object relationships with regards to crime and about object agency. By focusing on the policing challenges of one particular type of rural vandalism, we hope to contribute to the discussion of vandalism in rural spaces. Key Words: broken windows theory, graffiti, heritage crime, rock art, rural crime, vandalism.

R ock art sites of the U.S. Southwest are often located in very rural locations that are on or beyond the periphery of contemporary human activity. Rock art, images carved, painted, or scratched onto stone surfaces, is a physical testament to more than 10,000 years of history. It retains an important place within contemporary Indigenous religion and a salience that transcends cultures. Distant and inaccessible, these locations represent the human geographies of the past, when the climate was different or when these specific, if challenging, locations had active social or cultural significance. The remoteness of rock art sites means that many, perhaps the majority, are ' unknown ' and have not been documented. In Utah, for example, it is reasonable to estimate that there are between 80,000 and 100,000 rock art sites in the state, but only between 18,000 and 20,000 are ' known. ' 1 The rest exist within the landscape, waiting to be interacted with.

agencies at local, state, and federal levels, as does the protection of rock art from criminal damage.

Far from being inactive entities, rock art sites seem to exert a pull on humans, an attraction that not only inspires curiosity and wonder but also provokes what can be classed as destructive responses. Despite their rural or remote locations, people are drawn to rock art sites, and the sites experience numerous forms of crime. Although often broadly classified as vandalism, these activities form a varied corpus of illicit human -object interactions. These include the following:

-  Theft of rock art from its original location, either for personal use and display at a person ' s home or for sale within the market for illicit cultural objects.

The religious, cultural, historical, and artistic significance of rock art has inspired over a century of policy aimed at its conservation. Although the mosaic of cultural heritage protection across the ' checkerboard ' of rural land owned or overseen by federal, state, and private entities falls beyond the scope of this short article, the responsibility for the preservation of rural rock art falls to a variety of

-  Petty vandalism of rock art sites, with contemporary names, dates, and other tags added, either scratched into the rock or added via paint or marker.

-  Shooting rock art sites with guns ( ' target practice ' ).
