People need a land study because a lot of times they haven ' t had the oral historian in the family who has passed it on like my grandmother passed it on to me. So, they need to know where this can be found; it needs to be gathered and collected. (Interview, June 11, 2021)

These data can be surprisingly challenging to access and analyze in underfunded rural counties. Because tax maps contain spatial representations of ownership and are increasingly available as GIS files, we use property valuation assessment (PVA) records for quantitative and spatial analysis of ownership. PVA offices are charged with assessing the value of private property and sending quarterly tax bills based on locally established formulas. They maintain physical tax books that contain key details about properties, including parcel size, land use, building structures, and market values. Most counties also have digital PVA records in the form of spreadsheets, which can be accessed through open records requests in most cases. These spreadsheets are often not accompanied by metadata, however, and typically require significant effort to parse. They also do not include unique taxpayer identifiers, so linking multiple property holdings to a single entity can be challenging, especially considering that many corporations also operate under multiple names, subsidiaries, or both. Therefore, acquiring data and preparing them for analysis is a cumbersome and technical task. Because PVA records list taxpayers, rather than the owner on the deed, these records can only be considered a proxy for ownership, but in most cases, it is reasonable to assume that the taxpayer is also the owner (see also Randle, Barlow, and Gunnoe 2015; Macaulay and Butsic 2017).

A number of issues complicate the use of PVA records for the study of land ownership. The quality and availability of these records is highly variable: There is no standardization between counties or even within counties -as record administrators change, so, too, do the standards and practices of record keeping. In the example of Mingo County mentioned earlier, we found that numerous parcels held by one of the largest landholders were recorded as being zero hectares in official deed records. Interviews with county officials revealed that parcel size was routinely recorded inaccurately to simplify accounting in connection with a tax incentive program for managed timberlands. Comparison of this landholder ' s parcels in other states and counties revealed a similar pattern of inaccurate parcel size and valuation numbers. Moreover, many counties and states do not have GIS or sophisticated databases. We have found partnerships between professional academic researchers and locally informed rural residents essential to gathering, interpreting, and translating land records into useful maps and statistics that can serve as a springboard for public discussions about land ownership and public revenues.

Shade typically requests and processes data using a combination of Microsoft Excel and QGIS, and where feasible, works with community-based stakeholders and courthouse officials to further ground truth the records and analysis. We review summary statistics about concentrated ownership and assessed values, including parcel maps when available, and look for discrepancies between records and peoples ' direct knowledge of corporate practices and property relations. In southern West Virginia and southwestern Virginia, maps and figures resulting from that process have been used as a basis for dialogue in a series of public forums about economic transition (for media coverage, see Justice 2019; Workman 2019; Counts 2020). Still, the political sensitivity of questions of land and taxation have led to reluctance among some team members to approach county courthouses. We found through inside relationships that, when nonresidents visit the courthouse to gather this information and ask for clarity about records, workers are often grilled by their supervisors about researchers ' intentions after we leave (Interview, Mingo County, West Virginia, December 14, 2018).

Political stonewalling is further compounded by underfunding of counties, a direct consequence of undertaxation of land in extraction zones. Previous studies in the Appalachian region found that the share of local tax burden is borne disproportionately by smallholders compared to corporate entities who hold the majority of land in coalfield counties (ALOT 1983; Spence et al. 2013). Our research has identified an antagonism between state revenue offices that seek to consolidate land records and create public GIS portals and local county offices that are resistant to making property valuation data easily accessible. There are myriad possible reasons, but one issue is that counties are incentivized to limit records access, as they can sell data to third-party vendors as one strategy to make up for shortfalls in local revenues (Horn 2021). Some counties have also resisted sharing data for public research purposes such as our study, despite being covered by open records laws, and have sought to charge exorbitant fees to comply with data requests, ranging from $5,000 to $20,000 per county, per tax year. This problem has significantly stalled our work in Kentucky, leading to further inequalities in data access in which resident stakeholders are unable to access records that are hoarded by private data vendors who sell the data to speculators and developers. This also creates an ethical conundrum for our work: We want to maintain positive relationships with county officials and avoid undermining their interests, but also make data publicly accessible for social and environmental justice purposes, which could likewise inadvertently subsidize the cost of business for land speculators (Otts 2019).
sections.GIS and Spatial Statistics:
On the other end of the spectrum, states such as North Carolina and Tennessee have implemented robust, centralized state GIS systems. The consistency and quality of data in North Carolina has facilitated more rapid and complex statistical analyses. Shade worked with a graduate student at Appalachian State University to gather PVA data from twenty-nine western North Carolina counties, code for absentee ownership based on zip code, and calculate a Gini coefficient and Lorenz curve to estimate ownership inequality in each county. The student also completed econometric modeling of the relationship between high rates of concentrated absentee ownership and several socioeconomic variables, including county poverty rate, median household income, infrastructure investment, level of education, tax revenues, and mortality and disease rates (Meadows 2018). Building on Shade ' s (2017) prior work and the collective knowledge of land study researchers in both academic and grassroots venues, we also crafted an interview guide to gather qualitative data from local tax assessors. These interviews provide a richer context through which to interpret quantitative findings, and are also important for documenting the qualitative dimensions of property as a product of mundane human activities, such as record-keeping practices, which are integral to both the emergence and maintenance of systems of landed property (Rose 1985; Bhandar 2016).

We see many possibilities for using GIS and spatial statistics in our work, and are in the process of organizing more than 20 million PVA records covering four states into an interactive digital mapping system. As interactive maps have become more popular through mainstream media sources, we aim to deliver on an expectation of comprehensive data accessible through a well-designed interface. These products require significant skills beyond those possessed by most academic geographers, and as discussed earlier, can be challenging to create due to discrepancies in data quality and access. We anticipate building digital tools around narratives that can inspire further political engagement and action in local and state venues, but that will always be accompanied by additional community-based and qualitative efforts.

Van Sant ' s work in the Shenandoah Valley also combines GIS and qualitative methods, but has a slightly different research trajectory. The COVID19 pandemic forced them to change their plan to develop a wide network of community collaborators before beginning mapping of land ownership in the Shenandoah Valley. Instead, with the help of Shade and undergraduate research assistants, they initiated the quantitative phase of research virtually during the COVID lockdown. Using similar methods, they mapped rates of absentee ownership and degree of ownership concentration in the ten-county region. As public health restrictions have eased, they have developed research partners and are beginning qualitative research using the maps as prompts for interviews and focus groups. This kind of ' map elicitation ' method has multiple benefits: First, as mentioned earlier, it can help improve the mapping through a process of ground truthing; second, it provides an intimate forum for the spread of scholarship to community members; and third, the response of research participants to the maps and interview questions provides important qualitative data about the ways that community members interpret and experience land ownership change. Given the many challenges researchers face when attempting participatory land ownership research, we highlight this approach as a variation that nevertheless integrates qualitative methods and GIS.

Beyond the authors ' projects, GIS and spatial statistics about land ownership can inform a multitude of scholarly and public advocacy endeavors. For example, Khadka et al. (2021) recently examined how changes in land ownership structure correlated to changes in land use and land cover over sixteen years in three Kentucky counties. Similarly, extension faculty at the University of California created the CalLands portal to track land ownership and land-cover statistics (Macaulay and Butsic 2017).

As early as 2005, Fraser, Gayawali, and Schellas (2005) examined how rates of African American land ownership in the Black Belt correlate with forestry practices and indicators of socioeconomic well-being. Linking the increasingly powerful technologies offered through GIS packages with land ownership research can inform cutting-edge environmental and social policy research, bridge quantitative and qualitative subdisciplines in human -environment research, and provide accessible storytelling tools in public scholarship initiatives like the Appalachian Land Study.
sections.Conclusion: We have argued that critical engagement with land records and participatory methods that prioritize the insights of rural people in resource-based economies can both document and respond to the dynamics of U.S. land ownership. Although we have focused on Appalachia, the methods are more broadly applicable. A firm grasp on who owns the land can inform a range of economic, environmental, and cultural geographic inquiries. From rapidly changing land and commodity markets to mundane legal transactions such as mergers and acquisitions, land ownership is always in flux and therefore inherently challenging to document. We attempt to deal with this complexity by approaching records as material artifacts, while using available data to elicit public engagement about entrenched inequalities in rural environments. In this moment of overlapping political, economic, and ecological crises, we are hopeful that more land ownership research will engage diverse publics with important questions about who can access, make decisions about, and benefit from land. /H17039

sections.Introduction:
Who owns the land? It seems a simple enough question. It is, however, one which is alarmingly difficult to answer.

I n early 2021 a surprising story in the business press jumped to more popular media: Bill and Melinda Gates were now the largest private farmland owners in the United States. The former was lauded as a ' sustainable agriculture champion ' with a long-standing interest in climate change and dubbed ' Farmer Bill ' (Villarreal 2021; O ' Keefe 2021). Others wanted to know more. Exactly how much farmland do the Gateses own? Do they own more land that is not in agricultural production? Where are these landholdings? As Massey (1980) highlighted in the epigraph, these kinds of questions are ' alarmingly difficult to answer ' (263). One report estimates that the Gateses own 108,845 hectares (268,984 acres) in the United States stretching across nineteen states, 90 percent of which are agricultural land (O ' Keefe 2021). These numbers are only estimates, though. There is no publicly accessible centralized data source about land ownership in the United States. Even with scores of journalists and researchers working to uncover the details of the Gateses ' landholdings, it is difficult to know the answers with much certainty, let alone analyze broader trends such as gendered, racialized, and corporate patterns of land ownership and use.

Drawing from our experiences in coal, oil, and gas affected areas of Central Appalachia and in the more agriculture-oriented Shenandoah Valley of Virginia, we discuss some of the main challenges of rural land ownership research. Broadly, these challenges include administrative barriers to accessing and using records, political gatekeeping, and the proliferation of legal instruments that govern rights to land. As we outline these challenges, we discuss participatory approaches to studying land ownership that can help overcome these barriers and lead to meaningful application of land ownership data to real-world problems.
sections.Background: The Appalachian Land Study: From early land grabs by absentee speculators to later waves of timber production and energy extraction, scholars of Appalachia have long addressed how regional land tenure dynamics intersect with resource extraction economies (Gaventa 1982; Salstrom 1994; Banks 1995; Billings and Blee 2000). As part of a larger story of U.S. enclosure, colonization, and industrialization, these scholars have documented eighteenthand nineteenth-century land grabs by East Coast speculators that established contemporary land ownership paradigms in Appalachia and entrenched the domination of extractive industries within legal and bureaucratic regimes for governing land and minerals (Rasmussen 1994; Dunaway 1995; Stoll 2017).
sections.Designing a Regional Land Study: Methods: Following the model of its predecessor, the Appalachian Land Study employs participatory methods. Participatory action research facilitates participation, action, and reflection by those most affected by the research and its themes (Fals-Borda 1987). The Appalachian Land Study draws on the transformative potential of people ' s connection to land and place, which opens pathways for political dialogue in areas where civic space has been severely undermined by two centuries of corporate domination. Although a comprehensive account of the twoyear participatory planning process is not feasible in the space of this article, we want to highlight how collaborative study design can ground the objectives and methods of land ownership research in people ' s lived experiences -a methodological advantage that also requires significantly more time and resources to implement.

records.title: An Indicator Framework for Resilient Agroecosystems in Ontario, Canada
records.abstract: Southeastern Ontario presents a unique agricultural landscape in which both alternative and conventional farms operate. Each category of farm experiences a wide range of environmental and socioeconomic shocks and stresses that threaten each farm's longevity, raising questions about what constitutes resilient agriculture. Yet in Ontario there presently exists no unifying framework for building agricultural resilience. In response, this project mobilizes an analytical framework based on resilience indicators to create a qualitative method for assessing farm sustainability. Implementing this framework in the study area of Inverary, South Frontenac, semistructured interviews based on resilience indicators were conducted with both alternative and conventional farmers. The interviews enabled us to identify primary issues experienced at the farm level and account for the ways that their operations are structured to mitigate risks and achieve valued outcomes. Our research found that diverse farmers are facing overlapping threats but are prioritizing different responses to those threats by relying on distinct indicators of resilience. Key insights after using the indicator framework are summarized to create a deeper understanding of agricultural resilience in the province.

sections.An Indicator Framework for Resilient Agr:
Bryan Collins

<!-- image -->

SUNY Oneonta, USA

Southeastern Ontario presents a unique agricultural landscape in which both alternative and conventional farms operate. Each category of farm experiences a wide range of environmental and socioeconomic shocks and stresses that threaten each farm ' s longevity, raising questions about what constitutes resilient agriculture. Yet in Ontario there presently exists no unifying framework for building agricultural resilience. In response, this project mobilizes an analytical framework based on resilience indicators to create a qualitative method for assessing farm sustainability. Implementing this framework in the study area of Inverary, South Frontenac, semistructured interviews based on resilience indicators were conducted with both alternative and conventional farmers. The interviews enabled us to identify primary issues experienced at the farm level and account for the ways that their operations are structured to mitigate risks and achieve valued outcomes. Our research found that diverse farmers are facing overlapping threats but are prioritizing different responses to those threats by relying on distinct indicators of resilience. Key insights after using the indicator framework are summarized to create a deeper understanding of agricultural resilience in the province. Key Words: policy, qualitative research, resilience, rural studies, sustainable agriculture.

R esilience terminology has crept into governmental platforms within Canada, although it is often not clearly defined. The Pan-Canadian Framework on clean growth and climate change includes a broad section on adaptation and resilience, referring often to the agricultural industry. Despite being mentioned frequently in the report, resilience is never discussed, other than how embracing it will help communities move forward. Core concepts in the report include incorporating scientific information with traditional knowledge, investing in resilient infrastructure, and focusing on vulnerable regions of the country (Government of Canada 2018). At the provincial level, the Ontario Ministry of Agriculture, Food, and Rural Affairs (OMAFRA) broadcasts little in the way of resilient thinking in their sustainable farming information guides. Infrequent mentions of the term use it as a loose adjective to depict a broadly defined goal, such as achieving ' resilient agriculture. ' The ministry is much more oriented toward economic development, highlighted by the its mandate to promote ' a more competitive and productive agri-food and agriproduct sector ' (OMAFRA 2013).

However useful, generally there is no uniformity on these issues between the different levels of government in Canada. Furthermore, there is a clear gap between debates on resilience in the academic world compared to the governmental policy world. Other stakeholders in the space of agriculture include farmers, those in private industry that sell to farmers, and those in other agricultural organizations such as the Ecological Farmers Association of Ontario (EFAO) or the National Farmers Union (NFU). A framework that brings in resilience and examines farms through the lens of a coupled socialecological system, by combining biophysical, political, and socioeconomic factors, will improve on the ways in which we think about resilience compared to previous efforts made by organizations throughout Ontario. Therefore, the objective of this research is to introduce an analytical framework for assessing agroecosystem resilience in in rural Ontario, Canada.

<!-- image -->

The view of resilience presented here stems from the definition set forth by Folke et al. (2010), defining resilience as ' The capacity of a system to absorb disturbance and reorganize while undergoing change so as to still retain essentially the same function, structure, and feedbacks, and therefore identity, that is, the capacity to change in order to maintain the same identity ' (20). This definition is apt for examining social-ecological farming systems in Ontario given the diversity of farming identities in the province (Smith 2015) as well as the multitude of disturbances present that are forcing farmers to change (Caldwell et al. 2022). Using this framework, this work assesses farmer approaches toward resilience aimed to ensure that their farms maintain their identity when confronted with disturbances. Farm identities are the collection of values, goals, and meanings that drive the production system forward (Letourneau and Davidson 2022). Studies that measure the social-ecological resilience of farms are currently quite rare, including in Ontario, but possess great potential for further informing agricultural policy (Darnhofer 2014; Jacobi et al. 2015). Although the results from the pilot assessment are useful for analyzing the resilience of the agricultural landscape in Ontario, the key contribution of this project is to demonstrate that this framework can be applied in other geographic contexts to better understand the resilience of agricultural systems at the farm level.

This research first examines a range of existing frameworks and indicators used to assess farm resilience in ways that incorporate socioeconomic, environmental, and cultural characteristics. It then synthesizes these frameworks to create an approach suited for agriculture in this project ' s study area, Inverary, Ontario, and apply this comparatively across the divide between alternative and conventional farms. Both farm types are in different positions to manage shocks and stresses -both socioeconomic and environmental -underscored by their relative size and specialization.

Farms classified as conventional are those that make use of chemical input-based systems, work with mechanization to achieve economies of scale, and are strongly embedded in agri-business markets, both as consumers of external inputs and for the distribution of outputs (Therond et al. 2017). Conversely, farms classified as alternative typically adopt strategies for prioritizing environmental health of the farm. One strategy is to substitute chemical inputs with more environmentally friendly inputs (i.e., organic inputs such as manure for fertilizer) in efforts to preserve ecosystem and human health. These farms often tend to pursue biodiversity-based farming systems, which seek to substitute external inputs with ecosystem services to maximize biodiversity and integration of resources on the farm. Alongside this alternate approach to farming systems, alternative farms often seek to target local markets for distribution.

More broadly, this research fits into a renewed focus on agricultural sustainability at both regional and global levels, in part owing to concerns about the contribution of agriculture to greenhouse gas emissions as well as its potential vulnerability to climate change impacts. The global food system contributes to between 21 percent and 37 percent of greenhouse gas emissions, drawing attention from policymakers at all scales of government (Mbow et al. 2019). The conflict between maximizing economic potential and minimizing environmental impact is perhaps the primary issue of the debate over agricultural sustainability (McNeill 2019). This conflict, amplified by decreased availability of water and harsher socioeconomic conditions, including reduced incomes and rising land prices, among farmers globally and in Canada, puts debates around agricultural sustainability at a defining moment (United Nations 2013; Caron et al. 2018; Lawley 2020). Although addressing these challenges is important, this study is more limited to analyzing the ability of distinct farms ' operations to withstand shocks and stresses.

sections.Methodology:
Situating This Framework Within Resilience Theory

We have operationalized the theoretical frameworks existing in the agroecosystem resilience literature to design a resilience framework that assessed individual farmers ' attempts to maintain their farm identity while facing shocks and stresses. Key existing frameworks include Meuwissen et al. (2019), which offers a methodology to assess both specified and general resilience at the farm level, and the SHARP þ protocol used by the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO; Hern  andez Lagana, Phillips, and Poisot 2022), which offers a step-bystep resilience assessment tool specifically designed for farmer response to climate change. Both assessments use indicators and an integrated holistic approach, using both qualitative and quantitative methods. Meuwissen et al. (2019) presented a comprehensive methodology using multivariate statistical analysis, econometrics and modeling, visualization, system dynamics, structured surveys and workshops, and qualitative interviews with multiple stakeholders. The SHARP þ protocol presents a structured questionnaire consisting of thirty-five modules, with each module containing -between five and ten questions. Although these assessments offer an excellent starting point for conducting a comprehensive view of resilience, they require substantial time, labor, and planning. In response, this research proposes an assessment framework that can be conducted by a small team where the primary data collection method is through semistructured interviews without relying on quantitative or statistical methods.

The assessment framework uses a four-step process. First, we characterize the farming system by asking the resilience ' of what?, ' a concept promoted by Carpenter et al. (2001) and Cutter (2016) to help eliminate vagueness and provide a stronger assessment of the diverse needs and resources of each farm. Second, we ask resilience ' to what?, ' where we inquire into what specific shocks and stresses each farmer faces. Third, we ask about resilience ' for what purpose?, ' to identify overarching goals of diverse stakeholders within the study area. Fourth, we introduce resilience indicators to reconceptualize ways that farmers are enhancing resilience on their farm. This process borrows from the process put forth by Meuwissen et al. (2019), keeping aspects that are more applicable to a qualitative smaller scale analysis.

Asking Resilience of What, Resilience to What, and Resilience for What Purpose?

We introduce a specified resilience framework as opposed to a general resilience framework. Specified resilience identifies resilience of specific aspects of a farming system to specific kinds of shocks, whereas general resilience identifies resilience of broader systems to all kinds of shocks (Folke et al. 2010). For example, specified resilience would address how a farm ' s financial matters are resilient to supply chain disruptions from the COVID-19 pandemic. Therefore, taking this approach requires understanding the baseline characteristics of each farming system -asking resilience of what -before understanding what each farm is building resilience toward -asking resilience to what. To learn about the resilience of what for each farming system, we have identified five key farm characteristics from the food system resilience literature (Table 1; Jacobi et al. 2018). These five categories provide a wideranging index of characteristics for each farm, where we can then ask specifically about resilience to those characteristics through semistructured interviews.

Determining resilience to what required asking about the specific shocks and stresses each farmer faced. Questions posed to farmers covered both socioeconomic and environmental threats. The interview questionnaire is found in the Appendix. Overall, twenty-two interviews with farmers took place. All the farms are located in the Inverary region of southeastern Ontario, which is a farming community that is composed of both alternative and conventional farms. Six conventional farms and five alternative farms participated, each agreeing for an initial interview to discuss the goals of the project and agreeing for a second longer interview by answering the questions in the questionnaire. Semistructured interviews provided freedom for farmers to speak toward issues they felt were most important to them (O ' Keeffe et al. 2016). Initial interviews often lasted -fifteen to twenty minutes and the questionnaire interviews typically lasted between thirty and sixty minutes, but this was flexible depending on the interviewee and how much time and information they wanted to share. Some interviews spanned more than ninety minutes to two hours.

Determining resilience for what purpose required interviewing nonfarmer stakeholders. Interview templates with nonfarmer stakeholders were designed to learn more about what the interviewee ' s organization does, to learn how they interact with farmers and influence the agricultural space in Ontario, and to provide information and anecdotes about what they see as the key issues for farmers in the past and moving forward -in essence, to materialize resilience for what purpose in the study area. Interviews with provincial representatives with OMAFRA were designed to reveal a crucial outlook on agroecosystem resilience in the province and to see if what is being highlighted by the government matches what is highlighted by farmers. Employees from OMAFRA were interviewed to assess their views. Likewise, organization representatives from the Ontario Federation of Agriculture (OFA), the EFAO, Frontenac County Manager of the Economic Development Office, and the manager of the region ' s largest agricultural machinery dealer were interviewed to provide valuable information on how their respective organizations play a role in shaping agricultural policies and practices in the province.
sections.Resilience Indicators:
After asking resilience of what, resilience to what, and resilience for what purpose, we sought to explore each farm ' s capabilities for boosting their specific resilience to the threats they face. Commonplace with agroecosystem resilience assessment is using indicators to demonstrate resilience-enhancing attributes (Biggs et al. 2012; Cabell and Oelofse 2012; Jacobi et al. 2018; Meuwissen et al. 2019; Tittonell 2020). Although a multitude of indicators are applied in diverse resilience assessments, we have selected six for our framework. These six indicators can be captured through semistructured interviews, whereas many others found throughout the literature cannot be easily measured through qualitative methods. We sought questions that allowed interviewees to provide open-ended responses for elaboration on the connections between characteristics and indicators. The relationship between question number, characteristic, and indicator is listed in the fourth column of Table 1. Not having quantitative indicators is a limitation that prevents this assessment framework from being a holistic outlook into resilience, but it does allow this assessment to be performed solely through using a qualitative methodology.

Processing the data first required transcribing the interviews and then performing thematic analysis through open coding by linking key ideas to one or more of the eleven characteristics and indicators. Axial coding then helped thematically group key ideas together and help compare results across participants, such as finding what types of farms tend to operate in ways that prioritize certain indicators over others. Thematic analysis linked farmer responses to threats they face to our selected indicators. Thematic analysis is a commonly used analysis method for deriving relationships in qualitative data (Terry 2017) and has been used in similar scoping qualitative research to interpret semistructured interview data from farmers (Whitton and Carmichael 2024). We tracked how many farms were enacting management practices that linked to each indicator to see if there was a significant difference in the ability to respond to threats between each farm and farm types. Because this study does not make use of quantitative modeling or statistical analysis, we focused on indicators that can be captured through farmer narratives. Quantitative assessments that feed into modeling or statistical analysis might include indicators related to specific land use-trends, such as percentage of arable land that uses synthetic pesticides, or related to farmer income, such as the proportion of income from farming relative to total household income (Zong et al. 2022).

sections.Results and Discussion:
Resilience ' of What ' in Alternative and Conventional Agricultural Systems

This section assesses the resilience of the participating farms by synthesizing both alternative and conventional farms ' resilience of what, to what, and how they are building resilience by linking their actions on the farm to our assessment ' s indicators. We also review Inverary ' s resilience ' for what purpose ' by summarizing nonfarmer stakeholders ' perspectives on resilience in the region. There is a clear divide in scale, goals, and practical approaches when assessing the five selected characteristics between alternative and conventional farm types. These approaches feed into our resilience framework by characterizing resilience ' of what. ' After analyzing the coded transcripts, dominant patterns emerged, which are summarized in the top portion of Table 2.
sections.Resilience ' to What ': All farmers interviewed in the study area of Inverary described the main environmental and socioeconomic shocks and stresses their farms were facing, threatening their farms ' identity. Notably, there was strong overlap in the types of threats that were expressed by farmers. These threats are summarized in Table 3. The two most pronounced threats that were put forth by every farmer interviewed were drought and rising input costs. In 2016, there was an extreme drought in southeastern Ontario. Crop farmers recalled that the drought devastated their yields and dairy farmers recalled that the drought led to heat stress on their cows. Every farmer also noted the harsh impact of rising input prices, which peaked during the growing season of 2022. Increased costs for fuels, fertilizers, and machinery, as well as general inflation, reduced profit margins for all farmers interviewed.
sections.Thematic Analysis of Farmer Interviews:
All farms face similar threats, but some farms choose to direct their attention and resources to some threats more than others in efforts to maintain their farm ' s identity. Creating beneficial responses to socioeconomic shocks and stresses often relied on the human capital and social capital of the agroecosystem, whereas creating beneficial responses to environmental shocks relied heavily on natural capital. The top portion of Table 2 demonstrates the difference in characteristics and resources between the two types of farm groups assessed, whereas the bottom portion provides examples of how farms within each category are directing their resources to build resilience into their operation. We relate these examples to our selected indicators to further uncover patterns in the Inverary agricultural space.

Keeping their farm functioning over time and generating intergenerational renewal is extremely important to all the farm owners surveyed. The two key resilience indicators found for improving the longevity of the farm were (1) using reflective and shared learning, and (2) integrating local knowledge systems into the farm management plan. Reflective and shared learning, expressed through trial-anderror tactics as well as planned experimentation, were common themes discussed to continually adapt to changing environments. Reflecting on what has happened within the agroecosystem in the past and adjusting how things work to proactively anticipate future environmental conditions also ensures the farmers are continually expanding their knowledge base and skill set. Additionally, alternative farms have identified the benefit of integrating local knowledge systems into their agroecosystem through understanding the importance of growing locally adapted and high-quality products.

Although alternative farms form the minority of agricultural operations in the study area, they do have a strong social presence because of their heightened emphasis on connecting with their local community, given that their community members are predominantly buying their products. All of the participating farms had a unique specialty and are therefore facing different industry-specific risks. They also face common risks, however, and their responses to these risks follow a generally unified pattern. Major focuses included (1) building natural capital in their system, (2) keeping operations and markets local, and (3) integrating local knowledge concepts into operations. The majority of alternative farms noted having strong connections to provisioning their seeds from local nonprofit organizations like the Kingston Area Seed Saving Initiative, a prime example of integrating local knowledge into operations.

Alternative farms identified that having strong and reliable access to local labor allowed them to cope better during the turmoil associated with the pandemic. Strong social capital to source labor during the pandemic boosted response diversity, as alternative farms were able to keep functioning at near full strength, compared to conventional farms that relied on labor programs that were disrupted.

Alternative farms also found that building social capital within their community offset the need for seeking extra hired help, as well as using those community connections to better navigate economic challenges by sharing useful knowledge among their networks. They also described the benefit of increasing their temporal diversity, setting up their agroecosystem so that it is functioning and bringing in income for as many months of the year as possible. One farm used strong natural capital, represented by a picturesque apple orchard, and social capital, represented by integration into community networks such as providing field trips for local schools, to make ecotourism a central part of their income during the farm ' s offseason. This is a prime example of natural and social capital characteristics influencing one of the selected indicators.

Although the sampled alternative farms match up well with many of the selected indicators of resilience, there are still limitations to this form of farming. The first limitation is the systemic struggle to make this form of farming a reasonably profitable way to make a living. It was noted in the interviews that most farmers who farm this way require a direct household member with a secure second job, although this type of split livelihood was in no way confined solely to alternative agriculture. Some alternative farmers who do not require a second job are in a financial position where they are not currently relying on producing a steady income. Farmers in this situation might be retired or pursuing alternative farming more as a hobby than as a job to make a living because they are already financially comfortable. Overall, there is a diversity of financial situations for these types of farmers. There are farmers who operate as a business for profit and do not require second jobs, there are farmers who are reliant on diversified streams of income, and there are farmers who have built financial capacity from their previous careers to have flexibility in their operations.

Conventional farmers ' responses to financial and labor issues generally relied on using new technology to increase efficiency on the farm. Efficiency through mechanization was identified to both save money by using fewer inputs and reduce reliance on labor by introducing automation. All of the surveyed dairy farms have either upgraded to robotic milking systems or, in the case of one farm, have started using heat and motion tracking collars for their livestock. All dairy farms also have heavily relied on artificial insemination (AI) breeding to develop stronger and more productive animals, which has been noted by all to be a useful endeavor. Each farm also makes use of new technology through relying on genetically modified organism (GMO) seeds for their cash cropping operations. Improved efficiency is especially desirable for these farmers given their strong reliance on high-input farming. Knowledge of new technology was primarily initiated through informal network discussions between dairy farmers. Several dairy farmers mentioned that they learn about which technologies are useful and which are not by sharing knowledge with each other. One farmer specifically noted this as being critical, citing examples of how input dealers are not the best source of finding accurate unbiased information for new technology.

Whereas conventional farms are generally responding in a uniform way to short-term socioeconomic threats, long-term threats are being handled differently. To deal with shifting liberalized markets, some farms have shifted toward specialization and other have shifted toward diversification. Other farms are settled in between. For example, one farm is continually diversifying their farm away from solely cash cropping by introducing new ventures through greenhouses and growing several different products to be sold both locally as well as overseas. This diversification is a result of the farmer ' s hesitancy to continue participating in global markets owing to price volatility. Conversely, another farm is specializing in sheep production and has no intentions of diversifying away from this mission. Everything on the farm is designed to support lamb production, as it is their only income. This relies on expanding urban markets that purchase their product, but issues will arise if those markets decline.

Four other conventional farms are working on a hybrid specialization model. On each farm, dairy is the focus and most of the farm ' s operation works toward supporting the cows. Each farm within the last -ten to fifteen years, however, has diversified into growing cash crops as a secondary feature to earn supplemental income. Although not the focus of the farm, this diversification adds a cushion toward both short-term shocks through seasonal market disruption and long-term stresses if market forces or political forces, such as the disappearance of supply management, start to favor cash cropping over dairy farming. Diversification in this vein introduces spatial diversity, which was nonexistent prior to diversifying. Although these farms have pivoted from solely producing dairy products, the farmers still maintain that they are dairy farms. In essence, their identity as dairy farms is preserved because they now have extra incomes from cash cropping to support their dairy endeavors. Shifts in farming approach toward hybrid specialization strongly rely on natural capital, primarily by having the land to plant new crops. Of the three dairy farmers who have recently started growing cash crops, one farmer already owned the land to be set aside for growing crops, whereas the other two had to start renting land to begin their cash crop endeavor. Financial capital in the form of investment, as well as upgrades to physical capital were also precursors toward hybrid specialization. Investing in these capitals to create this new farming model resulted in examples of the farms demonstrating spatial diversity and response diversity by having a more spatially diverse farm that produces multiple products, as well as earning supplemental income to be used to address future threats.

In contrast to alternative farms, conventional farms are more uniform in their approaches to resilience building. This is likely due to their participation in conventional food systems that provide farmers with less autonomy over farm operations and, therein, restricting their potential resiliencebuilding pathways. The dominant short-term issue voiced by these farmers was rising prices for the inputs that they have become dependent on, such as fertilizers, fuels, and seeds. Equally, farmers have felt overworked because of the extreme difficulty in finding reliable sources of farm labor. These two issues combined have prompted a strong response in the form of searching for ways to improve efficiency on the farm at all costs. Efficiency reduces costs by using fewer inputs, which saves money, and efficiency also reduces the need to find labor by integrating automation into the system. Efficiency through mechanization, however, reduces resilience in agricultural systems because it leads to homogenized production and results in fewer people involved to make decisions or contribute their knowledge (Hendrickson 2015; Bennett et al. 2021).

Where these conventional farms diverge is how they approach long-term stresses. For the farms who diversified, the farmers noted the benefit of having multiple income streams to buffer against market volatility. The farm that diversified the most noted they can by virtue of having the financial resources -including stable access to bank credit -try out new ventures. The other farms maintain a focus on dairy in part because dairy is what they know best, so they do not want to risk moving away from their primary areas of expertise. Additionally, the infrastructure for dairy is so demanding that pivoting away from it would require a degree of operational flexibility that many conventional farmers do not possess.

One common theme in dealing with several of the threats in Table 2 was reliance on the ' family farm ' aspect of each farm by using existing social capital to integrate local knowledge and reflective and shared learning values into the farm management plan. Whereas the tightening of operating costs is threatening the longevity of each farm, the internal local knowledge possessed by each family acts to keep motivation high to carry on the family farm ' s tradition. All farmers noted that farms are going out of business in their region, but they all still argue that there exists a sense of farming community. Each farmer has strong social capital where they have existing relationships with several other farmers in the region, which offers several benefits both in the short term and long term. Short-term issues that rely on strong social capital, such as needing help with machinery or someone to watch the farm while the primary operator takes some time off, or long-term issues such as maintaining a presence in local agricultural organizations to lobby for long-term health of the area, were all highlighted by farmers as solutions toward preserving the longevity and intergenerational potential of family farms.

On one side of the debate, OMAFRA, the OFA, and input dealers are promoting one path -prioritized by boosting farmer incomes through new technological advancements -whereas the other organizations interviewed are promoting a second path -one that values building resilience through advocating for local food systems and assisting small farms. The effect is that both alternative and conventional farmers believe their farming operation qualifies as resilient. Alternative farmers believe they are farming with resilient qualities that are framed by the organizations they interact with, and vice versa for conventional farmers. Notably, interactions between organizations and farms are quite stratified by farm type. Interviewees from both the EFAO and local County Office of Economic Development stated they primarily interact with alternative farms. Conversely, every conventional farmer interviewed is a member of the OFA.

Interestingly, almost every farmer ' s response to what they hope to do to respond to threats (interview question 33) matched what is being put forth by the organizations that farm type tends to interact with. Alternative farmers ' primary responses revolved around protecting natural capital and keeping a small-scale local focus, which are also the visions put forth by the EFAO and County Office of Economic Development. Conventional farmers ' responses all described the importance of improving efficiency and making use of new technology, which are responses also promoted by the OFA, OMAFRA, and local input dealers. This acts as a barrier toward adaptation, as each farm type ' s vision of responding to threats matches that of the organization with which they interact. Because the study area ' s resilience ' for what purpose ' is divided, this poses issues for creating a unified vision of resilience. Both the EFAO and County Office of Community Development claimed efforts of enhancing outreach to conventional farmers to help bridge this gap.
sections.Conclusion:
This pilot study in Inverary, Ontario, that used our resilience assessment revealed several conclusions, including uncovering the goals and approaches of diverse farming types (resilience ' of what ' ), the key environmental and socioeconomic threats that both alternative and conventional farmers face (resilience ' to what ' ), and the visions for resilience promoted by nonfarmer stakeholders in Inverary ' s agricultural space (resilience ' for what purpose ' ). Then, farmer operations were assessed and compared to select resilience indicators. Although most farms displayed some traits that linked to the indicators, thematic analysis revealed insightful patterns. Both farm types strongly rely on reflective and shared learning to best respond to threats. Both farm types also recognized the importance of integrating local knowledge systems by connecting with their community for assistance in times of need. We observed that alternative and conventional farmers are enacting different methods to build resilience into their operation. Although alternative farms exhibited traits of temporal diversity and self-regulation, there was little to no evidence of conventional farmers exhibiting these traits.

This study ' s findings matter not only for the localized context of Inverary, but also for the broader goal of inquiring into the state of agricultural resilience in Ontario agriculture. Farmers tended to align their actions with the values and information provided by their affiliate networks -whether alternative or conventional. This suggests that nonfarmer stakeholders play a critical role in shaping how resilience to environmental and socioeconomic threats is understood and practiced. Yet, these nonfarmer stakeholders operate within divergent ideologies, which results in fractured visions of agricultural futures. Without shared meanings of resilience, and given that divergent ideologies have competing values and priorities, movements to support long-term agricultural sustainability risk ineffectiveness. Particularly concerning is the evidence of key traits fundamental to resilience theory being absent from conventional farming structures in the area. The coping mechanisms used by conventional farms might be effective in the short term. The absence of resilience indicators, though, such as temporal diversity and self-regulation, compromise the farm ' s abilities to maintain its identity under compounding environmental and socioeconomic stresses. The absence of these indicators might also suggest an inherent incompatibility between the principles of conventional farming and the resilience indicators proposed in this study.

Given the diversity of interpretations of agricultural success in this study, we propose a critical need for consensus building among nonfarming stakeholders to establish a common set of definitions and frameworks for resilience in Ontario agriculture. The indicator framework we have developed offers a scalable tool that could be applied across other regions to capture relevant knowledge while maintaining conceptual consistency. This framework also provides a foundation for evidence-based policy that supports resilience as a dynamic process that is shaped by ecological conditions, social relationships, and institutional support. Ignoring these dynamics risks reinforcing systems that are economically effective in the short term but unsustainable in the long term. /H17039

sections.Introduction:
R esilience terminology has crept into governmental platforms within Canada, although it is often not clearly defined. The Pan-Canadian Framework on clean growth and climate change includes a broad section on adaptation and resilience, referring often to the agricultural industry. Despite being mentioned frequently in the report, resilience is never discussed, other than how embracing it will help communities move forward. Core concepts in the report include incorporating scientific information with traditional knowledge, investing in resilient infrastructure, and focusing on vulnerable regions of the country (Government of Canada 2018). At the provincial level, the Ontario Ministry of Agriculture, Food, and Rural Affairs (OMAFRA) broadcasts little in the way of resilient thinking in their sustainable farming information guides. Infrequent mentions of the term use it as a loose adjective to depict a broadly defined goal, such as achieving ' resilient agriculture. ' The ministry is much more oriented toward economic development, highlighted by the its mandate to promote ' a more competitive and productive agri-food and agriproduct sector ' (OMAFRA 2013).

However useful, generally there is no uniformity on these issues between the different levels of government in Canada. Furthermore, there is a clear gap between debates on resilience in the academic world compared to the governmental policy world. Other stakeholders in the space of agriculture include farmers, those in private industry that sell to farmers, and those in other agricultural organizations such as the Ecological Farmers Association of Ontario (EFAO) or the National Farmers Union (NFU). A framework that brings in resilience and examines farms through the lens of a coupled socialecological system, by combining biophysical, political, and socioeconomic factors, will improve on the ways in which we think about resilience compared to previous efforts made by organizations throughout Ontario. Therefore, the objective of this research is to introduce an analytical framework for assessing agroecosystem resilience in in rural Ontario, Canada.

Riverine flooding events are expected to become increasingly severe in the coming decades due to climate change, resulting in an urgent need to build flood resilience in underserved areas of the country. West Virginia has some of the highest risk of flooding in the United States, which is often compounded by aging infrastructure and high levels of socioeconomic vulnerability. In June 2016, one storm caused flooding that killed twenty-three people, destroyed or damaged thousands of homes and businesses, and caused $1 billion in damages across the state. Some of the most affected towns have yet to fully recover. This mixed-methods community-engaged research project was the first systematic investigation of lessons learned from the 2016 floods in Greenbrier County, West Virginia, a place devastated by this disaster. Using a county-wide survey, focus groups, and participatory GIS (PGIS), this project resulted in the creation of community-informed geospatial products to communicate flood risk, as well as a set of community-identified recommendations for increasing resilience to future flood disasters. Findings offer critical insights for more effective flood response and recovery in West Virginia and other rural areas of the United States with high riverine flood risk. Key Words: community-engaged research, flood risk, natural hazards, participatory GIS, resilience.

A s made clear by flooding events in recent years from western North Carolina to eastern Kentucky to northern Vermont, rural inland communities in the United States are at a high risk of severe flooding. Such communities tend to have high levels of socioeconomic vulnerability and low capacity to respond to flood disasters (Poling and Shealy 2024). Nationally, West Virginia is ranked at or near the top in nearly every flood risk category including potential impacts of flooding on utilities, public safety infrastructure, commercial properties, and schools (First Street Foundation 2020), with at least one flooding-related federal disaster declared in each of the state ' s fifty-five counties since 1996 (West Virginia Division of Homeland Security and Emergency Management 2018; Land Use and Sustainable Development Law Clinic, WVU 2022). Between 1993 and 2017, floods resulted in an estimated $1.8 billion in property damage and 103 deaths across the state (Patterson 2020). These already regular disasters are expected to become more severe because of climate change (Environmental Protection Agency 2016), with significant expected annual losses from riverine flooding across the majority of West Virginia counties (Federal Emergency Management Agency [FEMA] 2025). Like rural communities across the United States, these risks are compounded by aging infrastructure (American Society of Civil Engineers 2020), high levels of socioeconomic vulnerability

<!-- image -->

(Agency for Toxic Substances and Disease Registry 2020), and low rates of flood insurance coverage (FEMA 2018b).

On 23 June 2016, one storm delivered ten inches of rain across West Virginia, or 25 percent of the state ' s mean annual rainfall (Shinn and Caretta 2020; Caretta et al. 2021; Figure 1). Small creeks rose rapidly, killing twenty-three people, tearing homes from foundations, damaging businesses, and causing $1 billion in damages across the state (Di Liberto 2016; Poling and Shealy 2024). Over 90 percent of those seeking FEMA assistance after the flood did not have flood insurance, and relied on a combination of personal finances, nonprofit assistance, and other government resources to rebuild (Poling and Shealy 2024). Some of the most affected towns continue to struggle with long-term recovery (Shinn and Caretta 2020; Lilly 2021; Poling and Shealy 2024; Shinn 2024). This article details findings from a community-engaged mixed-methods research project that investigated lessons learned from the 2016 flood in Greenbrier County, West Virginia. The project was the first systematic documentation of lessons learned from the 2016 event and findings offer critical insights for more effective flood response and recovery in West Virginia and other rural areas of the United States with high riverine flood risk.

Figure 1 Rainelle, West Virginia, the day after the 2016 flood. Image courtesy of Elevated Media.

sections.Conceptual Framework:
Community Vulnerability and Resilience to Flooding

The relationship between social vulnerability and natural disasters is well established (Burton 1993; Buckland and Rahman 1999; Cutter, Boruff, and Shirley 2003), including in relation to flooding (Few 2003). Vulnerability is understood as the susceptibility of an individual or group to harm, which in part determines their ability to effectively respond to natural disasters (Cutter, Mitchell, and Scott 2000; Adger 2006; Turner 2016). Flood risk results from a combination of flood magnitude, exposure of population and assets to the hazard, and vulnerability of the exposed population (Fedeski and Gwilliam 2007; Hallegatte 2014). Several social factors can moderate or exacerbate a community ' s capacity to anticipate, respond to, and recover from natural hazards (Cutter, Boruff, and Shirley 2003; Cutter and Finch 2008; Ka  zmierczak and Cavan 2011). Such factors include income levels (Morrow 1999; Cutter, Boruff, and Shirley 2003; Flanagan et al. 2011); age distribution (Morrow 1999; Cutter, Boruff, and Shirley 2003; Cutter and Finch 2008; Flanagan et al. 2011); racial and ethnic composition (Morrow 1999; Cutter, Boruff, and Shirley 2003; Flanagan et al. 2011); and other factors related to home values, employment, population growth rates, education levels, and home and vehicle ownership (Morrow 1999; Cutter, Boruff, and Shirley 2003; Thieken et al. 2008; Flanagan et al. 2011).

Communities can experience vulnerability to floods and other natural hazards while also exhibiting resilience (Cutter 2016). Community resilience is defined as ' the ability of communities to withstand and mitigate the stress of a disaster ' and is a key component of long-term disaster recovery (Chandra et al. 2011). Predisaster planning and coordination is an important part of enhancing community resilience, even -and perhaps especially -in the context of high levels of social vulnerability (Phillips and Jenkins 2010; Stajura et al. 2012).
sections.Participatory GIS for Predisaster Planni:
Effective predisaster planning requires accurate knowledge about flood risk. Research on climate knowledge has found that nearly all cases of successfully utilized data production and implementation employed some form of iteration between producers and users of the product (Dilling and Lemos 2011). Still, hazard mitigation planning often stresses expert-driven procedures that do not engage the most vulnerable groups and communities (Hendricks, Meyer, and Wilson 2022). One approach that is proven effective in engaging local communities is participatory geographic information systems (PGIS), which explicitly engages feedback from the user during product development. PGIS emerged as a response to criticisms of traditional geographic information systems (GIS), which tended to neglect social and cultural dimensions, with a focus on connecting scientific knowledge generation and policy formulation to enhance societal outcomes (Brandt et al. 2020).

The primary objective of PGIS is to include stakeholders in the GIS process to address issues that directly affect them, thereby harnessing local spatial knowledge and enriching outcomes. Prior research has demonstrated the value of PGIS for community-level disaster resilience in the context of climate change and geohazards (Haworth et al. 2018; Liu et al. 2018; Nkoana, Verbruggen, and Hug  e 2018; Pecl et al. 2019; Juh  asz et al. 2020; Williams, Pauli, and Boruff 2020; Nofal and Van De Lindt 2022), as well as flood mitigation specifically (Verplanke et al. 2016; Cruz-Bello and AlfieCohen 2022). PGIS fosters ownership among end users while increasing usability and filling knowledge gaps (Kemp 2008; Verplanke et al. 2016; Zolkafli, Brown, and Liu 2017; Yusuf et al. 2018; Ndzabandzaba 2020). As a result, PGIS can be a critical component of supporting communities with knowledge to improve resilience to natural hazards such as floods.
sections.Case Study and Methods:
Greenbrier County, West Virginia

This project focused on Greenbrier County, West Virginia, population 32,149 (U.S. Census Bureau 2023b), one of the counties most severely affected by the 2016 flood (Figure 2). Of the twenty-three casualties resulting from this event, fifteen were in Greenbrier County. Research activities centered on the towns of Rainelle and White Sulphur Springs. Both communities are situated in flood-prone narrow river valleys (FEMA 2018b; Caretta et al. 2021) and both were devastated in 2016 (Shinn and Caretta 2020), but they have divergent socioeconomic realities that led to uneven flood recovery and thus provide rich data on flood response and recovery in differing socioeconomic contexts.

Figure 2 West Virginia counties affected by 2016 flood with project study sites ( FEMA, 2016 ).

<!-- image -->

In Rainelle, population 1,250, 37.0 percent of households live below the federal poverty line. In White Sulphur Springs, population 3,036, 14.4 percent of households live below the federal poverty line (U.S. Census Bureau 2023a). Rainelle, located on the western side of Greenbrier County, has an economic history related mostly to the oncebooming timber industry in the region and has experienced decades of job loss associated with the decline of such extractive industries. This community has been deemed a bellwether for others with high flood risk across the United States (Hersher, Jingnan, and Schmidt 2021). On the eastern edge of Greenbrier County, White Sulphur Springs is a popular tourist destination and home of The Greenbrier -a luxury hotel, vacation community, and golf course -which provides a significant proportion of area employment (Alvey 2020). Together, the divergent experiences of recovery in these communities provide comprehensive insights into vulnerability and resilience to flooding in West Virginia.
sections.Methods:
The project integrated three distinct methods. First, a survey of Greenbrier County residents was conducted from December 2022 to January 2023 to capture experiences with flooding and awareness of flood risk (see Supplemental Material, Appendix A for complete list of survey questions). The survey was advertised via social media and flyers posted in the communities and was delivered through Qualtrics, as Web-based surveys provide the opportunity to reach many people in a short amount of time (Kaplowitz et al. 2012). Recognizing that a virtual survey could overlook those with low computer literacy or without access to broadband, paper surveys were also made available at the City Hall in both towns. No one took advantage of this opportunity, however. As such, although the project made a concentrated effort to reach as many residents as possible, there was a potential bias against some of the most vulnerable groups.

Second, the research team held three in-person community focus groups in public spaces in Rainelle and White Sulphur Springs in November 2022 (twenty-six total participants) and four virtual focus groups via Zoom in January 2023 (sixteen total participants). Focus groups are designed to bring together participants around a common topic of interest and are a robust method for collecting a relatively large amount of qualitative data in a short time (Watson and Till 2010). Participant recruitment focused on those with insights on the 2016 flood and was done through existing relationships of the research team, with a snowball approach to expand the initial sample. Participants in community focus groups included affected residents, emergency responders, floodplain managers, health care professionals, mayors and city council members, business owners, and nonprofit organization representatives. Participants in virtual focus groups included representatives of FEMA, country-level emergency management, AmeriCorps, West Virginia Voluntary Organizations Active in Disasters (WV VOAD), and several faith-based organizations. Focus groups were held during day and evening times to maximize participation and each participant was offered a gift card to offset participation costs.

Focus groups were facilitated to generate discussion on (1) lessons learned from response to and recovery from the 2016 flood, (2) priorities for future flood response and recovery efforts, and (3) the PGIS activities described later. The same questions were asked of participants in each of the seven focus groups, and analysis focused on identifying common themes that emerged across the groups, minimizing the risk that a small number of individuals could skew the overall findings (see Supplemental Material Appendix B for a complete list of focus group questions).

Third, at each of the seven focus groups, PGIS methods were used to gather input on visual tools created by the research team. The primary objectives of the visuals were to communicate flood risks facing these communities based on climate change models. Flood risk analyses incorporated data on several indicators: flood hazards, physical exposure, human exposure, social vulnerability, physical vulnerability, physical loss, human impacts, and mitigation (see Supplemental Material Appendix C for complete details and data sources for each indicator). The results were used to produce two-dimensional (2D) maps and three-dimensional (3D) visualizations that were presented to focus group participants for feedback and refinement (Figure 3).

sections.Findings:
Survey Findings

There were 1,168 valid survey responses, with an age range of 18 to 82 and an average age of 27.5. Annual household income ranged from less than $20,000 to more than $100,000. A total of 56 percent identified as female and 43 percent as male, and 80 percent identified as White. The average number of adults in households was 2.73, with 0.84 children. Approximately 75 percent reported full-time employment and nearly 70 percent had post-high school education, from trade school to advanced degrees.

Results indicate that the 2016 flood had widespread impacts on Greenbrier County. Nearly all respondents (98 percent) reported community impacts from the 2016 flood, with 76 percent reporting that their primary residence was either damaged (55 percent) or destroyed (44 percent). Of these, 87 percent reported being able to stay in their home despite damage, whereas some left their home for a short period of time (9 percent) and a few left permanently (3 percent). Of those whose homes were affected, over one-third did not believe they were vulnerable to flooding prior to the 2016 event (Figure 4).

Survey data revealed that recovery from the 2016 flood remains incomplete. When asked about the recovery level of their community, only 19 percent of respondents felt there had been a complete recovery, whereas 74 percent reported partial recovery. A full 92 percent of affected respondents received some kind of assistance for flood recovery, but only 52 percent of respondents reported a full recovery for their household (Figure 5). Respondents received help from a combination of sources, including FEMA, the National Guard, the Red Cross, faithbased organizations, and several nonprofit organizations. When asked how satisfied they were with the recovery process, 27 percent were very satisfied, 34 percent were somewhat satisfied, 34 percent were neither satisfied nor dissatisfied, and 4 percent were somewhat or very dissatisfied.

The survey indicated that the flood had widespread impacts on employment, including the necessity to take time off to repair damaged homes. When asked how the flood affected employment, 43 percent reported working more hours and 42 percent reported working fewer hours. As a result of these disruptions, over half of respondents whose jobs were affected by the flood experienced at least some reduction in income (Figure 6).

Respondents also reported emotional and mental health impacts related to the flood. When asked if the 2016 flood caused emotional or mental health impacts (diagnosed by a medical professional or not), 73 percent reported impacts, including new or increased levels of anxiety, depression, and fear of large storms. Over half (54 percent) of people received support for these impacts, including from family and friends (27 percent) or mental health professionals (23 percent). An additional 23 percent reported wanting but not receiving mental health care.

Figure 6 Impacts on income of 2016 flood.

<!-- image -->

Figure 7 Household preparation for future floods.

<!-- image -->

Finally, responses indicate a wide range of perceptions on preparation for future floods, with less than a quarter feeling that either their household or their community are ' very prepared ' for future flooding (Figures 7 and 8). When asked if they have flood insurance for their homes, 47 percent reported having none, 21 percent reported having mandated flood insurance, 26 percent reported voluntarily purchasing flood insurance, and 6 percent were unsure if they had it at all.

Three broad conclusions stand out from this survey. (1) The high response rate, with approximately 4 percent of the total county population participating, indicates a great deal of interest in the ongoing impact of the 2016 flood. (2) Many residents and communities were not fully prepared for the flood, as indicated by disruptions to living situations, physical and emotional health, and employment. (3) Levels of recovery vary significantly and are incomplete. Tellingly, 92% of respondents reported receiving some kind of assistance but only 52% reported full recovery over six years after the flood.
sections.Focus Group Findings:
Two broad themes arose from the focus groups: (1) the need for predisaster preparation (e.g., coordination with FEMA and other organizations, establishing clear communication channels and leadership roles, and volunteer coordination), and (2) the need for additional predisaster capacity building (e.g., hiring and training floodplain managers, providing accurate flood insurance information, and creating improved flood risk assessment tools). As one participant said, ' All disasters start local and end local, ' highlighting the importance of community capacity building. Additionally, virtual focus group participants also discussed issues of equitable access to assistance, including for disabled residents, those with low literacy rates, and the inability of lowincome households to access flood insurance. Focus group findings are summarized in Table 1, alongside representative participant quotes. Of note, although Rainelle and White Sulphur Springs had different socioeconomic contexts before the flood and are at different stages of postflood recovery, insights on lessons learned from the flood were similar across all seven focus groups and have been summarized accordingly.

Geovisualization Risk Indicators and Participatory GIS Findings

The following groups of indicators were used to analyze flood risk and create 2D and 3D visualizations of the results to present to the communities for their feedback.

Flood Hazard. In White Sulphur Springs, the effective 1 percent-annual-chance flood zone area, also known as the Special Flood Hazard Area (SFHA), is 266 acres or 21.9 percent of the community area, whereas in Rainelle it is 223 acres or 31.1 percent of the community area. These percentages are higher than the median ratio for all incorporated areas in the state (10.2 percent). Rainelle is potentially more exposed to higher flood depths, whereas in White Sulphur Springs, the primary concern lies in the considerable threat posed by flood velocity. Comparing the 2016 flood high-water marks in Rainelle with the estimated inundation depths by FEMA indicates the event was between a 1 percentannual-chance (100-year) and 0.2 percent-annualchance (500-year) flood event. In White Sulphur Springs, the 2016 flood exhibited similarities to a 500-year event.

Physical Exposure. Both Rainelle and White Sulphur Springs have a high level of physical exposure of primary structures in the high-risk floodplains (Table 2). The ratio of buildings in the floodplain to the total structures within the community is significantly higher for both areas compared to the state ratio. The median building value in the floodplain of White Sulphur Springs is higher than the statewide value, whereas it is lower in Rainelle. Most buildings in high-risk floodplains are residential; however, in Rainelle, the ratio of nonresidential structures is higher than the statewide ratio indicating higher risk of business interruption by flooding. In both communities, more than 75 percent of the flood-prone structures were constructed before the initial FEMA Flood Insurance Rate Map (FIRM)

Essential facilities, such as police and fire stations, emergency operations centers, schools, hospitals, and nursing homes, play a vital role in delivering critical services to communities. One such facility -the White Sulphur Springs Police Department -is in the high-risk (100-year) floodplain. In Rainelle, two essential facilities are located in the highand moderate-risk flood zones: the Rainelle Volunteer Fire Department and the colocated Town Hall and Rainelle Police Department. The location of these structures within the floodplain risks significant operational challenges during flooding events as well as the loss of critical governmental records and services. In White Sulphur Springs, eight community assets were identified within the high-risk floodplain, including four churches, the city hall, the municipal court, a U.S. Postal Service office, and a national fish hatchery. In Rainelle, there are six community assets in the high-risk flood zone including four churches, the Rainelle Public Library, and the Municipal Water Department. Findings also reveal that a considerable portion of the road network including U.S.

60 in both towns is at risk of inundation at flood depth of 1 foot or higher (Figure 9). Three bridges in White Sulphur Springs and two in Rainelle are also subject to flood inundation. These bridges can obstruct flow and increase the risk of impact by causing backwater flooding.

Human Exposure. A significant proportion of the population resides in the floodplains with a 1 percent annual chance of flooding in both communities. In White Sulphur Springs, 1,026 individuals are estimated to live in the high-risk area representing 39 percent of the city ' s total population. In Rainelle, the estimated population residing in the floodplain is 582 accounting for 43 percent of the total population (U.S. Census Bureau 2023a). This percentage is significantly higher than the statewide percentage of 10 percent for all incorporated areas.

Social and Institutional Vulnerability. This study identified several social vulnerability indicators for the two communities, as summarized in Table 3. Rainelle is more vulnerable in all categories compared to the state ratios. Both communities have a higher average of renter-occupied properties, making structures and residents more susceptible to flood loss.

Physical Vulnerability. Primary structures located in flood zones that have subgrade basements are more vulnerable to flooding. In comparison to the statewide ratio for all incorporated areas, both communities have a lower percentage of these structures (Table 4). One-story buildings are more vulnerable to flooding compared to multistory structures because if the flood water exceeds the first floor, the percentage of building damage will be higher and trapped occupants cannot escape to a higher level. The ratio of onestory residential buildings is higher than the statewide percentage. Rainelle has a much higher ratio of red tag structures (dilapidated, vacant, or buildings with appraised values equal to or less than $10,000) in the floodplain, which means they could be more vulnerable in terms of building quality and the cost-effectiveness of mitigation measures.
