Physical Loss. Field surveys of the 2016 flood for White Sulphur Springs and building-level loss models show that a significant number of structures will be substantially damaged at greater than 50

percent for flood events that exceed the 100-year base flood elevations (Table 5). Both building loss estimates and high-water marks indicate that the building damage percentages are considerable for both communities but are estimated to be higher in Rainelle due to the high inundation levels, longer flood duration, and wider flooding extent. Finally, the large amount of debris generated from major storms like the 2016 flood correlates to the high damage percentage of structures.

Both communities have higher amounts of paid losses compared to the state mean because of an increase in the number of claims from the 2016 flood disaster. Although the total number and value of structures in the high-risk floodplains of Rainelle is lower than White Sulphur Springs, the estimated debris, number, and amount of previous paid losses, and the number of repetitive loss structures is higher and indicative of repeated flooding events.

sections.Human Displacement:
In both communities, the ratio of estimated population displaced due to flood inundation of one foot or higher caused by a 1%-annual-chance (100-year) flood event is much higher than the state average for all incorporated areas. Moreover, the estimated number of individuals in need of short-term (up to two weeks) shelter in case of a 1%-annual-chance flood is also greater than the state average (Table 6).

Flood Mitigation. Mitigation measures implemented since the 2016 flood by the community were field verified and evaluated in accordance with the local floodplain management regulations (Table 7). Field verifications of both communities show that for most construction projects, the new structures were built to the base flood elevation of a 1 percentannual-chance event (Figure 10). Field surveys show, however, that substantially damaged residential structures were often repaired but not elevated above the base flood elevation.

The percentage of elevated structures in the highrisk floodplain built to the design flood elevation

(DFE) set by the local floodplain management ordinance, or a two-foot safety factor above the 100-year base flood elevation, is lower in Rainelle (35 percent) than White Sulphur Springs (59 percent) as the town of Rainelle is more exposed to higher flood depths.

To measure a community ' s recovery and resiliency against future floods, the net cumulative tax assessments of floodplain building values preand postdisaster were calculated. The net cumulative tax assessment reveals that the total floodplain building value in White Sulphur Springs has fully recovered and exceeded predisaster levels, whereas Rainelle has only partially recovered. Of the cumulative building values in the floodplain between 2015 and 2022, the predisaster values were $13.3 million and $23.0 million for Rainelle and White Sulphur Springs, respectively, and 2017 postflood decreased significantly to $5.0 million for Rainelle and $13.4 million for White Sulphur Springs. After mitigation efforts, in 2022 the cumulative building values in the floodplain for Rainelle and White Sulphur Springs increased to $12.3 million and $29.2 million, respectively (Figure 11).

A loss avoidance study (LAS) quantifies the losses avoided (also known as damage prevented or benefits) due to the implementation of mitigation projects. An LAS for these towns revealed mitigation measures from elevating buildings above the base flood and buyouts resulted in a damage loss avoidance amount of $2.3 million for Rainelle and $2.6 million for White Sulphur Springs. The loss avoidance was calculated by determining the difference between loss estimates for buildings with a firstfloor height of 1 foot (not elevated) and of a scenario in which those are elevated to DFE (2 feet above base flood elevation) or removed entirely. The ratio of areas preserved for open spaces in floodplains of both communities is lower than the average ratio for all incorporated areas statewide (5 percent), indicating limited use of this mitigation strategy.
sections.Participatory GIS Activities:
Geospatial visualizations created from the preceding findings were presented at each of the community focus groups with residents and city leaders to seek input and ensure the accuracy and relevance of the maps (Figure 12). The participation of residents allowed for real-time data validation, which was valuable for refining flood maps and addressing discrepancies to ensure that the data used for decisionmaking were accurate. Two maps were prepared for each community. These maps delineate the 100-year flood zone, buildings damaged or demolished by the 2016 Greenbrier flood, repaired buildings, flood buyout properties, and critical infrastructures. As a result of community feedback, several modifications were made to the maps, including listing two properties as buyout properties in White Sulphur Springs, removing one structure from the 100-year flood zone in White Sulphur Springs, marking a building as an unrepaired structure in White Sulphur Springs, and identifying a police department as in the flood zone in Rainelle. In addition to the feedback on the maps, participants also improved the mapping process by locating their homes or workplaces, describing the water height, inundated streets, and the location of shelters during the 2016 flood. At the conclusion of the project, dissemination meetings were held and updated maps were given to each community.

Engaging participants in the GIS process resulted in more reliable flood maps, which in turn can empower residents and local authorities to make more informed decisions regarding flood risk management and disaster preparedness, including through identifying critical infrastructure, evacuation routes, and vulnerable areas. More accurate flood maps can also empower individuals and communities to take proactive measures, such as purchasing flood insurance or implementing flood-resistant building practices, to mitigate the impact of future flooding events. As a result, these efforts promote resilience in flood-prone communities.

sections.Discussion and Conclusion: Building Floo:
It is well-established that high levels of social vulnerability decrease a community ' s ability to effectively respond to natural disasters such as floods (Cutter, Mitchell, and Scott 2000; Few 2003). This is due in part to socioeconomic factors related to employment, education, and home ownership rates (Morrow 1999; Cutter, Boruff, and Shirley 2003; Flanagan et al. 2011). Findings from this project show that Greenbrier County, West Virginia is no exception to these trends, even as flood disasters become increasingly likely for the region. The unique mixed-methods community-engaged approach employed by this project went beyond identifying risk factors; it also determined key knowledge gaps that need to be filled, resulting in the creation of geospatial products to communicate flood risk, as well as a set of community-informed recommendations for increasing resilience to future flood disasters (Table 8).

Research participants consistently articulated the need for improved flood risk education for everyone from residents to local officials. The PGIS approach used in this project not only provided critical knowledge about unique flood risk factors, but it also harnessed community knowledge to increase the accuracy of the products, a process that is known to increase ownership and use of the final outputs (Zolkafli, Brown, and Liu 2017; Yusuf et al. 2018; Ndzabandzaba 2020). As one focus group participant said, ' You can only work with the tools that are given to you … . And if you ' re not given the tools to make change before an event happens, then you are forever going to be saying, okay, well, what can we do differently? '

In addition to the geospatial tools, findings also resulted in several recommendations that are community-informed but also have broad application for other rural inland communities at risk of flooding. These recommendations articulate a clear need for improved comprehensive predisaster preparation and capacity building, which are known to be key aspects of improving disaster response (Phillips and Jenkins 2010; Stajura et al. 2012). Although findings from the two case study sites -Rainelle and White Sulphur Springs -make clear that socioeconomic differences between communities contribute to uneven flood recovery processes, focus groups in both communities generated similar recommendations for improving future flood response. This indicates that these recommendations are relevant to rural communities of varying socioeconomic contexts.

Flooding events are expected to become increasingly severe in the coming decades due to climate change, resulting in an urgent need to build flood resilience in underserved areas of the country. sections.Building Flood Resilience in West Virgin:
a , Behrang Bidadian b , Annie Mahmoudi b , Aaron Maxwell b , and

Jamie E. Shinn Julian Levine c







a SUNY College of Environmental Science and Forestry, USA; b West Virginia University, USA; c West Virginia School of Osteopathic Medicine Center for Rural and Community Health, USA

Riverine flooding events are expected to become increasingly severe in the coming decades due to climate change, resulting in an urgent need to build flood resilience in underserved areas of the country. West Virginia has some of the highest risk of flooding in the United States, which is often compounded by aging infrastructure and high levels of socioeconomic vulnerability. In June 2016, one storm caused flooding that killed twenty-three people, destroyed or damaged thousands of homes and businesses, and caused $1 billion in damages across the state. Some of the most affected towns have yet to fully recover. This mixed-methods community-engaged research project was the first systematic investigation of lessons learned from the 2016 floods in Greenbrier County, West Virginia, a place devastated by this disaster.
sections.Conceptual Framework:
Community Vulnerability and Resilience to Flooding

The relationship between social vulnerability and natural disasters is well established (Burton 1993; Buckland and Rahman 1999; Cutter, Boruff, and Shirley 2003), including in relation to flooding (Few 2003). Vulnerability is understood as the susceptibility of an individual or group to harm, which in part determines their ability to effectively respond to natural disasters (Cutter, Mitchell, and Scott 2000; Adger 2006; Turner 2016). Flood risk results from a combination of flood magnitude, exposure of population and assets to the hazard, and vulnerability of the exposed population (Fedeski and Gwilliam 2007; Hallegatte 2014). Several social factors can moderate or exacerbate a community ' s capacity to anticipate, respond to, and recover from natural hazards (Cutter, Boruff, and Shirley 2003; Cutter and Finch 2008; Ka  zmierczak and Cavan 2011). Such factors include income levels (Morrow 1999; Cutter, Boruff, and Shirley 2003; Flanagan et al. 2011); age distribution (Morrow 1999; Cutter, Boruff, and Shirley 2003; Cutter and Finch 2008; Flanagan et al.
sections.Participatory GIS for Predisaster Planni: Effective predisaster planning requires accurate knowledge about flood risk. Research on climate knowledge has found that nearly all cases of successfully utilized data production and implementation employed some form of iteration between producers and users of the product (Dilling and Lemos 2011). Still, hazard mitigation planning often stresses expert-driven procedures that do not engage the most vulnerable groups and communities (Hendricks, Meyer, and Wilson 2022). One approach that is proven effective in engaging local communities is participatory geographic information systems (PGIS), which explicitly engages feedback from the user during product development. PGIS emerged as a response to criticisms of traditional geographic information systems (GIS), which tended to neglect social and cultural dimensions, with a focus on connecting scientific knowledge generation and policy formulation to enhance societal outcomes (Brandt et al. 2020).

records.title: From the Right to Energy to the Right to the Countryside and Back Again: Contextualizing Rural Energy Transitions
records.abstract: Rural areas as well as their interlinkages with urban agglomerations have gained increasing attention as the main sites where the current energy transformation toward the use of renewable energy is taking place. Due to this, contestations over transitions and emancipatory efforts to transform energy infrastructures cannot be detached from the structural conditions of rural areas and their entanglements with other spatial scales. In this sense, sustainable energy transitions reflect various differences between as well as within rural areas. Consequently, rural energy transitions are embedded in broader processes of rural change. This contribution to the Focus section illustrates interconnections between energy transitions and rural change as they relate to issues of land-use change in rural areas, rural poverty, and marginalization, along with rural populism. In doing so, we argue that energy transition plays an important role for all these issues of rural development and advocate for a systematic integration of the transformation of energy systems and rural change. We, thereby, believe that contextualizing rural energy transitions can contribute to the realization of a right to the countryside and of just and sustainable rural futures within the energy sector and beyond.

Rural areas as well as their interlinkages with urban agglomerations have gained increasing attention as the main sites where the current energy transformation toward the use of renewable energy is taking place. Due to this, contestations over transitions and emancipatory efforts to transform energy infrastructures cannot be detached from the structural conditions of rural areas and their entanglements with other spatial scales. In this sense, sustainable energy transitions reflect various differences between as well as within rural areas. Consequently, rural energy transitions are embedded in broader processes of rural change. This contribution to the Focus section illustrates interconnections between energy transitions and rural change as they relate to issues of land-use change in rural areas, rural poverty, and marginalization, along with rural populism. In doing so, we argue that energy transition plays an important role for all these issues of rural development and advocate for a systematic integration of the transformation of energy systems and rural change. We, thereby, believe that contextualizing rural energy transitions can contribute to the realization of a ' right to the countryside ' and of just and sustainable rural futures within the energy sector and beyond. Keywords: land use, populism, poverty, rural areas, sustainability transitions.

C urrent transformations of energy infrastructures shape the development of cities and regions. Rural areas, however, have been particularly exposed to various effects of climate change but also transformed by responses to these threats, including the implementation of adaptation and mitigation measures such as the development of wind farms, solar parks, and biogas facilities. Rural areas have reemerged as locations where current energy transitions toward the use of renewable energy resources are being materialized (Naumann and Rudolph 2020). Rural areas have already been affected and transformed by the extraction of energy resources and the building of infrastructure for the large-scale production of electricity and heat, but the decentralized and horizontal deployment of renewable energy requires larger surface areas due a to a lower power density (Huber and McCarthy 2017). The expansion of renewable energies additionally incorporates areas in the energy system that had previously been less affected by energy infrastructures. Current energy transitions have the potential to reshape regions or result in the abandonment of spaces that have been integrated into fossil energy systems. This will produce both new energy landscapes and postcarbon landscapes in rural areas (e.g., Lennon and Scott 2017; Batel 2020; Pasqualetti and Smardon 2025). Therefore, the peculiarities and implications of rural energy transitions deserve attention from research and practice. The example of energy, however,

illustrates that rural areas are not separate, isolated entities but have complex and uneven relations with urban agglomerations (e.g., Regier, Berka, and Hoicka 2025), for example, as ' energy peripheries ' (Golubchikov and O ' Sullivan 2020), as parts of ' peripheralization ' (Langguth 2025) or ' urban -rural exploitation ' (Kelly-Reif and Wing 2016). Furthermore, Woods ' s (2007) notion of the ' global countryside ' reminds us how rural places are intertwined with global flows of capital, resources, people, and information.

In turn, energy transitions have become formative elements of ' planetary rural geographies ' and how they are contoured (Wang, Maye, and Woods 2025a, 2025b). Planetary rural geographies have been proposed as a research agenda to incorporate rural areas as spaces of crisis, conflict, and hope (Wang, Maye, and Woods 2025a). Although crisis and conflict dimensions of rural areas have been explicitly linked to rural change, such as marginalization and poverty, transformations of land use, and emerging populism in rural areas, rural spaces of hope are associated with more equitable and just rural futures as well as the use of participatory forms of democracy to reshape rural economies. As we argue in this short contribution to the Focus section, however, although all three geographies of planetary rurality resonate with rural issues connected to the global energy transition, the transformation of the energy system should be viewed more explicitly from the perspective of rural change to allow for its critical consideration in and as part of the formative processes that entail rural spaces of crisis, conflict, and hope.

Our argument is twofold. First, infrastructures related to resource extraction and energy supply as well as their transformation profoundly impinge on rural development. Second, the expansion of renewable energy is also shaped by broader trends of rural change that provide the fundamental conditions for energy transitions. Repercussions of structural rural change on energy transitions have remained less explicit in existing research, however.

In a first attempt to shed a critical light on the effects of rural change on energy transitions in rural areas, we follow the contours of the geographies of planetary rurality as identified by Wang, Maye, and Woods (2025a, 2025b) to consider challenges such as rural land-use change, rural poverty and marginalization, and rural populism and how they relate to the expansion and utilization of renewable energies.

First, the expansion of renewable energy facilities is dependent on what land resources are available. Therefore, the utilization of energy resources contributes to conflicts around rural land use and adds further pressure on already changing and contested agricultural, residential, and touristic uses of land, for example, in coastal and marine areas. Second, rural poverty and marginalization also have an energy dimension or, turning it around, energy poverty is one aspect of the social marginalization experienced in rural areas, which creates social demands on energy transitions. Third, contested issues around energy transitions are raised by right-wing populists, especially in rural contexts that cannot be detached from wider structural issues and hardships felt in rural areas.

Due to the entanglement of these manifestations of the energy transition with different aspects of rural change, we propose a more contextualized understanding of rural energy transitions. For that purpose, we briefly outline the debates about landuse change, rural poverty and marginalization, and rural populism as well as their dialectical interrelations with rural energy transitions. All three topics are affected by and enrolled in processes of energy transitions, and rural energy transitions are taking place in a context of land-use change, poverty, and populism.

Building on that, we advocate for a more holistic understanding of rural energy transitions, where the energy sector is only one strand among a multitude of rural transformations. We argue that such a critical contextualization of rural energy transitions can contribute to the realization of a ' right to the countryside ' (Barraclough 2013), of equitable and sustainable rural futures of the energy sector and beyond. In that sense, we connect not only to other approaches for democratizing infrastructure provision (e.g., Van Veelen and van der Horst 2018) but also to wider debates on rural planning (Gkartzios, Gallent, and Scott 2022) and livelihoods (Shucksmith 2018; Gallent et al. 2025).
sections.Rural Energy Transitions and Rural Chang:
Different modes of energy provision have historically influenced rural areas and have entailed specific challenges, while also presenting opportunities for rural development. From a geographical perspective, the transition from a system based on fossil fuels toward a system predominantly based on decentral, flexible, low-carbon, and renewable energy consists of more than just substituting fuels. It involves structural changes to the energy supply, distribution, and consumption of energy, as well as a reconfiguration of related spatial patterns of economic and social activities (Bridge et al. 2013). In what follows, however, we use the term energy transitions to merely focus on transformations on the side of energy supply and its energetic sources.

Access to variable renewable energy resources like water, biomass, wind, and sun, the availability of land for the deployment of energy infrastructures, and a lower population density are main reasons why material expressions of the energy transition mostly manifest in rural areas. The focus of academic and political attention has often been on urban energy transitions, however (e.g., Cast  an Broto 2019). It is only recently that a debate about rural energy transitions has started to emerge (e.g., Clausen and Rudolph 2020; Calvert et al. 2022; Uleri, Vigan  o, and Musolino 2025). The transition toward an energy system based on renewable energy sources requires the often-contested designation and allocation of locations where new energy infrastructures can be established as well as hopes and desires to realize emancipatory energy projects contributing to rural development (Naumann and Rudolph 2020). This transition entails profound sociotechnical transformations that will have spatially uneven consequences due to legacies of the declining energy regimes, the geographical distribution of renewable resources, land requirements, and public and industrial policies supporting their uptake (Slee 2020). Additionally, consequences of localized energy transitions are relevant for rural areas in the Global North and the Global South and are, thus, also embedded in and exposed to variegated politicaleconomic dynamics that inform rural change. For example, in the Global North the COVID-19 pandemic accelerated a trend toward remote working in rural areas due to migration from urban areas to the countryside (e.g., Gonz  alez-Leonardo, Rowe, and Fresolone-Caparr  os 2022).

Land-use change, poverty, and populism are not exclusively linked to rural areas. They each feature a specific rural dimension. In the following, the three issues are used as emblematic examples for shedding light on the interrelation of energy transitions and rural development in planetary rural geographies (Wang, Maye, and Woods 2025a, 2025b). All of these issues are highly relevant for rural development but are also contested within debates about the future of rural areas and their energy systems. Therefore, the following subsections briefly introduce each issue and its amalgamation with rural energy transitions.
sections.Land-Use Change and Energy Transitions i:
The large-scale rollout of renewable energy requires land on which infrastructures like solar and wind farms can be deployed, necessitating a far-reaching return to a horizontal surface-based energy regime in contrast to the use of subterranean fossil fuel sources (Huber and McCarthy 2017). Consequently, rural areas have gained critical attention in the energy transition, in particular, as contested resources for the deployment of renewables that undergo dual processes of revalorization and marginalization. In particular, linkages between available land resources in rural areas and renewable energy development have become the focus of critical scrutiny. Foremost in the rural context, renewables have turned into a formative element of the global land rush, green grabbing, and land deals (Scheidel and Sorman 2012).

The interrelationship of renewable energy infrastructures with rural areas remains ambiguous, however. On the one hand, the expansion of renewables has been associated in the Global North with expectations for rural economic development (e.g., Clausen and Rudolph 2020), linked to employment during the development and operation of the sites, the localization of the supply chain, increased tax revenues, and proactive benefit sharing. Regarding rural regions in the Global South, enhanced electrification and the local anchoring of the supply chain have also been highlighted as a positive. On the other hand, large-scale renewables are a key driver of land-use changes (Poggi, Firmino, and Amado 2018) that often interfere with the agricultural sector and contribute to the marginalization of already deprived and left-behind places, as precarious activities are displaced (Yenneti, Day, and Golubchikov 2016).

Thus, transformations of land use induced by energy transitions often involve significant contestations. As land-use changes affect agricultural landscapes and agrarian livelihoods (Paprocki and McCarthy 2024), they raise questions about the interplay between housing; tourism; nature conservation; the maintenance, intensification, or ecological modernization of agriculture; and the growth of renewable energy. The aforementioned influx of urbanites relocating (temporally) to the countryside affects the provision of housing, alters the character of rural communities, and changes the associated expectations of ' authentic ' rural landscapes. Despite the widespread articulation of a political desire to advance approaches to coexistence and creating synergies with other rural land uses, however, the commercial appetite from developers to integrate nature-based solutions remains negligible.

The energy transition imperative, the dominance of large-scale projects, coercive development practices, and land acquisitions have evoked associations of energy and infrastructural colonization (Dunlap 2021), especially in the Global South. The growing pressure on agricultural land due to the expansion of renewables is not unique to the context of the Global South. For example, the rapid expansion of large-scale solar and wind farms in Europe has increasingly been made possible partly through clandestine land acquisitions (e.g., Kirkegaard et al. 2023; M € uller and Pampus 2023). In contrast, there is a potential to reuse, repurpose, and replace energy infrastructures that enables a greater durability and a recycling of energy landscapes (Pasqualetti and Smardon 2025). For example, the use of agricultural bioenergy provides the opportunity to contribute to energy and heating self-sufficiency in rural areas, allowing residents to combine agrarian uses of land with energy production and supply while becoming independent from large and centralized energy providers (e.g., Rossi and Hinrichs 2011).

Current understandings of rural energy transitions that employ one-sided perspectives in terms of the provision of benefits, compensation, and placatory activities associated with the utilization of rural resources embedded in corporate social responsibility statements are insufficient to address the structural changes that rural areas are currently facing. Ambitions toward a large-scale rollout of renewable energy facilities in rural areas, therefore, need to be approached from a cross-sectoral perspective (Silva and Sareen 2021) that provides more flexibility through bottom-up and participatory solutions that address social issues as well.
sections.Poverty, Marginalization, and Energy in:
There is an increasing awareness of the problem of rural energy poverty, especially in the Global South (Acheampong et al. 2023). For the Global North, physical access to electricity and heat supply is a less critical issue, but increasing costs can contribute to energy or fuel poverty (Roberts, Vera-Toscano, and Phimister 2015). Rising tariffs on gas, fuel, heat, and electricity supply particularly affect low-income households in rural areas.

Studies have revealed the rural characteristics of energy poverty, for example, in terms of the interlinkages between fuel and mobility poverty (Mattioli, Lucas, and Marsden 2017). In remote rural areas, in particular, car dependence is connected to a higher vulnerability to fuel poverty. Energy poverty depends not only on the income of households but also on the level of education, the conditions of buildings, and technological equipment (Boardman 2009). This illustrates that energy poverty needs to be viewed as embedded in different expressions of social deprivation in rural areas, such as the shortage of affordable housing (Kordel and Naumann 2024), or rural poverty in general (Shucksmith et al. 2023).

Rural energy transitions have ambivalent impacts on the issue of poverty. On the one hand, new forms of electricity or heat generation can provide new income opportunities for rural areas. For example, the shift toward renewable energy can enable new modes of collective ownership of the energy provision that address issues of fuel poverty as well as economic and social development in rural communities, such as the establishment of energy communities (Morrison and Ramsey 2019). On the other hand, energy transitions can also be connected to the rising costs of fossil fuels and the need for existing buildings to be retrofitted. Furthermore, in regions that used to depend on the exploitation of fossil or nuclear energy sources, energy transitions can lead to job losses in these sectors -an issue that is closely connected to the rise of antienvironmental populism (Thorleifsson 2016).

In general, rural energy transitions tend to reflect existing social differences between urban and rural areas, as well as within and across rural regions and communities. Whereas some places (e.g., bioenergy villages or self-sufficient energy communities) are able to become actively involved in energy transitions and benefit from them, other places with fewer financial resources and social capital might largely be confronted with the detrimental impacts of energy transitions, without having the opportunity to shape their local trajectories (Hanke, Grossmann, and Sandmann 2023). This discrepancy raises numerous conflicts and is increasingly being coopted by right-wing populists.
sections.Rural Energy Populism:
The term rural populism (Jadhav 2021) illustrates the rural peculiarity of current populist movements. Rural concerns and issues have been increasingly coopted by populist movements in different countries (McCarthy 2019). A particular aim that echoes the antielitist element of populism (Mudde 2004) is to contest urban interests and transition narratives that make claims on rural areas, thereby creating tensions between urban and rural areas while neglecting their mutual coproduction within larger processes and structures of capitalist development (McCarthy 2025). On the one hand, populism preys on concerns about the expansion of renewables in rural areas and fears of rural livelihoods being converged and sacrificed to global and urban interests related to climate change (Wang, Maye, and Woods 2025b). On the other hand, populist rhetoric evokes and incites nostalgia and blame, thereby raising grievances directed toward the decline of fossil fuel industries in rural areas, along with a desire for their renaissance (Meyer 2022).

Hence, in recent years, energy infrastructures and the transformations they bring about have become an issue for right-wing populist mobilizations (Beveridge, Naumann, and Rudolph 2024). For example, Wanvik and Haarstad (2021) considered the right-wing populist resurgence against local energy transitions to merely represent ruptures and instabilities that are inherent in the transformation process toward sustainability. They, thereby omit the wider connections with the political-economic dynamics that exist. Further research has shed light on the populist struggles between renewable and fossil fuel industries (Knuth 2019), between different pathways and infrastructures of energy transitions (Batel and Devine-Wright 2018), or between the maintenance and decommissioning of fossil fuel infrastructures (Kojola 2019). In more detail, Batel, Valquaresma, and Alba (2024) explored the experienced territorial manifestations of renewable energy projects and far-right populist rhetoric in relation to the implications of the deployment of renewable energy in peripheral locations in Portugal.

As is often the case with right-wing populism in general, ' energy populism ' entails a specific rural dimension. Populist contestations over the locations of renewable energy infrastructures do not only often take place in rural regions (Dech  ezelles and Scotti 2022) but also focus on the ' values of rurality. ' Furthermore, infrastructural decline, deindustrialization, and the enclosure of land and natural resources in rural areas can serve as leverage points for rural populism. In that sense, the antienvironmental and anticlimate rhetoric of rural energy populism can be understood as a form of ideological backlash, responding to real and perceived threats to the economic position of rural regions ' left behind ' in global competition ( \_ Zuk 2025). Therefore, rural energy transitions are only one trigger for rightwing populism and they must be viewed in relation to additional issues that underlie and drive change in rural areas.

The main characteristics of right-wing populism such as the rejection of the established media, political institutions, forms of participation, and science can also be found in conflicts related to the realization of energy transitions (Haas et al. 2025). At the same time, rural energy transitions entail a potential for progressive change. Current efforts aimed at a decentralization of energy supply provide opportunities for new institutional solutions that provide ways for increased public participation and social equity within energy transitions (Becker and Naumann 2017), also in rural areas. For example, community energy projects facilitate energy democracy, aim to generate local benefits and deliver distributional justice (e.g., Creamer et al. 2019; Fichera et al. 2025). In summary, as pointed out by McCarthy (2025), rurally inflected populism has become an important element of contemporary politics that needs to be carefully considered when analyzing conflict dynamics related to rural energy transitions.
sections.From Rural Energy Transitions Toward a R:
As the three examples illustrate, energy transitions, in terms of the utilization and provision of renewable energy sources, and rural change are inextricably linked. The expansion of renewables has become increasingly entangled with specific problems, hardships, and wider challenges, but also hopes and desires within rural areas and for rural areas. The realization of energy transitions in rural areas has tangible consequences for their socioeconomic development. In turn, as land-use change, rural poverty and marginalization, and rural populism exemplify, rural change impinges on the possibilities and introduces barriers to the transformation of energy systems.

Therefore, we advocate for a more thorough contextualization and holistic understanding of rural energy transitions, one that situates them within general trends of rural change.

At first, such an understanding necessitates an extension of the empirical focus from energy to additional sectors in transition. Most prominently, this would need to involve the agricultural sector but also the transportation sector and efforts for their sustainable transformation, initiatives for sustainable water and waste management, the maintenance of social infrastructures, and the realization of housing justice. Such an extended focus would enable us to look at interlinkages and commonalities, along with contradictions, between different sectors of infrastructure provision and their transformations. There are numerous examples of such cross-sectoral linkages, such as the introduction of electric mobility, the energy retrofitting of affordable housing, and the use of wastewater and biofuels to generate heat and electricity.

Second, there is a need to connect different conceptual approaches to the establishment and formation of just and sustainable infrastructure futures; for example, the right to energy (Walker 2015), water

(Farhana and Loftus 2012), transportation (Sanchez and Brenman 2007), or housing (Rolnik 2014). Obviously, justice and sustainability have to be achieved through all of these (and many other) sectors and cannot be limited to one or only some of them. In turn, there is the need to elaborate the rural dimensions of these approaches, which brings us to our final point.

Third, various rights, forms of infrastructural justice, sustainability, democracy, and civic participation must become part of a ' right to the countryside ' (Barraclough 2013) to allow a ' good ' (Shucksmith 2018) or ' postcapitalist ' countryside (Gallent et al. 2025) that caters to its inhabitants, their livelihoods, and the their needs. Consequently, such rural futures question established paradigms of growth, the maximization of profit as well as the fierce competition between different rural places and regions. Like the extensive debates on the ' right to the city, ' its institutional forms, practical implementation, and contradictions, the ' right to the countryside ' requires further conceptual elaboration and practical operationalization. In that sense, the right to the countryside comprises not only just and sustainable energy provision, but also just and sustainable land use, housing, social infrastructures, and much more. A right to the countryside will not be exclusive for rural areas but needs to be considered in its entanglement and metabolism with urban regions as well (Charmes 2025). Likewise, it needs to be implemented locally but also incorporates further relations reaching beyond regions and nationstates that coconstitute rural spaces of crisis, conflict, and hope. Therefore, a right to the countryside entails new social and energetic spaces that are rural but at the same time ' glocal ' as well as ' rurban. '

As we briefly illustrated with this contribution, social change might start with the transition of energy infrastructures, but it goes far beyond it. Hence, rural energy transitions should be understood as an energy-related process rather than an energy-centered process. In a similar vein, they are addressing rural peculiarities but must go beyond them to become truly transformational. /H17039

Rural Energy Transitions and Rural Change

sections.Introduction: C urrent transformations of energy infrastructures shape the development of cities and regions. Rural areas, however, have been particularly exposed to various effects of climate change but also transformed by responses to these threats, including the implementation of adaptation and mitigation measures such as the development of wind farms, solar parks, and biogas facilities. Rural areas have reemerged as locations where current energy transitions toward the use of renewable energy resources are being materialized (Naumann and Rudolph 2020). Rural areas have already been affected and transformed by the extraction of energy resources and the building of infrastructure for the large-scale production of electricity and heat, but the decentralized and horizontal deployment of renewable energy requires larger surface areas due a to a lower power density (Huber and McCarthy 2017). The expansion of renewable energies additionally incorporates areas in the energy system that had previously been less affected by energy infrastructures. Current energy transitions have the potential to reshape regions or result in the abandonment of spaces that have been integrated into fossil energy systems. This will produce both new energy landscapes and postcarbon landscapes in rural areas (e.g., Lennon and Scott 2017; Batel 2020; Pasqualetti and Smardon 2025). Therefore, the peculiarities and implications of rural energy transitions deserve attention from research and practice. The example of energy, however,

illustrates that rural areas are not separate, isolated entities but have complex and uneven relations with urban agglomerations (e.g., Regier, Berka, and Hoicka 2025), for example, as ' energy peripheries ' (Golubchikov and O ' Sullivan 2020), as parts of ' peripheralization ' (Langguth 2025) or ' urban -rural exploitation ' (Kelly-Reif and Wing 2016). Furthermore, Woods ' s (2007) notion of the ' global countryside ' reminds us how rural places are intertwined with global flows of capital, resources, people, and information.

In turn, energy transitions have become formative elements of ' planetary rural geographies ' and how they are contoured (Wang, Maye, and Woods 2025a, 2025b). Planetary rural geographies have been proposed as a research agenda to incorporate rural areas as spaces of crisis, conflict, and hope (Wang, Maye, and Woods 2025a).
sections.Rural Energy Transitions and Rural Chang: Different modes of energy provision have historically influenced rural areas and have entailed specific challenges, while also presenting opportunities for rural development. From a geographical perspective, the transition from a system based on fossil fuels toward a system predominantly based on decentral, flexible, low-carbon, and renewable energy consists of more than just substituting fuels. It involves structural changes to the energy supply, distribution, and consumption of energy, as well as a reconfiguration of related spatial patterns of economic and social activities (Bridge et al. 2013). In what follows, however, we use the term energy transitions to merely focus on transformations on the side of energy supply and its energetic sources.

records.title: Geographical Disparities in Energy Access: Challenges and Opportunities for Ghana's Energy Transition
records.abstract: This study examines geographical disparities in energy access across Ghana, analyzing the spatial patterns and socioeconomic drivers that influence energy distribution. Using a mixed-methods approach combining geospatial analysis with statistical evaluation of regional data, the research reveals significant disparities between northern and southern regions, as well as between urban and rural areas. Although Ghana maintains an impressive national electrification rate of 89 percent, access varies dramatically from 99 percent in the Greater Accra region to as low as 61 percent in the Savannah region. The study identifies key factors contributing to these disparities, including proximity to power generation facilities, population density, and economic activity levels. Analysis of clean cooking fuel access shows similar spatial patterns, with liquified petroleum gas adoption ranging from 69 percent in Greater Accra to minimal levels in northern regions. The study proposes pathways for a just energy transition, emphasizing the role of decentralized renewable energy systems, public-private partnerships, and targeted policy interventions. Drawing lessons from successful initiatives in Kenya and Rwanda, the study provides actionable recommendations for addressing spatial inequities in Ghana's energy landscape. The findings contribute to the broader discourse on achieving universal energy access while highlighting the importance of geographical considerations in energy policy and infrastructure development.

Akwasi Adu-Poku a , Ivy Gladys Appiah b , and Francis Kemausuor a

a Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology, Ghana; b Multigeomatics Land, Mining, and Engineering Surveyors, Ghana

This study examines geographical disparities in energy access across Ghana, analyzing the spatial patterns and socioeconomic drivers that influence energy distribution. Using a mixed-methods approach combining geospatial analysis with statistical evaluation of regional data, the research reveals significant disparities between northern and southern regions, as well as between urban and rural areas. Although Ghana maintains an impressive national electrification rate of 89 percent, access varies dramatically from 99 percent in the Greater Accra region to as low as 61 percent in the Savannah region. The study identifies key factors contributing to these disparities, including proximity to power generation facilities, population density, and economic activity levels. Analysis of clean cooking fuel access shows similar spatial patterns, with liquified petroleum gas adoption ranging from 69 percent in Greater Accra to minimal levels in northern regions. The study proposes pathways for a just energy transition, emphasizing the role of decentralized renewable energy systems, public -private partnerships, and targeted policy interventions. Drawing lessons from successful initiatives in Kenya and Rwanda, the study provides actionable recommendations for addressing spatial inequities in Ghana ' s energy landscape. The findings contribute to the broader discourse on achieving universal energy access while highlighting the importance of geographical considerations in energy policy and infrastructure development. Key Words: clean cooking, electricity, energy access, energy transition, geographical disparities.

A ccess to modern energy services is a critical determinant of socioeconomic development and a cornerstone for achieving global sustainability targets (IRENA 2023). To measure progress toward United Nations Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 7.1 and for our future analysis, the International Energy Agency (IEA) defines energy access as a household ' s ability to reliably and affordably access both electricity and clean cooking facilities (IEA 2020). This access should provide enough energy to meet basic needs and, over time, reach the regional average for essential energy services. Official measures of access, however, often count only formal grid connections and registered energy providers, which could overlook the informal or illegal connections (e.g., shared meters, independent solar kits) that many Ghanaian households rely on.

O ' Sullivan 2020). Although significant progress has been made globally in expanding energy access, many regions, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa, continue to face profound challenges in bridging the energy divide (Bishoge, Kombe, and Mvile 2020; Omole, Olajiga, and Olatunde 2024). The 2024 SDG reports show that sub-Saharan Africa now accounts for 83 percent (or 570 million people) of the global access deficit in 2022, an increase from 50 percent in 2010 (United Nations 2024).

In recent years, there has been growing recognition of the importance of spatial dimensions in energy policy, highlighting how geography influences the distribution and accessibility of energy resources. The global initiative to achieve universal energy access by 2030, as outlined in SDG 7, underscores the necessity to tackle energy access disparities between and within countries (United Nations 2024). Disparities in energy access are often deeply entrenched in spatial inequalities, reflecting historical, socioeconomic, and infrastructural dynamics (Schafft, Brasier, and Hesse 2019; Golubchikov and Ghana is a leader in sub-Saharan Africa regarding electricity access, with an impressive national electrification rate of 89 percent (Energy Commission 2024). This achievement has resulted from decades of deliberate investments in energy infrastructure, policy reforms, and international collaborations. Ghana ' s energy sector has implemented significant initiatives, including the deployment of solar photovoltaic (PV) systems in the Northern, Upper East, and Upper West regions, which capitalize on the country ' s high solar irradiation. Additionally, the introduction of solar-powered minigrids in island and lakeside communities, such as those in the Volta Basin, has expanded electricity access to remote areas that are challenging to connect to the national grid (Adu-Poku et al. 2023). In the Ashanti region, the commissioning of the K1 Thermal Power Plant (formerly known as the AMERI Power Plant in the Western region) in 2024 marks another significant

<!-- image -->

milestone in boosting energy generation capacity (GRIDCo 2022; Volta River Authority 2024). This development aims to reduce transmission losses and enhance grid reliability in the middle belt of Ghana. Despite these advancements, substantial disparities persist in electricity access, particularly between northern and southern regions and between urban and rural areas.

Southern Ghana, home to major economic hubs such as Accra and Kumasi, has achieved nearuniversal access to electricity due to its proximity to energy generation facilities, higher population density, and concentrated economic activities (Energy Commission 2024). Conversely, northern Ghana continues to grapple with lower electrification rates, limited access to modern cooking fuels, and underdeveloped infrastructure. Similarly, whereas urban areas across the country enjoy relatively high levels of energy access, many rural communities remain underserved, facing both infrastructural and socioeconomic barriers to reliable energy, mirroring the subregional trend in rural electrification (Omole, Olajiga, and Olatunde 2024).

These spatial disparities in Ghana ' s energy landscape are influenced by a range of geographical and socioeconomic factors. Proximity to the national grid, population density, and levels of economic activity play pivotal roles in shaping energy access patterns. Access to clean cooking fuels such as liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) also follows a similar spatial pattern, with southern and urban areas enjoying better availability and affordability compared to northern and rural areas. These disparities not only highlight the inequities in Ghana ' s energy transition but also underscore the broader challenges of ensuring sustainable and inclusive energy development.

Globally, there are several successful initiatives aimed at bridging energy access gaps, many of which hold valuable lessons for Ghana. For instance, Rwanda ' s Renewable Energy Fund (REF) demonstrates the effectiveness of targeted public -private partnerships to expand off-grid solar plants in rural communities, a model that could be adapted to Ghana ' s northern regions (Climate Investment Funds [CIF] 2022). Similarly, Kenya ' s electrification efforts, through programs like the Last Mile Connectivity Project (LMCP) and Power Africa Off-grid Project (PAOP), particularly its focus on off-grid solar solutions, have significantly increased rural energy access, reducing dependence on fossil fuels and raising national access rates (USAID 2020; Davis 2021). In Bangladesh, the Solar Home Systems (SHS) program has transformed the energy landscape in remote areas by providing affordable and reliable solar energy solutions to millions of households (World Bank Group 2021). These initiatives underscore the importance of targeted, context-specific strategies that address the unique challenges of underserved regions while leveraging local resources and capacities.

Despite Ghana ' s progress and the wealth of global examples, gaps remain in the understanding and addressing of geographical disparities in energy access within the country. Existing research and policy efforts have often focused on aggregate electrification rates, overlooking the nuanced spatial patterns that characterize energy access and consumption (Mensah, Kemausuor, and BrewHammond 2014; Gyamfi, Modjinou, and Djordjevic 2015; Kemausuor and Ackom 2017). Furthermore, there is limited analysis of how geographical factors such as proximity to infrastructure, resource availability, and socioeconomic conditions shape energy access in different parts of Ghana. This gap in understanding not only limits the effectiveness of current policies but also constrains the ability to design interventions that are equitable, efficient, and sustainable.

This study aims to address existing gaps by examining the geographical disparities in energy access in Ghana and identifying pathways toward a just energy transition. Official statistics in Ghana, however, often rely on formally registered customers and energy service providers, potentially underrepresenting the true extent of energy access by excluding informal or illegal connections, which are common in slum areas and among low-income groups. Such informal access, often through unregulated or unsafe means, is prevalent in Ghana and complicates the energy access landscape. Although this study primarily uses official data due to availability, it acknowledges that actual disparities might be more pronounced when informal access is considered, highlighting the need for a nuanced understanding of energy access in policy planning. By combining geospatial analysis with statistical assessments and policy evaluations, the study seeks to provide a thorough understanding of how spatial factors affect energy access patterns. Additionally, it will explore strategies to bridge these gaps and contribute valuable insights to the ongoing discourse on energy transition, offering actionable recommendations for policymakers, energy planners, and other stakeholders.
sections.Methodology:
Study Area

Ghana, situated in West Africa, spans latitudes 4  44 0 N to 11  11 0 N and longitudes 3  11 0 W to 1  11 0 E, encompassing a total land area of 238,535 km 2 . The country ' s administrative structure comprises sixteen regions, each characterized by distinct geographical and socioeconomic features that significantly influence the distribution of energy infrastructure and patterns of energy access.

The country ' s electricity infrastructure is predominantly concentrated in the southern regions, with major power generation facilities distributed across strategic locations. The hydroelectric infrastructure includes the Akosombo hydroelectric plant (1,020 MW), Kpong hydroelectric plant (160 MW), and Bui hydroelectric plant (404 MW; Energy Commission 2024). Thermal power generation is centered around industrial hubs, with significant installations in Tema, Takoradi, and Aboadze. The transmission network extends approximately 6,472 kilometers, with sixty-eight bulk supply points consisting of high-voltage lines operating at 161 kV (76.5percent of the total circuit length), 69kV (3.4 percent of the total circuit length), 225 kV (1.5 percent of the total circuit length), and 330kV (18.6 percent of the total circuit length), whereas the distribution network comprises mediumand lowvoltage lines serving various communities across the country (GRIDCo 2022).
sections.Data Collection:
The study used the most recent disaggregated data available at the regional level, secondary data from multiple authoritative sources to examine electricity access patterns and cooking fuel usage across Ghana. Electricity access and demographic data were primarily sourced from the Ghana Statistical Service (GSS) Population and Housing Census 2021 (GSS 2022). Supplementary data on national and regional electrification rates were obtained from the Ghana Energy Commission and the Ministry of Energy ' s annual reports. These sources provided granular information on household energy usage patterns, differentiated by region.

Cooking fuel usage data were extracted from the 2021 Population and Housing Census, which provided detailed information on primary and secondary cooking fuel choices and accessibility to LPG distribution networks. This data set was particularly valuable in understanding the spatial distribution of clean cooking fuel adoption across different regions.

Infrastructure data were obtained through technical reports from GRIDCo and annual reports and maps. These documents provided comprehensive information about power plant locations and capacities, transmission line routes, distribution network coverage, and the spatial distribution of LPG marketing companies (LPGMCs) throughout the country. Solar resource potential was assessed using data and maps from Global Solar Atlas 1 and Solagis. 2
sections.Analytical Framework: The analytical framework adopted for this study combines geospatial and statistical methods to examine the spatial patterns and socioeconomic drivers of energy access disparities in Ghana. This dual approach allows a comprehensive understanding of energy access ' s physical and socioeconomic dimensions.
sections.Geospatial Analysis:
Geospatial analysis was to map and visualize disparities in energy access. Specific geospatial techniques, such as proximity analysis, were employed to examine the relationship between infrastructure availability and energy access levels. For instance, the locations of power plants were georeferenced using official coordinates from GRIDCo and other verified sources. The regions ' central points (centroids) were calculated, and proximity to power plants was determined using straight-line distances. These calculations were cross-validated with official infrastructure maps and reports from the Ghana Energy Commission to ensure accuracy.

The analysis also incorporated renewable energy potential data to assess the feasibility of deploying decentralized energy solutions in underserved regions. Solar irradiance data were spatially analyzed to identify optimal regions for renewable energy projects, particularly in northern Ghana, where grid extension is economically and logistically challenging.
sections.Statistical Analysis: Statistical analysis was conducted using Python to explore the relationship between energy access and socioeconomic factors. Correlation analyses were performed to quantify the influence of variables such as population, population density, and proximity to power plants on electricity and clean cooking fuel access. This analysis provided a nuanced understanding of the drivers of energy access disparities.

Proximity to power generation facilities plays a pivotal role in electricity access. For instance, Greater Accra, located 60 km from hydropower plants and 20km from thermal plants, exhibits the highest electricity access. Conversely, regions like Savannah and North East, situated 400 to 550km from central power plants, experience limited access due to higher transmission losses, infrastructure costs, and voltage drops. This highlights the critical need for decentralized energy systems to address access gaps in remote areas, particularly in northern Ghana.
sections.Clean Cooking Access and LPG Distributio:
Clean cooking access remains critically low at a national average of 37 percent, with stark regional disparities. Southern regions such as Greater Accra (69 percent), Western (38 percent), and Central (37 percent) lead in LPG adoption. These regions benefit from robust LPG distribution networks and higher household incomes, making clean cooking fuels more accessible. Greater Accra, for example, hosts 188 LPGMCs, far exceeding the numbers in northern regions such as Savannah (three) and North East (one), even though the Savannah and North East regions are several times larger than the Greater Accra region by land size.

In northern Ghana, households predominantly rely on traditional biomass fuels like firewood and charcoal. Savannah (95 percent), North East (95 percent), and Northern (88 percent) regions exhibit heavy dependence on firewood. This reliance, as shown in Figure 1, contributes to deforestation and indoor air pollution, exacerbating health and environmental challenges. Electricity for cooking remains minimal nationwide, with Greater Accra showing the highest adoption (10,116 households) due to its advanced electrification and economic status. Expanding LPG infrastructure and promoting alternatives like biogas are essential to addressing these disparities.
sections.Proximity to Power Plants and Infrastruc:
As shown in Figure 2, the correlation analysis provides valuable insights into energy access disparities. Proximity to power plants exhibits a strong negative correlation with access (Pearson ' s r ¼ -0.84), indicating that regions closer to generation sites have higher electrification rates. Regions like Volta and Eastern, located close to hydropower plants (80 km) and thermal plants (150 km), achieve high electricity access rates of 93 percent and 91 percent, respectively. By contrast, remote regions such as Savannah and North East, located 400 to 550 km from power plants, report access rates as low as 61 percent and 74 percent. This disparity arises from transmission losses, higher infrastructure costs, and voltage drops over long distances.

Population dynamics also play a significant role: A positive correlation of 0.65 was found between regional population size and electricity access, reflecting economies of scale, where larger populations incentivize investment in energy infrastructure. Urban regions like Greater Accra and Ashanti, with their large populations and economic activity, demonstrate this trend, achieving access rates of 99 percent and 96 percent, respectively. Even population density (in persons per square kilometer) correlates positively ( r ¼ 0.46) with access, although less strongly. Demographic variables alone, however, do not fully explain access patterns. For example, Ghana ' s electrification programs have sometimes been driven by political priorities, with infrastructure investments directed to support remote communities for electoral or strategic reasons (Briggs 2012). Such political factors can decouple the strict population -access relationship.

For clean cooking access, a similar but even stronger effect of population is observed, as clean cooking access correlates with population size ( r ¼ 0.91), underscoring the influence of urbanization and market dynamics. Urban regions like Greater Accra, with better infrastructure and higher incomes, lead in rates of LPG adoption. Conversely, rural regions such as Savannah and North East lag far behind due to limited LPG distribution and affordability challenges. These findings suggest that although population and infrastructure proximity are key determinants of energy access, they are interwoven with policy and investment choices that have reinforced urban -rural disparities.

sections.Urban -Rural Dynamics and Energy Inequit:
Regions with high urban populations, such as Greater Accra, Ashanti, and Central, demonstrate better energy access metrics due to concentrated economic activity, higher incomes, and advanced infrastructure. For example, Greater Accra region combines high electricity access (99 percent) with the highest clean cooking rates (69 percent) and LPGMC density. This urban advantage reflects economies of scale and prioritization in government policies.

By contrast, rural-dominated regions such as Savannah, North East, and Upper West face significant energy access challenges. Sparse populations increase the per-capita cost of grid expansion and LPG distribution, leaving many households reliant on traditional energy sources. These dynamics exacerbate energy inequities and highlight the need for targeted interventions in rural areas.

sections.Key Insights on Ghana ' s Energy Transit:
Spatial disparities in energy access significantly challenge Ghana ' s sustainable development goals. For instance, the lower level of electricity access in northern Ghana limits educational opportunities as schools struggle to provide lighting and power for digital resources. Health-care delivery is also hindered, with clinics facing difficulties running essential equipment and vaccine refrigeration. Furthermore, limited energy access curtails economic development, as businesses and industries in these regions cannot operate efficiently or expand. These combined impacts illustrate how uneven energy distribution perpetuates regional inequalities and undermines national development efforts. The results highlight how regional inequities in electricity and clean cooking fuel access undermine socioeconomic development and limit the country ' s progress toward achieving SDG 7. Regions in northern Ghana, such as Savannah, Upper East, and North East, lag in electricity access, with rates as low as 61 percent. These disparities are compounded by the physical remoteness of these regions, logistical challenges, and limited economic activity. Conversely, southern and urbanized regions like Greater Accra and Ashanti benefit from concentrated infrastructure investment and policy prioritization, achieving electricity access rates of nearly 100 percent.

In addition to geographical, socioeconomic, and infrastructural factors, political dynamics significantly shape energy access disparities in Ghana. Politicians often finance energy infrastructure projects as part of vote-seeking strategies, leading to development in remote locations with low population density and limited economic activity, which might not align with demographic or economic justifications. For instance, electrification projects under the National Electrification Project (NEP) and Self-Help Electrification Program (SHEP), by which communities and governments shared the cost of electricity access, have been influenced by political agendas, with resources sometimes disproportionately allocated to regions aligned with ruling parties. The SHEP was for communities within 20 km of existing 11/33 kV grid lines; where communities had to organize themselves and contribute some materials, like electricity poles for grid connection (IEA 2021). Towns vied with each other to be on the SHEP scheme, with communities putting up signboards that read ' Noelectricity, no vote. ' This politicization can both mitigate and exacerbate disparities, depending on whether investments prioritize politically strategic areas over those with greater energy poverty. Transparent and equitable energy planning, guided by objective criteria such as energy access needs, is essential to address these challenges effectively.

The findings align with global patterns observed in similar contexts, as highlighted in the literature. For example, the politicization of energy access in sub-Saharan Africa, as discussed by Briggs (2012), often leads to selective allocation of energy infrastructure, entrenching regional inequalities. MacLean et al. (2016), in their comparative analysis of Ghana and Uganda, also highlighted how divergent political histories have shaped citizens ' expectations for electricity access. For instance, the political dynamics highlighted by Cuesta Fern  andez (2018) are evident in our findings where subnational units significantly influence core -periphery linkages in electrification efforts. This is particularly apparent in the distribution of LPGMCs and grid infrastructure, which shows clear regional biases favoring southern and urban areas. The concept of electric territorialities proposed by Cuesta Fern  andez (2018) helps explain how these disparities become entrenched through political and infrastructural decisions.
sections.Policy and Implementation Gaps:
The study ' s findings reveal significant limitations in Ghana ' s energy policies, particularly in addressing regional and urban -rural disparities. Despite substantial progress in national electrification, policy frameworks often lack spatial considerations, focusing predominantly on aggregate access rates.

One critical gap is the uneven distribution of LPGMCs, which exacerbates clean cooking access disparities. Whereas the Greater Accra region hosts 188 LPGMCs, Savannah and North East regions have only three and one, respectively. This imbalance reflects broader policy failures to ensure equitable infrastructure deployment. Despite government efforts to promote clean cooking adoption, including the Clean Cooking Action Plan and the Rural LPG Promotion Program (RLP), which provides LPG stoves at no cost, evaluations have shown low sustained usage among beneficiaries (Broni-Bediako and Amorin 2018; Carri  on et al. 2021; Clean Cooking Alliance 2021). Moreover, the high upfront costs of clean cooking technologies, coupled with limited subsidies and financing options, further hinder adoption in rural areas (Dongzagla and Adams 2022).

Another limitation is the reliance on centralized energy systems, prioritizing urban and periurban regions due to their economic viability. This approach neglects remote and sparsely populated areas, where grid extension is economically unfeasible. Decentralized energy solutions, such as solar minigrids, remain underutilized despite their proven efficacy in addressing similar challenges in countries like Kenya, Rwanda, and Bangladesh.

Policy inconsistencies and political interference also undermine long-term energy planning. As demonstrated by Brass, Harris, and MacLean (2019), access to electricity has complex implications for political participation and citizen engagement. For example, Briggs (2012) reported that electrification projects under the NEP in Ghana were often influenced by political agendas, with resources disproportionately allocated to regions aligned with ruling political parties (World Bank Group 2010). Such practices resulted in the neglect of oppositionaligned regions and led to inefficiencies in energy infrastructure deployment. This inconsistent prioritization not only delays progress toward universal access but also deepens regional inequalities in energy access. Strengthening institutional frameworks and ensuring continuity in energy planning are essential to overcoming these challenges.
sections.Energy Access and the Energy Transition:
Achieving a just energy transition in Ghana requires strategies that prioritize equitable access to energy for all regions and socioeconomic groups. Decentralized renewable energy systems, such as solar minigrids and home systems, are critical for improving access in remote areas, particularly in northern Ghana, where solar potential is high (4.06 -4.45 kWh/kWp compared to 3.70 -4.10 kWh/kWp in the south). Challenges such as unreliable minigrid or off-grid electricity (Adu-Poku et al. 2023) and the capital costs of solar systems alongside energy-storage systems affect their adoption. A significant concern is the potential abandonment of decentralized systems on grid extension, as observed in contexts like Indonesia and Sri Lanka, where communities prefer centralized grid electricity due to social perceptions of reliability or cost (Tenenbaum, Greacen, and Vaghela 2018; Segura-Rodr  ı guez, Bhandari, and Sanogo 2025). In Ghana, grid unreliability and billing issues further complicate this dynamic, particularly in rural areas.

To ensure that decentralized renewable energy contributes to both energy access and a sustainable energy transition, policies must facilitate integration with the national grid. This includes technical standards for interconnection, feed-in tariffs to allow excess energy sales, and incentives for maintaining renewable systems after grid extension. Lessons from countries like India, with established minigrid regulations, and Kenya ' s off-grid energy policies suggest that hybrid systems combining grid and renewable sources can enhance sustainability. In urban areas, where grid access is high (e.g., 99 percent in the Greater Accra region), renewable energy adoption driven by cost declines and energy independence desires can reduce grid pressure, supporting the transition. A comprehensive strategy integrating rural and urban contexts, addressing grid reliability, and promoting equitable policies is essential for a just and sustainable energy transition in Ghana.

Furthermore, the Rwanda REF project highlights the importance of targeted and inclusive strategies in promoting private-sector-led off-grid renewable energy development (CIF 2022). This initiative provides lines of credit and creates an enabling environment for off-grid solar electrification. At the core of the project is the creation of lines of credit in local currency for financial institutions. These lines of credit are used to finance solar home systems, minigrids, and the solar companies that offer these solutions (CIF 2022). Local financial institutions leverage these funds to support private solar companies, enabling them to provide households with offgrid solutions through decentralized methods. Rwanda ' s solar power projects, such as the Agahozo Shalom Youth Village solar field, the first utilityscale, grid-connected solar project in East Africa. This demonstrates that intentional efforts can effectively close the energy access gaps faced by many communities. Kenya ' s electrification program also offers instructive lessons. Through initiatives like the LMPC, Kenya increased electricity access from 37 percent in 2013 to 79 percent in 2023 by connecting 9 million rural households (IEA 2025).

Concurrently, Kenya became a global leader in offgrid solar: In 2023 it accounted for nearly three quarters of all solar home systems sold in East Africa. These outcomes show the power of blending grid expansion with market-driven solar deployment. Ghana can emulate this approach by scaling up minigrid projects and innovative financing models (e.g., pay-as-you-go solar) alongside continued grid extension, ensuring both strategies work in tandem.

Renewable energy deployment should also be complemented by targeted policies that address socioeconomic barriers. Subsidies and financing mechanisms for clean cooking technologies, such as LPG and biogas, can enhance affordability and adoption in rural areas. Kenya ' s National Cooking Transition Strategy offers valuable lessons, demonstrating how multifaceted approaches involving policy implementation, private-sector participation, and innovative financing can drive progress (Ministry of Energy and Petroleum 2024). This approach has transformed Kenya ' s cooking sector into a sustainable and profitable industry, intending to achieve universal access to clean cooking technologies by 2028. Ghana can adopt similar models to mobilize resources and expertise for its energy transition.

International support is equally crucial. Development partners and multilateral organizations can provide technical assistance, concessional financing, and capacity-building initiatives to support decentralized energy projects and infrastructure development in underserved regions. By aligning these efforts with Ghana ' s broader development agenda, the country can achieve sustainable and inclusive energy growth.
sections.Conclusion:
This comprehensive study of geographical disparities in Ghana ' s energy access reveals complex patterns of inequity that must be addressed to achieve universal energy access and sustainable development. The research demonstrates that although Ghana has made remarkable progress in electricity access, achieving an 89 percent national electrification rate, significant regional disparities persist. These disparities are particularly pronounced between northern and southern regions, with access rates varying from 99 percent in Greater Accra to 61 percent in the Savannah region, reflecting deeper structural and socioeconomic inequalities.

The analysis reveals that proximity to power generation facilities, population density, and economic activity levels are key determinants of energy access. Urban regions benefit from concentrated infrastructure investment and economies of scale, whereas rural and remote areas face persistent challenges in grid connectivity and clean cooking fuel access. The study ' s findings on clean cooking access are particularly concerning, with stark disparities in LPG distribution networks and adoption rates between regions. The research also identifies significant opportunities, however, particularly in northern Ghana ' s superior solar resource potential. With specific PV power outputs ranging from 4.06 to 4.45 kWh/kWp, compared to 3.70 to 4.10 kWh/ kWp in southern regions, there is substantial potential for decentralized renewable energy solutions to address access gaps in underserved areas.

Drawing from successful examples in Kenya and Rwanda, the study demonstrates that targeted interventions and innovative approaches can effectively address spatial inequities in energy access. Success, however, requires sustained political commitment, robust institutional frameworks, and careful consideration of local contexts and needs. Future research should focus on developing more detailed implementation strategies for specific regions, evaluating the effectiveness of various policy interventions, and exploring innovative financing mechanisms to support energy infrastructure development in underserved areas. Additionally, continued monitoring and evaluation of progress toward energy access goals will be crucial for ensuring the effectiveness of implemented solutions.

The findings of this study contribute to our understanding of the spatial dimensions of energy access and provide insights for policymakers and planners. It highlights that achieving SDG 7 requires not only technological deployment but also deliberate attention to where and how energy services are provided. By addressing geographical disparities, Ghana can advance its energy transition in a way that is sustainable and inclusive, offering lessons for similarly situated countries in the pursuit of universal modern energy access. /H17039
