sections.Introduction:
C lassically, geopolitics, as it emerged over a century ago, has focused on the global, the imperial, and the national stages. Frequently, too, classical geopolitics invokes natural physical entities of land and sea, terrain, and relief, such as the ways that Hungarian geopolitical discourse took the Carpathian basin as a reference point (Balogh 2021). Organic understandings, enfolded from the outset as in Rudolf Kjell  en ' s ' The State as a Living Organism ' (Holdar 1992; Tunander 2001), evolved in the hands of right-wing nationalists and fascist regimes from the late 1930s. Similar subscriptions developed enduring focal points in Latin American military geopolitics, reflected in notions of the Left as a cancer to be eliminated from the body-politic, as in the widely promoted geopolitical narratives of the Chilean dictator Augusto Pinochet (Hepple 1992).

The development of critical geopolitics since the 1980s deconstructed and denaturalized such national and imperial discourses (  O Tuathail 1996) while positing alternative foci. Among other scales and sites, references to urban geopolitics have proliferated. As Bialasiewicz (2016) summed up:

Over the past decade, the term ' urban geopolitics ' has entered the policy as well as academic lexicon. In an oped piece published in the summer of 2012, Saskia Sassen prognosticated the emergence of a new sort of ' urban geopolitics, ' noting that from tackling environmental

geojds@nus.edu.sg questions to countering the threat of terrorism, in the decades to come it would be urban actors and city networks that would become key geopolitical actors and sites of geopolitics . (317, italics in original)

Although a valuable review of geopolitics and urban armed conflict in Latin America (Demarest 1995) had earlier surveyed urban counterinsurgency texts and revisited the literature on urban guerrilla warfare, it was Graham (2004b) who specified urban geopolitics as ' the telescoping connections between transnational geopolitical transformations and highly local acts of violence against urban sites ' (191). The wider expansion of references to urban geopolitics is relatively recent. A Research Companion to Critical Geopolitics (Dodds, Kuus, and Sharp 2013) published just over a decade ago contains neither chapter heading nor index references to ' urban, ' or ' cities, ' and a Google Ngram search reveals just how steep the growth of work citing ' urban geopolitics ' has been (Figure 1).
sections.Parameters of Urban Geopolitics: According to Spanu (2023) the turn to urban geopolitics means ' examining the connection between transnational geopolitical transformations, the production of space, and acts of violence at the urban scale ' (2). Describing urban geopolitics as ' a heterogeneous interdisciplinary engagement, ' Rokem and Boano (2023, 1671), noted, however, that ' generally it is not a theory-based approach -there is no ' urban geopolitical grand theory or theories '' (1672). Although chasing a grand theory might not be helpful, the stage is certainly ripe for careful examination and development of empirical and theoretical horizons.
sections.Surrounding the Cities from the Countrys: Although there are other examples of nationalist and conflict discourses that invoke the rural as a reservoir of national purity and attendant sacrifice, or conversely as contamination for a cosmopolitan city, such as those described regarding the wars accompanying the collapse of Yugoslavia by Jansen (2005) and Simmons (2001), one of most significant forms of geostrategic thought on city -countryside relations was born in twentieth-century China. The notion of the countryside surrounding the cities in a conflict was developed in the context of China ' s civil war and struggle against Japanese imperialism culminating in the communist victory on the Chinese mainland and Mao ' s proclamation of the People ' s Republic in Tiananmen Square on 1 October 1949. records.title: From Labor to Life in Vegetal Geography: Exploring Ontological Marginalization and Critical Externalities in the Plantationscape of a Global South Country
records.abstract: In the ever-expanding era of urbanization where the dominance of the urban human increasingly defines global society, marginalized subaltern groups in remote rural spaces remain stark reminders of systemic inequities. Nowhere is this more evident than in India, a rising superpower whose rapid growth paradoxically coexists with deep-rooted societal divides. Within its vegetal geographies, such as the tea plantations of the Global South, landscapes of cultivation are not merely sites of production; they are living terrains where plants, labor, and social hierarchies intertwine, reinforcing the very inequities that urban progress claims to transcend. This study explores the ontological marginalization within the tea plantationscape of the Dooars region in India. Ontological marginalization is conceptualized as the systematic exclusion of marginalized ways of being, rooted in colonial histories and perpetuated by modern socioeconomic systems. The findings reveal a paradox of livelihood duality. On one hand, subsistence practices rooted in collective labor, seasonal variability in livelihoods, and reciprocal exchange continue to sustain households. On the other, these practices are increasingly enmeshed in exploitative wage economies that define the vegetal geography of tea gardens. In this landscape, the very plants that anchor livelihoods also structure social relations, tying human survival to cycles of cultivation that reproduce dependency and marginality. The research reveals how historical disruptions, contemporary structural inequalities, and gendered dimensions of exclusion have perpetuated intergenerational poverty and systemic vulnerabilities. It argues that addressing ontological marginalization demands rejecting colonial development logics and embracing justice-based frameworks that value diverse ways of being, knowing, and surviving.

sections.From Labor to Life in Vegetal Geography::
Suranjan Majumder

Department of Geography and Applied Geography, University of North Bengal, India

In the ever-expanding era of urbanization where the dominance of the ' urban human ' increasingly defines global society, marginalized subaltern groups in remote rural spaces remain stark reminders of systemic inequities. Nowhere is this more evident than in India, a rising superpower whose rapid growth paradoxically coexists with deep-rooted societal divides. Within its vegetal geographies, such as the tea plantations of the Global South, landscapes of cultivation are not merely sites of production; they are living terrains where plants, labor, and social hierarchies intertwine, reinforcing the very inequities that urban progress claims to transcend. This study explores the ontological marginalization within the tea plantationscape of the Dooars region in India. Ontological marginalization is conceptualized as the ' systematic exclusion of marginalized ways of being, ' rooted in colonial histories and perpetuated by modern socioeconomic systems. The findings reveal a paradox of livelihood duality. On one hand, subsistence practices rooted in collective labor, seasonal variability in livelihoods, and reciprocal exchange continue to sustain households. On the other, these practices are increasingly enmeshed in exploitative wage economies that define the vegetal geography of tea gardens. In this landscape, the very plants that anchor livelihoods also structure social relations, tying human survival to cycles of cultivation that reproduce dependency and marginality. The research reveals how historical disruptions, contemporary structural inequalities, and gendered dimensions of exclusion have perpetuated intergenerational poverty and systemic vulnerabilities. It argues that addressing ontological marginalization demands rejecting colonial development logics and embracing justice-based frameworks that value diverse ' ways of being, knowing, and surviving. ' Key Words: developmental paradox, existential exclusion, indigenous livelihoods, ontological marginalization, vegetal geography.

T he concept of ontological marginalization, where certain lives are rendered existentially subordinate and excluded from legitimate political and human recognition, finds its most influential articulation within biopolitical thought, which locates governance as inherently producing zones of neglect and exclusion. Foucault ' s Society Must Be Defended lecture in 1976 instituted the ' shift ' from sovereign power to biopower: a form of governance that distinguishes between lives worth fostering and those that may be left to die, excluding certain groups at the level of their very being (Foucault 2003). This racialized administration of life constructs a ' biopolitical hierarchy ' in which marginalized populations, such as Indigenous and tribal communities, are governed as risks and anomalies rather than full political subjects. For Foucault, such marginalization occurs when groups are defined as naturally dangerous, inferior, or internal enemies, rendered less fully human within societal logics (Foucault 2003; Murray 2003; C. Taylor 2011). Extending this, Agamben (1998) theorized homo sacer as ' bare life, ' stripped of political value yet subject to sovereign force, crystallizing the condition of ontological marginalization. Whereas Foucault emphasized historical shifts in power regimes, Agamben universalized the logic of exception, producing a more metaphysical and juridical theory of exclusion. In the same milieu, Hardt and Negri (2000) argued that under late capitalism, life itself becomes the site of production and control, with the multitude simultaneously exploited and rendered ontologically malleable; their focus on collective resistance underscores the abstraction and disposability of subaltern life in a globalized order. Esposito ([2002] 2011), through his theory of Immunitas , reframed marginalization as a protective mechanism of the political community, negating ' othered ' life to preserve social coherence and enforcing exclusion through purification. Building on such critical engagements with the politics of life, Lemke (2011) provided the first systematic overview of biopolitics, offering a framework to understand how political power targets ' life itself ' as its explicit concern. Influenced by Foucault, Lemke examined how, in the modern era, politics increasingly aligns itself with biological laws, giving rise to forms of governance that regulate ' bare life ' and construct ' biological citizenship. ' He critiqued and expanded on the work of later theorists such as Giorgio Agamben, Hardt, and Negri, situating biopolitical mechanisms within the context of neoliberalism and bioscience. This orientation, however, carries problematic historical resonances, including eugenics and racism, underscoring the ambivalent and often exclusionary nature of biopolitical governance.

<!-- image -->

Positioned within the broader framework of ethnic marginality, biopolitical mechanisms take concrete form in the erasure of tribal and Indigenous ontologies in the Global South. Urbanization, as both demographic process and epistemic project, privileges the urban, mobile, rational citizen while casting remote-dwelling tribal communities into zones of invisibility and ontological liminality. In the current era of relentless urban expansion and the global ascendancy of the ' urban human ' paradigm, subaltern Indigenous and tribal groups remain confined to remote rural geographies, especially in the Global South. This urban-centric trajectory fosters a global sociospatial condition in which modernity, development, and citizenship are increasingly defined through urban logics (Parnell and Robinson 2012; Randolph and Storper 2023). India, as a rapidly ascending global power, exemplifies this paradox: Whereas its cities reflect global capital flows and technological growth, its tribal communities, such as the Oraon, 1 continue to face deep structural inequalities and exclusion from dominant sociopolitical frameworks (Nagendra et al. 2018). Within this developmental matrix, ontological marginalization serves as a critical lens for examining how certain ways of being, knowing, and relating to place are systematically rendered illegible within hegemonic systems of knowledge and governance (Shah 2007; Soguk 2007; Duarte and Belarde-Lewis 2015).

Rooted in critical theory, existential philosophy, and decolonial thought, the concept underscores how dominant paradigms of modernity construct hierarchies of being that exclude tribal and Indigenous ontologies from what is deemed real, legitimate, or human. As Fanon (1952) argued, colonial systems imposed an ontological rupture that reduced the colonized to objects devoid of subjectivity. Building on this, Wynter (2003) and Maldonado-Torres (2007) showed how coloniality continues to structure the postcolonial world through a racialized ' genre of Man ' that situates Black, Indigenous, and other racialized communities outside full humanity. This resonates with Peterson ' s (2015) insight on emplacement, wherein marginalized groups, despite economic deprivation, remain rooted in relational geographies, defying erasure through cultural endurance and place-based identity.

Recent scholarship shows that emplacement and relational personhood endure as acts of resistance and cultural survival. Far from vestiges of a premodern past, these alternative ontologies contest the extractive and homogenizing logics of capitalist urbanism. Addressing ontological marginalization thus demands a radical epistemic shift, redefining who and what is recognized as fully human within the frameworks of development, modernity, and the state.

India ' s sociocultural fabric has been shaped by successive waves of coerced displacement, ecological adaptation, and political conquest. As Kosambi ([1956] 2008) noted, India ' s history is not merely dynastic but a layered social history grounded in material conditions and the movement of peoples across diverse ecological zones. Colonial rule brought extensive displacement and dispossession to tribal communities of central India, particularly those from the Chotanagpur Plateau (Guha 1988; Damodaran 2006). To frame such uprooting as ' migration ' sanitizes historical violence and erases the lived experience of ontological marginalization, obscuring the coercive nature of displacement and the exploitative systems of indentured and corv  ee labor imposed on these communities (Guha 1988).

The marginalization of tribal communities, including the Oraon, is illuminated when situated within the evolution of geographical thought on human -environment relations and sociospatial stratification. Classical determinists like Ratzel and Semple emphasized environmental factors in shaping societies, positing that ecological advantages facilitated sociopolitical dominance. Although critiqued for determinism, this framework informed later theories such as G. Taylor ' s (1936) zones and strata model , which argued that successive waves of settlement pushed earlier racial or ethnic groups into environmentally marginal regions. In India, this produced concentric sociocultural zones in which newer arrivals occupied resource-rich cores, while Indigenous populations were relegated to peripheral spaces. For instance, in the colonial tea plantations of North Bengal, settlement policies reserved resource-rich cores for elites, such as planters, while relegating migrated indentured labor groups to the peripheries, thereby creating enduring socioeconomic dependency. The continued vulnerability of tribal communities thus reflects a persistent spatial logic in which access to ecological resources and proximity to political power determine ontological positioning within the Indian sociospatial hierarchy (Guha 1988; Chattopadhyay 2014).

Building on this, Soja ' s (2010) concept of spatial justice enriches the analysis by revealing how power operates spatially to create ' center ' and ' periphery, ' both geographically and in social consciousness. This spatial displacement was not uniform or absolute, however. In this light, Bendapudi ' s (1958) notion of negative areas , remote, resource-rich landscapes often avoided by mainstream settlement yet inhabited by tribal groups, shows that ecological richness does not equate to political and social advantage. Thus, while Indigenous communities might initially retain control over resource-rich areas but remain confined to isolated and less productive zones, they continue to be marginalized in terms of political power and socioeconomic inclusion. For example, tribal communities in the resourceabundant forests of the Chotanagpur Plateau remained marginalized politically and economically despite controlling these negative areas . The Oraon tribe ' s historical habitat in the Chotanagpur Plateau and surrounding uplands exemplifies this dual marginalization: Ecologically resource-rich yet distant from political centers and socially displaced through centuries of agrarian expansion, colonial plantation economies, and postcolonial development-induced displacements perpetuated ontological marginalization.

Harvey ' s critique of spatial inequalities, rooted in capitalist relations, frames spatial inequality not as mere physical distance but as a structural product of uneven development and capitalist exploitation, continually reshaping the socioeconomic landscapes of communities like the Oraon. First displaced under colonial extractive regimes and later marginalized by postindependence development dilemmas, the Oraon experienced the colonial imposition of administrative grids, economic logics, and ideological chronologies, which fractured their ontological unity, what was called the ' homogeneous, empty time of modernity ' imposed on ' plural, lived temporalities. ' Thus, their marginalization is not only spatial, social, or economic, but also a biopolitical production of ' life-as-risk, ' ' life-as-surplus, ' and ' life-as-outside. '

This article begins by contextualizing the research setting and outlining the ethnographic research design used to gather data from Oraon households. Subsequently, I 2 examine the concept of ontological marginalization across conceptual, narrative, and quantitative dimensions within the contexts of livelihood stress and diversification. Employing an ethnographic livelihood perspective, I analyze intersecting relationships beyond the immediate confines of village boundaries, focusing on contemporaneous dynamics rather than longitudinal trajectories (Clendenning 2024). Finally, I discuss how adopting a livelihood deprivation lens enhances data triangulation while presenting inherent challenges in portraying the complexities of marginalization.

sections.Dualism in Geography of Backwardness: Eq:
When the government comes with promises of development, we are the ones who always lose our forests, land, and homes. Who is this development really for? (#R49, M, Grassmore TG)

The preceding quote captures the irony of pseudodevelopment, a phenomenon I observed during my doctoral field work in a rural tea garden in the Dooars region, at the foothills of the Darjeeling Himalaya. This apprehension, ' progress ' for some and ' disposability ' for others, emerged intensely through interviews and focus group discussions, which revealed among Oraon inhabitants a sense of exclusion not limited to poverty and neglect but extending to invisibility within developmental discourse: a basic absence from contexts defining modern progress (Paradies 2020). What surfaced was not only the irony of pseudo-development, where ' growth ' narratives mask deepening precarity, but also the existential ' weight of being ' relegated to the periphery of normative imaginaries of citizenship, value, and development.

In India, where blunt wealth divides reinforce social stratification and economic expansion coexists with entrenched hierarchies, development programs claiming to foster inclusivity often reproduce structural inequalities. They displace and dismantle Indigenous forms of life, disrupt relational economies, and impose extractive logics on already vulnerable communities (Byrd et al. 2018; Paradies 2020; Clendenning 2024). This is absolute in the plantationscape 3 of Dooars, where the Oraon, historically recruited into colonial tea plantations, continue to earn subsistence wages under labor regimes replicating colonial succession of command. This article examines how the Oraon persist within and respond to systemic marginalization. Following Peterson ' s (2015) framing of emplacement as ontological resilience, their continued inhabitation of tea gardens is recited not as inertia but as a relational survival strategy. They do not merely reside in these geographies; they exist through them, resisting displacement despite persistent hardship.

This study further contributes to debates on rural marginality and the geography of backwardness by foregrounding multiple deprivations, the simultaneous experience of economic, infrastructural, and symbolic exclusion. Geographical isolation compounds these vulnerabilities, producing chronic underfunding of public infrastructure and restricted access to state services (Woods 2009; Peterson 2015; Majumder 2025a). Yet, despite these constraints, communities remain anchored to place, reflecting not passivity but an ontological commitment to land, memory, and identity.
sections.Historical Foundations of Marginalizatio:
Historically, Oraon social structures centered on collective labor and reciprocal exchange, fostering solidarity and equitable resource sharing. These systems were disrupted by colonial interventions and later neoliberal state policies, which formalized land ownership and replaced shared governance with private landholding (Majumder 2025a). Colonial land revenue systems (Guha 1968, 1980) prioritized extraction and surplus production, displacing the Oraon from ancestral lands and weakening mutual labor exchange, thereby introducing new stratifications. Land alienation became widespread, pushing many to forest fringes, a legacy that continues today, intersecting with postcolonial development agendas, industrial expansion, and displacement.

As one elder from Abhihill Tea Garden lamented:

The land that once sustained our ancestors now operates by others. Four generations ago, we were compelled to leave our ancestral homeland and were resettled here … laboring in the tea garden. We have spent our entire lives working relentlessly, hoping for a better livelihood, decent living conditions, and enough food for our families. Nothing has truly changed. (#R56, M, Abhihill TG)

The preceding testimonial underscores the persistent dissonance between externally imposed development models and the community ' s intrinsic rights to livelihood, identity, and territorial belonging. Experiences of dispossession reveal the compounded effects of state-led interventions, capitalist market forces, and urban expansion, which not only reproduce intergroup inequalities but also erode intracommunity solidarities and traditional mechanisms of equity. Like many rural working-class groups, the Oraon remain distanced from political engagement; economic marginalization extends beyond material deprivation to political exclusion (Majumder 2025a, 2025b). Dependence on low-wage labor and landlessness limits their capacity for collective action, as survival needs override political participation. As Spivak (1988) noted, subaltern groups struggle to access platforms for expression, leaving their concerns absent from mainstream discourse. This aligns with Marx ' s assessment of ' class domination, ' where the ruling class wields the state to perpetuate economic and social inequities (Marx and Engels 2023), further restricting the Oraons ' visibility in governance and policymaking (Guha 1980).

In the Dooars, the (re)settlement of the Oraon reflects a historical and ontological rupture rooted in colonial displacement. From the Chotanagpur Plateau, they were forcibly migrated to North Bengal to meet indentured labor demands in the tea plantations (Xaxa 1992; Sarkar 2017). Coercive mobility, driven by land alienation, indebtedness, and the collapse of indigenous agriculture under colonial revenue systems, shifted livelihoods from self-sufficient farming to precarious plantation work (Xaxa 1992; Deb 2022). The tea plantation system entrenched socioeconomic dependence through exploitative labor relations, curtailed autonomy, and cultural erosion (Thompson 1959; Bhowmik 1981), disrupting traditional knowledge systems and subjecting the Oraon to enduring marginalization under both colonial and postcolonial labor regimes (Purkayastha 2015; Sarkar 2017).

sections.Case Study, Methods, and Settings:
This study is based on a cross-sectional, ethnographic investigation conducted over fifteen months, employing a mixed-methods approach at the household level. The site, also the primary field location for my doctoral research, enabled sustained engagement with the Oraon community and deeper contextual understanding. Data collection (July 2022 -September 2023) combined semistructured interviews, participant observations, case histories, and social mapping. Using purposive sampling, the Draft Electoral Roll of 2020 identified areas of high Oraon concentration in Jalpaiguri district, with Mal subdivision selected for its spatial variation and demographic density.

Mal subdivision, located in the Dooars region at the foothills of the Sikkim Himalayas, includes three community development blocks (Mal, Matiali, and Nagrakata), further divided into twenty-two Gram Panchayats (Figure 1). This population-based observational study employed both ethnographic observations and a systematic ' door to-door ' household survey, using a predesigned interview schedule. Random sampling selected 200 households per block (total 600 households; 2,909 individuals), with 487 male- and 113 female-headed households. The sample was designed using Daniel ' s (1999) formula for infinite populations, ensuring statistical robustness. The methodological rigor was further enhanced through landscape transect walks and repeat visits in late 2023 and early 2024, providing comprehensive insights into the socioeconomic and cultural dynamics of the Oraon community.

A geotagging approach based on geographic information systems was employed to spatially triangulate data, providing a localized spatial representation of sampled households and enabling comparative neighborhood visualization. Each household was geotagged as a point feature using geographic coordinates, facilitating spatial analysis within the study area. Household surveys were administered with the partial support of field investigators (Figure 2). Surveys were conducted in Bengali, Hindi, Sadri, and Kurukh (the latter used minimally), with Sadri serving as the primary communication medium. A presurvey training session was conducted for field investigators, covering research objectives, survey protocols, and data collection techniques, supplemented by field demonstrations. Twelve in-depth interviews with key stakeholders (village headmen, Panchayat Pradhan, nongovernmental organization [NGO] workers, teachers) and five focus group discussions provided historical and contextual perspectives on marginalization, sustainable livelihoods, conflict, displacement, land acquisition, economic negotiation, and social contestation. This integrated design allowed for robust triangulation of qualitative, quantitative, and spatial insights.

sections.Fragments of Ontological Marginalization:
Modern governance in the Global South selectively supports certain populations while consigning others to systemic neglect and the slow violence of abandonment. For the Oraon community and other marginalized groups inhabiting forested landscapes, tea plantation belts, and tourism circuits, livelihoods are neither static nor merely adaptive; they arise at volatile intersections of traditional subsistence economies, informal labor regimes, and violent restructuring of land and resource access under late-capitalist expansion. Everyday survival becomes an act of navigating spaces of dispossession, contested territorialities, and abandonment.

Unlike many tribal communities in eastern and central India engaged in marginal farming or forest economies, the Oraon in this study are intrinsically pushed into the tea plantation economy, possessing little or no agricultural land and lacking viable livelihood diversification. Dependence on shadow plantation economies, combined with state neglect, perilous leasehold settlements, and landlessness, produces a form of entrapment where shifting capabilities is unattainable. This establishes marginality across generations, reproducing not only economic deprivation but also ontological exclusion, shaped by illicit arrangements, 4 seasonality, and chronic unemployment. Ethnographic and quantitative mapping reveal multifunctional socioeconomic dynamism within this marginality, arising from processes of simultaneous ' inclusive exclusion ' and ' exclusive inclusion, ' where state-led development and market forces seize land, water, and labor while eroding social and cultural capital. In this paradox, inclusion within development frameworks becomes another form of exclusion (Figure 3).

Based on observations and narrative accounts integrated into a geographical perspective, four interconnected ontological dimensions emerge, shaped by historical processes of systemic exclusion, entrenched contemporary backwardness, and intersecting identities. First, the Oraon experience marginalization at the level of ' being and recognition ' (Deb 2022; Majumder 2025a), as their Scheduled Tribe identity is filtered through exclusionary discourses, erosion of indigenous knowledge systems, and enduring stereotypes that restrict mobility and erase cultural presence.

Second, their inability to secure food, shelter, and clean water reflects structural abandonment rather than mere economic failure; reliance on precarious, low-wage, seasonal labor positions them in chronic existential insecurity (Majumder 2025b).

Third, education remains largely inaccessible, constrained by poverty, poor infrastructure, and structural demands for child labor, representing not just an unfulfilled right but exclusion from systems that could expand futures (Banerjee 2015; Sarkar 2019).

Finally, fragile economic conditions, ranging from insecure tea garden work to exploitative forest-based labor, signify a forced adaptive existence in which traditional ways of life are dismantled without viable alternatives. Dispossessed and confined to precarious labor markets, the Oraon are rendered visible only as ' surplus labor, ' and their claims to space, dignity, and futurity are systematically denied. The denial of land rights is embedded in state interventions, capitalist enclosures, and exclusionary legal frameworks (Guha 1985, 1988; Bhandar 2018; Sarkar 2019).

sections.Epistemic Exclusion: Living as the ' Per:
In Mal subdivision, the Oraon tribe endures entrenched deprivation and prejudice, rooted in the convergence of historical marginalization and present socioeconomic challenges. Despite being among the most populous tribal communities in the region, the Oraon remain systematically excluded from mainstream development, perpetuating material and existential vulnerabilities. This exclusion undermines their capacity to sustain cultural heritage, safeguard traditional practices, and envision futures beyond poverty and discrimination (Majumder 2025a).

Colonial land alienation and state-led development projects have produced landlessness, displacement, and the erosion of subsistence livelihoods, forcing a shift toward low-paying, insecure wage labor. This dependence on precarious employment limits their socioeconomic agency. The nexus of deprivation and prejudice transcends economic hardship, manifesting in persistent social discrimination and stigmatization. Such prejudice operates through restricted access to resources, ethnicized hierarchies that cast them as ' inferior, ' and the constraining of aspirations through deep-rooted stereotypes about the community ' s worth.

During the field survey, it became evident that the Oraons ' deprivation and lack of opportunities are rooted in systemic neglect, perpetuating a cycle of poverty. The lack of infrastructure and effective government support compounds their marginalized status, leaving them trapped in poverty with limited opportunities for advancement. One respondent illustrated the situation, their words tinged with sadness.

I always read about the ideals of equality and justice. However, in reality, my experiences have shown me the opposite. My perspective on society changed drastically when I completed my graduation. I noticed how differently people were treated. . . . I am the only one in my house and in my village, who pursued higher education, despite facing enormous challenges. It did not take long for me to see the stark inequalities between social classes. People judged us based on our appearance, the way we speak, and how much money we have. (#R23, M, Mathachulka)

He further elaborated on the situation with a tone of sadness, ' The desperation and prejudice I witnessed were not isolated events … part of a system that continues to damage the lives and livelihoods ' (#R23, M, Mathachulka).

Such perceptions lead to social exclusion, depriving individuals of their ontological standing as ' equal ' members of society. This aligns with belief of a ' failure of recognition, ' where the denial of recognition ' harms ' identity formation itself (Cooke 1997).

Studies indicate that persistently low incomes and exclusion from formal financial systems compel tribal communities to rely on local moneylenders, entrenching cycles of indebtedness, poverty, and eventual land dispossession (Mohindra, Haddad, and Narayana 2006; Meher 2007; Estrada-Carmona et al. 2020). These structural constraints are compounded by socioeconomic marginalization and culturally embedded livelihood practices (Maharatna 2000). Health insecurity further deepens this precarity: In remote tribal settlements, limited health-care infrastructure and the prohibitive cost of transport to urban facilities heighten vulnerability. Approximately two-thirds of residents depend on local ' quacks, ' herbal remedies, and home-based treatments; formal care, when accessed, is often through tea garden dispensaries, which remain inadequate for chronic and serious conditions. Such cases are typically referred to Mal Hospital, an underresourced facility physically and economically distant from most settlements. The spatial isolation of tea gardens, even when urgent medical attention is needed, exemplifies how territorial marginalization constrains the Oraon community ' s mobility, forecloses their choices, and establishes their position within what might be described as zones of sociospatial neglect, stripping them of ' mobility and choice. '

The intergenerational narratives gathered during field work reveal a profound temporal dislocation (Box 1 and 2). Elders recall ancestral land lost decades ago, forests transformed into plantations, whereas their descendants can neither reclaim nor even imagine return. The story of Sukanta (Box 2) encapsulates a life fractured across generations: a childhood in deprivation, children lost to accidents, and an old age bereft of care or continuity. This fracture between memory, present suffering, and any conceivable future exemplifies how colonial time (denial and forced labor) and neoliberal time (migration and wage work) collide with Indigenous temporalities grounded in community, seasonality, and ancestral continuity.

The absence of adequate support for Sukanta ' s son and wife (Box 2) or of modern agricultural tools for Subodh (Box 1) shows how the community ' s needs and aspirations are dismissed, their humanity unrecognized by state and society. Despite expertise in local agroforestry and tea cultivation, Oraon voices remain excluded from development planning, a systematic exclusion rooted in institutional prejudice that renders tribal needs ' peripheral ' and sustains their status as ' other ' within the polity. This silencing constitutes an ontological denial, making Oraon perspectives inconsequential. Their heavy reliance on quacks and traditional healers, rather than certified doctors, further reflects the institutional neglect and discrimination perpetuating their Box 2. Born into deep poverty, sixty-seven-year-old Sukanta has endured a lifetime of physical frailty and emotional hardship. Married at fifteen, with two sons, he began tea garden work early but could not afford his children ' s education, foreclosing their prospects for upward mobility. His only perceived option was to send them out of state as construction laborers. Modest financial improvement was shattered when his wife suffered a paralytic stroke following a heart attack. Six years ago, both sons returned home briefly; soon after, a two-wheeler accident left the elder son disabled and claimed the younger ' s life.

Box 1. Subodh, 5 a forty-six-year-old marginal landholder and farmer in Bidhannagar Gram Panchayat of Matiali block, has endured the harsh realities of deprivation throughout his life. The land he cultivates has been passed down through generations of his family, but without access to modern agricultural techniques, irrigation support, or any substantial government aid. His yields are often low, and his family struggles to make ends meet. Alongside this material deprivation, Subodh faces the persistent societal prejudice that marginalizes his community as ' backward ' or ' primitive. ' This stigma, rooted in entrenched caste and racial hierarchies, prevents many Oraon individuals, including Subodh, from accessing opportunities that are readily available to other, more privileged groups. Prejudice in this context operates not only in the economic sphere, where access to resources is unequal, but also in social and educational contexts, where the community ' s potential is undermined by discrimination. This prejudice creates a cyclical pattern of exclusion, limiting upward mobility and reinforcing the marginalization of indigenous communities like the Oraon.

Asked about treatment for his son, Sukanta recounted repeated but futile attempts to secure help, and empty promises from others, ' prohibitive transportation costs to the nearest medical college 78km away, ' and his ' inability to carry ' his disabled son. Now, too frail for regular work, he survives through ' occasional odd jobs for neighbors, ' food donations, and a cow that offers minimal sustenance.

Sukanta ' s life reveals prejudice operating on multiple fronts. Economic prejudice is embedded in his position as an Oraon, excluded from development programs and viable economic opportunities. Institutional prejudice is evident in the absence of state support despite acute need, reflecting how tribal populations are structurally bypassed by welfare mechanisms. Social prejudice emerges in perceptions of his community as less capable or deserving, reinforcing systemic neglect. Together, these intersecting prejudices entrench a cycle of deprivation, curtailing access to health care, eroding survival capacity, and perpetuating intergenerational inequality. Sukanta ' s experience is not an isolated misfortune but a manifestation of broader structural marginalization in which survival ' itself ' becomes a precarious, daily negotiation.

marginalization. Social and institutional rejection thus reinforces their alienation, trapping them in cycles of poverty and ontologically framed prejudice.
sections.Denied Essentials: Living at the ' Limit:
The Oraon tribe in the Mal plantationscape endures precarious living conditions, reflected in the dilapidated state of housing (Figures 4 and 5). The lack of stable shelter reinforces structural vulnerability and perpetuates marginalization. Among tea garden workers, employer-provided houses are typically semipermanent, yet many fall into kaccha 6 or semikaccha categories, and even semi-pucca 7 dwellings often lack durability and basic amenities. Kaccha homes, built with mud and bamboo walls and tin, thatch, or clay-tiled roofs, are highly vulnerable to rain, leakage, and flooding.

Housing conditions reveal more than material scarcity; they embody ontological marginalization. One respondent (#R25, F, Sukhanibasti) described ' decades of overlooking ' that left ' roofs leaking and walls collapsing ' during rains. Another respondent (#R28, F, Grassmore TG) recalled a roof ' partially repaired more than a decade ago ' but never since, due to financial constraints. Rain disrupts sleep, rooms fill with water, and containers are placed under leaks to manage intrusion. Such dwellings, lacking permanence and formal ownership of homestead land, are not simply ' homes in disrepair ' ; they materialize a history of being overlooked, rendering Oraon habitation politically and existentially invisible to the state as ' permanent or worthy. '

The struggles of the Oraon community go beyond the visible decay of housing, permeating the very core of their daily existence through aggregate downgrading. Here, marginalization also saturates basic utilities, particularly water and sanitation (Figure 4). Nearly two-thirds of households rely on unprotected wells for drinking water, with some using untreated river water. Seasonal extremes intensify risks: Summers bring shortages as the water table declines; ' monsoon rains contaminate open wells, leaving water dirty and dark with a foul stench ' (#R3, M, Dakshin Khalpara). Such dependence is inherited -' What my parents did and what most people in my village do ' (#R11, M, Jogesh Chandra TG) -and persists despite recurring health problems. Safer, protected sources installed by a few garden authorities remain inaccessible to those ' residing in far-off areas ' (#R3), reflecting how spatial exclusion deepens basic and everyday infrastructural neglect. Sanitation indicators are equally stark: Only onefifth of households have enclosed facilities for exclusive family use, whereas over a quarter of respondents practice open defecation due to absent infrastructure. The normalization of such practices stems not from cultural preference but from infrastructural absence, an emblem of deeper ontological backwardness.

The absence of dignified housing, clean water, and safe sanitation in Oraon tea garden settlements is not merely a symptom of poverty; it represents a deeper form of ontological backwardness, one that positions this community in a condition of disposability (Figure 5). As noted by a local NGO member, ' lacking legal protection over housing and homestead land, many workers remain confined to overcrowded, deteriorating quarters, without security of tenure or inheritance rights '-a situation that ' disproportionately affects women and non-working dependents. ' Displacement often pushes families toward forest-fringe villages or informal settlements, where they again lack formal land rights (Pattas) and tenure recognition.

This condition resonates with Mbembe ' s (2003) theoretical framework of necropolitics, which conceptualizes sovereignty as operating through the regulation of life and death. In this context, the systematic exclusion of households from essential services, health care, potable water, and secure housing constitutes a mode of spatial abandonment, rendering their lives governable only in terms of survival and disposability. Such geographies of exclusion are not accidental developmental deficits; they are deliberately maintained architectures of marginality, sustained through infrastructural neglect and economic extraction.

As one Oraon political leader aligned with the current opposition observed, the persistent denial of necessities signals more than neglect, it reflects an ' active refusal to recognize them [tribal indentured workers] as full citizens, entitled to dignity and care. ' In his words, their suffering has become ' routine, absorbed into the bureaucratic and social order, ' marking material deprivation from the symbolic and institutional life of the state.

The ontological marginalization of the Oraon community becomes starkly evident when material deprivation intersects with deeper epistemic and existential exclusions. This goes beyond deficits in wealth and infrastructure, revealing how the community ' s way of life, daily choices, and survival strategies are rendered invisible, devalued, and dismissed. A forty-six-year-old household head described his socioeconomic vulnerabilities as, ' I felt trapped in a relentless cycle of economic and social anxiety. I was exhausted from trying to meet the immediate demands of my family, let alone imagining a better future for my children … desperately wished to escape this trap and help lift my family members out of the darkness that had descended upon us ' (#R17, M, Ranicherea TG).

In the region, forest products remain the primary fuel source for most Oraon households, with only a small share using liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) or cow dung. Although many accessed LPG through the Pradhan Mantri Ujjwala Yojana (PMUY), regular use was constrained by rising refill costs (Figure 5). Surveys indicate that despite initial adoption, some households reverted to traditional fuels. As one respondent observed: ' It is paradoxical that the government subsidized our LPG connection, but we do not have enough means to actually use it ' (#R24, F, Abhihill TG). This remark, although seemingly economic, ontologically exposes the disjuncture between the state ' s developmental logic and the community ' s lived realities. The PMUY, launched under the promise of modernity and upliftment, presumes beneficiaries can transition to ' clean ' energy. Yet for respondents like R24, the subsidy is hollow, signaling inclusion without enabling it. Statistically recognized as a scheme beneficiary, she remains existentially excluded, her capability to act on that ' inclusion ' undermined by persistent poverty.

This sentiment is echoed by another respondent: ' LPG prices keep rising, but our wages stay exactly the same ' (#R15, F, Matiali TG). She underscores the stagnancy of their socioeconomic condition, where inflation and neoliberal cost-push policies operate within a vacuum of wage immobility and organizational neglect. Marginalization here means being trapped in a system where economic agency is frozen, expected to mirror the consumption patterns of others but denied the means and dignity to do so. Another woman noted, ' the main fuel of our cooking is wood collected from neighborhood and forest … we do this work regularly …' (#R33, F, Sathkaya TG). This status quo reveals both economic imperatives and conflicting interpretations: For women, firewood gathering is social, communal, and embedded in their relationship with land and ecology. The LPG case is not merely about fuel but signals figurative dislocation, whereas the firewood practice extends beyond energy needs to embody traditional ecological knowledge. These fragments expose a deeper pattern, a governance logic that treats them as bodies to be managed, not voices to be heard, where state apparatuses and mainstream development frameworks construct the community as ' backward ' and render their labor invisible within the hegemonic ideal of ' collective progress. '
sections.(Un)Making Futures: Education as Absence:
The Oraon people in the study area remain significantly behind in social and economic progress, with limited engagement in education and skill development hindering meaningful livelihood and societal advancement. This stems from extreme poverty, socioeconomic marginalization, and poor access to educational facilities. In line with the Plantation Labor Act 8 (PLA), elementary schools were set up in tea garden residential settlements, 9 but these, often far from workers ' lines, were the only option for most children and suffered from poor maintenance, inadequate infrastructure, teacher absenteeism, and weak oversight. Attendance remained low, as parents frequently kept children home for household or subsistence labor. This reflects systemic neglect by both employers and government, reinforcing the cycle of educational deprivation.

Most respondents dropped out after middle or secondary school due to financial stress, the need to work, the death of an earning family member, school distance, and poor transportation. Mediums of instruction at the primary level are typically Bengali, with some Hindi and Nepali, whereas Eklavya Model Residential Schools (EMRS) use English. Although consistent with state and national policies, this poses linguistic and cognitive barriers for Oraon children, whose cultural language is Kurukh and everyday lingua franca is Sadri. Many enter school with little or no exposure to Bengali, making classroom comprehension and formal interaction difficult. This disconnection fosters poor performance, alienation, low self-esteem, and early dropout.

The exclusion of their native language from schooling is not merely a practical obstacle but an ontological form of exclusion, erasing the child ' s mode of existence, cognition, and expression within the institutional structure. Conversations with elder community members reveal a troubling trend: The absence of mother-tongue instruction, combined with the dominance of Sadri in daily life, is eroding Kurukh, weakening intergenerational transmission, threatening cultural continuity, and undermining the community ' s linguistic heritage.

This case reflects a ' common reality ' for many who are facing socioeconomic challenges and limited access to education (Box 3). Among the Oraon community, formal education remains a distant aspiration: Nearly one-third of household heads lack any formal schooling, roughly one-fourth have education below the primary level, and only 0.66 percent have graduated. Fewer than one in six have reached secondary schooling, and only about one in fifteen progressed to higher secondary levels. Bachelor ' s degrees are held by barely one in thirty, and over a quarter of the population have had no access to formal education at all.

Box 3. Sunita, a 19-year-old girl from a tea garden settlement, lives with her parents and three siblings. Despite her aspirations for higher studies, she was forced to abandon school after the eighth grade due to entrenched generational poverty. Born into a family struggling to meet basic needs, she witnessed her parents ' daily battle to arrange sufficient food. Household responsibilities, traditionally and disproportionately assigned to young women, combined with the ' burden of insufficient income ' compelled her withdrawal from education. Financial necessity and unspoken social expectations that prioritize subsistence over personal advancement, especially for girls, framed her sacrifice. She now works in the tea garden, supplementing the family ' s fragile income with occasional agricultural wage labor.

Her case illustrates prejudice operating through multiple, overlapping channels. Structurally, the persistent neglect of educational infrastructure reflects institutionalized prejudice: underfunded schools, prohibitive distances to secondary institutions, and scholarship schemes undermined by bureaucratic inefficiencies and corruption. Socially, gendered prejudice compounds her marginalization, casting girls as supplementary earners and caretakers.

Decades of promises of development and upliftment have failed to improve wages, which remain abysmally low, forcing families to prioritize ' survival ' over schooling. Prejudice here is silent and systemic, manifesting not only through direct exclusion but through conditions that render advancement virtually impossible. Sunita ' s dropping out is thus not a personal misfortune alone; her future is foreclosed by the intersecting forces of poverty, gendered expectations, and structural neglect.

Educational vulnerability is particularly pronounced among female-headed households, as nearly two in five are illiterate, and only one in twenty have attained higher secondary education. Interestingly, the findings show that male-headed households have a lower share of members completing secondary education (ten years of schooling) and graduation compared to female-headed households. Female-headed households show a significantly higher rate of no formal education, however, underscoring gendered disparities in access. The larger proportion of female-led families with education below primary level further indicates systemic constraints limiting adolescents ' ability to pursue and complete primary education (Box 3).

These figures reveal not only structural marginalization but also ontological exclusion, where denial of institutional learning entails erasure of ' being, voice, and value. ' Despite affirmative action rhetoric, lived realities remain largely unchanged. To frame this merely as a lack of education risks legitimizing a ' continuum of neglect ' stretching from colonial disregard to present institutional indifference. Denial of education here signifies denial of full personhood and epistemic presence within dominant frameworks.

Twenty-one-year-old Pusphi (close friend and neighbor of Sunita) from the same village, said:

My experience is much like Sunita ' s. I had to leave school after completing secondary education. Although my parents encouraged and tried to support me, poverty made it impossible. The school I hoped to attend was nine kilometres away, and even the daily bus fare was unaffordable … that is why the cycle of poverty continues across generations … children in my neighborhood aspire to get an education to support their families and uplift our community, but we are largely ignored. (#R30, F, Sathkaya TG)

Pusphi ' s narrative reflects a double consciousness, simultaneous aspiration and resignation. Her remark that ' education is not for us ' signals the internalization of structural inequality.

Similarly, a respondent shared:

When the household economy was in crisis, schooling was no longer an immediate concern but became an unattainable goal. My children ' s innocent eyes held hope for a better tomorrow as they longed for education … . But all I could do was make empty promises, because I did not have the means to help them escape our grave circumstances ( … ). (#R17, M, Ranicherea TG)

The ' empty promises ' and inability to ' escape grave circumstances ' reveal deep ontological guilt, economic helplessness, and powerlessness. Such accounts embody generational trauma: lives shaped by poverty, where aspirations like education and social mobility remain distant ideals. Education symbolizes hope, dignity, and liberation from intergenerational deprivation, yet remains inaccessible due to financial hardship, infrastructural barriers (e.g., distance to school and unaffordable transport costs), and sociopolitical neglect, turning their generational space into one of emotional and existential defeat.
sections.Devaluation of Livelihoods: Insecure Wor:
From a Marxist perspective, ' labor is the fundamental source of value in society ' ; yet under capitalism, workers are alienated from their products; their contributions are undervalued and poorly compensated (Marx 2023). Among the Oraon, this is evident in informal labor such as tea garden work and sand quarrying. Their labor sustains industries and enriches employers, but they remain trapped in poverty, reflecting Marx ' s theory of surplus value, where workers receive only a fraction of what they produce. Over half of Oraon households rely solely on tea garden wages, heightening vulnerability to poverty, food insecurity, and malnutrition. Most households require two or more members in garden work, yet wages, 232 Indian rupees per day (approximately US$2.62 10 ) during the survey, later rising marginally to 250 Indian rupees per day (approximately US$2.85), remain far below a dignified standard of living. Formal workers average 180 to 210 workdays a year, and casual workers face irregular and seasonal employment.

In small gardens, women engage in informal leaf plucking for five to six Indian rupees per kilogram (approximately US$0.07), typically collecting fortyfive to fifty kilograms per day, highlighting the precarious, informalized nature of female labor. A respondent ' s (#R36, M, Chalsa TG) claim, ' It is just not possible to support a family on 200 to 230 Indian rupees a day (approximately US$2.28 -2.62) '

conveys a lived reality of undervalued work. His statement that ' our livelihoods have become increasingly uncertain ' points to the erosion of futurity, where even next-day planning is uncertain. Repeated but ignored appeals to the government and owners reveal a paradox of hypervisibility and erasure: visible as workers, voters, and ' poor tribal people ' in political rhetoric, yet excluded from decisionmaking and development priorities (Golay and Hannan 2025). They exist as ' bare life '-used but not valued, visible as labor yet invisible as persons.

The study found a clear generational divide in employment. Casual workers, often first-generation laborers from nonplantation backgrounds, lack experience and access to long-term benefits, whereas permanent workers are typically third-generation laborers in the formal plantation system, reflecting tea garden labor as intergenerational entrapment. Despite working over eight hours a day, including unpaid tasks beyond hazira hours, wages remain rigid and inadequate, tied strictly to fixed quotas. Plantation management justifies low pay through statutory provisions under the PLA, housing, health care, subsidized rations, and basic education, available only to permanent workers and their dependents. Casual laborers, a significant share of the Oraon workforce, are excluded and receive only basic wages. During lean seasons or closures, many migrate for short-term informal work, returning through contractual intermediaries, further eroding job security.

This dispossession is economic, relational, political, and historical (Majumder 2025b). Oraon marginalization emerges at the intersection of caste, ethnicity, and capitalist reorganization. Without land rights or subsistence farming, they remain trapped in exploitative labor regimes, stripped of autonomy and treated as disposable. The degradation of plantation work stems not from the labor itself but from the systemic devaluation of workers ' social worth; their labor sustains industries, yet their lives remain expendable. Historically, a rigid colonial hierarchy, managers, assistant managers, babus, munshis, dafadars, and at the lowest rung, the so-called coolies, structured plantation life (Banerjee 2015; Deb 2021). As one official noted, tea gardens run on a ' shadow economy ' that publicly projects order and productivity while concealing exploitative hierarchies of class and labor. Even so, resistance has emerged: With the ' collapse of managerial oversight, ' worker-led cooperatives have disrupted colonial disciplinary structures, emerging as counterpoints to structural domination, asserting a fragile but potent reclamation of agency. The establishment of worker-led cooperatives has emerged as a form of economic and political resistance (Deb 2021). These cooperatives are typically initiated through collaborations between local worker collectives, and occasionally external advocacy groups, rather than being directly driven by management. Local trade unions sometimes participate in mobilizing members or providing support during the formation stage, but their involvement is often inconsistent due to internal political divisions. Representation within these spaces is far from equitable (Bhowmik 2011). These acts, although often small in scale, represent attempts to reclaim dignity, assert collective agency, and challenge the very conditions that render workers simultaneously indispensable and disposable (Bhowmik 2011; Bhaduri 2018; Deb 2021; Wolf 2022). Regarding Oraon representation, although they form the backbone of the plantation workforce, their leadership within both trade unions and cooperatives remains limited. They are often participants rather than agenda-setters, which constrains the transformative potential of these spaces of struggle. Yet these moments of resistance, whether in the form of wage petitions, strikes, or the establishment of cooperatives, unfold under the lasting shadow of deprivation, where the disgrace lies not in the work itself but in the devaluation of those whose labor sustains the industry while they themselves remain food insecure (Bhaduri 2018; Deb 2021).

The economic sustainability of tea gardens in North Bengal is in jeopardy. Once framed as a path to stability, plantation labor has become emblematic of distress. Although the government has periodically introduced interim wage hikes, including the latest in June 2023 (Bag 2025), these remain far below subsistence levels and fail to account for inflation, rising living costs, and the historic undervaluation of plantation labor (Majumder 2025b). Low wages trap workers in cyclical poverty, a condition worsened by recent garden closures. As a community head noted, this is ' pushing many toward starvation, precarious migration, or debt-bondage in distant urban peripheries. '

Paradoxically, the industry hosts a multitude of trade unions 11 with divergent political affiliations, fragmenting collective bargaining power in the vegetal geography. This results in fragmented agendas and diminished collective bargaining strength. Most workers come from marginalized communities, whose social positioning limits access to resources and political influence (Banerjee 2015; Deb 2021, 2022). Although the majority of plantation workers belong to tribal communities, including the Oraon, positions in local trade unions are frequently occupied by individuals from nontribal or politically dominant caste groups. This has historically limited the capacity of unions to prioritize tribal-specific concerns such as land rights, cultural recognition, and language preservation. Instances where Oraon workers hold leadership positions, often in smaller, grassroots-led organizations, are exceptions that illuminate the potential for genuine worker agency, yet remain limited in scale. These institutions therefore embody both resistance and reproduction of exclusionary structures. Plantation owners cite financial constraints and high labor costs, about 60 percent of production expenses, to resist substantial wage hikes. Even though a Minimum Wage Advisory Committee 12 was formed in 2015, a statutory minimum wage remains unrealized (Bag 2025), with state inaction persisting despite years of deliberation (Nag 2022).

Community narratives reveal how Oraon fragilities are compounded by entrenched political opportunism. As one elder observed (#R16, M, Abhihill TG), ' electoral cycles bring fleeting visibility ' through promises of ' wage hikes and development, ' only for leaders to ' disappear ' after elections, reinstating structural invisibility. An active union member from Neoranadi TG stressed that the ' failure to achieve even minimal wage reforms, despite repeated protests, ' reflects deep-rooted apathy and neglect in state -society relations. Their marginalization is not mere ' underdevelopment, ' but a politically sustained condition aligned with Lefebvre ' s ([1974] 1991) notion of the production of space, where power relations inscribe inequality into everyday life. For the Oraon, confinement to degraded ecologies, informal settlements, and labor-extractive plantations is the product of historically accumulated, state-mediated spatial practices (Sushma 2015; Majumder 2025a).

Tea garden workers face worsening socioeconomic conditions due to low wages and frequent garden closures. As of 1 April 2025, their daily wage remains below the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (MGNREGA) rate of

260 Indian rupees (approximately US$2.97), which pays unskilled manual workers more. The absence of predictable work erodes not only income but also the rhythm, structure, and hope in daily life. As one worker noted, ' Most of us … used to work as casual laborers under the 100-day scheme [MGNREGA] just to survive. Now even that work has become irregular … hard for me to run family depending only on tea garden …' (#R2, M, Neoranadi TG).

Casual laborers in sand quarrying along the River Teesta and other local rivers illustrate similar socioeconomic threats, performing strenuous, hazardous work for 250 to 350 Indian rupees per day (approximately US$2.85 -4.00), depending on age and physical capacity. Both tea and quarry work are seasonal and irregular, leaving workers without job security and social safety nets (Das and Sharma 2009; Chatterjee 2010; Kenney-Lazar, Suhardiman, and Dwyer 2018). Income is directly tied to physical labor, so illness or work disruption can trigger severe financial crises. Ontologically, these workers remain trapped in a survival cycle that limits upward mobility and political engagement (Sutradhar 2016; Chhetri and Kasemi 2018).

State policy, which privileges formal labor sectors and infrastructure, largely overlooks such informal workers (Lahiri-Dutt 2016; Sutradhar 2016; Hannan 2024). Consequently, their voices stay marginalized, and socioeconomic conditions stagnate. The primacy of daily survival over civic participation entrenches their exclusion from decision-making processes directly shaping their livelihoods (Breidahl and Clement 2010; Lahiri-Dutt 2016).

Quantitative data reflects this fragility. Eighty-six percent of respondents identify unemployment as a major threat to survival (Table 1), and nearly all attribute worsening conditions to the closure of tea gardens, which once anchored both livelihood and social rhythm. This signals not only economic distress but also a collective awareness of an ontological crisis, a rupture in the conditions of being. Over four in five cite seasonal employment as a key destabilizer, and nearly all highlight meager wages as a pressing burden (Table 1). For almost two-thirds, multiple forms of precarious labor are not a choice but a strategy for ontological maintenance in systemic scarcity. These are survival strategies, not traditional expressions of agency, aimed at preserving existence in a system that denies stability, dignity, and recognition.

Economic insecurity among Oraon households is acute, with the majority reporting ' no capacity to save. ' Average monthly savings stand at 189 Indian rupees (approximately US$2.17). Annually, 33.65 percent save only up to 500 Indian rupees (approximately US$5.70), and just 13.34 percent exceed this. These figures are not mere poverty markers but indicators of enduring ontological fragility, where saving is less future planning than a precarious act of survival.

One widowed respondent (#R9, F, Neoranadi TG) expressed, ' Since my husband passed away, we have struggled economically. … The struggle will never end. Now, I have to struggle relentlessly to make ends meet … . Savings for the future is like an illusory. Her account mirrors the quantitative findings, revealing how gender, loss, and poverty combine to prevent even minimal financial resilience. This insecurity manifests not only in the inability to save but also in daily survival, particularly for women caregivers. As she further recounted, ' Sometimes, I am unable to offer my family a proper meal … hunger was evident on their faces, but as a mother and elder, I could do nothing … . ' Here, food insecurity and maternal helplessness illustrate a sustained erosion of the capacity to project into a stable future, a quiet violence confining life to the immediacy of bare survival.

In this excruciating reflection, ontological marginalization is seen to penetrate the most intimate ' sphere of protective identity. ' Respondents like R17 express a sense of frozen time, struggling to survive today with no capacity to plan for tomorrow, an ontological as much as economic condition. Her very sense of being, as both mother and household head, is bound to the ability to nourish and protect her family. When respondent R9 states she ' could do nothing ' as hunger overtook her household, she not only recounts economic hardship but also exposes the affective toll of prolonged marginalization and the failure of care systems. This is temporal paralysis, no forward movement, no long-term plans, and no arc of change. To be unable to fulfill that role is to experience a collapse of self, purpose, and dignity. Ontological marginalization is thus being alive without time, where social and economic relations obstruct the secure construction of selfhood, future planning, and sustained well-being.
sections.Conclusion:
To deepen understanding of recurring everyday noncompliance in achieving sustainable equity, this article presents a case study of the resettled Oraon community in northern West Bengal, India. Drawing on key findings, I foreground the concept of ontological marginalization to capture informal dynamics that perpetuate de facto inequalities, uneven wealth distribution, and gender contrasts. Ethnographic and mixed-methods research reveals the complex nature of this marginalization and the acute livelihood vulnerabilities faced by marginalized tribal populations. The findings highlight a profound disconnection between developmental ideologies and the lived experiences of a marginalized group.

Systemic exclusions faced by the Oraon are not incidental by-products of progress but are rooted in colonial legacies and contemporary neoliberal frameworks that sustain ' hierarchies of being, existence, and value. ' Their survival has been bound to the tea economy for over a century, spanning three to four generations, with the present households continuing this inherited dependence for at least the past twoand-a-half decades. The divergence between development as a state-imposed agenda and livelihood as a lived reality constitutes epistemic injustice, whereby dominant systems of wisdom and governance erase indigenous ontologies, reduce communities to passive subjects of intervention, and sever relational ties to land, labor, and culture. This study emphasizes the intersection of historical displacement, structural inequality, and present-day socioeconomic challenges. The findings reveal a paradox in which externally framed progressive interventions often intensify inequalities and disrupt traditional systems of equity, leaving communities like the Oraon further marginalized.

The Oraon community ' s livelihood duality, between traditional subsistence practices and wage labor in tea gardens, construction, and quarrying, reflects not mere economic diversification but ontological downgrading. Their ways of knowing, being, and living are devalued within a development paradigm that views them solely as labor, not as skill bearers or ecological stewards. As Spivak (1988) observed, the subaltern ' cannot speak ' not for lack of voice, but because dominant structures refuse to listen in their language. This marginalization is manifest in occupational instability and volatile livelihoods. Wage labor in tea gardens or Teesta River quarrying remains precarious, poorly paid, and without social protection, and migrant work, often a forced strategy for men, leaves women managing households through insecure, feminized labor. Viewing poor housing, inadequate health care, deficient education, and unsafe drinking water as ' normal ' underdevelopment obscures their reality as material expressions of dual marginalization, both as a constitutionally recognized Scheduled Tribe and as a population bound for generations to an uncertain plantationscape.

The community ' s opportunities and inequities reveal systemic failures in which external interventions and political neglect deepen vulnerability. From an existential geographical perspective, development must move beyond reductive materialism toward ontological justice, recognition of historically denied ways of being, knowing, and living. Education, touted as a pathway to mobility, becomes another site of ' inclusive exclusion, ' as state quotas ignore linguistic and cultural disconnects. The absence of mother-tongue instruction accelerates intergenerational cultural loss, threatening language, memory, and identity.

Addressing the systemic inequities sustaining ontological marginalization requires a transformative policy agenda grounded in philosophical reflection and pragmatic justice. Key directions include (1) embracing ontological pluralism by recognizing indigenous epistemologies, practices, and systems of equity, prioritizing relational, community-led processes over extractive, top-down interventions; (2) implementing land redistribution with legal protections against displacement, focusing on marginalized, especially female-headed households; (3) facilitating livelihood diversification beyond monoculture economies through skill development, market access, and infrastructure for sustainable agriculture, forest-based livelihoods, and microenterprises that enhance security without eroding cultural ties; and (4) ensuring inclusive education by removing economic and spatial barriers through free, quality schooling, stipends, transportation, and culturally relevant curricula.

Although this study draws on diverse empirical data, its scope and representativeness are limited. The findings provide valuable localized insights but cannot fully capture the structural complexity of ontological marginalization and systemic exploitation. Time and logistical constraints limited field work depth, particularly on seasonal livelihood shifts and evolving vulnerabilities. These constraints point to the need for longitudinal, comparative ethnographic and socioeconomic research involving other tribal communities in the plantationscape facing similar livelihood disruptions and cultural dislocations.

Ultimately, this article advocates for development as a virtuous praxis, recognizing marginalized lives as equally ' real, vocal, and valuable ' within broader sociopolitical and economic structures. Centering the Oraon community ' s voices, it calls for policy frameworks that address both material deprivation and the deeper structural roots of exclusion, challenge entrenched hierarchies, and ensure genuine participation in decision-making. Only through such transformation can development move beyond tokenism toward justice, dignity, and meaningful inclusion for historically marginalized communities.

sections.Notes:
1. Oraon are an aboriginal people belong to Dravidian group, presently settled in Jharkhand, Chattisgarh, Bihar, West Bengal, and Assam (Xaxa 1992). The original native place of Oraon was the Konkan region, from where they have migrated to the
2. Chotonagpur Plateau (Xaxa 1992). During the colonial period, Oraon further migrated toward Assam and the northern part of West Bengal to find opportunities for jobs in the tea plantation (Xaxa 1992; Sarkar 2017). The Oraons are the fifth-largest tribe in South Asia and the second largest tribal group (after Santhal) in West Bengal. According to the Census of India in 2011, the population of the Oraon community in West Bengal is approximately 8.83 lakh, which is 2.7 percent of the state ' s total population.
2. In all instances where I is used in this article, it refers to my direct, in-person involvement in conducting interviews and engaging in conversations with community members.
3. The term plantationscape refers to the spatial, social, and economic environment shaped by plantation economies. It encompasses not only the physical landscape of tea gardens or other plantations but also the lived realities of laborers, their housing, social relations, and cultural practices within this setting.
4. Informal systems within the plantation economy entrench workers in debt cycles, restricting mobility. Chronic underpayment and reliance on casual labor maintain a precarious, easily replaceable workforce. Informal recruitment, often mediated by middlemen, exploits newcomers through bribes, deductions, and, at times, human trafficking of vulnerable women and children. Such practices are overlooked by political -corporate alliances that maintain a fac ¸ade of legality while suppressing dissent and weakening unions. Despite legal obligations under the Plantation Labor Act, essential welfare provisions like health care, housing, and education are systematically denied, reinforcing structural marginalization and deepening dependence on exploitation.
5. All names mentioned in this article are pseudonyms.
6. Kaccha houses refer to dwellings constructed using temporary, nondurable materials such as mud, thatch, bamboo, and wood.
7. Pucca houses are dwellings built with durable materials such as brick, cement, concrete, or stone, providing greater structural stability, protection from weather, and access to basic amenities.
8. The Plantation Labor Act (1951) is a legislative framework intended to regulate the welfare of plantation workers in India, mandating provisions such as housing, medical care, and education. Enforcement remains inconsistent, however, with many plantations failing to meet even the basic statutory requirements.
9. In local Sadri language, residential quarters refers to Girmik Lines historically built in North Bengal ' s tea plantations to control and discipline workers. These cramped, poorly maintained clusters endure as visible legacies of plantation capitalism. Intergenerational dependence on plantation jobs, tied to residence in these lines, perpetuates economic vulnerability and entrenches structural marginalization within the tea economy.

10. Equivalent in U.S. dollars is based on the midmarket exchange rate of Indian rupees (as of August 2025).
11. The Joint Forum, an apex body of about thirty tea trade unions in North Bengal, was formed to oppose the prolonged delay in fixing a minimum wage for tea workers (Bag 2025). Political divisions between ruling-party-aligned and opposition-affiliated unions have fragmented decision-making. Consequently, the decade-long wait for wage reform has demoralized workers, many of whom continued working during protests, reflecting eroded collective motivation and trust (Bag 2025; Sinha 2025).
12. The Minimum Wage Committee, comprising industry, union, and state representatives, was tasked with determining fair wages within six months (Bag 2025). Yet, after nearly a decade and around twenty meetings, no consensus emerged (Sinha 2025). Tea planters argue that fringe benefits, such as housing, health care, and rations should count as wages, justifying low cash payments, whereas unions demand higher wages based on inflation and economic indicators. The issue was later referred to the State Productivity Council on the labor minister ' s advice (Sinha 2025). These fringe benefits are often nominal, masking systemic exploitation under legal pretenses, while mandated welfare under the Plantation Labor Act remains widely neglected.
