The public utility in the fair distribution of waters . . . has excited in all times continuing controversies.

-Ambrosio Cerd  an de Landa, Lima Water Judge (1828, 3 -4)

H istorical perspectives have long been considered integral to political ecology (Zimmerer and Bassett 2003; Peet and Watts 2004; Robbins 2004), although how and to what end historical content and analysis could be incorporated into this research approach has not been fully resolved and remains an ambiguous pursuit (Offen 2004). In general, the historical political ecology approach calls for the application of historical perspectives within a broadly de fi ned political ecology point of view and has been de fi ned as ' a fi eld-informed interpretation of society -nature relations in the past ' (Offen 2004, 21). This includes using historical material to contextualize current environmental con fl icts, especially the continuing in fl uences of European expansion and colonialism, often with the explicit motivation of improving social justice or environmental conservation in the present (Brannstrom 2004; Offen 2004; D. K. Davis 2009). Historical political ecology might also include asking questions about environmental change or natural resource use in historical periods, either recent (e.g., Swyngedouw 1999; Biehler 2009; Carey 2010; Lane 2011; Carey, French, and O ' Brien 2012) or more distant (e.g., Watts 1983; Sluyter 1999; Zimmerer 2000; Carney 2001; M. Davis 2004; End fi eld and Fern  andez Tejedo 2006; D. K. Davis 2007; End fi eld 2008). Although this latter purpose -using a political ecological analysis to closely examine nature -society relations in the past and not just provide context for current-day issues -is lesser used, it represents a powerful framework for historical research.

In this article, I apply such a framework to municipal drinking water access and governance in colonial Lima, the capital city of the Viceroyalty of Peru. I draw on approaches and questions inspired by political ecology to examine patterns and politics of water use in a colonial context, focusing on the in fl uence of power dynamics on sociospatial patterns of resource access and control (following McCarthy 2002; Ribot and Peluso 2003; Turner 2009). Using material analysis of water infrastructure and technology recorded in sixteenth- and seventeenth-century archives, I explain how water access formed, reinforced, and re fl ected

colonial social divisions, as well as in fl uenced the spatial development of the colonial city.

The city of Lima, originally called Ciudad de Los Reyes , was founded in 1535 as the seat of the Spanish Viceroyalty of Peru. It can be considered one of the most prominent of the Spanish colonial cities, second perhaps only to Mexico, the capital of New Spain. Lima is located on the central coast of Peru in a desert climate where true rainfall rarely occurs. All water used for drinking, irrigation, sanitation, and industry must be drawn from river watersheds and related aquifers. The urban design of Lima followed the wellknown Spanish colonial grid pattern, and the city was speci fi cally sited along the banks of the Rímac River and in relation to the numerous pre-Hispanic irrigation canals drawn from this river. 1 The Spaniards, however, established their own drinking water pipeline infrastructure. This underground pipe network, fi rst inaugurated in 1578, was controlled by the Cabildo (City Council) and was one of the earliest in the New World. The Cabildo, or municipal branch of colonial government, was of fi cially charged with managing Lima ' s water and, not surprisingly, the careful division of measured amounts of drinking and irrigation water occupied much of its energy. 2 Although the Cabildo ' s explicitly stated objective was to provide access to clean and copious drinking water for the entire urban population, this goal was only partially achieved. Therefore, this article seeks to examine how municipal governance strategies contributed to inequality in access to drinking water among colonial Lima ' s urban residents. The methodological approach to answering this question incorporates two major components: fi rst, asking questions inspired by political ecology and, in particular, the political ecology of water and, second, applying data collection and analysis techniques appropriate to the historical period being studied.

Three key themes drawn from the recent literature on the political ecology of water inform my interpretations of the Lima case. Most important, unequal water access (Swyngedouw 2004; Bakker 2011; Loftus 2011) and the related politics of surface water or aquifer management (Swyngedouw 1999; Norman and Bakker 2008; Brooks and Linton 2011; Jepson 2012) have proven integral themes in understanding current-day water systems and have been shown to have both important historical antecedents and long-term legacy effects. Second, analyses of urban development and urban -rural relations related to water demonstrate strong urban bias, with urban uses often privileged in cases of con fl icting multiple uses of water (multifunctionality). This bias, or unequal relationship between urban and rural areas, is evidenced by the urban hydraulic reach (or water footprint; Swyngedouw 1997, 2004; Bakker 2003; Kaika 2005; Scott and Pablos 2011). Third, combining spatial, social, political, and economic aspects of the previously mentioned themes, Bakker (2003) indicated that water supply in urban areas, especially urbanizing areas of the Global South, should be understood in terms of archipelagos instead of networks, given the discontinuous and partial coverage of public water supply and the frequency of multiple and overlapping methods of public and private water delivery mechanisms. Together, these themes provide a foundational perspective from which to examine urbanization, water supply, and inequality. They suggest the primacy of urban water use and indicate unequal infrastructural coverage and access to water within urban spaces.

Although these topics, questions, and themes from political ecological research can be easily transferred to historical contexts, the research methods typically used by political ecologists might not always be applicable, especially when more distant historical periods are studied. For such older cases, it is necessary to combine multiple methods and data sources, which might include fi eld-based ethnographic and landscape observations, archival analysis, archaeological investigation, biophysical data, mapping, and more. The multidisciplinary research area called hydraulic archaeology provides a framework for analysis of (pre) historical water systems (Kirchner and Navarro 1996; Glick and Kirchner 2000; Barcel  o 2004; Glick 2005). Here, practitioners seek to reconstruct the design, layout, construction, and modi fi cation of hydraulic systems, to identify the social groups participating in the use of these systems and thus to determine the relative political and demographic strengths of these groups as demonstrated by their ability to access water resources. The major unit of investigation in hydraulic archaeology is the concept of hydraulic space (Barcel  o 1996), which is basically equivalent to what Swyngedouw (1999) termed the ' waterscape ' and can be de fi ned as a landscape of water use, at once both natural and social. It is a space designed to take advantage of a natural fl uvial system, and incorporates (1) the aquifer or drainage area, (2) the local and regional topography in relation to desired water conduction, and (3) the irrigated parcels or other uses of water. It includes the biophysical context controlling the quantity of water available and the direction of its fl ow, as well as the human division of water among houses, fi elds, orchards, and other uses. The orientation and design of a hydraulic space is based on features of the fl uvial system, but the conduction and distribution of water in canals and pipes follows patterns that are neither natural nor casual. This water infrastructure is closely linked to the organization of productive activities and therefore to social, political, and economic relationships.

The focus on infrastructure (e.g., canals, pipelines), achieved through consideration of a range of data sources (e.g., archaeological survey and excavation, historical documents and maps, legal traditions, toponyms, and remotely sensed imagery), makes hydraulic archaeology a useful guide for pursuing historical political ecology work on water in colonial Lima. Given the nearly 500 years of Lima ' s urban development, few material or archaeological remains of colonial water infrastructure can still be found (or

reasonably accessed), so in this case archival sources contain the best information. The major source for the analysis of Lima ' s hydraulic space is the Libros de Cabildos de Lima (the books of the City Council of Lima, hereafter LCL ). These books, which record the minutes from the weekly or biweekly meetings of Lima ' s Cabildo, span almost the entire colonial period, from the city ' s foundation in 1535 to after Peru ' s independence in 1821, 3 and provide an incredibly comprehensive and continuous record of the Cabildo ' s actions related to drinking water governance. 4 In this article I examine the period 1578 to 1700, which was the interval during which most of Lima ' s public and private drinking water infrastructure was installed, the vast majority of potable water connection licenses were issued, and the most signi fi cant water management and governance strategies were developed. Speci fi cally, I analyze all references to springs, reservoirs, pipes, tanks, fountains, petitions for water connections, and other related topics in the LCL of the period in question to determine both spatial and temporal aspects of water supply in the pipeline network. I consider such basic questions as these: Where were pipelines constructed and when? Which residents and populations did these pipelines serve? How reliable was water supply in the network overall? This included mapping the pipeline routes and the locations of public and private running water connections. 5 I used this analysis of written descriptions of material aspects of Lima ' s hydraulic space to interpret the biophysical, social, political, and economic signi fi cance of patterns of drinking water access and control in the early colonial period and to evaluate the Cabildo ' s role in contributing to or alleviating inequality in water access.
sections.Lima's Hydraulic Space and Its Governanc:
In 1671, Lima ' s solicitor general called water ' the element most necessary after air ' ( LCL 29.X.1671), 6 and indeed it was the natural resource most frequently discussed by Lima ' s Cabildo. The provision of drinking water was considered one of the principal responsibilities of the Cabildo: ' the fi rst thing given attention in the foundation of all of the cities of the world [is] that this element, inexcusable for human life, is provided with cleanliness and security ' ( LCL 17.XI.1649). To this end, the Spanish located their capital city along the banks of the Rímac River, to provide residents with water for irrigation, drinking, sanitation, and industry. The Rímac dominates Lima ' s hydraulic space (Figure 1). Like all of Peru ' s coastal rivers, it fl ows westward, cutting down from the glacial lakes of the high Andes to the Paci fi c, descending from a height of over 5,500 m above sea level to its mouth near Lima ' s port El Callao over a distance of about 130 km. Its fl ow varies seasonally, increasing during the highland rainy season (October -April), when it often threatens to overrun its banks, and all but drying up during the dry months (May -September). The Rímac was the source of the irrigation canals that supported all agriculture in the region around the city (Domínguez 1988). It was also the source of numerous springs used for drinking water during the colonial period. Seepage and fi ltration from the river and the Andean cordillera fi lls the large alluvial aquifer -of approximately 390 km 2 in area and 100 to 500 m in depth -located underneath the city and its surroundings, recharging this resource on a seasonal basis (Lerner et al. 1982; Quintana and Tovar 2002).

The Spanish designed and built their linked agricultural and hydraulic system ( fi elds, canals, reservoirs, and pipelines) around the natural topography as well as the pre-Hispanic canals already in existence. This multipurpose hydraulic space linked Lima ' s urban core with its rural surroundings and was of fi cially controlled by the Cabildo, which exercised jurisdiction over the urban zone (approximately 2.6 km 2 ), as well as the surroundings of the city (approximately a 113km radius around the city). A diverse population resided within this larger territory, primarily made up of Spaniards, Africans, and Indians. 7 Although the Cabildo claimed great authority over the city, it actually governed through a complicated relationship with other branches of colonial government, especially the Viceroy (the Spanish monarch ' s representative in Peru) and the Real Audiencia (Royal Audience, the highest court in Peru). With respect to water administration, responsibilities of the Cabildo included protection of the urban riverbank and construction of levees, distribution of rights to irrigation waters, canal maintenance, concession of milling licenses, and, of primary importance here, construction and maintenance of a municipal drinking water pipeline network and allocation of permits to install private connections to this network for homes and other institutions. To manage all aspects of municipal water governance, a water judge ( Juez de Aguas ) was elected annually from among the city councilmen ( Regidores ). The water judge post was established in 1556, with power to enforce the water ordinances for the city and surrounding countryside. It was a lucrative position, with a salary of 800 pesos a year, yet election as water judge rotated among the councilmen and did not seem to require much specialized knowledge (Bell forthcoming).

To provision the city with drinking water, Lima ' s Cabildo carried out three functions: (1) It secured the source of the water in springs on the outskirts of the city; (2) it installed and maintained a network of reservoirs, tanks, and pipelines; and (3) it awarded licenses for running water connections from the pipes to private houses, monasteries and convents, and other institutions. For this, beginning in 1611, each year the Cabildo named three or four pipeline commissioners ( Comisarios de Ca ~ nerías ). 8 These pipeline commissioners were councilmen or mayors, and in fi fty-eight of the seventy-nine years for which we have data in the seventeenth century, one of the commissioners was simultaneously the water judge (or

The pipeline commissioners ' work centered on evaluating petitions for private water connections through site visits and engineer ' s reports, determining how much water should be awarded and from which pipeline, and setting the price and conditions of each license or concession. Commissioners also attempted to ensure that no one took more water than their title allowed and coordinated the construction and maintenance of the pipe network in general. In this case some specialized knowledge was developed; for example, Councilman Ordo ~ no de Samudio was selected thirty times as pipeline commissioner between 1650 and 1683 and was considered an expert on the topic.

The engineer ( alarife ) in charge of the pipelines was another important person and one who gained in fl uence over the course of the seventeenth century. In 1609 the Cabildo determined that the municipal pipelines and public fountains should be maintained by a specialist ( LCL 14.XII.1609), and from 1625 the post was always held by one of the of fi cial city engineers (see also San Crist  obal 1993). 10 In reality, only three engineers managed the pipelines for the majority of the century: Clemente de Mansilla (1625 -1634), Juan de Mansilla (1635 -1661), and Pedro Fern  andez de Vald  es (1661 -1706). 11 The inheritance and concentration of knowledge about the urban drinking water system in these men was extraordinary, and their opinions were commonly heard (and heeded) during Cabildo meetings. Finally, it is necessary to mention that the engineers worked with African slaves, for whom little documentary evidence exists. In only one Cabildo meeting from the period in question was one of these men mentioned by name: Pedro Angola, who was Juan de Mansilla ' s slave ( LCL .18.IV.1654). 12 Apparently this was a position requiring skill, but also entailing damp and dif fi cult conditions.
sections.Lima's Drinking Water Pipelines and the:
The pipeline network began at the springs located on the outskirts of the city (Figure 2). In the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, Lima drank mainly from two springs located approximately 6 km from the Plaza Mayor, called locally Atarjea and Sabana

(Bromley and Barbagelata 1945, 41; Raimondi [1824] 2009, 257 -58). The location of both springs, topographically above the city by approximately 100 m, provided the necessary inclination to canalize the water toward the main water tank located in the urban core, called the Caridad water tank ( Caja de Agua de la Caridad ) for its location next to the Caridad Hospital ( Hospital de la Caridad ). Water was distributed from this central storage point into the public and private pipelines. From the outset, this infrastructure contributed to inequality in water access. The pipeline network ' s center of gravity was the Caridad water tank in the northeast section of the city center. Those who lived above this key point in the network, including the farmers in the rural area around the springs, had to cede their rights to the zones lower in the fl ow of water. 13

The momentous inauguration of the fi rst public fountain in Lima ' s Plaza Mayor in 1578 was part of a larger municipal project to bring piped drinking water to city residents. 14 This project, in planning since 1552, culminated in the three main municipal pipelines that were constructed by 1613 (Bromley and Barbagelata 1945; see also LCL 26.XI.1610). The pipes were ceramic, made by city potters, and buried below city streets ( LCL 14.IX.1660; see also San Crist  obal 2005, 185 -86). The water for all three fl owed from the Caridad water tank (routes and construction dates summarized in Table 1 and illustrated in Figure 3). The Cabildo received petitions for private connections of running water from these three main municipal pipelines, to be installed in homes, monasteries and convents, and institutions (like hospitals). These connections were for speci fi c amounts of water withdrawn from the main pipelines, called pajas or reales , which were units of measurement based on the fl ow of water through pipes of controlled circumference (Table 2). The majority of petitions were submitted during the twenty-year period in which the three pipelines were being constructed (summarized in Table 3).

A total of sixty-three petitions for drinking water connections were recorded in the LCL from 1578 to 1700 for Municipal Pipelines 1 to 3, and a total of eighty connections could be identi fi ed for these three pipelines using additional data from Bromley and Barbagelata (1945). 15 Information about these petitions and the eventual concession of titles is listed in Tables 4 through 6, including biographical and institutional information about the petitioners and the locations of these concessions are mapped in Figures 3 and 4. Several signi fi cant patterns can be observed. Spatially, below the Caridad water tank the three original municipal pipelines were distributed fairly evenly over the central section of Lima ' s original thirteen-bynine city block grid, which would have been the main area populated when the original water system plans were initiated in the 1550s. As visible on the map of the pipeline system in 1613 (Figure 3), however, there is a clear concentration of concessions in the area just below (west and northwest of) the Caridad water tank, with distribution tapering off the farther outward one travels below this tank (especially to the southwest). The map of concessions along the municipal pipelines after 1613 demonstrates a similar geographic concentration, albeit with more connections, especially to the immediate southwest of the Caridad. The branching of Municipal Pipeline 3 speaks to the need to serve several key points, including religious institutions (e.g., the Jesuit Novitiate College and the Encarnacion Monastery, map references n and c, respectively), and residences of important people not included along prior municipal pipeline routes (e.g., Councilmen don Martin de Ampuero and don Diego de la Presa, map references i and j).

Straightforward social patterns are also apparent. Of the eighty concessions, seven were for public fountains, four were for government institutions (Cabildo and Viceregal), twenty were for religious or charitable institutions (including schools), and forty-nine were for private individuals. Of these private individuals, twenty-eight were for members of the Cabildo or their

Women seem to be mentioned on water petitions only when they were high-status individuals themselves; for example, if they were daughters, mothers, or widows of conquistadores, Cabildo members, or high-ranking royal or viceregal of fi cials. Among the religious and charitable institutions, convents and monasteries received the most water: 82 percent of total water conceded (see Bell [forthcoming] for this calculation), with the Jesuits controlling the largest water concessions of all -nearly nine reales of water -among their various properties. 16

Taken together, the sociospatial patterns of the water concessions paint a picture of the distribution of power in the city. The Cabildo designed and implemented the original municipal water system and, not surprisingly, it served many of the homes of the mayors and councilmen. Indeed, many of these connections were awarded for free, in recognition of service to the pipeline projects and other public works. Public fountains, ostentatiously part of the original plans, experienced delays in construction and many interruptions in service. For example, in 1596 the San Sebastian fountain was completed but no water was fl owing ( LCL 19.IV.1596), in 1612 the drainage of the San Marcelo fountain failed, causing problems, and in 1621 the public fountains were found to be in a general state of disrepair ( LCL 5.VII.1621). When an important individual ' s house was located outside of the basic layout of the three pipelines, this layout was adjusted, as demonstrated by the repeated branching

Additional water connections were easier to install near previous connections. For example, Captain Juan Fernandez de Heredia ' s connection on Municipal Pipeline 3 (map reference i) was facilitated by the prior existence of a water storage tank at the corner of the Carvajal Statue ( Marmol de Carvajal ) that served both a public fountain and don Diego de la Presa ' s connection (map references k and i). Religious institutions also in fl uenced pipeline routes: The powerful Dominican, Franciscan, and Jesuit orders, among others, were all served by the original municipal pipelines. These features all contributed to the concentration of water connections in certain sectors of the city; power, wealth, status, and water connections went hand in hand.

Nearly no concessions were given to merchants or professionals (who were not royal of fi cials) and none at all to artisans, laborers, or other lower ranking members of society. The Indian neighborhood -Santiago del Cercado -was not served at all by the three original municipal pipelines and was only provided with one public fountain. 17 This neighborhood, reported to be home to 800 Indians and eighty African slaves in 1629 (Bromley and Barbagelata 1945, 59), provides a key illustration of the sociospatial patterns of access described earlier: The Cercado was actually located right along the water main leading from the springs to the Caridad water tank, very near to the main area with springs. Because it was located ' above ' the Caridad, however, it had only limited access to the city ' s drinking water (Ram  on 2011). The African population is only referenced with regard to the pipelines in terms of slave labor toward their construction and maintenance and as water sellers. These lower status populations used the public fountains, purchased water from sellers who made deliveries via mule cargo, or collected water from the river, even though from 1552 river water was considered too polluted for most domestic uses (Cogorno 2011).

of private pipelines. Private pipelines were designed to serve only their fi nal points, and typically petitions could not be submitted to install additional connections to take water from along their courses (although there were several exceptions). The person or group who requested a private pipeline paid for its construction. These pipes generally served religious orders or neighborhoods where the municipal pipelines did not reach, which were called far neighborhoods ( LCL 28. XI.1651; San Crist  obal 2005). The Cabildo supervised the construction of at least twenty-one private pipelines between 1600 and 1700. Information about these pipelines is presented in Table 7 and they are mapped in Figure 4.

Examination of the petitions for private pipelines demonstrates that from the perspective of potable water provision, the city below the Caridad water tank was divided into two zones: that of ' above ' and that of ' below. ' The zone below suffered from continuous water shortages. This zone, identi fi ed as ' below the principal plaza ' and ' the bottom half of the city ' ( LCL 20.III.1629), included the far neighborhoods ( LCL 28. XI.1651) like La Merced, La Encarnaci  on, San Sebastian, San Marcelo, and Guadalupe (see also LCL 9. III.1620, 29.X.1671). These neighborhoods all had public fountains that experienced water shortages. The word below references actual topographic position but also location at the end of the pipelines; in other words, the lowest point in the water fl ow, to the northwest and southwest of the Plaza Mayor. These zones lacked water because those located above (along the pipeline) used the water, often taking water in excess of what their titles allowed and consequently letting little water fl ow to the end of the pipe ( LCL 9. III.1606, 11.VIII.1621, 20.III.1629). Other ' poor ' zones were left totally outside of the network; their residents had to buy water from water sellers or collect it themselves from distant public fountains or the river ( LCL 11.VII.1621, 20.III.1629). 18

The construction of private pipelines was an imperfect solution to the problem of supplying the general population with drinking water. For example, each monastery or convent that constructed a private pipeline was also required to install a public fountain for general use. In theory, this would contribute to a more egalitarian distribution of water. In practice, though, the convents did not comply with this obligation. In 1670, for instance, the Cabildo found that none of the public fountains were running as they should, and some were not even built ( LCL 3.IX.1670; see also 25. II.1671, 12.V.1671). These fountains are mapped in Figure 4, but this is an important case where installation of infrastructure did not necessarily equate to proper functioning of infrastructure. Therefore, in the second half of the century, the Cabildo decided that it was also necessary to expand the municipal pipeline network. It built two new municipal pipelines. The fi rst was built for a new fountain in the Plaza Mayor and was fi nished in 1650. The second was constructed to serve the San Marcelo neighborhood. Plans for this were initiated in 1668, although the pipeline was still not completed or functioning properly in 1692, mainly due to lack of funding ( LCL 20.IV.1668, 20.VII.1668, 30.VII.1668, 16.1.1669, 12.II.1669, 16.IX.1692). Details about these pipelines are also included in Table 7 and Figure 4.

In general, the Cabildo was not able to provide adequate drinking water to all of the residents of the city. Some problems were due to the slow construction of the municipal pipelines, like that of San Marcelo, which took nearly thirty years to complete. Others were due to the dif fi culty of controlling illegal water connections ( LCL 21.I.1605, 7.I.1611, 2.I.1636), which was compounded by the fact that the Cabildo lacked a registry -either a list or a map -that detailed the legal connections. The Cabildo had sought to create such a map of the pipelines and connections at several times throughout the seventeenth century without success (Bell 2012). In 1665 it ordered engineer Clemente de Mansilla to make a pipeline map, but he died before completing this work. In 1691 Pedro Fern  andez de Vald  es was similarly reprimanded for failing to submit his Cabildo-ordered map. As far as is known, the fi rst map of the pipeline network was made in 1787, of which only a copy from 1862 remains (Ram  on 2010). It is unclear why this project was so dif fi cult to complete, although it might relate to the way knowledge of the pipelines was stored: as practical working knowledge held by the engineers and their slaves. This was observed in Cabildo records from 1790, which described the ' depositing ' of knowledge of the water system in an elderly engineer and his still living slave (Ram  on 2011, 88).

From a broader perspective, it is easy to note social distinctions in the patterns of drinking water access that were both purposefully and inadvertently in fl uenced by the Cabildo ' s governance strategies. Even though the Cabildo (and some religious orders) employed a discourse supporting the necessity of providing water to all, and especially to poor neighborhoods, in reality it was the most powerful residents and the monasteries and convents that enjoyed running water. These areas were strategically located just below the Caridad water tank in the city center or, perhaps better said, the Caridad water tank had been strategically located near this neighborhood. No titles were awarded to either African or Indian individuals, and the Indian neighborhood (Santiago del Cercado) had only one public fountain, located ' above ' the Caridad water tank and thus in a relatively low-power location in the network. Moreover, the spatial distribution of the pipelines was one of the features that produced the differences between a rich neighborhood and a poor one. The division of water not only re fl ected social inequalities but also created and reinforced divisions between groups and zones. sections.Discussion and Conclusions:
Lima ' s hydraulic space was oriented by the east -west fl ow of the Rímac River and the location of the springs to the northeast and topographically above the city. The installation of its components, though, especially the drinking water pipeline, followed the desires, objectives, and values of Lima ' s human residents more than it did natural features. The LCL demonstrates that effective governance of Lima ' s hydraulic space was dif fi cult. The Cabildo repeatedly failed to achieve its primary objective of securing a clean and copious fl ow of drinking water in the municipal pipeline network. Problems with water supply were nearly always attributed to infrastructural and management problems, rather than ' natural ' issues like aquifer depletion or spring location. Although biophysical aspects of water availability and conduction were signi fi cant to drinking water supply, especially the seasonality of aquifer levels and the slope needed for gravity-based fl ow, drinking water access was most closely linked to the installation of infrastructure and to the spatial proximity down- fl ow from the Caridad water tank. The unequal distribution of drinking water infrastructure re fl ected colonial social divisions but also helped to create and widen gaps between groups based on access to water. Although the Cabildo made grand statements about the importance of providing water to all city residents, only the most powerful members of colonial society had running water in their homes.

This interpretation of Lima ' s municipal water system was only possible through interrogation of the Cabildo archives from a political ecology perspective. Most signi fi cantly, this perspective asks direct questions about the linked biophysical, material, social, political, and economic in fl uences on patterns of water access of individuals, groups, and regions. Political ecological analysis of contemporary urban drinking water systems shows strong inequality in access, and historical cases like that of Lima suggest that such patterns are not new (although the speci fi c relationships between past inequality and current conditions need to be clearly demonstrated and not assumed). Bakker ' s (2003) archipelago metaphor is also helpful for historical water analysis because it suggests that multiple, overlapping strategies are commonly used in urban drinking water delivery, including public and private supply systems, and that spatial coverage of water infrastructure is typically partial and uneven. This level of nuance is not always considered in historical situations, even though it was likely present. Finally, political ecological work has shown how uneven water access also leads to further social differentiation and thus shapes and in fl uences power relations, instead of merely re fl ecting or responding to them (Swyngedouw 1999; Gandy 2004; Loftus 2009). This can also be observed at a broader level, in terms of urban -rural relations, and usually results in signi fi cant urban bias. In colonial Lima, the governance strategies applied in the management of potable water resources not only led to the development of the urban space and the speci fi c sociospatial patterns of access to water within the city but also contributed to differentiation between urban and rural spaces. A signi fi cant urban bias was observed, with the city ' s hydraulic reach or water footprint extending beyond the urban zone into surrounding farmland. Although these questions and approaches might seem basic to political ecology, they have not frequently been applied to the study of early colonial natural resource access and never before to water in colonial Peru.

The relationship between the history of water systems and the history of cities also warrants further consideration (Swyngedouw, Kaika, and Castro 2002; Gandy 2003, 2004; Swyngedouw 2004). As Bakker (2003, 332) wrote, ' The water network is, in part, an artefact of urbanization. ' Given the great investment in construction and the dif fi culty of changing a pipeline network already built, water systems typically re fl ect water needs at one point in time and generally only cover a portion of a city, usually the most af fl uent part. Although such observations are generally made for contemporary urban situations, they are also true for colonial Lima and likely for other colonial Spanish cities in the Americas, which were established early in the colonial period and incorporated complicated and sophisticated water systems from the start. There are interesting remnants and traces of these colonial water systems in modern ones. For example, even though the city of Lima now draws drinking water from distant Andean lakes, the location of the Atarjea spring used from 1578 is still the location of Lima ' s central reservoir and water treatment plant (SEDAPAL 2013). This speaks to an enduring orientation of Lima ' s hydraulic space, even amidst modernization, development, and great change. With further historical analysis, it might be possible to reconstruct additional legacies of the colonial system with greater signi fi cance to modern patterns of water access.

There are clear advantages of applying a political ecology approach to historical water systems, but moving backward in time has methodological implications for the types of questions that can be asked and the types of data that might be available. Closer attention to material traces left on the landscape, including both biophysical and sociocultural features, is necessary, and a useful guide can be found in the hydraulic archaeology approach. In this article, I used written descriptions to explain the design and construction as well as the day-to-day management of infrastructure. In other cases, archaeological analysis of infrastructure might provide a useful complement, as historical documents have signi fi cant limitations for a political

ecological analysis. With the LCL we have only the fi nalized or ' clean ' version of the Cabildo meeting agendas, and rarely hear dissent among Cabildo members, let alone direct contributions from lesser heard voices, like Indians or African slaves. The LCL and other similar sources do, however, provide key insights into ' how Europeans conceptualized ' their ' colonial landscapes and how those imaginations produced material consequences for colonized people, environments and wildlife ' (Offen 2004, 29). In the case of Lima ' s water, we have a clear representation of the administrative, legal, engineering, and measurement concepts developed and applied to water. Understanding these colonial practices and conceptualizations, as well as their consequences and legacies for postcolonial resource management and environmental science, is a principal goal of historical political ecology (Offen 2004; D. K. Davis 2009). Although here I have delved only brie fl y into one history of water access, I have endeavored to show the utility of the historical political ecology perspective for explaining sociospatial patterns of natural resource access in the past. &

records.title: Protecting a Broken Window: Vandalism and Security at Rural Rock Art Sites
records.abstract: The majority of the ancient rock art sites of the U.S. Southwest are located in rural locations that are difficult to monitor or police. These sites seem to exert a pull on humans, an attraction that not only provokes curiosity and wonder but also what can be classed as destructive responses or vandalism. Many crime control methods for reducing vandalism are based on traditional theories such as defensible space and broken window theory. In the case of rock art, however, these methods do not yield expected results and in some cases are even detrimental. Rural crime, including rural vandalism, as a whole is marginalized in criminology, which has been dominated by urban-focused approaches and theories. In the case of rock art, considering how security is approached and maintained ultimately leads to questions about human-object relationships with regards to crime and about object agency. By focusing on the policing challenges of one particular type of rural vandalism, we hope to contribute to the discussion of vandalism in rural spaces.

records.title: Chasing Moving Targets in Rural Spaces: Local Policing and Drug-Related Interventions
records.abstract: Globalization in rural areas is commonly described in terms of both challenges and opportunities. Opportunities include increased communication and reduced distance. These factors, however, are also favorable for illicit activities such as increased opportunities for marketing drugs on the Internet and reduced barriers for transporting drugs. The drug industry is global and involves cross-site processes, but the drug problem is very local. This article discusses how drug activities infiltrate the work of professionals in rural places and the way this affects rural people and their living environment. In local communities, the police have the authority to counteract the spread and use of drugs, an authority that is described as geographically thinned. That is, police as well as other professionals combating the effects of drug abuse are affected as local cooperation, which is often encouraged by short distances, dense networks, and local knowledge, is weakened. Using a qualitative interview approach, this study argues that local practices related to prevention of drug-related crime are poorly equipped to deal with the speed and range of the contemporary drug trade.

sections.Richard Yarwood:
<!-- image -->

University of Plymouth, UK

This focus section aims to identify, conceptualize, and understand the emerging geographies of rural crime, in particular those of globalized rural crime, and evaluate their impact on different rural places. Contributions to this focus section reflect an interdisciplinary array of fields from geography, economy, and criminology to rural studies, fully engaged with pertinent theories and state-of-the-art literature. The focus section also critically examines how security and policing of rural areas is delivered by existing and emerging agencies, drawing from evidence from different country contexts in Brazil, the United States, the United Kingdom, and Sweden. Key Words: globalization, interdisciplinary, policing, rural crime.

T he study of crime and policing has largely been driven by a ' metropolitan criminology ' (Carrington, Hogg, and Sozzo 2016) that has focused attention on urban places of the Global North. Recently, this approach has been challenged by work that has identified the significance of crime in rural places and critically examined efforts to police and secure the countryside (Mawby and Yarwood 2010; Ceccato 2015; Donnermeyer 2016; Donnermeyer and DeKeseredy 2013; Carrington et al. 2018). There has also been a realization that rural places are no longer, if they ever were, based on isolated communities but, rather, are part of global, hybrid networks that connect them to a global countryside (Woods 2007). To date, most work on rural globalization has examined legitimate networks but, as Hall (2013) argued, illegal activities and organized crime make significant contributions to the processes, flows, and impacts of globalization. In a rural context, issues such as people trafficking, drug dealing, environmental crime, theft for international markets, and unregulated food production are examples of criminality that reflect, rely on, and strengthen global networks of crime. Recently, ' southern criminology ' (Carrington, Hogg, and Sozzo 2016) has sought to draw attention to the ways in which the world is connected through crime and, at the same time, to destabilize and challenge the largely Western-centric ways in which it has been studied and understood.

Despite these developments, the study and practice of rural policing has often been focused on the rural community, with an emphasis placed on identifying particular crimes in particular localities and encouraging community action to police them. Although a wide diversity of agencies and agents, both networked and fragmented, have attempted to deliver policing and security in pluralistic or autonomous ways (Loader 2000; Peterson and Åkerstr € om 2014), rural policing is often underresourced, exclusionary, and too parochial to deal with globalized, multiscalar threats (Yarwood 2015). These can contribute to exclusionary practices that reinforce the idea that communities are the cause and solution of these issues and fail to recognize the significance of global organized crime.

There is therefore a need to understand better the geographies of crime and policing in the global countryside. This focus section aims to identify, conceptualize, and understand the emerging geographies of rural crime, in particular those of globalized rural crime, and evaluate their impact on different rural places. It also critically examines how security and policing of rural areas is delivered by existing and emerging agencies, drawing on evidence from different country contexts: Brazil, the United States, the United Kingdom, and Sweden. Contributions to the focus section also reflect an interdisciplinary array of fields, from geography (Yarwood 2015; Stenbacka this issue), economy (Aransiola, Ceccato, and Justus this issue), criminology (Yates, B  erzin ¸a, and Wright 2021), and rural studies (Ceccato et al. this issue), fully engaged with pertinent theories and state-of-the-art literature. sections.Framing the Contributions to the Special:
The first article by Richard Yarwood introduces the special section by providing an overview of work that has examined the geographies of crime and policing in rural areas. It starts by examining the significance of organized and serious crime in rural places using the United Kingdom as a jumping-off point and argues that global rather than community-based perspectives are needed in its study and policing. This global perspective opens up a number of opportunities, including for ' care of others ' beyond the locality.

This theme is developed and exemplified by Susanne Stenbacka, who examines the challenges faced by police officers when dealing with crimes that are committed against rural populations but are global in nature and perpetrated by people in other places. Given a lack of clear global policing strategy, this article draws on interviews to examine the experience of policing local crime in a global context.

The third article draws on evidence from the Global South to examine the commodification of rural security. High rates of crime, an ineffective criminal justice system, and failing policing practices have driven some people to seek self-protection in Brazil. Using data from the Brazilian National Household Sampling Survey, James Temidayo Aransiola, Vania Ceccato, and Marcelo Justus assess the determinants of adopting safety devices in different urban and rural contexts. Their article draws attention to the unequal commodification of security across the country that penalizes the rural poor.

The fourth article is devoted to an underresearched area of study, namely vandalism in rural areas. The empirical material reported in the article by Donna Yates, Diana B  erzina, and Aaron Wright was gathered from a series of interviews with managers of rock art heritage in the Southwestern and Western United States. Yates and colleagues first describe the nature of heritage crimes to provide a context to discuss the complexity of policing in these types of rural landscapes in the United States.

With an increasing awareness of animal rights and of the environmental impact of consuming animal products, conflicts between animal rights activists and those who defend ethical animal production have increased worldwide. Drawing on answers from a national survey directed to animal farmers in Sweden, Vania Ceccato, Peter Lundqvist, Jonatan Abraham, Eva G € oransson, and Catharina Alwall Svennefelt characterize farmers ' victimization with a focus on crimes related to animal rights activists. Long distances and poor police presence are often associated with high rates of underreported crimes against animal production. In this final article, Ceccato and colleagues also highlight the importance of incorporating farmers ' safety needs into sustainable rural development policies. /H17039

records.title: Regional Drinking Water Supply in Pakistan: Regional Disparity, Inequality, and Development Pattern
records.abstract: This article explores the regional disparities in water supply coverage in Pakistan in the context of intraregional development patterns. We applied the Gini index, Esteban and Ray index, and Moran's I to measure regional development patterns in terms of inequality, polarization, and spatial concentration and build an integrated framework combining them with other widely accepted factors to understand regional differences in water coverage quantitatively. Our results show that improved water (tap and pump water) is more widely supplied in Pakistan with lower inequality but higher spatial concentration than tap water supply coverage, although the patterns differ by urban-rural divisions and provinces. Western regions with smaller populations tend to have higher tap water coverage, and eastern regions with large populations are more covered by improved water. The regression models show various mechanisms of improved water and tap water coverage. Both are related to local economic conditions but tap water coverage is more related to local environmental conditions, and improved water is more related to local demographic conditions. Strong and dense population centers decrease improved water coverage but promote tap water coverage. Urban planners and policymakers should address polycentric regional development to fulfill various development targets and improve regional equity of drinking water coverage in terms of accessibility, availability, and quality.

records.title: Geographies of Land Ownership Change in the Rural United States: Challenges, Methods, and Possibilities
records.abstract: Both academic and popular sources have recently pointed to important changes in rural land ownership across the United States: from consolidation and financialization to racialized dispossession. Although land and land ownership are foundational themes in geography, and a wide range of disciplinary attention focuses on land ownership, much of the basic empirical information about U.S. land ownership remains obscured-due in large part to difficulty accessing and analyzing property data. This article draws on our experiences with a participatory action research project called the Appalachian Land Study to outline some of the challenges of studying the geographies of land ownership in the United States as well as some possibilities for new directions. We briefly situate this kind of research in the context of the overlapping political, economic, and ecological crises of the present, and argue that geographical studies of land ownership in the rural United States have many important applications across the discipline and beyond.

records.title: An Indicator Framework for Resilient Agroecosystems in Ontario, Canada
records.abstract: Southeastern Ontario presents a unique agricultural landscape in which both alternative and conventional farms operate. Each category of farm experiences a wide range of environmental and socioeconomic shocks and stresses that threaten each farm's longevity, raising questions about what constitutes resilient agriculture. Yet in Ontario there presently exists no unifying framework for building agricultural resilience. In response, this project mobilizes an analytical framework based on resilience indicators to create a qualitative method for assessing farm sustainability. Implementing this framework in the study area of Inverary, South Frontenac, semistructured interviews based on resilience indicators were conducted with both alternative and conventional farmers. The interviews enabled us to identify primary issues experienced at the farm level and account for the ways that their operations are structured to mitigate risks and achieve valued outcomes. Our research found that diverse farmers are facing overlapping threats but are prioritizing different responses to those threats by relying on distinct indicators of resilience. Key insights after using the indicator framework are summarized to create a deeper understanding of agricultural resilience in the province.

sections.An Indicator Framework for Resilient Agr:
Bryan Collins

<!-- image -->

SUNY Oneonta, USA

Southeastern Ontario presents a unique agricultural landscape in which both alternative and conventional farms operate. Each category of farm experiences a wide range of environmental and socioeconomic shocks and stresses that threaten each farm ' s longevity, raising questions about what constitutes resilient agriculture. Yet in Ontario there presently exists no unifying framework for building agricultural resilience. In response, this project mobilizes an analytical framework based on resilience indicators to create a qualitative method for assessing farm sustainability. Implementing this framework in the study area of Inverary, South Frontenac, semistructured interviews based on resilience indicators were conducted with both alternative and conventional farmers. The interviews enabled us to identify primary issues experienced at the farm level and account for the ways that their operations are structured to mitigate risks and achieve valued outcomes. Our research found that diverse farmers are facing overlapping threats but are prioritizing different responses to those threats by relying on distinct indicators of resilience. Key insights after using the indicator framework are summarized to create a deeper understanding of agricultural resilience in the province. Key Words: policy, qualitative research, resilience, rural studies, sustainable agriculture.

R esilience terminology has crept into governmental platforms within Canada, although it is often not clearly defined. The Pan-Canadian Framework on clean growth and climate change includes a broad section on adaptation and resilience, referring often to the agricultural industry. Despite being mentioned frequently in the report, resilience is never discussed, other than how embracing it will help communities move forward. Core concepts in the report include incorporating scientific information with traditional knowledge, investing in resilient infrastructure, and focusing on vulnerable regions of the country (Government of Canada 2018). At the provincial level, the Ontario Ministry of Agriculture, Food, and Rural Affairs (OMAFRA) broadcasts little in the way of resilient thinking in their sustainable farming information guides. Infrequent mentions of the term use it as a loose adjective to depict a broadly defined goal, such as achieving ' resilient agriculture. ' The ministry is much more oriented toward economic development, highlighted by the its mandate to promote ' a more competitive and productive agri-food and agriproduct sector ' (OMAFRA 2013).

However useful, generally there is no uniformity on these issues between the different levels of government in Canada. Furthermore, there is a clear gap between debates on resilience in the academic world compared to the governmental policy world. Other stakeholders in the space of agriculture include farmers, those in private industry that sell to farmers, and those in other agricultural organizations such as the Ecological Farmers Association of

<!-- image -->

Ontario (EFAO) or the National Farmers Union (NFU). A framework that brings in resilience and examines farms through the lens of a coupled socialecological system, by combining biophysical, political, and socioeconomic factors, will improve on the ways in which we think about resilience compared to previous efforts made by organizations throughout Ontario. Therefore, the objective of this research is to introduce an analytical framework for assessing agroecosystem resilience in in rural Ontario, Canada.

The view of resilience presented here stems from the definition set forth by Folke et al. (2010), defining resilience as ' The capacity of a system to absorb disturbance and reorganize while undergoing change so as to still retain essentially the same function, structure, and feedbacks, and therefore identity, that is, the capacity to change in order to maintain the same identity ' (20). This definition is apt for examining social-ecological farming systems in Ontario given the diversity of farming identities in the province (Smith 2015) as well as the multitude of disturbances present that are forcing farmers to change (Caldwell et al. 2022). Using this framework, this work assesses farmer approaches toward resilience aimed to ensure that their farms maintain their identity when confronted with disturbances. Farm identities are the collection of values, goals, and meanings that drive the production system forward (Letourneau and Davidson 2022). Studies that measure the social-ecological resilience of farms are currently quite rare, including in Ontario, but possess great potential for further informing agricultural policy (Darnhofer 2014; Jacobi et al. 2015). Although

the results from the pilot assessment are useful for analyzing the resilience of the agricultural landscape in Ontario, the key contribution of this project is to demonstrate that this framework can be applied in other geographic contexts to better understand the resilience of agricultural systems at the farm level.

This research first examines a range of existing frameworks and indicators used to assess farm resilience in ways that incorporate socioeconomic, environmental, and cultural characteristics. It then synthesizes these frameworks to create an approach suited for agriculture in this project ' s study area, Inverary, Ontario, and apply this comparatively across the divide between alternative and conventional farms. Both farm types are in different positions to manage shocks and stresses -both socioeconomic and environmental -underscored by their relative size and specialization.

Farms classified as conventional are those that make use of chemical input-based systems, work with mechanization to achieve economies of scale, and are strongly embedded in agri-business markets, both as consumers of external inputs and for the distribution of outputs (Therond et al. 2017). Conversely, farms classified as alternative typically adopt strategies for prioritizing environmental health of the farm. One strategy is to substitute chemical inputs with more environmentally friendly inputs (i.e., organic inputs such as manure for fertilizer) in efforts to preserve ecosystem and human health. These farms often tend to pursue biodiversity-based farming systems, which seek to substitute external inputs with ecosystem services to maximize biodiversity and integration of resources on the farm. Alongside this alternate approach to farming systems, alternative farms often seek to target local markets for distribution.

More broadly, this research fits into a renewed focus on agricultural sustainability at both regional and global levels, in part owing to concerns about the contribution of agriculture to greenhouse gas emissions as well as its potential vulnerability to climate change impacts. The global food system contributes to between 21 percent and 37 percent of greenhouse gas emissions, drawing attention from policymakers at all scales of government (Mbow et al. 2019). The conflict between maximizing economic potential and minimizing environmental impact is perhaps the primary issue of the debate over agricultural sustainability (McNeill 2019). This conflict, amplified by decreased availability of water and harsher socioeconomic conditions, including reduced incomes and rising land prices, among farmers globally and in Canada, puts debates around agricultural sustainability at a defining moment (United Nations 2013; Caron et al. 2018; Lawley 2020). Although addressing these challenges is important, this study is more limited to analyzing the ability of distinct farms ' operations to withstand shocks and stresses.

sections.Methodology:
Situating This Framework Within Resilience Theory

We have operationalized the theoretical frameworks existing in the agroecosystem resilience literature to design a resilience framework that assessed individual farmers ' attempts to maintain their farm identity while facing shocks and stresses. Key existing frameworks include Meuwissen et al. (2019), which offers a methodology to assess both specified and general resilience at the farm level, and the SHARP þ protocol used by the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO; Hern  andez Lagana, Phillips, and Poisot 2022), which offers a step-bystep resilience assessment tool specifically designed for farmer response to climate change. Both assessments use indicators and an integrated holistic approach, using both qualitative and quantitative methods. Meuwissen et al. (2019) presented a comprehensive methodology using multivariate statistical analysis, econometrics and modeling, visualization, system dynamics, structured surveys and workshops, and qualitative interviews with multiple stakeholders. The SHARP þ protocol presents a structured questionnaire consisting of thirty-five modules, with each module containing -between five and ten questions. Although these assessments offer an excellent starting point for conducting a comprehensive view of resilience, they require substantial time, labor, and planning. In response, this research proposes an assessment framework that can be conducted by a small team where the primary data collection method is through semistructured interviews without relying on quantitative or statistical methods.

The assessment framework uses a four-step process. First, we characterize the farming system by asking the resilience ' of what?, ' a concept promoted by Carpenter et al. (2001) and Cutter (2016) to help eliminate vagueness and provide a stronger assessment of the diverse needs and resources of each farm. Second, we ask resilience ' to what?, ' where we inquire into what specific shocks and stresses each farmer faces. Third, we ask about resilience ' for what purpose?, ' to identify overarching goals of diverse stakeholders within the study area. Fourth, we introduce resilience indicators to reconceptualize ways that farmers are enhancing resilience on their farm. This process borrows from the process put forth by Meuwissen et al. (2019), keeping aspects that are more applicable to a qualitative smaller scale analysis.

Asking Resilience of What, Resilience to What, and Resilience for What Purpose?

We introduce a specified resilience framework as opposed to a general resilience framework. Specified resilience identifies resilience of specific aspects of a farming system to specific kinds of shocks, whereas general resilience identifies resilience of broader systems to all kinds of shocks (Folke et al. 2010). For example, specified resilience would address how a farm ' s financial matters are resilient to supply chain disruptions from the COVID-19 pandemic. Therefore, taking this approach requires understanding the baseline characteristics of each farming system -asking resilience of what -before understanding what each farm is building resilience toward -asking resilience to what. To learn about the resilience of what for each farming system, we have identified five key farm characteristics from the food system resilience literature (Table 1; Jacobi et al. 2018). These five categories provide a wideranging index of characteristics for each farm, where we can then ask specifically about resilience to those characteristics through semistructured interviews.

Determining resilience to what required asking about the specific shocks and stresses each farmer faced. Questions posed to farmers covered both socioeconomic and environmental threats. The interview questionnaire is found in the Appendix. Overall, twenty-two interviews with farmers took place. All the farms are located in the Inverary region of southeastern Ontario, which is a farming community that is composed of both alternative and conventional farms. Six conventional farms and five alternative farms participated, each agreeing for an initial interview to discuss the goals of the project and agreeing for a second longer interview by answering the questions in the questionnaire. Semistructured interviews provided freedom for farmers to speak toward issues they felt were most important to them (O ' Keeffe et al. 2016). Initial interviews often lasted -fifteen to twenty minutes and the questionnaire interviews typically lasted between thirty and sixty minutes, but this was flexible depending on the interviewee and how much time and information they wanted to share. Some interviews spanned more than ninety minutes to two hours.

Determining resilience for what purpose required interviewing nonfarmer stakeholders. Interview templates with nonfarmer stakeholders were designed to learn more about what the interviewee ' s organization does, to learn how they interact with farmers and influence the agricultural space in Ontario, and to provide information and anecdotes about what they see as the key issues for farmers in the past and moving forward -in essence, to materialize resilience for what purpose in the study area. Interviews with provincial representatives with OMAFRA were designed to reveal a crucial outlook on agroecosystem resilience in the province and to see if what is being highlighted by the government matches what is highlighted by farmers. Employees from OMAFRA were interviewed to assess their views. Likewise, organization representatives from the Ontario Federation of Agriculture (OFA), the EFAO, Frontenac County Manager of the Economic Development Office, and the manager of the region ' s largest agricultural machinery dealer were interviewed to provide valuable information on how their respective organizations play a role in shaping agricultural policies and practices in the province.
sections.Resilience Indicators:
After asking resilience of what, resilience to what, and resilience for what purpose, we sought to explore each farm ' s capabilities for boosting their specific resilience to the threats they face. Commonplace with agroecosystem resilience assessment is using indicators to demonstrate resilience-enhancing attributes (Biggs et al. 2012; Cabell and Oelofse 2012; Jacobi et al. 2018; Meuwissen et al. 2019; Tittonell 2020). Although a multitude of indicators are applied in diverse resilience assessments, we have selected six for our framework. These six indicators can be captured through semistructured interviews, whereas many others found throughout the literature cannot be easily measured through qualitative methods. We sought questions that allowed interviewees to provide open-ended responses for elaboration on the connections between characteristics and indicators. The relationship between question number, characteristic, and indicator is listed in the fourth column of Table 1. Not having quantitative indicators is a limitation that prevents this assessment framework from being a holistic outlook into resilience, but it does allow this assessment to be performed solely through using a qualitative methodology.

Processing the data first required transcribing the interviews and then performing thematic analysis through open coding by linking key ideas to one or more of the eleven characteristics and indicators. Axial coding then helped thematically group key ideas together and help compare results across participants, such as finding what types of farms tend to operate in ways that prioritize certain indicators over others. Thematic analysis linked farmer responses to threats they face to our selected indicators. Thematic analysis is a commonly used analysis method for deriving relationships in qualitative data (Terry 2017) and has been used in similar scoping qualitative research to interpret semistructured interview data from farmers (Whitton and Carmichael 2024). We tracked how many farms were enacting management practices that linked to each indicator to see if there was a significant difference in the ability to respond to threats between each farm and farm types. sections.Results and Discussion:
Resilience ' of What ' in Alternative and Conventional Agricultural Systems

This section assesses the resilience of the participating farms by synthesizing both alternative and conventional farms ' resilience of what, to what, and how they are building resilience by linking their actions on the farm to our assessment ' s indicators. We also review Inverary ' s resilience ' for what purpose ' by summarizing nonfarmer stakeholders ' perspectives on resilience in the region. There is a clear divide in scale, goals, and practical approaches when assessing the five selected characteristics between alternative and conventional farm types. These approaches feed into our resilience framework by characterizing resilience ' of what. ' After analyzing the coded transcripts, dominant patterns emerged, which are summarized in the top portion of Table 2.
sections.Resilience ' to What ': All farmers interviewed in the study area of Inverary described the main environmental and socioeconomic shocks and stresses their farms were facing, threatening their farms ' identity. Notably, there was strong overlap in the types of threats that were expressed by farmers. These threats are summarized in Table 3. The two most pronounced threats that were put forth by every farmer interviewed were drought and rising input costs. In 2016, there was an extreme drought in southeastern Ontario. Crop farmers recalled that the drought devastated their yields and dairy farmers recalled that the drought led to heat stress on their cows. Every farmer also noted the harsh impact of rising input prices, which peaked during the growing season of 2022. Increased costs for fuels, fertilizers, and machinery, as well as general inflation, reduced profit margins for all farmers interviewed.
sections.Thematic Analysis of Farmer Interviews:
All farms face similar threats, but some farms choose to direct their attention and resources to some threats more than others in efforts to maintain their farm ' s identity. Creating beneficial responses to socioeconomic shocks and stresses often relied on the human capital and social capital of the agroecosystem, whereas creating beneficial responses to environmental shocks relied heavily on natural capital. The top portion of Table 2 demonstrates the difference in characteristics and resources between the two types of farm groups assessed, whereas the bottom portion provides examples of how farms within each category are directing their resources to build resilience into their operation. We relate these examples to our selected indicators to further uncover patterns in the Inverary agricultural space.

Keeping their farm functioning over time and generating intergenerational renewal is extremely important to all the farm owners surveyed. The two key resilience indicators found for improving the longevity of the farm were (1) using reflective and shared learning, and (2) integrating local knowledge systems into the farm management plan. Reflective and shared learning, expressed through trial-anderror tactics as well as planned experimentation, were common themes discussed to continually adapt to changing environments. Reflecting on what has happened within the agroecosystem in the past and adjusting how things work to proactively anticipate future environmental conditions also ensures the farmers are continually expanding their knowledge base and skill set. Additionally, alternative farms have identified the benefit of integrating local knowledge systems into their agroecosystem through understanding the importance of growing locally adapted and high-quality products.

Although alternative farms form the minority of agricultural operations in the study area, they do have a strong social presence because of their heightened emphasis on connecting with their local community, given that their community members are predominantly buying their products. All of the participating farms had a unique specialty and are therefore facing different industry-specific risks. They also face common risks, however, and their responses to these risks follow a generally unified pattern. Major focuses included (1) building natural capital in their system, (2) keeping operations and markets local, and (3) integrating local knowledge concepts into operations. The majority of alternative farms noted having strong connections to provisioning their seeds from local nonprofit organizations like the Kingston Area Seed Saving Initiative, a prime example of integrating local knowledge into operations.

Alternative farms identified that having strong and reliable access to local labor allowed them to cope better during the turmoil associated with the pandemic. Strong social capital to source labor during the pandemic boosted response diversity, as alternative farms were able to keep functioning at near full strength, compared to conventional farms that relied on labor programs that were disrupted.
