To improve geographical accessibility to health  facilities in rural Ghana, it has been recommended  that additional health  facilities be  built.  Resource  constraints  make  this  recommendation  infeasible. Using  location-allocation models, this paper demonstrates that in the Suhum District of Ghana substantial improvements in accessibility  can be  achieved  with  better locational choices and  without additional facilities. Also, additional facilities will  produce little  improvement  in  accessibility if  location  is  not  explicitly  considered.  The paper  demonstrates  the  utility  of location-allocation  models  for  improving  accessibility  to  services  in  the  Third  World. Key  Words:  Ghana, geographical accessibfiq, location-allocation  models, rural health, Third World.
sections.Introduction:
eveloping countries  face the problem  of D improving their health  care delivery systems  but  lack  the  necessary  resources  to  do this.  Health  facilities are  often  geographically inaccessible to the majority of the rural population  (Freund  1986; Lasker  1981; McEvers 1980; Stock  1985). Women  and  children,  in particular, experience difficulties in reaching a source  of  care (Phillips  1990),  but  the  explosion of  health  care costs makes it increasingly difficult to improve  geographical accessibility to  services.  Attempts  to  extend  care  are  frequently hampered by financial and human resource  shortages  and  other  barriers  (Phillips 1990).

Given this problem, better spatial organization of existing health care delivery systems is a  logical  strategy  to  follow.  Rushton  (1984, 1988)  has argued strongly for the role locationallocation models might play in using limited resources more efficiently  to provide access for those currently without access. In their work in Nigeria,  Ayeni et al.  (1987) show that accessibility to maternal and child health clinics could be improved substantially through careful location  of new facilities. Yet, critics such as Phillips (1990) question the usefulness of  locationallocation models in the Third World. Phillips (1990,  145), citing  the problem  of  data availability and reliability, states that 'optimally designed spatial health  delivery systems are not practical in the Third World.' In response to such  criticism,  Rietveld  (1  990)  has  correctly noted  that  critics tend  to  exaggerate the  data requirements of location-allocation models.

This paper contributes to this debate by applying a simple location-allocation model using readily available local data to evaluate a recent public health  policy recommendation  for improving accessibility to health facilities in rural Ghana. The results indicate that simple applications  of  location-allocation models  provide important information for general spatial decision making and data limitations do not preclude  their  application  in  the  Third  World. Furthermore,  location-allocation models may be used to improve spatial accessibility  without increasing  the  number  of  facilities  and  with minimum disruption to the existing system of facilities.

The  paper  is  organized  in  the  following manner. First, there is a brief description of the geographic  inaccessibility  problem  in  Ghana and the rationale  for  the  latest policy recommendation. This is followed by a brief description  of  the  study area  and  the  modelling  approach used. The analysis  begins by evaluating, using the p-median  criterion,  the  accessibility provided by the system of facilities in place. It demonstrates  how  accessibility might  be  improved, and evaluates  the potential for improving accessibility by providing additional facilities. This is  followed by  an  evaluation, using the maximum coverage criterion, of the ability of  mid-level facilities to supervise low-level facilities. The paper  considers the potential  for

enhancing  supervisory  capability  by  adding more facilities and the costs that would be involved in relocating facilities. It concludes  with a discussion of how location-allocation modelling might be included in primary health  care planning in Ghana.
sections.The Geography of Health Services in Ghan:
Historically,  the Ghana Ministry of Health has grappled with  an  'unacceptable disparity between  service  coverage  and  quality  in  urban areas compared with rural  areas' (Adjei et al. 1984). In 1972,149 of 298 government doctors worked in the Accra-Tema metropolitan  area which  contained  about  8%  of  the  country's population (Sharpston 1972). In 1978, an estimated  70%  of  the  population were unable to use the official  health  system  (Ministry  of Health  1978) because of  prohibitive distances to rural  facilities.

The  dilemma  of  the  Ghana  Ministry  of Health  has  been  how  to  provide an  efficient and equitable system of service throughout the country with a highly constrained budget. To accomplish  this,  Ghana  adopted  a  Primary Health  Care  (PHC)  policy  in  1978 with  a stated goal to 'maximize the total health of the Ghanaian people' (Mmistry of Health 1978,9). Details of Ghana's PHC  are presented in Morrow (1983). In brief, the system is based  on a three-level  hierarchical structure  (Ministry of Health  1978) of  A-level,  B-level,  and  C-level facilities. Each A-level facility is usually staffed with  a  minimally trained  health  worker. This level  provides  first  level  curative  measures, pregnancy management, child health  promotion,  environmental protection,  and mobilization for health-related community projects. Blevel facilities are usually staffed with  a  community  health  nurse  and  a  trained  midwife. They provide technical supervision of A-level workers, routine  immunizations,  and  care  of patients including those referred from A-level facilities. C-level facilities are based on the district  hospital,  have  at  least  one  doctor,  and provide mostly curative services including inpatient care  and some  preventive  services. Within each district, a  District  Health Management  Team  (DHMT)  is  responsible  for identifylng  locations  to  host  PHC  facilities and overall  health  care  programming  in  the district.

Ghana's PHC policy has three aims (Ministry  of  Health  1978,  10):  (1)  to  improve  the accessibility  (coverage) of health services  by setting  up  a village-based system of  health  care; the aim will be for everyone to obtain essential basic services rather  than  for a few to receive sophisticated care; (2) to improve the quality of PHC at the point 'where it is most needed in the  village and peri-urban  areas . . . to meet priority health problems of all the people; and (3) to improve and strengthen the management capacity to support the PHC system at all levels; the aim will be to make more effective use of existing resources.

Between  1978  and 1988  it  appears  that Ghana's PHC policy had  little  effect  on  the spatial  imbalance  in  accessibility to  services. Only 20% of doctors served the rural population (80%) in  1982 (Ministry of Health  1982). In 1984  more than 605 of the 818 government doctors  in  Ghana were found in  the  Greater Accra  and  Ashanti regions  (Fig.  1).  Furthermore,  54%  of the 262  private practitioners in the country were in the Greater Accra region. Two of 11 districts surveyed by the Ministry of Health had no physicians. The population per doctor ranged from 20,944 to 113,322 in districts with doctors (Adjei et al.  1984).

In 1986,  Dr.  Moses  Adibo,  Director  of Health  Services, observed  that  'of  the  1031 physicians in  Ghana, one-third  were at Korle Bu Teaching Hospital, another one-third were in  Kumasi  and  Sekondi, the  remaining  onethird in the other communities. An analysis of the  distribution  of  some other  health  professional groups would  reveal a similar pattern' (Adibo 1987, 154). Similarly, in 1987 only 186 (28%) of the 665 government physicians  served the rural population. The two teaching hospitals accounted for 47% of the total number of doctors (Adjei et al.  1988).

Ten years  after  the  adoption  of  the  PHC program, spatial accessibility  to health facilities was still a major problem, especially  in the rural areas. A PHC Review  Committee within the Ministry  of  Health  recommended  that  many more  facilities  be  set  up  with  consideration given to 'the geographical coverage and population  of  the  c o ~ n t r y ~ ' (Adjei et al.  1988, 15). This paper refers to this approach as the 'addmore'  strategy.  It  was  assumed  that  establishing additional facilities in rural areas would increase both accessibility  and coverage. There are two major problems with this recommen-

dation. First, the resources available  to the government are limited  and  preclude  locating  a health facility, or even a health worker, in every village.  Even  if  this  were  possible,  the  additional cost o f  equipping, staffing,  and supplying these additional facilities would still be  a large obstacle. Second, additional facilities may not provide the greatest potential increase in coverage and accessibility if location is not explicitly  considered.  Furthermore,  evidence  from the locational analysis literature questions such an  approach.  For  example,  in  their  work  in Nigeria,  Ayeni  et  al.  (1987,  1093) show that 'the  proliferation  o f locations  of  the  health service delivery facilities of maternity and child welfare centers cannot eliminate the inefficiencies of location.'

This  study  examines  the  'add-more'  prescription to determine if it is based on a correct evaluation  of  the  accessibility  problem.  The rationale  is  that if  the diagnosis is wrong  the prescription w i l l also be wrong and is unlikely to fiu the problem. It is essential to determine the  extent  to which  the  spatial inaccessibility problem is a result of an inadequate number of health  facilities  or  of  deficient  locations. To accomplish this objective, the study will evaluate  the  'add-more'  recommendation  in  the Suhum District of Ghana (Fig.  1) and explore other alternatives to improving accessibility. In effect, the study uses location-allocation models as tools for measuring spatial accessibility.
sections.Studv Area:
The Suhum District is in the Eastern  Region of Ghana (Fig. 1). It is  one  of  10 pioneering districts which  the government  of  Ghana  selected  to  implement  the  PHC policy in  the country.  Consequently,  it is  the  focus  of  ongoing research into the planning and delivery of health services in Ghana. In fact, at the time of  fieldwork for this research, the district was involved in a World  Health Organization  assisted project to delimit the catchment areas o f health  facilities  and  identify  gaps  in  service delivery.

According to the latest available (1  984) census, Suhum has  a  population  of  146,100 and encompasses  about 877.5 sq km (District Health Management Team 1987). The district is located  on the  edge of Ghana's forest belt. The district capital, Suhum, has a population of 19,298  and is 60 km from Accra, the national

Figure 1: Ghana and location of Suhum District.

<!-- image -->

capital. Suhum has several central place functions, including education, administration, commerce,  and  health.  Besides  Suhum,  only Nankese has a population exceeding  3,000  people  (3,414),  and  just  14 communities  exceed 1,000. The remainder of the population is located predominantly in small rural farming villages (Fig. 2). Because of  this skewed  population  distribution,  Suhum  is  the  hub  of  most activities in the district.

The district has 30 government health facilities altogether:  the  C-level  facility at Suhum, six B-level  facilities, and  23 A-level  facilities. The system is  successively inclusive; higherlevel facilities offer all the services provided at lower-level facilities in addition to services that are not provided at lower levels. Thus  there are 30 facilities providing A-level services, seven of which  provide  B-level  services,  and  Suhum hospital provides all three levels  of service. Like most other districts in Ghana, health facilities

Figure 2: Population size of villages and towns in Suhurn District

<!-- image -->

are located primarily in the larger centers with very few in the remote rural centers. Access to government health services is quite limited for rural residents.

Walking is the most popular means of travel in  the  district  because  few  people  own  any mode of transportation including bicycles. Access  to  commercial passenger vehicles is  limited. Where access is not a problem, the high fares charged, especially during the rainy season when the roads become difficult to travel, restrict use.
sections.Accessibility and the Goals of Ghana's P:
I n  location-allocation modelling, geographical accessibility  may be conceptualized  in  two main  ways-proximity and  coverage.  When defined in terms of proximity, accessibility has a  distance minimization connotation  and may be measured using the average travel distance. As a locational goal, proximity translates into the simple  p-median problem which selects facility locations to minimize average travel distance  for  users.  Previous  research  has  found distance to be a major determinant  of  facility use (Stock 1982). Accessibility  may also be expressed using a coverage distance. If  a  facility is within the specified coverage distance from a person, it is considered accessibie to the person and the person is said to be covered. Those people beyond  this  distance are not  covered. The measure of accessibility in this context is the  proportion  of  people covered. As a locational  goal,  this  approach  translates  into  the maximal covering location problem (MCLP).

The first  goal  of  the  Ghana  government, improved accessibility,  may thus be seen as reducing  the  distance  between  health  facilities and users. The goal can also be viewed in coverage terms, i.e.,  improving the proportion of

people who are within a specified distance of a health care facility. The  second goal,  improving the quality o f   PHC, is not as easy to interpret or deal with because location-allocation models do not explicitly address quality issues. Therefore, this goal is not directly addressed in this study. It  could  be  argued,  as  has  the  Ghana government,  that by  improving other aspects of  the  system,  supervision  for  example,  the quality of service would be improved.

The third goal emphasizes management and interfacility  relationships including referral. There are  many  dimensions to management, but the government has isolated supervision of low-level  facilities  for  special  attention.  The government's a i m is to ensure that all facilities work effectively, and it has stressed that supervision  of  rural  health  workers  is  absolutely critical  (Adjei  et  al.  1988). To facilitate this, there must be a B-level facility  within eight km of  every  A-level facility.  Location-allocation models can address this problem effectively.

From the government's goals, therefore, two central locational problems emerge: accessibility of facility locations to users (involving distance minimization and coverage) and accessibility for suppliers (coverage considerations for supervision, supplies, and referral). This paper uses  the  p-median  and  maximum  coverage models  to  measure  the  level  of  accessibility provided by the existing system of facilities and to determine if this level of accessibility can be provided  without  considerable  additional  resources. Using these  results, the  paper  evaluates  the  'add  more'  recommendation and shows  how  location-allocation  models  could help to improve accessibility.
sections.Data Requirements and Modelling Approach:
Essential data for this study included population  and locational information  for each community.  Population  data  were  obtained  from the  1984 population  census.  Because  Ghana does not have  a  digital spatial database, locations  were  digitized  as x and  y  coordinates from the Ghana  1:50,000 map series obtained from  the  Ghana  Geologic  Survey  in  Accra. There were no major problems with the maps, but the population  data of some smaller communities had been aggregated with larger centers  close  by.  Another  minor  problem  was communities with different locations but simi- lar  names.  These were carefully organized to avoid assigning the wrong population figure to any location. A simple distance generating algorithm  was  used  to  generate  Euclidean distances between locations.

The analysis involves 150 population centers in the Suhum district as demand points and the population  at each center as the proxy for demand.  Euclidean  distances  are  used  because walking is the main mode o f   travel in Suhum district.  This  avoids the  problem  of  seasonal inaccessibility  along  different  types  of  roads. The Tietz and Bart (1968) heuristic algorithm was  used. The modelling approach treats  the three  levels  of  service  independently  and  locates an optimal system of 30 facilities in keeping with the successively  inclusive nature of the system.  Seven  of  these  will  provide  B-level services, and  one  of  these  seven will  provide C-level services.
sections.Proximity to Health Facilities:
The  immediate  question  is  proximity to Alevel  services. How  does  the  existing (actual) system of facilities compare with an optimally located set of 30 facilities? The optimal p-median system  @=30)  results in an average weighted  distance ( A m ) of  1.09 km compared  to  1.38 km  in  the  existing system,  the latter involving 26%  more travel distance than the  optimal  system (Table  1). Thus, A-level services are not as accessible as they could be. Figure 3 presents proximal (nearest facility) allocations for the actual system while Figure 4 illustrates the optimal p=30 system. Next,  the possibility of providing the  same level  of  accessibility to  A-level  services with fewer facilities is considered. How many optimally located facilities would provide the same level of  accessibility? In  order  to  answer this question, the level of accessibility for different values of p (i.e., numbers of facilities) needs to be determined. Table 1 presents the results for p ranging between 1 and 30. The level of  accessibility provided  by  the  actual  system (a n average travel distance of 1.38 km) can be provided with only 23 facilities.  This suggests that it is possible to reduce the travel distance  in the actual system (improve accessibility) even with fewer  facilities. sections.Proximity to Facilities: Quantity or Loc:
Optimally located  facilities exhibit decreasing accessibility returns to the number of facilities (Table l), a known  characteristic of p-median optimality. After initially huge increases in accessibility, additional  facilities  produce  rather marginal improvements. Between p=11 and p=20, accessibility improves from 2.4 km to 1.52 km but the reduction  in average  travel  distance  per  additional  facility declines to 0.11  km. sections.pMedian Accessibility to Higher-Level Se:
Next, the provision of higher-level services beginning with B-level  is  considered. Because it is successively  inclusive, seven of the 30 facilities in the actual system provide B-level  services.  In  order  to confomi  to  this  hierarchical structure, the optimal model must select seven facilities from the 30 providing A-level services to maximize proximity to users. The results are presented in Table 2. Hodgson (1  984) demonstrated  that  such  a  bottom-up  approach  can result  in  suboptimal  higher-order facilities. This effect is  evaluated by  selecting seven facilities  freely  from  the  open  system  of 1.50 demand points. This system, however, differs from the bottom-up  solution by less than 1% (Table 2). The optimal p=7 system would provide an AWD of 3.28 compared to 3.7.5  in the actual system. The actual B-level system is thus not as accessible  as it could be, since it involves 1. 5   % more  travel  distance than  the p-median system. In  fact, six optimally located facilities would provide an AWD of 3.6 km and involve less travel than  the actual system (Table  1).

Finally,  the  location  of  C-level  services  is considered. Only one facility, Suhum, provides C-level services. To conform with  this structure, one facility  to provide C-level services  will be  selected from  the  seven providing  B-level services. The  goal  is  to  verify  whether  it  is possible  to  improve  accessibility  to  C-level services. In  this  analysis, the  bottom-up  approach identified the same location, Suhum, as the  best  location  for  C-level  services. When one facility is  selected freely from the  150 demand points, however, only a  slight improvement  in  efficiency  (less  than  1%) could  be achieved.
sections.Modelling the 'Add More' Recommendation:
To model the recommendation that additional facilities  be established to improve accessibility requires the retention  of all 30 actual facilities and establishing  additional facilities.  The result of  this  approach  is  presented  in  Table  3.  It shows that, even if they were optimally  located, five  additional  facilities would  be  required  to provide  the  same  level  of  proximity  that  30 optimally located facilities would provide (AWD=1.09). If  additional  facilities were  not located  optimally,  many  more  might  be  required.

Achieving an optimal 30-node system would involve  relocating  11  of  the  actual  facilities. This brings up the question of relocation costs: would it be more costly to construct five new facilities  than it  would be to relocate 11  existing facilities? In  the  absence of  accurate data  on cost, it is  impossible to  provide a precise  answer. In  the  Suhum  district,  existing A-level facilities have  very  little  in  the  way  of  infrastructure.  Most  facilities have  little  furniture and  only  one  health  worker  with  minimum training.  Relocation would  mean  transferring

sections.Supervision Coverage:
Coverage models are based on the simple notion that there is a distance (travel time or cost) within which patrons are served (covered) and beyond which  they  are not (Church and  ReVelle 1974). The amount of coverage provided by  a  system of  facilities depends  critically on the  coverage  distance. A small coverage distance requires many facilities whereas a larger distance requires few. The Ghana government has  not  explicitly stipulated  a  coverage criterion  for A-level  facilities, but  desires a  B-level facility within eight km of  every A-level  facility.  This  would  ensure  that  B-level  workers supervise and  hold  clinics in  A-level facilities much  more  easily.  In  turn,  A-level  workers could  visit  B-level facilities  for  consultation when necessary with little effort.

The maximum  coverage model  is  used  to deal with the problem of covering the 30 existing  facilities.  The  objective  is  to  determine what proportion of existing  A-level facilities  are within  eight  km  of  a  B-level  facility. Also,  if facilities  were located optimally, how many facilities would  provide  complete  coverage  for existing  A-level facilities?  This  analysis  involves choosing only from the 30 existing facility locations.  Coverage  distances ranging  between four and 10 k m will be considered.

Furthermore,  the  actual B-level  system provides complete coverage at nine  km, but  this could be  provided with  only  four  optimally located facilities. If  the  relocation  of  B-level  facilities was not possible, the alternative would be  the provision  of  additional  B-level  facilities. The analysis indicates that  two  additional facilities would raise coverage to 100%. Thus, building upon  the  present  system would  require  that nine  facilities  be  provided  whereas  complete coverage could be  provided with  only five facilities if  four were relocated.

Frequently, decision makers require help in formulating  their  location  goals. When  they see the locational outcome of specified decision criteria,  they  may want  to revise  the  original location  goals.  For  example, the  government has  specified a  coverage distance of eight  km for B-level facilities without knowing the exact number of facilities that would be necessary to achieve that goal. It is likely that if they knew the costs involved in achieving this goal, they might  want  to  choose  a  different  goal.  This situation is where modelling is most useful and supports Rushton's (1989) contention that location-allocation models can be used as spatial decision support systems.

T o  provide  total  coverage with a  four km coverage distance, 17 facilities would be required. If resources were restricted to only  10 facilities and the coverage distance was four km, only 87.8% of total demand could be covered. Through this type of analysis, location-allocation  models can be useful for identifymg  decision  alternatives,  trading  off  resource inputs against alternative locational outcomes, and  even  in  defining  or  refining  the locational objectives.
sections.Conclusions:
A systematic evaluation of proximity to health facilities in Suhum district using the p-median and coverage models as the bench mark consistently shows that  accessibility could be improved without  additional facilities. Providing additional facilities is not the only way to improve  accessibility to  services in  Suhum  district.  Depending  on the relative costs of  relocation,  greater  accessibility  can  be  provided with  the  same amount  of  resources currently employed. The relocation costs of  A-level  facilities would  probably be  minimal,  while the gains in accessibility could be substantial.

Regardless of what action the Ghana government takes, these results confirm that data lirnitations do not preclude the use of simple location-allocation analysis to support spatial decision making in the Third World. Rather, performing simple analysis using readily available data can provide invaluable inputs for making difficult spatial decisions.

The results also show the importance of location-allocation models as objective tools for measuring spatial  accessibility.  Without  satisfactory  measurement  tools,  it  is  difficult  to evaluate policy  options  effectively.  Moreover, there is no way of telling when adequate accessibility  has been established. A large number of facilities does not necessarily imply greater accessibility.  Rather,  as  Rushton  (1984) has  argued, the selection of optimal locations might be an important, but neglected, key in the effort to improve accessibility to health facilities in  the  Third World.  Spatial efficiency at  the district  level  could  be  the  key  to  an  efficient national system of facilities.

One of the difficulties of improving accessibility to health facilities in the Third World is that  'health care  delivery systems have  often grown up in a fragmented manner, provided by public, private, charitable and aid  sources and they have frequently been non-complementary or even competitive in their functions and locations' (Phillips 1990, 145). This problem is at the root of the redundancy and present day maldistribution  of  facilities,  especially where government facilities have not sought to maintain a spatial balance. The decentralization of decision making being promoted under Ghana's PHC program  provides an  excellent opportunity to address and solve this problem.

Under Ghana's PHC program, the District Health  Management  Team  (DHMT) is  responsible for all health planning and programming  within  the  district. A team  member, trained in the use of simple optimization models, could work with the DHMT  to identify an 'optimal' and desirable set of facility locations for  the  district. This  could  be  the  basis  of  a health facility location plan for the district, and the selected locations could be prioritized for development. District resources for additional facilities could be allocated based on these priorities. In addition, any organization seeking  to develop  a  health  facility  within  the  district could be encouraged to select one of the priority locations. Improved accessibility and efficiency at the district level will surely be the basis of a more accessible  and efficient national health care system. W

records.title: MIGRATION PATTERNS DURING A PERIOD OF POLITICAL AND ECONOMIC SHOCKS IN THE FORMER SOVIET-UNION - A CASE-STUDY OF YAROSLAVL-OBLAST
records.abstract: This paper examines migration in Russia during the period that preceded the breakup of the former Soviet Union (FSU) and during the current transition period. An unusually rich dataset is used to conceptualize the impact that the political and economic collapse of a world superpower has on a migration system. A regional case study of migration in Yaroslavl' Oblast from 1989 through 1992 is used to examine the relevance of expected outcomes given standard theories of migration, empirical regularities found in capitalist economies, and past trends in the FSU. The data clearly show a migration system undergoing political and economic shocks. A significant decline of the volume of flows and a relative increase in the importance of interrepublic movement indicate disruptions. Increased relative mobility for those in the later years of the working-age population and increased importance of urban-to-rural migration flows are also important changes evident in this migration system undergoing shock.

sections.Beth Mitchneck and David Plane:
University o f Arizona

This paper  examines migration in Russia  during the period  that preceded the breakup  of the former Soviet Union (FSU)  and during the current transition period. An unusually rich  dataset is used to conceptualize  the impact that the  political  and  economic collapse  of  a  world  superpower has  on  a  migration  system. A regional  case  study of migration in Yaroslavl' Oblast h-om 1989 through 1992 is used to examine the relevance of expected outcomes given standard theories of migration, empirical regularities  found in capitalist economies, and past trends in the FSU. The data clearly show a migration system undergoing political and economic shocks. A significant decline of the volume of flows and a relative increase in the importance of interrepublic movement indicate disruptions. Increased  relative mobility  for  those  in  thc  later  years  of  the  working-age  population  and  increased  importance  of  urban-to-rural migration  flows  are  also  important  changes  evident  in  this  migration  system  undergoing  shock. Key  Words: migration, Russia, USSR, economic shocks.
sections.Introduction:
oncern about potential climate change has C led  to a  number of studies addressing the possible  impacts  on  agriculture  (e.g.,  Santer 1985; Hodges  et  al.  1987; Smit  et  al.  1989; Cooter  1990; Curry  et  al.  1990; Rosenzweig 1990).  Two themes emerge from these studies. First, global climate change could alter agricultural productivity, requiring adjustment of certain agricultural  practices. Second,  present strategies used  to estimate climate impacts on agriculture have several shortcomings. Perhaps the most critical shortcoming involves accurate representation  of  climate  change  at  a  spatial scale where agricultural impacts are felt. Clearly,  the  impact  of  climate  change  over broad  agricultural regions should result  from the aggregated effects at local levels. Yet projecting climate change down to the local scale remains difficult. Many climate impact studies rely on general circulation model (GCM) output to  provide  initial  estimates  of climate change. Even  though  GCM results presently represent the most reliable and comprehensive means of  estimating potential climate change, the spatial and temporal resolution of the output is  typically too coarse to use directly with crop  yield  models  at  a  local  scale (Riebsame 1990; Rosenzweig 1990).

Most  researchers  have  acknowledged  the uncertainty  associated with  regional and local scale climate change scenarios and have recognized the need to present a range of potential impacts that conform  to  such  uncertainty (Cooter 1990;  Riebsame 1990;  Rosenzweig
sections.Review of Migration Trends:
For  Western  social  scientists conceptualizing migration  patterns  in  Russia,  standard  tools such as Ravenstein's laws of migration, life-cycle  theory,  the  Harris-Todaro  model,  public choice models, and many others may be useful. These  models  help  us  to  predict  migration patterns  according  to  variables  such  as  distance,  gender,  age,  unemployment,  and  local government policy. The relevancy of these traditional models, however, to non-Western, developing countries has been questioned (Brown  and  Sanders  1981). Approaches  that relate to both  less developed and more developed  contexts should be  considered here  due to  the  prevalence  of  multiple  development contexts in Russia and the USSR.

In  the  particular  context of  the  disintegration  of  the FSU, we  question the relevancy of previous  work  on  forced  refugee  flows  and international return migration, particularly repatriation. Most of this literature explains refugee flows during times of violent revolution or temporary labor migrations related to refugee

flows (e.g., Pessar 1988;  Marmora 1988;  Koehn 1991; Shami  1993). Literature on repatriation often deals with decolonization where the origin country was not contiguous to the receiving country (e.g.,  Smith  1981) or w i t h a  situation  of  returning  exiles  (e.g.,  Pessar  1988). This  literature  lacks  relevance  to  the  Soviet and post-Soviet cases because few places in the FSU violently  overthrew  the  Soviet regime, sending Russians packing. Returning Russians are not  exiles-they left their  homelands voluntarily, in some cases several generations earlier, to  seek fortunes  in  contiguous territories of  the country.

The appearance of crises or major economic 'shocks' requires the modification of tradition theory. As described by Long (1981), the 1930s Great Depression in the United  States caused a  stagnating  of  the  streams of  rural-to-urban migration, as people stayed on the farms where at  least  they  could  eat.  Explanations  of  the 'clean break' of US. migration patterns in the 1970s (Vining and Strauss 1977) included consideration of the severe recession early in that decade that was brought on by the shock of the Arab oil embargo of  1973. The persistence of the  metropolitan-to-nonmetropolitan movement trends through the late 1970s suggested, however, that a variety of factors were operating  synchronously  (Long  and  DeAre  1980). Among  those  factors  was  the  demographic shock of  extraordinarily large baby boom  cohorts  flooding  regional  labor  markets  (Plane and Rogerson 199 1; Plane 1992).  Interestingly, an oil glut (and recession) shock has been identified  to  help  explain U.S.  migration  patterns in the 1980s  (Plane and  Rogerson 1989; McHugh and Gober 1992).

Plane (1984) provided a theory of migration system  change  involving  'steady-state''  and 'non-steady-state' movement  patterns that vary in relative proportions  as a nation  passes through periods of rapid structural change followed  by  longer  interregnums  during  which movement patterns exhibit equilibrating trends.  Of considerable current interest in regional science are the  economies of  unscheduled,  major  events,  as  attested  to  by  several special  theme  sessions  at  the 1994  North American  Meetings in  Houston. To  date, however,  we are  unaware  of any  of  these emerging  ideas  having  been  applied  to  the impact  of  a  major  social  and  economic  dis- location  on  interregional  population  movement patterns,
sections.Soviet and Russian Case:
Questions  relevant to  the  changing  direction and composition of migration flows in the Soviet and Russian context during a shock period include: What  happens  to  the  direction  and composition  of  migration  flows  when  a  socially,  economically, and  politically integrated multinational state with distinct ethnic homelands breaks apart? What happens when strong government control over social and economic processes  begins  to  fade? When,  if  ever,  do major systemic changes occur?

The answers to these questions lie, in part, within  the  context of  the  previous migration system, one that was not well-studied by Western social scientists.  Many studies of migration in the FSU successfully predict the volume and direction  of migration  flows  using  standard economic models despite the contextual problems related  to the  noncapitalist setting (Rybakovskiy  1973; Zaytsev 1973; Lysenko  1977; Ball  and  Demko  1978;  Fuchs  and  Demko 1978; Grandstaff 1980;  Maksakova 1986; Mitchneck 1990, 1991).  These studies note the improvement of material welfare and quality of life  as  determining  factors in  the  decision  to migrate and destination choice. Standard economic  models  produced  highly accurate predictions  of  the  volume  and  direction  of  the flows  (Grandstaff  1980; Mitchneck  1990 and 1991). Ball  and  Demko  (1978) note  variable influences over  migration  flows  according  to level and type of regional  developmentagrarian, frontier, less industrial, and more industrial-supporting the  Brown  and  Sanders (198  1) thesis regarding the importance of contextual  influences over migration patterns.

Relatively little information is available about  gender, age, and  ethnic differentials of migration  flows  in  the  FSU.  Research  has shown generally balanced flows with respect to gender  (Lewis  and  Rowland  1979). Mobility appears to be highest among the youngest age groups in the labor force and among children (Lewis and  Rowland  1979). Also, substantial ethnic  differentials appear  to  exist,  with  the Slavs and several minority ethnic groups, such as  Jews,  Tatars,  and  Armenians,  having  the highest mobility rates (Lewis et al.  1976).

During  the  1970s  and 1980s  a  relatively small proportion of the total Soviet population moved interregionally each year. Topilin (1988) estimates  that about  5%  of  the  Soviet population  moved annually, with less than half of  those moves between  republics or economic regions.  T h e 5% figure places mobility in the FSU  well  below  that  of  developed  countries (Long 1991). Although Long's (1991) data are not  directly  comparable,  the  small  figure  is striking when  compared  to data  on changing place  of  residence circa 1981,  for  example, 17.5% in the United States and 9.6% in Great Britain.  T h e  majority  of the  moves  were  between  closely  located  oblasts  and  thus  were short-distance moves.  In  the  1970s between 40%  and 60% of moves were intraoblast (Rybakovskiy  1973). Evidence  of  a  trend  toward long distance moves, i.e., an increasing proportion of interrepublic  moves or interoblast moves, would indicate a change to the Russian migration system.

The direction and composition of migration flows in the  1970s and 1980s were largely stable,  but  we  see  the  first  evidence  of  social upheaval  with  the changing direction of some net migration interchanges in the  1980s. In a broad  regional perspective, the Soviet  (and Russian) population traditionally  redistributed from  central  Russia  eastward  towards  Siberia and  the  Far  East,  and  southward  towards Kazakhstan,  Central  Asia,  and  the  Transcaucams  until  the  1980s when  the  pattern  reversed  (Lewis  and  Rowland  1979; Mitchneck 1990).

The reversal  of this  long-term,  established pattern  of  migration  signals  social  and  economic  change.  Indeed,  cities  and  regions  in central  Russia  appear  to  have  attracted  migrants from farther rather  than  closer  origins in the mid-1980s.  Destination-specific  spatial interaction  models  of  intercity  migration  in 1985 for cities  in central  Russia  have  positive distance  coefficients,  indicating that  migrants were coming from distant rather  than nearby origins (Mitchneck  199  1).

Large-scale rural-to-urban migration  was also  an  important  feature  in  the  migration processes  of  Russia,  in  particular  in the postWorld War I and I1 periods (Lewis and Rowland 1979).  Although rural-to-urban  migration was a significant trend in the USSR, it became relatively  less  important  in  Russia  over  time.

Interurban  migration  became  predominant  in the  1970s and  1980s  in  Russia  and  for  the ethnic Russian population (Lewis and Rowland 1979).  A change to the migration system would be  indicated  by  the decreasing  importance  of interurban  moves.  This  did  occur  in  Russia after  the  1917 Revolution  when many urbanites left the cities of  northern  Russia  for rural places  in the south and east in  search of food and land  resources  (Lorimer 1946).
sections.Yaroslavl' Case Study:
The  Russian  and  Soviet  migration  systems have undergone shocks in the past due to major  violent  events  such  as  the  I917  Russian Revolution, civil  war, and  World  War  1 1 . Characteristics of the migration system persisted  despite  these  events-the north-to-south and west-to-east flows and rural-to-urban flows.

The essential  problem  here is to conceptualize  how  the  direction  and  composition of migration flows within the migration system(s) of  Russia  may  change  during the  post-Soviet period-a time  of  instability,  disintegration, and reintegration, not a wartime period. There are likely to be several overlapping yet distinct phases  of  migration.  The reality  of  the  situation suggests that although the phases may be distinct,  no one phase will be evident in isolation  in  any one place  or at any one point in time. Phase I, destabilization, describes the late 1970s and early 1980s  when the reversal of the north-to-south  net exchange occurred. Phase I foreshadows Phase 1 1 ,  disintegration,  when the chaotic patterns occasioned by the current destabilization and politicaVeconomic shocks become evident.  The initial  period  of  destabilization  ended  in  the  late  1980s just  as pereswoyka was ending. Phase I1 migration should be  evident  in  the  1990s, with  1989 being  a transition year  when both  Phase I  and  Phase I1 patterns co-existed.
sections.Yarosla vl':
Migration  in and  out  of  Yaroslavl'  Oblast should  be  seen  as  representative of central Russia. Data on migration in the Central Economic  Region  (a  statistical  accounting region to which Yaroslavl' belongs)  for 1970 through 1989 indicates that Yaroslavl'  is not atypical for the region with respect to losses of  population

in  the  1970s due  to  migration,  gains  in  the 1980s, persistent inflows of  migrants to urban places from the  1970s through  1989, and consistent outflows of  migrants  from rural  places (Goskomstat  RSFSR 1990).  Although the Central Economic Region has received a large portion  of the forced migrants returning from the  former  Soviet republics, Yaroslavl' Oblast received  about  the  average  number  for  the region  (Vitkovskaya  1994). Despite  the  relatively  large  number  of  returning  Russians in Yaroslavl', the oblast was  not  designated as  a receiving location by  the  central  government (Schwartz 1993).

Other regional  issues also support  the  description of Yaroslavl' as typical for the region. The politics are not overwhelmingly  liberal or conservative, although the region can boast of early  'democratic' movements  (Hahn  199  I). Although the oblast capital is located within a five-hour train  ride,  Moscow does not  dominate  the  region;  the  oblast capital, Yaroslavl', is  itself  a  regional  center  due  to its  industrial importance and role as a transportation center. Industrial employment in the oblast is concentrated in petrochemicals,  machine-building, the  automobile  industry,  and  light  industry (textiles).  These industrial sectors provide the oblast economy  with the combination of growth possibilities and an obsolete, fixed capital  base.  The oblast  is  not  dominated  by  the military  industrial  complex,  although  some factories  did  produce  for  it.  Yaroslavl'  does differ  from  other  central  Russian  oblasts  in that it has a higher proportion of its population living  in  urban  areas  (about  80% urban  and 20%  rural  in  1989), but  like other  oblasts in the central region its population is mainly ethnic Russian (95% in  1989).
sections.Data and Methods:
Migration  data  for  Phase  I 1   come  from  the annual  population  register  data  collected  in Yaroslavl' by  the oblast government. Register data  collected at the oblast level are probably of  higher  quality than  those  presented  at the national  level; by  the  time  the  national  level receives  the  data,  they  have  passed  through several  government  offices,  each  having  the potential  to introduce  error. Trained  sociologists calculated this dataset by hand  using the original registry forms. Although human error can occur in the absence of computerization in

Russia, the population accounting in this dataset is  the best available to date.

Several major drawbacks, however, exist due to the nature  of  the registry system. First, inmigration data are more accurate than outmigration data. Individuals must register as  they migrate into a  place  in order to receive social services,  including  housing, education,  and public assistance, but  no  such incentives exist to  register  outmigration.  Outmigration  data are  generally underestimated,  but  due  to  the absence of  place-to-place migration  data,  we cannot  estimate  the  level  of  undercounting. Within this particular dataset, however, we can measure 6% undercounting for intraoblast migration. Second, the urban accounting systems are  more  accurate than  the  rural  ones. Rural inmigration and outmigration are likely undercounted. Third, there are two separate counts of intraoblast migration. Differing levels of accuracy  between  urban  and  rural  accounting systems and  differing levels  of  self-reporting for  inmigration  and  outmigration  explain the latter  problem.

Accounting  and  data  quality  problems  are not  unique  to  Soviet  or  Russian  population data. These problems exist  in many contexts, particularly those with less technologically advanced data management systems. These data are,  however,  the  best  quality  and  most  detailed available on migration trends in Russia. Our approach is to analyze the time series with respect to trends without giving undue weight to  absolute figures. We  rely  most  heavily on the inmigration  data-rather than  the  outmigration  data-and the  data collected in urban places.

Because the goal of this work is to conceptualize the nature of a migration system undergoing shock and, in part, because of data limitations,  simple  descriptive  techniques  rather than causal modeling techniques were used  to describe and analyze the migration data. Other than  presenting  the  raw  data  themselves, we calculate simple ratios to describe the composition of the migration flows, such as a sex ratio and an age ratio of the 15-34  age group to the 35-59 age  group.  We  also  calculate  demographic  effectiveness ratios  to  measure  gains and  losses due to  the  exchange of  population at varying geographical levels. A high positive or  negative ratio  indicates a  large imbalance between the stream and counterstream. An in-

creasing ratio  over time  signifies regional net gains. The ratio is calculated by subtracting the counterstream  from  the  stream,  dividing  by the sum of migrants, and multiplying by  100.
sections.Evidence on Phase II Migration Pattern H: The hypotheses associated with Phase I1 focus on an acceleration of trends noticeable toward the end of Phase I, such as returning migration flows  to  Russia  from  other  republics and  the concentration of  ethnic groups in their homelands.  We  expect  to  see  gradual  structural change becoming evident from  1989 through 1992.
sections.Hypothesis 1: Decreasing volume $jaws:
The absolute volume  of  the migration  flows in and out of Yaroslavl' Oblast should decrease during the 1989-92  time period. We  should see the decreasing  volume  for  intraregional  flows  and gross interoblast  and interrepublic flows.

Decreasing flows  should  indicate the  presence of  economic shock. The decline of volume for total in- and  outmigration  would  be consistent with  the  United  States experience during  the  Great  Depression  and  the  experience  of  Russia  after  the  Civil  War  in  1917 (Lewis and Rowland  1979). We would  expect a  temporary  increase of  migration  associated with  cataclysmic  events,  such  as  the  commencement of  armed conflict in  the southern tier  or the perception of  revolutionary events. The volume should gradually decrease as  the migrant pool diminishes and as  people decide to wait out the economic downturn in place to reap  the  benefits  of  place-specific knowledge and social and  economic networks.

The time  period  under  investigation here, 1989-92,  does  in  fact show a  decline of  total in-  and outmigration, and net migration  (Table  I)  preceded  by  an  increase.  We  do  not consider the  decrease to be  a normal year-toyear  variation  of  migration  flows  because  of the  sharp decline for both  in- and oumiigration  between 1989  and 1992  (19,686  and 16,974, respectively).  The decline is especially noteworthy because from  1979 through  1988 Yaroslavl'  Oblast  experienced  an  average annual  net  increase  due  to  migration  of  about 2,900 persons  (Goskomstat  RSFSR 1990). Goskomstat RSFSR data show a steep increase of net  migration  between 1988  and 1989 followed by  a  gradual  decline  evident in  the current  dataset  as  well.  Intraoblast  migrants decline  as  do  the  interoblast  flows, while  the interrepublic  level  flows  fluctuate  (Table  1). The decline is a major change in the migration system,  while  fluctuating  interrepublic  flows also suggest changes to the migration system.
sections.Hypotbesis 2: Increasing proportion of:
The proportion of long-distance migrants should increase  over  the  period  as  interrepublic  flows increase in importance.

Interrepublic  (i.e., long-distance) flows consist of refugees  and return migrants.  We should be  seeing relatively more interrepublic moves relative to short-distance moves as part of  the effect of the shock. The breakup of the FSU should have precipitated an acceleration of south-to-north flows as Slavs return to Russia, Ukraine, and Belarus from the non-Slavic republics.

The data show that the proportion  of interrepublic  inmigration  and  thus  long-distance movers  does  increase over  the  period  (Table 2).  The growing proportion  of  long-distance movers in Yaroslavl' reflects the growing social unrest and economic instability outside Russia. The proportion  of  in-migrants  to  Yaroslavl' Oblast  from  republics  outside  of  Russia  increases from an estimated 12% in  1989 to an estimated 22% in 1992,  with the proportion of out-migrants going to other republics remaining fairly stable during the period. Hypothesis 3: Women predominate  in  long-distance mow

The proportion of women relative to men should increase  in  long-distance  flows  as  part  of  the return migration motivated by social conflict and by  economic conflict.

If  the  return  migration  is  politically or socially motivated, then more women than men should  make  the  long-distance  moves  as  is characteristic  of  international refugee  flows.

The long-distance moves would  be motivated by social  unrest, perceived or real ethnic conflict, and  political  change  rather  than  job seeking. We expect women to precede men, as wives  and  children  move  first while  the  men stay  behind,  continue  working,  or  join  the military.

While the dataset is rich, it does not include a breakdown of the flows by origin and destination.  Using  data  on  the  ethnic  and  gender composition of the flows,  we extrapolated long-distance  movers  by  ethnicity, given  two considerations. First, non-Russian in-migrants will most likely be long-distance movers. NonRussian ethnic groups with  homelands in the FSU  were  concentrated  in  their  homelands. Second, Russians will predominate in the refugee  inflows  to  Yaroslavl'  as  they  leave  nonRussian regions due to real or perceived ethnic conflict and social unrest.

In support of the hypothesis, Russian women  do  surpass  men  for  inmigration  to Yaroslavl'  in  each  year  (Table  4).  Ukrainian and  Belorussian  women  do  not  outnumber men  but  increase  their  representation  in  the flows between 1989 and 1992. The category of 'other,'  comprised of ethnic groups with homelands within Russia (the  Mordovian, Dagestani, Osetian,  Chechen,  Ingush,  Bashkortostan, Udmurt, Komi, and Chuvash republics),  also increased its  proportion  of  women. These increases are consistent with  more traditional refugee flows. Many of  the non-Russian  ethnic  homelands  in  Russia  experienced both  armed  conflict and  social  unrest  during 1991 and  1992.

sections.Hypothesis 4: Changing ethnic composit:
Ethnic composition of the migration flows should  change during  this period. The proportion  of  Slavs  to  non-Slavs  in-migrating  should increase  over  time,  as  should  the  proportion  of non-Slavs to Slavs out-migrating.

We expect changing ethnic composition to reflect a trend  toward further reconcentration of  Soviet national  groups within  their  homelands as a manifestation of social and economic changes  during Phase  1 1 .  Table 5  shows  support for this hypothesis.  Slavs do increase their proportion of total inflows from 89% in 1989 to  93%  in  1992  and  Russians  increase  from 84% to 89%. This indicates a trend toward the reconcentration  of  Russians and  Slavs in central Russia and a structural change in the composition  of migration flows.

The data  clearly  reflect  outmigration  from central Russia by non-Slavic  ethnic groups. In 1989, more non-Slavs migrated into Yaroslavl' Oblast than migrated out of the oblast  (Table 5).  Few non-Russian  ethnic groups had negative  net flows. But by  1992, the  situation had reversed with a negative net flow appearing for almost all  non-Slavic  ethnic  groups  and  with the  overall  non-Russian  proportion  of  inflow decreasing from 1  1 % to 8%. This supports the hypothesis that non-Slavic  groups were leaving central Russia. Although the data do not specify  the destinations of  out-migrants,  it is possible  that non-Slavs  leaving Yaroslavl' are  returning  to  their  ethnic homelands  or joining kin  in other places  in Russia.

sections.j a w s Hypothesis I : Changing age cump:
The  labor  force  peak  of  the  age  schedules  of migrants should broaden and the volumes of migrants  for all age groups should decrease due to the  economic and political shocks. Over the period,  mobility  for  older  age  groups  within  the working-age  population  (including  mid-career) should increase relative  to the  younger age groups. We expect the changing age composition to  be  evident  for  men  and  women  in  the  total and urban  flows.

Due  to  economic  and  political  instability, migration should become a viable response of persons in  all age groups, not just of  persons in  the  younger  years of  labor force participation  with  children, as  was  the  case during the Soviet period  (Lewis and Rowland 1979). We expect two trends to become evident: (1) older age groups will increase their proportion of the total  flows  because  migration  becomes  a  response  of  the  entire  population,  and ( 2 ) the volume of flows for all age groups will  decline at the end of  the period because fewer people will be at risk of migrating, and those remaining will choose to wait out the crisis in place.

The  changing  ratios  of  younger  to  older labor  force  age  migrants  for  both  total  flows and for urban  places  strongly support the hypothesis concerning the changing age structure of  migrants (Table 6). The ratios decline over the period for gross migration flows, inmigration, and outmigration, signifying greater  balance of age-specific flows. The declining ratios hold  constant  for total,  male, and  female migrants, further highlighting the pervasive changes in  mobility. The largest  relative  declines are evident for the 15-34  age group, the group  with  the  previously  highest  mobility rates. These data provide strong evidence that the age structure  and  the  volume of  flows  by age  group  have  changed  dramatically during the  crisis  period.  This  trend  has  important implications for  the changing composition of the labor force in Yaroslavl' during the transition period.

Hypothesis  6:  Changing  rural-to-urbnn migration flows

The volume  and  demographic effectiveness of urban-to-rural migration flows should increase as the  urban  crisis intensifies, reversing  the  longterm urbanization trend.

Recent  research  has  shown  that  in  Russia during the 1989-1992  period, urban places began  to  lose  population  while  the rural  places gained population due to migration (Zayonchkovskaya 1994). This trend should be particularly  evident  on  the  interrepublic  scale  since many  returning  migrants  and  refugees are forced  to  live  in  rural  places  due  to  governmental urban  residential  controls. The urban response  to shock at this point should include outmigration to rural locations. This response occurred in the United States during the Great Depression  of the  1930s and in  Russia imme- diately following the 191  7 revolution  (Lorimer 1946).

The information  for Yaroslavl'  Oblast suggests  a  concurrence  with  the  general  change for Russia. T h e  direction of flows changed and the  importance  of  rural-to-urban flows  declined  during the transition  period  (Table 7). The proportion  of  rural-to-urban  flows  also declines over time at the intraoblast level (from 41%  in  1989  to  30%  in  1992)  and  at  the interrepublic level (from 24% in 1989 to 10% in  1992). T h e  effectiveness  of  urban-to-rural flows increases  on the intraohlast,  interoblast, and  interrepublic  levels  (Table  8).  Urban-torural  flows increase  at the  intraohlast and  interrepublic levels (Table  7).  Information from the database also shows a trend toward declining urbanization over the 1989-92  period. Given  that 1992 was the year of the breakup of the Soviet Union,  the  structural  change may  be  an indicator of the deepening urban crisis and severe economic disarray that followed. We also see a  change  from  negative to  positive  effectiveness  for  interoblast  migration  (Table  8),  but the  change occurs earlier than  for  intraoblast migration. Urban-to-rural  effectiveness on the interrepublic  scale was  positive  and  increased during the period.

The redistribution  to rural places  at the interrepublic scale most likely reflects the urban residential  controls  in  place  at  the  time  that affected the long-distance return migrants. The  declining  importance  of  rural-to-urban migration  and  increased  importance  of  rural destinations  may  also  reflect  an  element  of choice on behalf of the migrants. Urban-to-rural migrants position themselves  in places where they have access to productive resources (land  and  livestock  for  food  production)  that are not available in the cities or for which they must pay substantial amounts. The early 1990s was  a time of  declining availability of  food in urban places and rising interest on the part of urban  dwellers in  obtaining  plots  of  land  to grow their  own food supply. A second reason that  migrants  may  choose  rural  places  over urban  ones is that land  reform,  including the allocation of land, structures, and farm equipment, was beginning in the experimental stage and seemed an inevitable event. People located in rural places prior to land reform physically position  themselves  in  places  where  they  are likely to reap benefits to which urban dwellers do not have access.

We expect the volume and effectiveness of interurban flows to decrease for Yaroslavl' Oblast on the interoblast scale due to the increasing  relative  importance  of  intraoblast  migration  (see Table  2).  The data reflect decreased volume of  interurban  flows  at  the  intraoblast and interoblast scales (Table 7 ) and decreased effectiveness of interurban  flows within Russia (Table  8).  The  data  also  show  the  striking increased migration to urban places in Yaroslavl' at  the  interrepublic  scale, with  the greatest  gains  occurring  in  1992, the  year  of the  breakup  (Table  8).  These trends  are  significant because they signal further disruptions to the previous system where interurban moves predominated at all scales.
sections.Conclusions:
One  primary  conclusion  from  the  empirical analysis  of  migration  in  Yaroslavl'  Oblast  is that  despite  dramatic  political  and  economic disruption  in  the  FSU,  the  structure  of  the migration system is predictable using an analysis of historical trends and standard approaches.  Despite  dramatic contextual differences between capitalist and socialist economic systems, concepts derived from capitalist contexts  can  serve  as  a  guide  to  the  analysis of migration  flows in socialist contexts.  Contextual differences exist, however, and are important for the study of migration flows.  For example,  the  increasing  migrant  flows  to  rural places in Yaroslavl' are due, in part, to the lack

of a housing market and to government regulation.

The data  clearly show  a  migration  system undergoing  political  and  economic  shocks. A significant decline in the volume of  flows and a  relative increase in  the  importance  of  longdistance  (interrepublic)  moves  are  results  of social  and  economic  disruption.  This is particularly evident when  we  look  at the  demographic  composition  of  the  flows.  Increased relative mobility for those in the later years of the  working-age  population,  reflected  in  the declining age ratios, is one of the most important  changes evident in  the migration system. Also, a  significant change of  direction  of  migration  flows, in particular the increasing importance  of  urban-to-rural  flows,  was  found. Despite only minor changes to the  migration patterns  by  ethnic group,  the reconcentration of  ethnic  groups  into  their  respective  homelands within the FSU was evident. The process is  likely  to  accelerate  during  the  1990s and deserves  greater  attention  in  future  analysis. This change also suggests that whereas Yaroslavl' may be an ideal locale to study many aspects  of  current  changes  in  the  migration system, much of the migration by non-Russian ethnic groups is taking place elsewhere.

Some  continuity  with  the  past  migration system does exist. For example, Yaroslavl' Oblast had  had  a net  gain of population  through migration for a long time; however, during the crisis  period  the  gains  increased.  Interurban migration is still dominant, but less so relative to the increased importance of  urban-to-rural flows at the interrepublic and intraoblast scales.  Also,  for  the  total  population,  gender differentials in  mobility  are  slight;  however, when  disaggregated by  ethnicity, gender  differentials increase. These  examples highlight the  importance  of  disaggregating the  migration data in order to reveal the composition of broad changes in the migration system.

We expect that when the  crisis phase ends, the patterns established in Phase I1 will lay the foundation for a new migration system distinct from previous patterns. There are several possible scenarios,  however, about how the system will evolve. If the economic and political crises worsen, we can expect Phase I1 migration patterns to persist to the extent that at-risk pools remain. A postshock transition  phase may  be characterized by stepwise migration evident on a  system-wide  basis  as  migrants  respond  to changing individual and environmental conditions in places. An  example of  changing environmental  conditions would  be  the  lifting or institution  of  residential controls  in  different locations in  the  system. Another  phase could be  a  temporary  new  stability with  a  gradual return  to certain pre-crisis migration patterns such as interurban moves predominating. But the spatial configuration of the system will differ dramatically from the pre-crisis period. For example, during the 1970s and 1980s,  large net inflows  were  concentrated  in  relatively  few places  like  Siberian  boom  towns  and  capital cities of  republics. Provincial capitals were attractive destinations for their own hinterlands but  did  not  present  intervening obstacles for nonlocal migrants.  New  centers of  economic growth  and  cultural primacy  are  likely to emerge that will  change the  configuration of the system of  origins and destinations. We are likely  to see less primacy under  capitalism or some  economic  system  other  than central planning. This new migration system will ultimately depend on the success of economic reforms in particular places, including changing regional levels of economic prosperity.

The structure  and  composition of  the  migration flows and the resulting migration rates after the shock will not look entirely like those in the United States or any other country.  The historical social and  economic context of  the FSU  and  the  dynamic  nature  of  migration flows suggest that while there  may  be  a  convergence  of  economic  systems and  some  related similarities  of the migration systems, significant differences will persist. The accuracy of  impact estimates relating  climate change to regional-scale agricultural production  is  constrained by  the  temporal  and  spatial  resolution  of  climate  change  projections.  Several  techniques  have  been  used  to compensate for these limitations in order to provide reasonable estimates of the impact of climate change on crop yield.  One approach assumes that variability over time  can  substitute for spatial variability, thereby  reducing the need to estimate the impacts at a  spatially dense network of  stationsan assumption that  has  not been generally tested.  This  study  evaluates  this  assumption  using  methods  similar to  those  employed  in  the  climate  impact literature. The findings suggest that current practices are generally defensible if  the  goal is to provide a range of possible  crop responses to climate change. However, the results also show that  the assumption is highly sensitive to  specific  interactions  at  the  soil-plant-atmosphere  interface  and,  consequently,  does  not  hold  under  certain circumstances. Key Words: climate change, agricultural impacts, scale, temporal variability, spatial variability.

records.title: COTTAGERS IN AN URBAN FIELD
records.abstract: The use of rural areas by the urban population is an important organizing principle in the study of the rural hinterland of urban centers. One of the important land uses identified within the urban field is recreation. This paper focuses on cottage property ownership in one part of the urban field, the rural-recreational countryside. Using three case studies from Canada, it was found that cottage properties account for a large proportion of local residential property. Although most cottage properties are owned by urban residents, up to one-quarter are owned by local residents. Using a questionnaire survey, it was also found that cottage owners are more likely to be older, better educated, and have higher incomes than rural residents.
