Near the end of the colonial period farmers began to focus their efforts on making planted maize seeds repulsive to crows. Some adopted the indigenous seed treatment with roots of false hellebore, also called 'Indian poke.' 7 These were boiled 'for  hours' and the kernels soaked in the concoction before planting (Eliot  ,  ). Sprinkling the soil with the liquid after the corn had been sowed was sometimes part of the operation. Manasseh Cutler, Hector St. John de Crèvecoeur, Samuel Deane, and Alexander Wilson all remarked that this botanical brew kept crows from digging up corn seeds (Cutler  ,  ; Deane  ,  ; Wilson  - ,  :  ; St. John de Crèvecoeur  ,  ). Other farmers sought more readily available and easily processed crow repellents. Coating maize with coal tar, often mixed with train oil or grease, soon became popular. Wood ashes or gypsum prevented the seeds from sticking together. A three-day delay in germination was the disadvantage of this coating. Those who knew chemicals came up with a number of other seed treatments that included saltpeter, copperas, ammonium nitrate, and lime chloride (Drown and Drown  ,  ; Enfield  ,  ). A strychnine treatment developed at

the Massachusetts State Agricultural Experiment Station was expensive but effective. Various commercial crow repellents, some with a strychnine base, came on the market in the early twentieth century.

Outfoxed by the treated corn kernel, crows redirected their foraging on farms to other edibles, including seed potatoes and phaseolus beans, whose pods crows learned to strip open in order to reach the seeds. In the South, crows figured out how to excavate peanuts, a legume that develops underground. Cherries, berries, pecans, and grapes have attracted crows, too. Chicks and eggs are part of their buffet, but to obtain those morsels involved flying dangerously close to the farmstead. An early motive for keeping guinea fowl, known for their raucous shrieks, on American farms was as barnyard sentinels against such incursions (De Kay  ,  ). Effective but not to be counted upon, farmers found that a breeding pair of eastern kingbirds ( Tyrannus tyrannus )  nesting  nearby  effectively  kept  crows  at  bay  (St.  John  de Crèvecoeur [  ]  ,  - );  Wilson  - ,  :  ;  Nuttall  ,  ).  The kingbird pursues with impetuosity any bird of whatever size that enters its territory.
sections.to kill or not to kill:
From the Euro-American perspective, firearms seemed to offer the immediate solution to the crow threat. In Captain John Smith's Virginia colony, the fact 'the very many crowes . . . are kld [killed]' indicates the use of that method ([  ]  ,  ). Destroying crows was framed as a civic duty, as exemplified by a  North Carolina law covering eight counties that required 'each taxable he or she' to yearly kill seven crows or squirrels (Clark  ,  ). That may have been prompted by a legal requirement in Maryland implemented in  and in place for thirty years that every taxable person deliver yearly 'three squirrel scalps or crow heads' (Edwards  ,  ). When, in the early eighteenth century, land use in eastern Virginia shifted from tobacco to corn and other grains, exterminating crows and squirrels became imperative (Hening [  ]  ,  :  ;  :  - ). Periodic deliveries of crow heads to the county courthouse demonstrated concern for the common good as it was then interpreted. Citizen responsibility, however, could not match the incentive of monetary reward for destroying crows. Most eastern states instituted a bounty for killing these unloved birds. In  Pennsylvania started such a reward system (Jones  ,  ). The Maryland one, started in  , paid the reward in tobacco. To finance the  bounty, some states instituted a crow tax; the one in Maine, for example, amounted to  .  a year (C. A. Day  ,  ). In the colonial period counties and townships, aware that failure of the corn crop was a public disaster, sometimes set their own stipulations. In Deerfield, Massachusetts, a  town vote proclaimed that 'whosoever shall kill crows this summer shall have four pence apiece peayed them by ye Town' (Sheldon  ,  :  ). In Buckfield, Maine, proof of each crow killed before the first of July received a reward of one shilling (Cole and Whitman  ,  ). Generous bounties on crows depended upon using unreliable muskets. The shotgun, as it improved through the nineteenth century, made it possible to kill many crows with one pull of the trigger. Funds to pay crow bounties became so

oversubscribed in New York, Pennsylvania, and New Jersey that compensation had to cease.

Technology aside, killing crows has always been the challenge presented by a species prescient about human intent. Individual wariness extends to group strategy. When a small flock lands on the ground, one bird serves as a designated sentinel and stands guard as its conspecifics feed. Many farmers alluded to the automatic flight response that the mere appearance of a man with a gun elicited. Alexander Wilson wrote of the 'jealous sagacity' of the crow in distinguishing a person with a firearm and reacting accordingly (  - ,  :  ). Crow hunters confirm that reaction, although assertions that crows learn to recognize the difference between a rifle, which kills at a distance, and a shotgun, which requires a closer quarry, stretch credulity (see, for example, Mermon  ). John Marzluff's research, however, suggests that crows recognize and remember human faces (Nijhuis  ).

Farmers killed crows as vermin on the assumption that they had no or little larger value. Edward Samuels's remark that crows were 'not only worthless, but ruinously destructive' and that they were 'not deserving of a moment's indulgence or protection at the hands of the ruralist' summarized a prevailing nineteenthcentury attitude (  ,  ). Countering views like that of M. W. Davis, who saw the crow as a 'friend to the agriculturalist' who lived in 'copartnership' with it, were exceptions (  ,  ). In that same vein was St. John de Crèvecoeur, who wavered between philosophy and practicality when he asked, 'Are they not the children of the great Creator as well as we? They are entitled to live and to get their food wherever they can get it. We can better afford to lose a little corn than any other grain because it yields above seventy for one' ([  ]  ,  ).

Beginning late in the nineteenth century, ecologically minded individuals called 'agricultural reformers' began to contest the negative view of crows by providing stark evidence of what they ate. Analysis of stomach contents of dead birds showed that crows consumed larger amounts of harmful insects than they did crops (Bendire  ;  Barrows  ;  Judd  ,  - ).  Most widely disseminated of these studies were Edwin Kalmbach's reports based on stomach analysis of  ,  dead crows (  ,  ).  Kalmbach found that their intake consisted of  percent vegetable matter and  percent food of animal origin and that one-half of the plant-food category came from corn. Sixty-one percent of the analyzed crows had eaten corn. Kalmbach distinguished the spring planting period of April-May, when one-third of the crow diet was corn, from the October harvest period, when that dietary proportion rose to one-half. These researchers did not deny the damage crows wrought on crops but emphasized the important summertime consumption of harmful insects, which made it difficult to simplistically categorize crows as noxious.

Notwithstanding the more balanced information about what crows ingested, laws that emerged in the late nineteenth century protecting wild bird species exempted crows (Palmer  ). Rural attitudes still held strongly against crows, so it is not surprising that the Federal Migratory Species Treaty Act of  excluded crows from any protection. In the  s  rising  concern about food production and the

army of pests depressing it hardened attitudes. Several states reinstated bounties. Sporting groups and so-called conservation clubs organized crow shoots. Dynamite bombs became an acceptable way to destroy them. In a highly publicized case in  near Rockford, an inspector from the Illinois State Department of Conservation killed  ,  roosting crows with dynamite (Bent [  ]  ,  :  ). That crows are vermin was an accepted idea through the  s. The bounty in Michigan, implemented in  , paid  cents for each crow head and is still on the books.

The earlier two-decade spurt of anti-crow sentiment dissipated in the  s as the rural vision changed. North American agriculture, with its transformed scale of operation through consolidation and mechanization and the generalized use of pesticides, fertilizers, and hybrid seeds, created food surpluses. Losses due to crows were simply written off as the cost of doing business. The chemical coating applied to maize seed was meant not to discourage crows but to prevent seed rot and disease. Bounties were once again removed. The  Migratory Species Act included crows on its list of protected species. However, to satisfy anti-crow sentiment, hunting them was permitted for part of the year. The state of Wisconsin, for example, which has had a crow-hunting season since  , harvests about  ,  birds a year.
sections.Crows in Cities:
The creation of a particular kind of residential landscape in North American cities encouraged crows to nest and feed there. In the  s  an  urban model adopted from western Europe favored the establishment of city parks and tree belts along most streets (Lawrence  ). Single-family dwellings surrounded by grassy swards and trees emerged as the preferred urban residential pattern in North America. Such artfully constructed habitats provide crows with open ground to feed on and treetops to nest in. Unlike the rock dove ( Columba livia ),  introduced from Europe in the early  s, crows rarely raise their young on human-made structures. Cities offer diverse food sources. Lawns have worms, often near the surface because of irrigation. Eggs and nestlings of song birds, especially robins, are abundant. Streams, ponds, or lakes offer other edibles. More recently crows have learned to take advantage of trash bins and dumpsters. Food wastes from these and other points receive daily replenishment, which enables crows to count on them as a reliable source of edibles. In addition, food litter from the American habit of eating snacks on the run has created a nutrient bonanza for commensal birds of several species.

Habituation to an urban food supply explains why resident crow populations in North American cities increased until the year  .  The annual Christmas Bird Count in New York City enumerated  ,  crow sightings in  , but  ,  in  (Martin  ). 8 Food supply, however, can not explain why, beginning in the midtwentieth century, towns and cities began to harbor large winter roosts of crows. Huge flocks now descend regularly to roost, tightly packed, in trees over an entire neighborhood. No nineteenth-century writer mentioned large winter concentra-

tions. The best explanation of this major development in crow synanthropy is that cities provide protection from being shot, safety from hawks and owls  their major predators  and greater ambient warmth. The pattern is for crows to congregate at staging areas and from there fly to an urban roosting locale for the night. Crows that winter in these roosts are a combination of flocks that summer in the surrounding countrysides and flocks that have migrated from more northern locales. The occupants of these roosts sleep in town at night and commute to the countryside to forage early in the morning.

Certain cities acquired a measure of notoriety for the large crow roosts they have harbored year after year (see Figure  ).  Since  especially  ,  Auburn, New York (population  ,  ), has had winter roosts comprising  ,  - ,  crows. Kalmbach indicated, however, that a winter roost was there as early as  (  ), and Emlen identified a large rural roost  kilometers south of Auburn in  - (  ).  The  notoriety of the recent Auburn roost generated National Geographic coverage, a Web site, a state bill, protests, and a controversial crow shoot in  . A cemetery provides a staging area for crows before they move downtown to sleep in an area around City Hall. A small river and the bright lights of the nearby large prison that may make crows feel more secure are other possible attractions to explain their concentrations there. Another small eastern city, Hagerstown (population  ,  ) in the Maryland Piedmont, shelters a winter roost of  ,  crows. As in Auburn, each morning the birds fly out to forage in the surrounding farm country (Gilbert  ).

Other major concentrations are Lancaster, Pennsylvania, with an estimated crow roost of  ,  crows; Springfield, Ohio (  ,  crows), Terre Haute, Indiana (  ,  crows), and Danville, Illinois (  ,  crows). Rich agricultural land is within foraging range of all four cities. The largest urban roost in North America may be in  Chatham, Ontario, where wildlife officials estimated the presence of  ,  crows in  ,  ,  in  , and  ,  by the fall of  (Riverdeep  ). Substantial sums of city money have gone to disperse or kill them, but this small city (population  ,  ) also hired a falconer and discussed a household requirement of crow-proof trash cans. Chatham, located in the cornbelt of southeastern Ontario, has abundant food in the surrounding rural area for crow foraging. Similar rich foraging possibilities seem to occur near most winter roosts. Why a particular area is chosen for a roost presents another question. In Chatham crows gather around industrial plants, where they are not bothered at night. Winter temperatures in town would be higher than in the surrounding rural areas. However, global warming since  may be a more significant temperature factor than the urban heat island to explain the broad North American pattern of winter crow roosts centered in areas where the winter average nighttime temperature is well below freezing.

Seasonal residency of mass concentrations of roosting crows creates a vexing problem for a municipality. The din of intense avian sociability during their lateafternoon arrival reaches a decibel level that aggravates most humans. Accumula-

tions of crow excrement are judged to be unaesthetic, odoriferous, and a potential source of histoplasmosis. In some places crows damage lawns in search of grubs. Residents in the affected neighborhoods typically unite to persuade the city to drive away the cawing and defecating hordes in their midst. Efforts to drive crows back to a rural habitat involve various hazing methods: pyrotechnics, firecrackers, sirens, amplified distress calls, spotlights, and laser beams. None has been successful in permanently dispersing roosts. In some cases the crows return to the site they left; in other cases they simply move elsewhere. Two constraints make lethal control measures a last resort. Many municipalities maintain a prohibition against firing guns within city limits. More recently, animal protectionists have organized to protest planned elimination of city roosts.
sections.Perturbation in Numbers:
The ornithological literature, together with the record of long-term landscape change, propels a series of thoughts about the crow population in eastern North America. More than any other process, the human imprint on the land has created the fragmented habitat that crows need to satisfy the high demands of their food quest. Daily food intake approximates half the bird's weight, and that requirement cannot be met by foraging in the forest. By my extrapolations, Euro-American farmers and loggers had by  cleared more than  million hectares of land in the eastern United States and Canada. Indians had earlier modified considerable expanses through fire, although they actually farmed less than  percent of that extent at  any one time. Farms provided more sources for crow sustenance than would simply burning the land to change the vegetation from closed to open. Each farm carved out of the forest formed a nutrient focus for crows: the crops themselves, insects feeding on the crops, and food wastes (see Figure  ). Densities of crows have often been a measure of how much food is available and may vary from five to sixty crows per square kilometer (Emlen  ). By my estimate, a conservative crow density of  per square kilometer of open land would have translated into a population of  ,  ,  crows in eastern North America in  .  Forty million more crows would have been added between  and  , when at least  million square kilometers of forestland were cleared.

Since then, two opposite land-use trends have occurred that probably canceled out further increases and decreases in numbers of crows. Agricultural abandonment has allowed forests to reclaim much land, especially in New England, eastern Canada, and Appalachia. Expansion of suburban and exurban landscapes around large and small cities everywhere in North America creates conditions for crow survival. Within them, housing developments, parks, cemeteries, campuses, golf courses, and strip malls offer crows either the kind of habitat they like or the availability of food. Kevin McGowan found that suburban crows have higher rates of nest survival than do rural crows (  ). One study, using Christmas Bird Counts, argued that American crow populations are increasing most rapidly in urban areas (Marzluff and others.  ). Meanwhile, the large rural roosts historically de-

scribed between New Jersey and Virginia have disappeared. Over the course of the nineteenth century four uninhabited islands in the Delaware River once harbored more than a million crows (Wilson  - , vol.  ; Rhoads  ,  ; Nuttall  ,  ). Rural crows have moved into cities. As northern areas have become warmer, fewer crows may have migrated southward. On the other hand, the decline in agriculture in some places has also caused a diminution in wintertime crow populations.

Some regional difference in crow numbers is systemic. Crows have always been more common from Virginia northward than in the Deep South. Two efficient scavengers, the black vulture ( Corgyps atratus ) and the turkey vulture ( Cathartes aura ) are abundant in the latter region, and the former species has in recent decades also competed with crows in urban areas. As one moves north, vultures become scarce, and beyond latitude  °  they drop out, thus allowing crows to occupy a full  scavenger niche. An early colonial reference to crow scavenging on human corpses during the  - epidemic in Massachusetts puts the bird's gravitation to roadkill in wider perspective (Adams [  ]  ,  :  ). Their incompatibility with wilderness is another systemic difference that affects crows. Both the forested mountainous areas and the subarctic taiga of eastern North America have small crow populations (Gauthier and Aubry  ).  In  New Y ork State, for example, the crow is notably absent only in the largely wilderness area of the Adirondacks (Bonney  ).

Regional decreases and increases in crow populations have always occurred. In central Ohio in the late nineteenth century, John Wheaton found few crows (  ,  ). He attributed the small number to the decimations of a cholera-like disease and the cutting of trees along streams that had been their nesting and roosting sites. Elon Eaton noted an epidemic of mortal blindness ('roup') that resembles what John Emlen had described in New York State in  - (Eaton  ; Emlen  ). Heavy persecution of crows reduced their numbers. Between circa  and  , official vilification of crows had its effect in the agricultural Midwest. Richard Graber and Jean Graber argued for a major decline in the crow population in Illinois, from  ,  ,  in January  to  ,  in February  (  ,  ).

Most recently, crow populations have fallen with the spread of West Nile virus, a disease introduced in  from Africa to New York City. Substantial die-offs of crows began in  , when researchers identified the species as the prime reservoir for the virus spread by infected Culex mosquitoes. Diagnosis of thousands of dead crows throughout North America implicated the virus over the ensuing five years (Caffrey, Smith, and Weston  ). The American crow soon became the sentinel organism for the spread of the disease. Its decline in some places was as much as  percent from  levels (LaDeau, Kilpatrick, and Marra  ,  ). For a time the disease wiped out virtually the entire crow population in the Chicago metropolitan area. By  crow die-off had subsided, suggesting the emergence of immunity of Corvus brachyrhynchos from the virus.
sections.The Crow in Context:
The crow is part of a larger synanthropic phenomenon that merits attention on an increasingly humanized earth. Certain animals, to enhance their survival, attached themselves to the human presence at some point in the past without undergoing domestication. Vertebrates, especially mammals and birds, capture most of this attention, although synanthropy also applies to a host of invertebrates such as the bedbug and clothes moth. Every continent has representatives of this broad category of synanthropic organisms, some of which are pests and some of which are not. Some species have established a quasi-obligate relationship with humans; others, like crows, are facultative in their response. For North America, Richard Johnson classified  native bird species in a continuum of mutualistic intensity (  ). One well-known avian in this category is the eastern robin ( Turdus migratorius ),  which extended its numbers and range enormously as lawns and shade trees graced North American towns and cities. At some time in history the chimney swift ( Chaetura pelagica ) found the benefits of making its nests on human-made structures. Harvesting insects on the wing around farms was so rewarding that nesting in nonhumanized settings was abandoned. The purple martin ( Progne subis )  has carried an implicit quid pro quo one step further by accepting colonial birdhouses, many of which are predator proof, in exchange for snaring large daily allotments of mosquitoes. A sizable raptor, the barn owl ( Tyto alba ), brokered its own ancient bargain with people when it moved into buildings in exchange for destroying harmful vermin. Because this species occurs throughout the world, its synanthropy must have emerged in Eurasia.

The crow-human relationship, in which the food intake of the former overlaps with that of the latter, historically presented a good deal more conflict than has the human relationship with most other bird species. Antagonism would have been less if farmers had recognized the full value of crows, not only in destroying harmful insects but also as a source of nutrition. History suggests that the crow once had a role as a game bird. Four seventeenth-century observers found crows to be perfectly acceptable to eat. Gabriel Sagard wrote of catching crows in cornfields and eating them ([  ]  ,  ); Nicolas Denys made the analogy that crow meat was as good to eat as chicken ([  ]  ). Thomas Morton announced that 'the crows (which I have much admired, what should be the cause) both smell and taste of muske in summer, but not in winter' ([  ]  ). In Virginia, William Byrd proclaimed crows 'as good to eat as doves' ([  ]  ,  ). By the nineteenth century positive assessments of the flesh of crows were rarely noted. Among the failed twentieth-century efforts to popularize crow meat as food was its presence on Chicago restaurant menus disguised under the name of 'Italian woodcock' (Brennan  ). During World War II a food purveyor at the Illinois State Fair tested the idea of crowburgers to find some use for the dead crows hunted in large numbers at that time. Gourmets who partake of crow breasts roasted in wine may concur on culinary value, but for the larger North American society an unconscious food prejudice has trumped nutritional acceptance and ecological benefit.

Notwithstanding that gap, the relationship of this black-plumed avian and us the talking primate has increasingly intertwined. Acceptable crow nourishment has expanded from the  items that Kalmbach catalogued in the early twentieth century. The processed snack foods of North American culture, including beef jerky, cheese puffs, tortilla chips, and bagels, suit corvine palates as well. Among the commensals that now converge on places where waste food of humans accumulates, crows manage to acquire their share. Crows may dominate the fauna around landfills, especially if modern management techniques are not used. Garbage in plastic bags does not deter crows, and anecdotal reports of crows memorizing the schedule of garbage pickups now abound. Observations suggest that crows position themselves near interstate highways to retrieve roadkill. Adaptability goes beyond scavenging. Lawrence Kilham documented crows feeding on lice and ticks found on the hide of hogs and cows (  ). Nesting components of rural crows also reflect changing technology and culture. In the nineteenth century, many nests had linings of horse hair from the time when animal power prevailed on farms. In the late twentieth century, pieces of plastic began to line nests. Eastern cities demonstrate a gradual shift away from total dependence of crows on trees as nesting sites to bridges, powerline platforms, chimney tops, building ledges, and even neon signs.

In less than a century the advance of urbanization and large commercial farming have made humans more tolerant of crows. Reduction in crows' classic wariness, especially apparent in cities where guns are disallowed, forms a behavioral response to that change. The future of American crow demeanor as a species is suggested by intercontinental analogy of a congener. In India the house crow ( Corvus splendens ) has lived for many centuries in an essentially unarmed, animal-friendly, and densely populated culture. Its audacity extends to stealing food from street vendors and entering dwellings to remove food from the table (Kilham  ,  ). The extreme watchfulness of the American crow has grown out of a long history of persecution. As people treat crows with insouciance rather than aggression, less wariness results in reproductive success, and another kind of corvine conduct asserts itself. Unlike the now-extinct dodo, the crow's innate intelligence has enabled it to adapt its behavior to anthropogenic changes in the environment (Marzluff and Angell  ,  ).

Around the middle of the nineteenth century George Perkins Marsh, noting that crows 'no longer respected' the presence of a scarecrow in the field, opined that 'it is commonly said in New England, and I believe with reason, that the crows of this generation are wiser than their ancestors' ([  ]  ,  ). Marsh's proposition that a behavioral change could have occurred within a period of approximately  years  was  not  put  into  a  Darwinian framework of natural selection. Individual crows able to outwit humans passed on their genes to offspring, which, in turn, made humans even more valuable as a source of nutriments. Worthy of speculation is how human-crow interaction had hereditary consequences on maize as it diffused through the eastern half of the continent. Subtle anatomical changes in seedlings and husks may have occurred in the plant as native farmers planted the

seed deeply in the ground and selected the ears for thick husks to protect their crop from corvine depredation (Hart  ).

Both intelligence and sociality explain the malleability of crow behavior. Nikolaas Tinbergen and Konrad Lorenz conceptualized an innate releasing mechanism in the brain that enables birds in the whole corvid family to react creatively to new situations (Lehrman  ).  A  hereditarily  determined neural capacity plausibly emerged in their evolution as highly social creatures keenly attentive to their conspecifics. Crows applied that sensitivity to social information about their fellow crows to information about unrelated organisms from which they could derive food. As part of their cognitive tool kit, crows honed traits of ruse and deception facilitated by their brain, which is proportionately larger than that of most other birds. The crow manifests causal reasoning, imagination, flexibility, and prospection in advance of most other vertebrate species (Emery and Clayton  ; Lefebvre  ). Transmission of new knowledge to kin and then to the flock makes a crow a culture-bearing organism overqualified for the ecological niche it occupies. Cognitive complexity has enabled crows to adapt to changes in human technology that have enhanced their survival.
sections.Bridging Ontological Divides:
A broad perspective on the crow raises procacious questions about how the traditional organization of knowledge has failed to fully address synanthropy as a category. Neither historical geography, which employs the methods of the academic discipline of history, nor biogeography, which follows the canon of the biological sciences, has creatively engaged the realm of the other. Historical geographers, who by inclination or training subconsciously label phenomena as either 'historical' or 'unhistorical,' view the nonhuman as an immutable backdrop to changing human circumstances. Yet many animals have their own time-space tapestry, in which social intelligence has evolved over centuries to change collective behavior. Configuring the animal over the long term  an exercise that always requires inference and supposition  opens another window into understanding biotic change and geographical context. Seen in that way, a synanthropic organism becomes a useful indicator of change and, as such, a way to further probe the myth of virgin nature. Synanthropic organisms, like people, are in the process of becoming ( natura naturans ) and never a finished product ( natura naturata ). Anthropocentrism crumbles when humans perceive animals as more like, rather than unlike, themselves. If humans have an innate potential for personal development, how can we know that the crow is not self-powered to do the same?

Biogeographical assumptions fall in an opposite direction. Studies of fauna and flora have typically marginalized anthropogenic influences as inconvenient intruders into nature's exquisite web. That view becomes unsustainable for those who want to understand the earth as it really is. Biogeography cannot ignore the stark fact that less than one-fifth of the world's land area has escaped direct human impact and that creative assessment of the world's biodiversity cannot disregard the

manifold anthropogenic interventions in biotic patterns and processes. The classic procedures of mainstream science are not the privileged path to knowledge in melding the biotic and anthropic with insight and discernment. A delicate empiricism is required to see comprehensively rather than selectively and to think not about crows but with them. The biggest hindrance to an alternative way of thinking is the false assumption that nature and culture are separate ontological entities. Crows in their relationship to humans offer a compelling narrative to ponder the need to reevaluate the presumptions that animals are without history or culture.

-  . An extensive literature on crows provides abundant evidence of their intelligence and adaptability (Verbeek and Caffrey  ). People who have kept crows as pets are astonished by their capacity  to  learn  and  their  reasoning power (Bendire  ,  - ;  Bent  [  ]  ,  - ;  Kilham  ). William Bartram, one of America's earliest writers on natural history, wrote that 'it would be endless . . . to recount instances of this bird's understanding, cunning, and operations, which certainly exhibited incontestable demonstrations of a regular combination of ideas, premeditation, reflection and contrivance, which influenced his operations' (  ,  ).
-  . European entomologists introduced the word 'synanthropy' into scientific usage in the  s. Dalibor Povolny, in particular, gave the term precise meaning and its English-language forms (  ,  ).  Scientists  extended the use of 'synanthropy,' which had initially been applied to insects that were attracted to humans and their places, to encompass avifauna (Tomialojc  ). Other vertebrates are now included in this term, but, contrary to its usage by Gordon Whitney (  ,  ), synanthropy is not limited to introduced exotic commensals such as the rock dove, European starling, or Norway rat. Three forms of the word are in use: 'synanthropy,' as the condition; 'synanthrope,' as the organism; and 'synanthropic,' as the adjective. This cluster of neologisms has not yet entered the unabridged dictionaries of the English language.
-  . Inspiration for a holistic view of biological phenomena comes from the delicate empiricism of Johann Wolfgang Goethe (  - ). Though better known for belles lettres and philosophy, Goethe formulated a style of inquiry that employed careful description, avoided mechanistic explanation, and sought to discover the unity of the thing studied (Seamon and Zajonc  ).

-  . References to 'blackbirds' in historical sources raise the question about which species was being addressed: the crow, in the Corvidae family; the red-winged blackbird ( Agelaius phoeniceus ) and the common grackle ( Quiscalus quiscula ), both in the Icteridae family; or the European starling ( Sturnus vulgar is), in the Sturnidae family, introduced from England in  . References to the blackbird in the remarks of Adriaen van der Donck and Izaak De Rasieres about the island of Manhattan in the seventeenth century and those of Luigi Castiglioni about Maryland in the eighteenth century could have applied to any of the three native species (De Rasieres [  ]  ,  ; Donck [  ]  ,  - ;  Castiglioni [  ]  ,  - ).  However, Pehr Kalm provided the necessary ornithological detail to distinguish grackles and red-winged blackbirds as separate species, both of which he described as 'maize-thieves' (  ,  :  - ).
-  . Originally a scarecrow was a person employed in scaring birds by shouting, banging pans, waving sticks, or moving clappers. Only in the sixteenth century did it acquire its current meaning of an immobile effigy meant to frighten birds from growing crops ( Oxford English Dictionary  ,  :  ).
-  . David Jones inventoried the American Indian groups who knew false hellebore and its effects (  ,  - ). When ingested, the many steroidal alkaloids found especially in the roots, which are five to ten times more poisonous than the leaves or stems, cause convulsions. Manasseh Cutler described the root as a 'most drastic cathartic' and poisonous to swine (  ,  ).
-  . The Christmas Bird Count started in  , when the American ornithologist Frank Chapman proposed counting birds around the holiday season (officially between  December and  January)

rather than hunting them as had been the custom. Collected mainly by amateur bird-watchers, this information is useful not only to document the presence of bird species in a place at that time of year but also to make temporal comparisons within any one species.

records.title: FEMALE ACTIVITY SPACE IN RURAL BANGLADESH
records.abstract: Mobility and employment opportunities of women have traditionally been restricted in rural Bangladesh. As poverty increases, women in poor families seek work to support families. This trend has resulted in expansion of female activity space, after many years of stability. This article analyzes female space in the context of purdah, the patriarchal family structure, and the spatial organization of rural settlements. It discusses ethnic and other differentials that influence female space. Governmental and nongovernmental organizations are urged to create additional employment opportunities for rural women, so as to expand further their activity space.

sections.BIMAL KANTI PAUL:
ABSTRACT. Mobility  and  employment opportunities of women  have  traditionally  been  restricted  in  rural  Bangladesh. As  poverty  increases,  women in  poor families  seek  work  to  support  families.  This  trend  has  resulted  in  expansion of female  activity  space,  after  many  years  of  stability.  This  article  analyzes female space  in  the  context  of  purdah,  the  patriarchal  family  structure,  and  the  spatial organization of  rural settlements. It discusses  ethnic  and  other  differentials  that influence  female  space.  Governmental  and  nongovernmental organizations are urged  to create  additional  employment opportunities for  rural women, so as to expand  further  their  activity  space.

IN  many developing  countries, women  in rural areas usually perform their daily  activities at home or in their own  neighborhoods. Beyond  the  neighborhood  boundary, open  fields, public roads,  and markets are male  space, traversed  by  women  only  on  special  occasions and in  appropriate company or dress. The  presence  of women  in  male  space  is  generally  considered  to be both  provocative  and offensive  (Mernissi 1975).  Evidence  suggests,  however,  that  many  changes  occurred in  gender  relations  throughout  the  developing  world  during  the U.N.  Decade for Women,  from 1976 to  1985,  and that female  space  has  expanded  as a result. Most work  on  this  subject  has dealt with  the  spatial  behavior of urban women  in industrial countries, with little attention  given  to the  spatial  behavior  of rural women  in  developing countries.  This  article examines  the  changing  structure of  female  activity space  in  rural  Bangladesh.  A  holistic  approach  links  female  activity  space with  cultural, social,  political, religious,  and economic  systems.  Unless  otherwise  noted,  the  term  female  space  here  represents  the  space  of  Muslim women.  The  predominant  religion  in  Bangladesh  is  Islam, which  covers 85 percent  of  the  population.  Hindus  account  for  13  percent,  Buddhists  0.61 percent,  and Christians 0.31  percent (BBS  1985, 97).

*  DR. PAUL is an assistant  professor  of  geography at Kansas State  University,  Manhattan, Kansas 66506.

Copyright  ? 1992  by  the American  Geographical  Society of  New  York

NUMBER 1

Until  recently,  the  mobility  and  employment opportunities  of rural  women in  Bangladesh  have been limited both  spatially  and  functionally.  However, women  are now  increasingly  forced to seek  employment  outside the homestead to  support  their  families.  Age-old  norms  segregating  and  protecting women  have  been  broken  during  the  last two  decades  (World  Bank 1990, 1).  This  pattern  has  resulted  in  the  areal  expansion  of  the  female  activity space,  which  had  been  severely  restricted  by  tradition  (Greeley  1983, 42; Khandker 1987, 93).  After  providing  background,  this  article discusses  differentials of  female  activity  space  in  rural  Bangladesh, analyzes  the  recent changes  in the extent of female  space  at the national level,  and offers some policy  recommendations.
sections.BACKGROUND:
The extent  of  female  space  in  rural  Bangladesh  is  closely  linked  to the purdah, which is  deeply  rooted in Islamic doctrines. The word  literally  means curtain or  veil,  and  the  practice epitomizes  the  exclusion  of  women  from public  male  space  and  their  seclusion  in  the  home  compound,  which  is surrounded and shielded  by  houses,  foliage,  and  fencing  (Feldman  and McCarthy 1983,  949;  Chen  1986,  217).  Purdah is often one of several instruments of  patriarchal  family  structure that enable men to dominate women  in rural Bangladesh (Cain, Khanam, and Nahar  1979, 1).  Men  usually  exert  power and  authority  over  women,  because the  former control  property,  income, and women's  labor,  and because husbands  generally  are five to fifteen  years older than  their  wives.  Purdah and  patriarchal family  structure have  produced a  rigid  division  of labor  by gender  and a  system  of social stratification that makes women  extremely  dependent  on  husbands  and  places  them  at extreme  risk when  husbands  prove  unreliable  or withdraw  support.  The women's  apparent  insurance  against  such  potential  risks  is  children,  especially  sons,  the  birth  of  whom  confers  some  status and  autonomy  on  a young  woman  (Chen  1986, 217-218).

To understand the extent of sex-based  activity space  in rural  Bangladesh, it is  necessary  to have  knowledge  of the  spatial organization  of rural settlements.  Their  primary  unit  is  a  bari,  which  generally  consists  of  two  to six houses around a  square  or  rectangular courtyard.  The residents of a bari are in most instances divided  into households  living  in  separate  houses that are used  for  sleeping,  storage,  and  cooking.  If a household  has  cattle, there  is likely  to be a shed in the outer  courtyard  (Fig. 1).  There  may  also be a kitchen garden  accessible to the bari without  exposure  to the outside world. A household  usually  consists of a nuclear  family  and  represents  the  primary  economic unit,  being  the locus of  production  and  consumption.  All the residents of a bari are members  of  a  patrilinear family.  Most  daily  activities  of  married women  and  young  unmarried  girls  are confined  to a bari.

Women  perform  a wide  variety  of  jobs  and  activities  to  maintain  the family.  However,  the  existent  social  system  dictates that women  specialize

<!-- image -->
FIc.  1-Rural settlement in  Bangladesh.

only  in the tasks that can be  performed  in or near a bari.  They  fetch water, clean  houses,  cook and serve  meals,  wash  dishes  and  utensils,  and care for the children. Other tasks for women  are  tending  of livestock,  raising poultry, preparing  and  storing  foodstuffs, and  growing  vegetables.  In  nonagricultural communities  women  do other work: in  fishing  communities,  for  example,

they  weave and  repair  nets,  prepare drying  racks,  and  protect  the catch from birds. Men are  primarily responsible  for the fieldwork related to  production and for all other activities  requiring  social interaction outside the homestead. Irrespective  of  occupation,  men also  participate  in some  farmyard  and homestead-based activities  such  as  feeding  and  raising  cattle.  Similarly,  women sometimes  work with  husbands  in  the  nearby  fields to harvest  pulses  and mustard or at  ponds  to clean  jute.  Until  recently,  however,  those were  rare exceptions,  where  labor-intensive,  location-specific  tasks  required poor  families  to use the  labor of both  sexes  (Greeley  1983, 40).

The  next-highest  rural  settlement unit is the  para,  or  neighborhood,  which is intermediate between  the bari where  an individual  lives  and the  village in  which  it  is  located.  A  neighborhood is  a  cluster  of  adjacent  baris,  the formation of which  is  usually  conditioned  by occupational, religious,  social, or  topographical  factors  (Bertocci 1975, 353).  Several  neighborhoods,  which are  physically  detached from each other  by cropland,  wasteland,  or woods, together  form a  village.  Small  villages  often  comprise only  one  neighborhood. In some  villages  there  may  be a  post  office, schools,  or  shops,  generally  at the  junction  of two or more roads.  Beyond  the  village  are  weekly  or  biweekly markets  (hats),  where  men  do all the  shopping  for household  items and the principal selling  of a household's  agricultural  and  nonagricultural produce.

People living  in a  neighborhood  are  generally  related,  and a  majority  of them have the same basic  occupation,  whether in  agriculture, fishing,  weaving,  or  pottery.  The  pattern  holds  true with  respect  to  religion  and  caste, especially  in Hindu-dominated areas. Sometimes households  from one  patrilinear  kinship  group  cluster in  one  neighborhood  of a  village.  Women  are usually  allowed  to  visit  other  homesteads  in  the  neighborhood without wearing  a veil. Because few families in a  neighborhood  own  a well  or  pond, most  women  must  go  to  the  site  of  one  to  obtain  potable  water  for their households  and to bathe and wash clothes.  They  also  occasionally  visit other homesteads to borrow or return  goods.  The sheltered  paths connecting neighborhood baris are used  for these  visits.  Movement  of women  beyond  their own  neighborhood  is  rarely required  and is not  permitted  unless  they  wear a  burkah, which  is a loose  garment  that covers the  body  from crown  to toe, or  carry  an  umbrella to shield  them  from the  gaze  of men  along  the  way. However,  only  the  wealthy  can afford to have  burkahs, so an alternative is for most  women  to  cover their  heads  with  a sari  arranged  like  a burkah. Women of  prosperous  families often travel in curtained  carriages.  Thus the activity space  of most women  in rural  Bangladesh  extends to the  boundary of their  neighborhood.  Male  space  covers a broader area, encompassing  the boundaries of their own  and  nearby villages.
sections.DIFFERENTIALS IN FEMALE SPACE:
Although  the  neighborhood  boundary generally  determines  the  extent of female  space  in  rural  Bangladesh,  the area  may vary  in size  according  to

a woman's  economic  status,  age,  and  religion,  as well  as the  geographical location and size  of the  neighborhood  (Fig. 2).  Women  from different economic classes are  subject  to varied  types  and  degrees  of  patriarchal  control. The  poorer  the  family,  the  more  egalitarian  the  relationships  and  responsibilities between  the sexes. The social  prescription  of  purdah  is least  rigidly followed  by  women  of the  poorest  families  (Feldman 1983,  1894),  which  need women's  involvement  in  income-producing  activities.  Women  of  landless and  land-poor  families  thus  often  work  outside  their  neighborhoods.  The female  space  of women  of  poor-to-very-poor  families  may  include their own and  adjacent neighborhoods.

Wealthy families,  which  have  enough  land and other income sources to provide  food and other necessities  year-round,  do not need the labor of the women  for survival and can afford the costs  implicit  in their strict seclusion. Indeed, they employ  women  of  poor families, mainly  widows  and divorcees, to  perform  work  that  involves breaking  the  norms  of  purdah.  The  hired laborers  wash  clothes,  carry  water,  and husk rice,  tasks not  usually performed by  women  of so-called  high-status  families for reasons of honor. Purdah thus symbolizes  the  social status of  rural families  and  bolsters class differences among  them  (Abdullah  and Zeidenstein  1982, 56).  The nature of their work means that women  of  relatively  affluent families need not leave their homesteads. With decreased familial  wealth,  the  range  of female  space expands; likewise  with  increased  wealth,  the  range  contracts. This  relationship  contrasts  markedly  with the situation in Western countries:  there affluent women have more  mobility  and hence  a  larger activity space  than do  poor  women. Obviously,  wives  of  village religious  leaders also maintain strict  purdah  and stay  within  their homestead  compounds.

The  status  and  position  of  women change  at different  points  in  their life  cycles,  which may  broadly  be  divided  into  two  stages:  the  orientation stage  in  the  parental home,  and the  procreation stage  in  the  affinal home. Marriage  is the nexus between these  stages.  Before  marriage,  girls pass through infancy,  childhood,  and adolescence in the  parental  home.  They usually  are secluded there between  menarche and  marriage.  Notions  of  purity  and morality  underlie this restriction on  spatial  movement.  After  marriage,  women acquire  new  roles  as  daughter-in-law,  mother,  mother-in-law,  and  grandmother. Because of the  large  differences in  age  between  husbands and wives, many  mothers-in-law and  grandmothers  are widows. Mothers-in-law in  joint families  supervise  and direct the  work and social relations of other female family  members,  especially  young  wives  and  adolescent  daughters.  With advancing age,  the demands for  purdah diminish,  and female members are allowed more  open physical  movement  in the  neighborhood  as well as some outside it.  Elderly women,  especially  widows,  have the most  autonomy  and mobility  in  their  own neighborhoods  and  in  adjacent  ones.  Their  activity space  often  exceeds the  boundary  of overall female  space.

The  space  of  a  young  wife,  in  contrast, falls  short  of  the  boundary  of

overall  female space.  The  mobility of  a new wife  is  severely restricted  even within the  homestead compound. In  the  first  year of  marriage, she  is  not allowed to  visit  other  homesteads without an  older  female escort  from  the husband's family. She  is  rarely  sent  to  bring  water  or to  borrow  goods  from nearby homesteads. She  must  bathe  in  the  pond or  river  only when most men  are at work  in the fields.  Nearly  the  same  is true for unmarried  adolescent girls:  they  may  fetch  water,  bathe,  and  do  many other  tasks,  but  they  must be  accompanied by  friends of  their age  or  by  younger siblings.

The  activity  space  of  Hindu  women,  who  do  not  practice purdah,  encompasses  a  larger  area than  overall female  space.  Hindu  female  space  includes  the  women's  own  neighborhood,  plus  a  part  or all  of  the  adjacent neighborhoods.  It thus  more  or less  corresponds  to  the  space  of  the  nonHindu  very  poor  women  or those  of  older  ages.  Irrespective  of  economic status,  age,  and  religion,  female  space  often  extends  to  adjacent neighborhoods  if  two  or  more  of  them  are close  together  or  are  homogeneous in kinship  and other social criteria  (Cain, Khanam, and Nahar  1979, 32). This is  also  true  for  women who  live near  the boundary  of  two adjacent neighborhoods.

The  pattern  contrasts  sharply among  women  of tribes,  which  account for almost 1  percent  of the total  population.  The  activity space  of these women is  larger  than  that  of  the  poorest  nontribal  women,  because  tribal  society does not restrict women's  movements  outside  their homesteads.  The tribal groups  are  concentrated  in  the  southeastern  and  northern  hilly  areas of Bangladesh  and on the  plains  of North  Bengal.  Unlike  the vast  majority  of women  in  Bangladesh,  the tribal women  have a dominant role in all  aspects of life.  They  work  both  at home  and in  the  fields and are involved,  as are men,  in  marketing  of  agricultural produce.  Female  participation  in  all economic  spheres  in  tribal  society  has  been  induced  by  the  harsh realities of pressing  socioeconomic  problems.  Male and female  spaces  of the tribal  groups are similar to male  space  in the rest of  Bangladesh.

The size of female  space  varies  regionally  in  Bangladesh,  as the districts of the  country  differ from each other in economic condition and in  practice of  purdah.  Noakhali  and  Chittagong  are considered the  most  conservative districts,  and  the  female  activity  space  there  should  be  smaller  than  the overall  female  space.  The  opposite  is  true  for  Bogra, usually  considered  a nonconservative  district. The  range  of  local female  activity  space may  also be at variance with  the size of overall female  space  because of the  proximity and the  accessibility  of the  neighborhood  to urban centers.  Generally,  female space  for women  who live in urban  fringe  areas  should be  larger  than overall female  space.  Persons in  such  neighborhoods  are  relatively  less strict about observing  purdah  than are those  in rural areas.
sections.RECENT CHANGES IN FEMALE SPACE:
The  employment  opportunities  traditionally  available  to  rural women were as  paid  labor in other  households,  preferably  in the same  neighborhood. Paid labor is defined  here to include  both  agricultural  and  nonagricultural tasks  performed  for cash or kind. The  type  of work  performed  as  paid  labor is  essentially  household  related  (Table I).  Although  paid  labor is  still  the largest  source  of  female  employment in  rural  Bangladesh,  the  number  of women  seeking  wage  employment  is  increasing.  The chief  distinction  between paid  labor  and  wage  labor  is  that  the  former  is  restricted to  the household  compound,  while  the  latter is not.  Because  wage-labor employ-

ment involves  greater  movement  from home,  it is reasonable to contend that female  space  in  rural  Bangladesh  has been  expanding.

One  way  to  support  this assertion is to adduce national-level information on  the  absolute  size  of  the  female  civilian  labor force in  rural  Bangladesh for two  or more consecutive  censuses.  Unfortunately,  the definition  of this segment  of  the  labor force  has  varied  in  Bangladeshi  censuses.  The  1961 census,  for  example,  defined  the  female  civilian  labor force as  comprising women  ten  years  of  age  or  older  who  were  gainfully  employed or  were seeking  work. In  1974, by  contrast, female  children  below  ten  years  of  age but above  five  years  who  claimed to have  worked  for  wage  or  profit  were included  in  the  civilian  labor force  (Census  Commission  1975, 148).

Despite  the  definitional  problems,  the available labor-force data  suggest that more women  have been  employed  or  looking  for work in recent  years than in the  early  1970s. The 1983-84  survey  of the labor force  (BBS  1985,  77) showed that the absolute size of the female  portion  increased  by  half a million persons  during  the  1974-1981 intercensal  period  and  by  0.8 million  from 1981 to  1984. These trends cannot be  explained  merely  by  the  expansion  of the absolute number of the rural  female  population aged  ten or above  (Census Commission  1975, 111, 135;  BBS  1985).  Moreover, the  average  annual increase in  the  absolute  size  of  the  female  civilian  labor force was  much  higher  in the  1981-1984  period  than in the  1974-1981  period.

Empirical  studies  in  rural Bangladesh during  the  past  decade or earlier suggest  that  women's activity  space  has  been  expanding  (Abdullah  and Zeidenstein  1982, 24; Chen  1983, 70; Feldman and  McCarthy 1983;  Greeley 1983, 43; Chen  1986, 220; Aziz  1990, 3). According  to these  studies,  women have been seen  working  in the fields alone or  alongside  men;  participating

in  weeding,  transplanting,  and  harvesting  of  crops; carrying  harvest  from the  fields;  and  tending  cattle  (Safilios-Rothschild  and Mahmud  1989). They also  work  at  public-sector  construction  sites  (World  Bank  1990, 30).  More and more women  have also been observed  begging. By contrast,  in  previous years  all work  outside  the  homestead,  other  than  begging,  had  been  done by  men.
sections.EXPANSION OF FEMALE ACTIVITY SPACE:
Several  independent but  mutually  correlated factors have  forced rural women  to seek both  paid  and  wage  labor outside their homes  or  neighborhoods.  Bangladesh  is now  undergoing  rapid  socioeconomic  change  marked by  increased rates of rural landlessness  and  impoverishment.  The  country has one  of the  highest  population  growth  rates in  the  world;  that  growth, in  turn, slashed the  average  area of cultivable land  per  rural  household,  from 1.21 hectares in  1961 to  approximately  0.61 hectare in  1981  (BBS  1985, 255). Available  evidence  further  suggests  that  the  proportion  of  landless  rural households  rose from 18  percent  in  1960 to 33  percent  in  1977 and to  nearly 45  percent  in  1983-84  (BBS 1973, 12; BBS 1985, 205).  In  contrast with  and complementing  the  growing  numbers of  land-poor  and landless families is an increased concentration of  landholdings.  In the  1960s, 17  percent  of farm households  controlled 50  percent  of the cultivated land  (BBS  1973, 12).  The latest national-level  survey  of  landownership  recorded that in  1977, 11  percent  of  the  households  owned  more  than  50  percent  of  the  land  (Jannuzi and  Peach  1980). Disparities  between  landowners  and  landless  probably heightened  during  the  1980s,  as households  continued  to  grow.

In the  absence  of  land,  most  poor  households  depend  entirely  on  agricultural  wages  for subsistence. This has  generated  an abundant  pool  of labor and has caused  wages  to  drop,  even as inflation has boosted the cost of  living. Consequently,  wage  incomes of the male members of landless families have proved  insufficient  for  subsistence,  and women  in  such families  are forced to  leave  their  homes  in  search of  employment. One  field  survey  of  eight Bangladeshi villages  concluded  that  dependency  of landless households  on female  wage  labor  had  risen  (Greeley  1983, 46).  Additionally,  women  in families  owning  a little land must work their own  fields, because the families cannot afford hired male labor.

With increased  poverty  in  rural  Bangladesh,  the traditional  family-support systems  are  changing  (World  Bank  1990, 9).  Under the norms of  patriarchy,  when  a woman  loses her husband  through death, divorce, separation, or  abandonment,  her in-laws,  adult  children, or  parental family  should  support  her. In the face of economic  pressures,  this  support increasingly  is not forthcoming.  The  incidence  of  divorce  and  desertion  has  risen  as  poverty has  advanced  (Chowdhury  and Jahan 1984; Chen  1986, 219).  Whereas the number of divorced males  consistently  decreased in the  past  three censuses, the number of divorced females  consistently  increased. A similar trend also emerges  when  the  numbers  are  expressed  as a  percentage  of total married

persons. Marriage  instability apparently  is  highest among  the  poorest  households  (Miranda 1980).  The number of widows  also increased  during  the last two  decades  (BBS  1985, 90),  even  as the  number  of widowers  decreased.

The  rising  incidence  of  divorce  and  widowhood among  rural women clearly points  to an  increase in  the  number  of  female-headed  households. Traditionally,  most widowed  and destitute women  in  lower  socioeconomic classes  sought  paid-labor opportunities  in  other  households  of  their  own neighborhoods.  Few, if  any, sought wage  labor. As their numbers have risen, however,  they  have  recently begun  to seek both  paid  and  wage  labor.  Married women  of other  age groups, previously  outside the rural labor market, have become  its main  participants  in  recent  years (Ahmed  1987, 30).  The  age  at which  women  have  begun  working  outside the home  has become  younger and  younger.  A  survey  of  two  hundred  female  laborers in  four  areas of Bangladesh  found  that 23  percent  were  under  25  years  of  age;  43  percent were  between  26 and 40  years  of  age;  and  the  remaining  34  percent  were more than 40  years  old  (Feldman  and  McCarthy 1983, 956).  Some 60  percent were married at the time of the  survey;  13  percent  were divorced or  separated; 27  percent  were  widowed.

These data all  imply  that increased  landlessness,  poverty, escalating prices, inflation,  weakened  male  obligations  to  support  women,  and  rapid  increase in number of households headed  by  women have contributed to new  patterns of  activity  for rural  women,  specifically  those of  poor  families. This shift has led  to  the  expansion  of  female  space  in  recent  years.  As  the  World Bank (1990, 708) observed,  "Social norms  of  'proper'  behavior  are no  longer  restricting  women  from  entering  employment."  Many  nongovernmental  organizations,  multilateral and bilateral aid  agencies,  local  voluntary  organizations,  and  Bangladeshi  ministries  have  economic  and social  programs  for rural  women,  most  of  whom  have  been  influenced  in  some  way.  These organizations  also  provide employment  opportunities  for rural women.  For example,  the  Population  Control and  Family Planning  Division  of the Ministry  of  Health  and  Population  Control  employed  11,533 rural women  as family-planning  workers in  1985  (BBS 1989, 564).  These workers visit  rural houses to deliver  contraceptive  devices and advice.  They  travel  through  fields, on dirt or  paved  roads,  and across rivers-activities that extend female  space in  rural  Bangladesh.

Nonetheless, several factors  have constrained  employment  of rural  women. The Islamic revival  movement,  which  has  swept  across the  Muslim  world, strongly  advocates seclusion of women  in the bari  compounds  (Ahamed  and Nazneen  1990,807).  Other  constraints  on women's  employment  have stemmed from certain  developmental  interventions.  Capital-intensive  investments  in the  textile  industry  in  recent  years  have  displaced  rural women  from employment  in  handloom  crafts  (Chen  1986, 222). Expanded  use  of  rice-processing  machines  in  the  wake  of the  green  revolution  also  displaced many poor  rural women  from tasks in other households.  According  to an official

estimate,  the  rapid growth  of mechanized  milling  in  Bangladesh displaced 3.5 to  5 million  days  of  female  labor  annually.  In  1984, most  of  the  11,000 rice mills  in  the  country  were  using  electric- or  diesel-powered  rice hullers (Ahmed 1985, 29).  Yet  green-revolution  technology  has also enhanced  wageemployment  opportunities  for women  from landless and  land-poor  households  in  transplanting,  weeding,  and  harvesting  the  paddy  (Ahmed  1985). It is  thus  difficult to estimate  the  net  effect of  green-revolution  technology on women's  agricultural employment.
sections.CLOSING COMMENTS:
The  perimeter  of female  space  in  rural  Bangladesh  has been  expanding in  recent  years,  as  a  consequence  of  socioeconomic  changes  related to  increasing  landlessness  and  impoverishment.  However,  rising poverty  is not affecting  all  rural women equally.  Women  from  the  poor  and  very  poor classes face a  greater  threat to their survival than do women  of rich families. As a  result,  the  expansion  of female  space  is not uniform across  socioeconomic classes. Yet the overall female  space  has  expanded,  as  poor  women  constitute the  overwhelming  majority  of  the  rural families.  Usually,  the  standard of living  rises when  activity space  also  expands. Unfortunately,  this  relationship has not  emerged  in rural  Bangladesh.

Many  more women  now seek access to a labor market that has  long  been dominated  by  males. In such a  situation,  public policies  should  be devised to facilitate women's  entry  into the  wage-labor  market. Such  policies  should not be  designed  exclusively  for the  poor  women,  whose  behavior has little influence  on  others,  but must also include  women  from rich families,  who set  the  standards for the  village.  Additionally,  governmental  and other organizations  involved  in  rural  development  should  continue  to  support  existent  projects  aimed at  improving  the conditions  of rural women.  Without further  expansion  of  their  space, living  conditions  will  continue  to  deteriorate. There is  also the  need  to  create new  employment  opportunities  for rural women.

sections.BEEKEEPING AND LOCAL SELF-RELIANCE IN:
PETE M. ILLGNER,  ETIENNE L. NEL, and MARK P. ROBERTSON

ABSTRACT. Beekeeping  has  the  potential  to supplement  incomes  in  rural  southern  Africa.  In light of regional  economic constraints,  self-reliance  strategies  that  draw  on local  knowledge and skills  take  on a renewed  importance.  We  consider  the advantages  and disadvantages  of beekeeping and examine appropriate  forms of development support. A short case study from Zimbabwe illustrates these issues. Keywords: honeybees,  rural  southern  Africa,  selfreliance,  Zimbabwe.

Beekeeping may  be  seen  as  aperfect  model  of  responsible, sustainable agriculture.  It can  greatly  benefit  rural  communities  by  providing  additional  food, medicine  and income.

-Elize  Lundall-Magnuson, "Developmental  Beekeeping," 1997

Economic marginalization, the  frequent  failure  of  past  development  interventions, and the need of local communities  in rural  Africa  to secure  economic survival  have encouraged  a focus on indigenous  knowledge  and self-reliance  strategies  (Burkey 1993;  Binns 1995).  The academic and policyattention  increasinglybeing  paid to these considerations  represents  a fundamental  shift  in development  foci and  a  concerted response  to  the  perceived negative  effects  of  structural adjustment  programs  in  rural Africa  (Taylor and  Mackenzie  1992).  Where  local  self-reliance strategies exist  and,  in certain  instances,  where  they  are  supported  by  external  agencies,  they  often  "constitute  the only  means  of survival  for  local  communities,  providing  an  invaluable basis for  reviving  local  self-reliance  and  restructuring regional  development  on more  indigenous and self-reliant  lines"  (Gooneratne  1992,  3). These issues  have  particular relevance  to indigenous  beekeeping  in the rural  areas  of the  countries  that  make  up the Southern  African  Development  Community (Louw  1992)  (Figure  1).  Beekeeping, it can  be argued,  is an  ecologically  and  technically  appropriate form of income generation  for  communities  in  some  of  the  most  economically  and  environmentally poor areas  of  Africa.  Its  role  in  promoting  economic  self-reliance and  the  need  to  enhance  this  role  were  identified  in  the  important  Banjul  Bee  Declaration  of 1991 (Bees for Development  1991).

Although  beekeeping  can  only  rarely become  the  sole  source  of income  and  livelihood for  people  in  the  Third  World,  its  role  as  a  source  of supplementary earnings, food, and employment should not be underestimated.  Key  points in the argument that beekeeping  is a key  element in promoting  rural  self-reliance  are  that:
